Watch your application come to life:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
<Steps>
  <Step title="View Deployment Progress">
    Click on your application to see:
    - **Build logs**: Container image creation
    - **Deployment logs**: Kubernetes deployment status
    - **Application logs**: Your app's output

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/deployment/deployment_logs_view.png" alt="View deployment logs in real-time" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Wait for Running Status">
    Deployment typically takes 2-5 minutes.

    Status progression: `Building` → `Deploying` → `Running`

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/deployment/deployment_status.png" alt="Application deployment status" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Access Your Application">
    Once running, click the application URL to view your live app!

    The URL format: `https://your-app-xxx.qovery.io`
  </Step>
</Steps>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="CLI and API">
    Follow the deployment logs of the environment:

    ```bash
    qovery environment deployment logs --project "My First Project" --environment production
    ```

    Check the status of the service. Use `qovery application list` for a service built from Git:

    ```bash
    qovery container list --project "My First Project" --environment production
    ```

    Get the URL of the service with `GET /application/{applicationId}/link`, or `GET /container/{containerId}/link` for a container. It lists the Qovery domain and any custom domain:

    ```bash
    APPLICATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_APPLICATION_ID"  # from qovery application list --json

    qovery api "application/$APPLICATION_ID/link"

    # For a container
    CONTAINER_ID="REPLACE_WITH_CONTAINER_ID"  # from qovery container list --json
    qovery api "container/$CONTAINER_ID/link"
    ```

    Print the output of your app with `qovery log -a my-api`, or `qovery log -n my-api` for a container.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Check it worked

`qovery application list` (or `qovery container list`) shows your service with the status `DEPLOYED`. Open the URL returned by the `link` call: your app answers. If the status ends with `ERROR`, run `qovery environment deployment logs --errors-only` and see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## What Happened Behind the Scenes

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Git Repository Deployment">
    When deploying from Git, Qovery automatically:

    1. ✅ Cloned your Git repository
    2. ✅ Built a Docker image using your Dockerfile
    3. ✅ Pushed the image to container registry (ECR, GCR, etc.)
    4. ✅ Created Kubernetes deployment, service, and ingress
    5. ✅ Configured automatic HTTPS with Let's Encrypt
    6. ✅ Started health checks and monitoring
    7. ✅ Made your app accessible via `https://your-app-xxx.qovery.io`

    <Info>
    Qovery handles the entire build and deployment pipeline for you!
    </Info>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Container Registry Deployment">
    When deploying from a container registry, Qovery automatically:

    1. ✅ Pulled your pre-built Docker image from the registry
    2. ✅ Created Kubernetes deployment with your specified image
    3. ✅ Configured networking and load balancing
    4. ✅ Set up automatic HTTPS with Let's Encrypt
    5. ✅ Started health checks and monitoring
    6. ✅ Made your app accessible via `https://your-app-xxx.qovery.io`

    <Info>
    No build step needed - your image is deployed directly to Kubernetes!
    </Info>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Build Failed (Git Repository)">
    **Common causes**:
    - Missing or invalid Dockerfile
    - Build dependencies not installed
    - Syntax errors in Dockerfile
    - Insufficient build resources

    **Solutions**:
    - Read the build error lines: `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only` (see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment))
    - Verify Dockerfile builds locally: `docker build .`
    - Ensure all dependencies are in package files
    - Contact Qovery support to increase build resources if needed
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Image Pull Failed (Container Registry)">
    **Common causes**:
    - Registry not connected to Qovery
    - Image name or tag incorrect
    - Authentication issues
    - Image doesn't exist

    **Solutions**:
    - Verify registry is connected: [Container Registry Setup](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/container-registry)
    - Check image name matches exactly (case-sensitive)
    - Use specific tags, not `latest`
    - Verify image exists in your registry
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Application Crashes">
    **Check**:
    - Application logs for error messages
    - Environment variables are set correctly
    - Port configuration matches your app (Git: check Dockerfile EXPOSE)
    - Resource limits (CPU/memory) are sufficient
    - Health check endpoints are accessible
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Cannot Access Application">
    **Check**:
    - "Publicly Accessible" is enabled
    - App listens on `0.0.0.0:$PORT` not `localhost:$PORT`
    - Health checks are passing (if configured)
    - Wait 2-3 minutes for DNS propagation
    - Check firewall rules if using custom domains
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Dockerfile Not Found (Git Repository)">
    **Solutions**:
    - Ensure Dockerfile exists at repository root
    - If in subdirectory, set "Root Application Path"
    - Check filename is exactly `Dockerfile` (case-sensitive)
    - Verify branch contains the Dockerfile
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Quick Tips

<Tip>
**Start Small**: Begin with minimal resources (500m CPU, 512MB RAM) and scale based on actual usage.
</Tip>

<Tip>
**Use Health Checks**: Configure `/health` or `/healthz` endpoints in your app for better reliability.
</Tip>

<Tip>
**Enable Auto Deploy**: For development environments, enable auto-deploy to automatically deploy on Git push.
</Tip>

<Tip>
**Check Logs First**: When troubleshooting, always check application logs - they contain valuable debugging information.
</Tip>

# Create a Database
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/connect-database

> Add a database to your environment and connect your application to it with the connection URI and the environment variables Qovery creates.

<Note>
**Haven't deployed an app yet?** Start with the [Quick Start Guide](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart) to set up your first application, then return here to add a database.
</Note>

## Overview

This guide shows you how to create a database in your environment and connect it to your application.

<Tip>
For production, deploy a cloud provider managed database (for example Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL or MySQL, or Amazon ElastiCache for Redis) with a [Blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints). See [Creating a Blueprint Service](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints#creating-a-blueprint-service).
</Tip>

## Supported Databases

Managed databases are supported through [Blueprints](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints). For development and testing, Qovery can also deploy the following databases as containers on your cluster, as described in this guide:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="PostgreSQL" icon="database">
    Most popular relational database
  </Card>
  <Card title="MySQL" icon="database">
    Traditional relational database
  </Card>
  <Card title="MongoDB" icon="database">
    Document-oriented NoSQL database
  </Card>
  <Card title="Redis" icon="database">
    In-memory key-value store
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

## Creating a Database

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
<Steps>
  <Step title="Navigate to Your Environment">
    In the Qovery Console, go to your project and select the [environment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment) where you want to add the database.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add a Database via New Service">
    Click the **New Service** button, then either:
    - Select **Database** from the service type list, or
    - Search directly for the database you want (e.g., "MySQL", "PostgreSQL")
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Basic Settings">
    Configure your database:

    - **Database Type**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, or Redis
    - **Name**: Give your database a name
    - **Version**: Choose the database version
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Resources">
    Set the resource allocation for your database:

    - **vCPU**: CPU assigned to the database container
    - **Memory**: RAM assigned to the database container
    - **Storage**: Size of the persistent storage attached to the database
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create and Deploy">
    Review your settings and click **Create**. You can choose to create the database alone or create and deploy it immediately.
  </Step>
</Steps>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="CLI and API">
    You need the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), signed in with `qovery auth`. The `qovery api` command sends authenticated requests to the [Qovery API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/introduction).

    Create the database with `POST /environment/{environmentId}/database`. `name`, `type`, `version` and `mode` are required:

    ```bash
    ENVIRONMENT_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ENVIRONMENT_ID"  # from qovery environment list --json

    qovery api "environment/$ENVIRONMENT_ID/database" \
      --field name=my-db \
      --field type=POSTGRESQL \
      --field version=17 \
      --field mode=CONTAINER \
      --field accessibility=PRIVATE \
      --field storage=10
    ```

    Then deploy it:

    ```bash
    ENVIRONMENT_NAME="REPLACE_WITH_ENVIRONMENT_NAME"

    qovery database deploy --environment "$ENVIRONMENT_NAME" -n my-db --watch
    ```

    See [Databases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/database#create-a-container-database) for all the fields.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Terraform">
    ```hcl
    resource "qovery_database" "my_db" {
      environment_id = "<environmentId>"
      name           = "my-db"
      type           = "POSTGRESQL"
      version        = "17"
      mode           = "CONTAINER"
      accessibility  = "PRIVATE"
      storage        = 10
    }
    ```

    Deploy the environment with a [`qovery_deployment`](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/Qovery/qovery/latest/docs/resources/deployment) resource, then run `terraform apply`.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Check it worked

```bash
ENVIRONMENT_NAME="REPLACE_WITH_ENVIRONMENT_NAME"
qovery database list --environment "$ENVIRONMENT_NAME"
```

Your database shows the status `DEPLOYED`, with its host and port. Add `--show-credentials` to print the login and password.

## Connecting Your Application

Qovery automatically injects database credentials as [environment variables](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables) when your application runs. You'll have access to a connection URI and individual connection details.

### Using the Connection URI

The easiest way to connect is using the connection URI environment variable:

```javascript
// Node.js with PostgreSQL example
const { Pool } = require('pg');

const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z9XXXXXX_DATABASE_URL,
});
```

### Available Environment Variables

For each database, Qovery provides:

- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_DATABASE_URL` - Complete connection string
- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_HOST` - Database host
- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_PORT` - Database port
- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_LOGIN` - Database username
- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_PASSWORD` - Auto-generated password
- `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_<DBID>_DEFAULT_DATABASE_NAME` - Default database name

Replace `POSTGRESQL` with your actual database type (`MYSQL`, `MONGODB`, `REDIS`, etc.) and `<DBID>` with the database ID shown in the Console (visible in the **Variables** tab of your service).

<Note>
The exact variable names are always visible in the **Variables** tab of any service that has the database attached. You can copy them directly from there.
</Note>

From the CLI, list them with `qovery application env list -n my-app`. To expose one under the name your code expects, create an alias on it:

```bash
# Copy the exact name from qovery application env list
DB_URL_VARIABLE="REPLACE_WITH_QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_DBID_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL"

qovery application env alias create -n my-app \
  -k "$DB_URL_VARIABLE" \
  --alias DATABASE_URL
```

Redeploy the application to apply it. See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases).

## Database Management

### Backups

Databases created this way run as containers and have no automated backups or snapshots. For production, provision a cloud provider managed database with a [Blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints) and configure and verify the provider's backup and retention settings.

## Best Practices

<Tip>
Start with small CPU and memory values and scale up as needed. For production workloads, use a [Blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints) to provision a managed database.
</Tip>

<Warning>
Database passwords are generated automatically. Store them securely and rotate regularly.
</Warning>

# Database Seeding with Lifecycle Jobs
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/others/database-seeding-lifecycle-job

> Seed a PostgreSQL database from SQL scripts with a Qovery Lifecycle Job, including idempotent, conditional and per-environment seeding.

## Overview

This guide shows you how to use Qovery Lifecycle Jobs to seed your PostgreSQL database with SQL scripts. This approach is ideal for initializing databases with sample data, setting up database schemas, or restoring database backups during deployment.

<Info>
**What are Lifecycle Jobs?** Lifecycle Jobs are special jobs in Qovery that run at specific events during your application lifecycle, such as START, STOP, or DELETE. They're perfect for database initialization, migrations, and cleanup tasks.
</Info>

## Prerequisites

- A Qovery account with an environment set up
- A PostgreSQL database deployed in your Qovery environment
- A SQL script file for seeding your database
- Basic knowledge of Docker and shell scripting

## Goal

Set up an automated database seeding process that runs when your environment starts, using a secure approach that downloads SQL scripts from external storage (like S3) and executes them against your PostgreSQL database.

<Warning>
**Security Best Practice**: Never store sensitive data or production database dumps in public repositories. Always download SQL scripts from secure locations like AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or private repositories.
</Warning>

## Architecture Overview

The solution consists of three main components:

1. **Dockerfile**: Builds a container with PostgreSQL client and curl
2. **Seed Script**: Shell script that downloads and executes SQL files
3. **Lifecycle Job**: Qovery job configured to run at environment start

## Step 1: Prepare Your SQL Script

First, prepare your SQL script and store it in a secure location.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create Your SQL Script">
    Create a SQL file containing your database schema and seed data:

    ```sql seed.sql
    -- Create tables
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
      id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
      username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
      email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
      created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS posts (
      id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
      user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),
      title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
      content TEXT,
      created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    -- Insert sample data
    INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES
      ('john_doe', 'john@example.com'),
      ('jane_smith', 'jane@example.com')
    ON CONFLICT (username) DO NOTHING;

    INSERT INTO posts (user_id, title, content) VALUES
      (1, 'First Post', 'This is my first post!'),
      (1, 'Second Post', 'Another great post'),
      (2, 'Hello World', 'My introduction post')
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Upload to Secure Storage">
    Upload your SQL script to a secure location:

    **AWS S3 Example:**
    ```bash
    aws s3 cp seed.sql s3://your-bucket/database-seeds/seed.sql
    ```

    **Generate a presigned URL (valid for limited time):**
    ```bash
    aws s3 presign s3://your-bucket/database-seeds/seed.sql --expires-in 604800
    ```

    <Info>
    You can also use Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or any HTTP-accessible location with authentication.
    </Info>
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Step 2: Create the Seeding Script

Create a shell script that will download and execute your SQL file.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create seed.sh">
    Create a file named `seed.sh` with the following content:

    ```bash seed.sh
    #!/bin/env bash

    set -e
    set -u
    set -o pipefail

    # Check if psql is installed
    if ! command -v psql &> /dev/null; then
      echo "psql could not be found. Please install it and try again."
      exit 1
    fi

    # Check if curl is installed
    if ! command -v curl &> /dev/null; then
      echo "curl could not be found. Please install it and try again."
      exit 1
    fi

    # Download the SQL dump
    echo "Downloading SQL seed file from: ${SEED_URL}"
    curl "${SEED_URL}" -o seed.sql

    # Check if seed.sql exists in the current directory
    if [[ ! -f "seed.sql" ]]; then
      echo "The seed.sql file could not be found in the current directory."
      exit 1
    fi

    echo "Database seeding started."

    # Seed the database
    if [[ "${RESTORE_METHOD}" == "pg_restore" ]]; then
      pg_restore -d "$DATABASE_URL" seed.sql
    elif [[ "${RESTORE_METHOD}" == "psql" ]]; then
      psql "$DATABASE_URL" < seed.sql
    else
      echo "Invalid restore method. Please set the RESTORE_METHOD environment variable to either 'pg_restore' or 'psql'."
      exit 1
    fi

    echo "Database seeding completed successfully."
    ```

    <Note>
    - **psql**: Used for plain SQL files (.sql)
    - **pg_restore**: Used for custom PostgreSQL dump formats (.dump, .backup)
    </Note>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Make Script Executable">
    If you're testing locally, make the script executable:

    ```bash
    chmod +x seed.sh
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Step 3: Create the Dockerfile

Create a Dockerfile that packages the seeding script with required dependencies.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create Dockerfile">
    Create a file named `Dockerfile`:

    ```dockerfile Dockerfile
    FROM debian:11-slim

    # Install PostgreSQL client and curl
    RUN apt update && apt install postgresql-client curl -y

    # Set working directory
    WORKDIR /app

    # Copy the seed script
    COPY seed.sh .

    # Make the script executable
    RUN chmod +x seed.sh

    # Set bash as entrypoint
    ENTRYPOINT [ "/bin/bash" ]
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create Repository Structure">
    Your repository should have this structure:

    ```
    database-seed/
    ├── Dockerfile
    └── seed.sh
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Push to Git Repository">
    Push your code to a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket):

    ```bash
    git init
    git add Dockerfile seed.sh
    git commit -m "Add database seeding lifecycle job"
    git remote add origin <your-repo-url>
    git push -u origin main
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Step 4: Create Lifecycle Job in Qovery

Now create the Lifecycle Job in the Qovery Console.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open Qovery Console">
    Navigate to [Qovery Console](https://console.qovery.com) and select your environment.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create New Lifecycle Job">
    Click **New service** → **Create lifecycle job**

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/lifecycle-job/service_creation.png" alt="Create Lifecycle Job" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Repository">
    Configure the service:

    - **Name**: `database-seed`
    - **Source**: Select your Git provider and repository
    - **Branch**: `main` (or your default branch)
    - **Root application path**: Leave empty if Dockerfile is at root, or specify path if in subdirectory
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Build Settings">
    - **Build mode**: Docker
    - **Dockerfile path**: `Dockerfile`
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select Lifecycle Event">
    - **Event**: Select **START**

    This ensures the database seeding runs when your environment starts.

    <Info>
    You can also select multiple events if needed:
    - **START**: Run when environment starts
    - **STOP**: Run when environment stops
    - **DELETE**: Run when environment is deleted
    </Info>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Job Settings">
    - **Number of restarts**: 0 (job should run once and complete)
    - **Max duration**: 300 seconds (adjust based on your database size)
    - **Port**: Leave empty (not needed for this job)
    - **CMD Arguments**: `["seed.sh"]`

    <Warning>
    Don't forget to add the CMD Arguments `["seed.sh"]` - this tells the container to execute your seeding script.
    </Warning>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Resources">
    Set appropriate resources:

    - **CPU**: 0.5 vCPU (adjust based on database size)
    - **Memory**: 512 MB (adjust based on SQL file size)

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/lifecycle-job/cronjob_recap.png" alt="Lifecycle Job Configuration" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create Without Deploying">
    Click **Create** (not **Create and deploy**)

    We need to set up environment variables before deploying.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Step 5: Configure Environment Variables

Configure the environment variables required by your seeding script.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open Variables Section">
    In your Lifecycle Job, navigate to the **Variables** section.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/lifecycle-job/variables.png" alt="Environment Variables" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add DATABASE_URL">
    Add the database connection string:

    - **Variable**: `DATABASE_URL`
    - **Value**: Use the built-in alias from your PostgreSQL service
    - **Type**: Alias

    **Example value format:**
    ```
    postgresql://username:password@hostname:5432/database_name
    ```

    <Info>
    **Using Qovery Database Aliases**: If your PostgreSQL database is deployed in Qovery, you can reference it using built-in aliases like `$QOVERY_DATABASE_YOUR_DB_NAME_CONNECTION_URI`. This automatically provides the connection string.
    </Info>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add SEED_URL">
    Add the URL to your SQL script:

    - **Variable**: `SEED_URL`
    - **Value**: The URL to your SQL script (e.g., S3 presigned URL)
    - **Type**: Secret (if URL contains sensitive information)

    **Example:**
    ```
    https://your-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/database-seeds/seed.sql?AWSAccessKeyId=...
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add RESTORE_METHOD">
    Specify the restore method:

    - **Variable**: `RESTORE_METHOD`
    - **Value**: `psql` (for plain SQL files) or `pg_restore` (for PostgreSQL dumps)
    - **Type**: Value

    <Note>
    - Use `psql` for `.sql` files created with `pg_dump --format=plain`
    - Use `pg_restore` for `.dump` or `.backup` files created with `pg_dump --format=custom`
    </Note>
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Step 6: Deploy and Test

Deploy your Lifecycle Job and verify it works correctly.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Deploy the Lifecycle Job">
    Click **Deploy** to start the deployment.

    The job will build the Docker image and wait for the next lifecycle event.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Monitor Deployment">
    Watch the deployment logs to ensure the container builds successfully.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Trigger the Job">
    The seeding job will automatically run when:
    - You deploy or redeploy your environment
    - You start a stopped environment
    - The START event is triggered

    To test immediately, you can redeploy your environment.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Check Job Logs">
    View the Lifecycle Job logs to verify successful execution:

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/lifecycle-job/job_output.png" alt="Job Output Logs" />
    </Frame>

    You should see output like:
    ```
    Downloading SQL seed file from: https://...
    Database seeding started.
    INSERT 0 2
    INSERT 0 3
    Database seeding completed successfully.
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Verify Database Contents">
    Connect to your database and verify the data was seeded:

    ```sql
    SELECT * FROM users;
    SELECT * FROM posts;
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Advanced Scenarios

### Idempotent Seeding

To make your seeding script safe to run multiple times, use idempotent SQL commands:

```sql
-- Use IF NOT EXISTS for table creation
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

-- Use ON CONFLICT for inserts
INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES
  ('john_doe', 'john@example.com')
ON CONFLICT (username) DO NOTHING;

-- Use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE to update existing records
INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES
  ('john_doe', 'john@example.com')
ON CONFLICT (username)
DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email;
```

### Using Multiple SQL Files

Modify your seed script to handle multiple SQL files:

```bash
#!/bin/env bash

set -e

# Array of SQL files to execute in order
SQL_FILES=(
  "01-schema.sql"
  "02-seed-users.sql"
  "03-seed-posts.sql"
)

for sql_file in "${SQL_FILES[@]}"; do
  echo "Downloading ${sql_file}..."
  curl "${SEED_BASE_URL}/${sql_file}" -o "${sql_file}"

  echo "Executing ${sql_file}..."
  psql "$DATABASE_URL" < "${sql_file}"
done

echo "All database seeding completed successfully."
```

### Conditional Seeding

Only seed if database is empty:

```bash
#!/bin/env bash

set -e

# Check if database is empty
TABLE_COUNT=$(psql "$DATABASE_URL" -t -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'public';")

if [ "$TABLE_COUNT" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Database is empty. Proceeding with seeding..."
  curl "${SEED_URL}" -o seed.sql
  psql "$DATABASE_URL" < seed.sql
  echo "Database seeding completed."
else
  echo "Database already contains tables. Skipping seeding."
fi
```

### Environment-Specific Seeds

Use different seed files for different environments:

```bash
#!/bin/env bash

set -e

# Determine seed file based on environment
if [[ "${QOVERY_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE}" == "PRODUCTION" ]]; then
  SEED_FILE="production-seed.sql"
elif [[ "${QOVERY_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE}" == "STAGING" ]]; then
  SEED_FILE="staging-seed.sql"
else
  SEED_FILE="development-seed.sql"
fi

echo "Using seed file: ${SEED_FILE}"
curl "${SEED_BASE_URL}/${SEED_FILE}" -o seed.sql
psql "$DATABASE_URL" < seed.sql
```

## Troubleshooting

### Job Fails with "psql: command not found"

**Issue**: PostgreSQL client not installed in container

**Solution**: Verify your Dockerfile installs `postgresql-client`:
```dockerfile
RUN apt update && apt install postgresql-client -y
```

### Connection Timeout to Database

**Issue**: Cannot connect to database from Lifecycle Job

**Checklist**:
- ✅ Database is deployed and running
- ✅ `DATABASE_URL` environment variable is correctly set
- ✅ Database and Lifecycle Job are in the same environment
- ✅ Network connectivity between services is enabled

### SQL File Download Fails

**Issue**: Cannot download SQL file from storage

**Solution**:
- Verify the `SEED_URL` is correct and accessible
- Check if presigned URLs have expired (regenerate if needed)
- Ensure the container has network access to external URLs
- Test the URL manually with curl

### Duplicate Key Errors

**Issue**: Seeding fails with duplicate key violations

**Solution**: Use idempotent SQL commands:
```sql
-- Instead of INSERT, use:
INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES ('john', 'john@example.com')
ON CONFLICT (username) DO NOTHING;
```

### Job Runs Too Long and Times Out

**Issue**: Seeding job exceeds max duration

**Solution**:
- Increase the **Max duration** in job settings
- Optimize your SQL script (use COPY instead of INSERT for large datasets)
- Split large seeds into multiple smaller files
- Consider using `pg_restore` with parallel jobs flag for large dumps

## Best Practices

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Store Secrets Securely">
    Never commit sensitive data to your Git repository:
    - Use presigned URLs with expiration for S3
    - Store SQL files in private buckets with IAM authentication
    - Use Qovery Secrets for sensitive environment variables
    - Rotate presigned URLs regularly
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Make Seeds Idempotent">
    Design your SQL scripts to be safely re-runnable:
    - Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`
    - Use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
    - Check for existing data before inserting
    - Use transactions to ensure all-or-nothing execution
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Environment-Specific Data">
    Use different seed data for different environments:
    - Minimal data for development
    - Realistic test data for staging
    - Migration scripts only for production
    - Use environment variables to select appropriate seeds
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Monitor Job Execution">
    Always check job logs after deployment:
    - Verify successful completion in Qovery logs
    - Check database contents after seeding
    - Set up alerts for job failures
    - Review execution time to optimize performance
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Version Control Your Seeds">
    Track changes to your seed data:
    - Keep seed SQL files in version control
    - Use semantic versioning for seed files
    - Document changes in commit messages
    - Tag releases that include seed changes
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Test Before Production">
    Always test database seeding in non-production environments:
    - Test with preview environments
    - Verify on staging before production
    - Test rollback procedures
    - Document the seeding process
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Alternative Approaches

### Using Database Migrations

For schema changes and ongoing database updates, consider using migration tools instead:

- **Flyway**: Version-controlled database migrations
- **Liquibase**: Database-independent migration management
- **Alembic**: Python-based migration tool for SQLAlchemy
- **TypeORM/Sequelize**: Built-in migration support for Node.js

### Using Qovery Clone Environment

For duplicating existing data:

1. Create a database backup in your source environment
2. Use Qovery's Clone Environment feature
3. The cloned environment includes database snapshots

### Using Init Containers (Helm)

If deploying with Helm charts, use init containers:

```yaml
initContainers:
  - name: db-seed
    image: your-seed-image
    command: ["/bin/bash", "seed.sh"]
    env:
      - name: DATABASE_URL
        value: "postgresql://..."
```

- Explore other Lifecycle Job use cases (backups, cleanup, monitoring)

# Deploy a Django Application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/frameworks/django

> Deploy a Django application with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes in your own cloud account with Qovery: production Dockerfile, Gunicorn, health check, migrations as a lifecycle job, static files with WhiteNoise.

This guide deploys a Django project served by Gunicorn, with a PostgreSQL database and migrations that run before each release. Qovery builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it on a Kubernetes cluster in your own cloud account.

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Prerequisites

- A Django project in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, with a `requirements.txt`.
- A Qovery account and a cluster: [create one in your cloud account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cloud), [connect your own cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/kubernetes), or [try it on your laptop](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/try-with-an-agent).
- These packages in `requirements.txt`: `gunicorn`, `psycopg[binary]`, `dj-database-url` and `whitenoise`.

## Prepare the settings

Read the configuration from environment variables in `settings.py`:

```python settings.py
import os
import dj_database_url

SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY")
DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "False") == "True"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h for h in os.environ.get("DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS", "").split(",") if h]
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = [f"https://{h}" for h in ALLOWED_HOSTS]
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")

DATABASES = {"default": dj_database_url.config(conn_max_age=600)}

STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "staticfiles"
STORAGES = {
    "default": {"BACKEND": "django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage"},
    "staticfiles": {"BACKEND": "whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage"},
}
```

Add `"mysite.health.HealthCheckMiddleware"` first in `MIDDLEWARE`, and `"whitenoise.middleware.WhiteNoiseMiddleware"` right after `"django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware"`. Replace `mysite` with your project package.

Kubernetes probes call the pod by its IP address, which is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, so Django would answer them with `400 Bad Request`. This middleware answers `/healthz` before Django checks the host:

```python mysite/health.py
from django.http import HttpResponse

class HealthCheckMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        if request.path == "/healthz":
            return HttpResponse("ok")
        return self.get_response(request)
```

## Add a production Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile Dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PORT=8000

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec gunicorn mysite.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:${PORT} --workers 3"]
```

- `python:3.13-slim` is the official Python image without build tools. `psycopg[binary]` ships its own PostgreSQL client library, so no system package is needed.
- `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` sends logs straight to stdout, where Qovery reads them.
- Copying `requirements.txt` before the code keeps the dependency layer cached when only the code changes.
- `collectstatic` runs at build time and writes the files to `STATIC_ROOT`. WhiteNoise serves them from there.
- The container runs as a non-root user.
- Gunicorn binds to `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`, so Kubernetes can reach it. `exec` makes Gunicorn the main process, so it receives the stop signal and shuts down cleanly.

Add a `.dockerignore` with at least `.git`, `.venv`, `__pycache__` and `staticfiles` to keep the image small.

## Port and health check

The application listens on port `8000` and answers `GET /healthz` with `200`. Use both values when you create the application in Qovery.

## Connect PostgreSQL

The application and the migration job read the connection string from `DATABASE_URL`. Create PostgreSQL, then expose its connection string under that name at the environment scope, so every service of the environment gets it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Qovery database (development)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** and pick **PostgreSQL**. Keep the visibility private, then create and deploy it. See [Create a Database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/connect-database).
    2. Open the **Variables** section of the environment, find the built-in variable `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z<ID>_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL`, select **Create alias**, and name it `DATABASE_URL`.

    From the CLI, once the application exists:

    ```bash
    # Copy the exact name of the ..._DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL variable
    qovery application env list -n my-app

    qovery application env alias create -n my-app \
      -k "QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z1234ABCD_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL" \
      --alias DATABASE_URL --scope ENVIRONMENT
    ```

    This database runs as a container on your cluster, with no automated backups. Use it for development and testing.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Blueprint (production)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** › **Blueprint** and pick a managed PostgreSQL, such as [Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/aws-rds-postgresql) or [Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/scaleway-managed-postgresql). Deploy it.
    2. The Blueprint publishes its outputs as variables named `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z<ID>_<OUTPUT>`, and by default Qovery also creates an alias for each output, named `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>` after the Blueprint name. See [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs) for the naming rules and the cases where no alias is created. Copy the prefix from the **Variables** section, then create an environment secret `DATABASE_URL` that composes the outputs with `{{...}}` interpolation. The output names differ per Blueprint.

    Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_ADDRESS}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_IP}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Interpolation inserts the values as they are, without URL encoding. Leave the Blueprint's `db_password` input empty so Qovery generates the password, or set one made of letters and digits only: characters such as `#`, `?`, `%` or `:` break the URL.

    Make sure the Blueprint is deployed in a [deployment stage](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline) that runs before the migration job.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) and [Variable Interpolation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#variable-interpolation) for the rules.

## Set the variables

| Variable | Value | Secret |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | The alias or secret from [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql) | Yes |
| `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` | A long random string | Yes |
| `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | The domain of the application, for example `my-app-z1234abcd.z5678efgh.qovery.io` | No |

The `qovery.io` domain shows in the Console once the application is created. Add your custom domains to `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, separated by commas.

## Run the migrations

Run `migrate` in a [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) built from the same repository and Dockerfile, triggered on the **Deploy** event, with these CMD arguments:

```json
["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
```

The job runs once per deployment. In the default [deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline), jobs run after the databases and before the applications, so the schema is up to date when the new code starts.

Running `migrate` in the start command instead works for a single instance, but every instance then runs it at boot, and a failed migration leaves the application crashing in a loop.

## Deploy

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
    <Steps>
  <Step title="Create a project and an environment">
    Follow steps 1 and 2 of [Deploy Your First Application](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/deploy-your-first-application#step-1-create-a-project). Pick the cluster the environment runs on.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Add PostgreSQL">
    Create the database and the `DATABASE_URL` variable as described in [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the application">
    In the environment, click **New Service** › **Create application**, select **Git Repository**, then your repository and branch. Leave **Root Application Path** empty unless the Dockerfile is in a subfolder.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Set the port">
    Add port <code>8000</code> with the protocol **HTTP**, and turn on **Publicly Accessible**. Qovery serves it over HTTPS on port 443.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Set the health checks">
    Set the readiness and liveness probes to type **HTTP**, path <code>/healthz</code>, port <code>8000</code>. See [Service Health Checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-health-checks).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Add the variables">
    Click **Create**, without deploying yet. Then open the **Variables** section of the environment and add the other variables listed in [Set the variables](#set-the-variables) at the environment scope, so the migration job gets them too. `DATABASE_URL` already exists from the previous step. Mark keys and passwords as secrets.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the migration job">
    Click **New Service** › **Create lifecycle job**, select the same repository, branch and Dockerfile, and trigger it on the **Deploy** event (`START`) with the CMD arguments <code>["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]</code>. Set the number of restarts to 0. See [Run the migrations](#run-the-migrations).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Deploy">
    Deploy the environment. Qovery deploys the database, then the job, then the application, builds the image from your Dockerfile and gives the application a URL on `qovery.io`. Follow the progress in the **Deployment logs** tab.
  </Step>
</Steps>
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="With a coding agent">
    Install the Qovery skills once:

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://skill.qovery.com/install.sh | bash
    ```

    Open your agent in the repository and paste:

    Deploy this Django project with Qovery, with a PostgreSQL database and a lifecycle job that runs the migrations.

    The agent writes the Dockerfile if there is none, creates the database, the variables, the job and the application, and gives you the URL. See [Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills).
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Troubleshooting

The CLI commands below use the organization and project selected with `qovery context set`. Run it first, or add `--organization` and `--project` to each command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Deployment fails on the health check">
    Gunicorn listens on another port, or on `127.0.0.1`. Check that the port in Qovery is `8000`, that Gunicorn binds to `0.0.0.0:${PORT}`, and that `HealthCheckMiddleware` is first in `MIDDLEWARE`. Read the error lines with `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Bad Request (400) in the browser">
    The domain is missing from `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Add the `qovery.io` domain and your custom domains, then redeploy. A `403 CSRF verification failed` on forms has the same cause, because `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` is built from the same list.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="relation does not exist">
    The migrations did not run against this database. Check that the job and the application read the same `DATABASE_URL` at the environment scope, and read the job output with `qovery log --job "<job name>"`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Static files return 404">
    `collectstatic` did not run at build time, or WhiteNoise is not in `MIDDLEWARE`. Check the build logs for the `collectstatic` step. With `DEBUG` off, Django itself serves no static files.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

For other errors, see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment).

# Deploy a Ruby on Rails Application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/frameworks/ruby-on-rails

> Deploy a Ruby on Rails application with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes in your own cloud account with Qovery: production Dockerfile, Puma, the /up health check, migrations as a lifecycle job, precompiled assets.

This guide deploys a Rails application served by Puma, with a PostgreSQL database and migrations that run before each release. Qovery builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it on a Kubernetes cluster in your own cloud account.

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Prerequisites

- A Rails 7.1 or later application in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, using the `pg` gem.
- A Qovery account and a cluster: [create one in your cloud account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cloud), [connect your own cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/kubernetes), or [try it on your laptop](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/try-with-an-agent).
- The `RAILS_MASTER_KEY` of the application (the content of `config/master.key`).

## Add a production Dockerfile

`rails new` generates a production Dockerfile since Rails 7.1. You can keep it (see [the port note](#port-and-health-check)), or use this shorter one at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile Dockerfile
FROM ruby:3.4-slim AS base
WORKDIR /rails
RUN apt-get update -qq && \
    apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y libpq5 && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ENV RAILS_ENV=production \
    BUNDLE_DEPLOYMENT=1 \
    BUNDLE_PATH=/usr/local/bundle \
    BUNDLE_WITHOUT=development:test

FROM base AS build
RUN apt-get update -qq && \
    apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y build-essential git libpq-dev libyaml-dev pkg-config && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock ./
RUN bundle install && rm -rf ~/.bundle "${BUNDLE_PATH}"/ruby/*/cache
COPY . .
RUN SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 ./bin/rails assets:precompile

FROM base
COPY --from=build "${BUNDLE_PATH}" "${BUNDLE_PATH}"
COPY --from=build /rails /rails
RUN useradd rails --uid 1000 --create-home --shell /bin/bash && \
    mkdir -p db log storage tmp && chown -R rails:rails db log storage tmp
USER 1000:1000
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["./bin/rails", "server", "-b", "0.0.0.0", "-p", "3000"]
```

- `ruby:3.4-slim` is the official Ruby image without build tools. Match the version to your `.ruby-version`. It installs `libpq5`, the PostgreSQL client library that the `pg` gem loads at runtime.
- The `build` stage has the compilers and headers that native gems such as `pg` need. The final stage copies only the installed gems and the application, so the image stays small.
- `BUNDLE_WITHOUT=development:test` leaves out the gems you do not need in production.
- `SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1` lets `assets:precompile` run at build time without the real secret.
- The container runs as a non-root user that owns `db`, `log`, `storage` and `tmp`, the folders Rails writes to.
- Puma binds to `0.0.0.0`, not `localhost`, so Kubernetes can reach it.

## Port and health check

The application listens on port `3000`. Rails 7.1 and later add a `GET /up` route that answers `200` when the application boots, so use it as the health check path.

The Dockerfile that Rails 8 generates starts Puma behind Thruster on port `80`. If you keep it, set the port to `80` in Qovery instead of `3000`.

If you set `config.hosts` in `config/environments/production.rb`, exclude the health check from host authorization, because Kubernetes probes call the pod by its IP address:

```ruby config/environments/production.rb
config.hosts << ENV["APP_HOST"] if ENV["APP_HOST"].present?
config.host_authorization = { exclude: ->(request) { request.path == "/up" } }
```

## Connect PostgreSQL

The application and the migration job read the connection string from `DATABASE_URL`. Create PostgreSQL, then expose its connection string under that name at the environment scope, so every service of the environment gets it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Qovery database (development)">

    2. Open the **Variables** section of the environment, find the built-in variable `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z<ID>_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL`, select **Create alias**, and name it `DATABASE_URL`.

    2. See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) and [Variable Interpolation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#variable-interpolation) for the rules.

Rails reads `DATABASE_URL` and merges it into the `production` entry of `config/database.yml`. If that entry also declares `cache`, `queue` and `cable` databases (the Rails 8 default for Solid Cache, Solid Queue and Solid Cable), give each one a database it can reach on the same server, or remove the ones you do not use.

## Set the variables

| Variable | Value | Secret |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | The alias or secret from [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql) | Yes |
| `RAILS_MASTER_KEY` | The content of `config/master.key` | Yes |
| `APP_HOST` | The domain of the application, if you use `config.hosts` | No |

## Run the migrations

Run `db:migrate` in a [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) built from the same repository and Dockerfile, triggered on the **Deploy** event, with these CMD arguments:

```json
["./bin/rails", "db:migrate"]
```

The job runs once per deployment. In the default [deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline), jobs run after the databases and before the applications, so the schema is up to date when the new code starts. The job needs `DATABASE_URL` and `RAILS_MASTER_KEY` too: create them at the environment scope.

The Dockerfile that Rails generates also runs `db:prepare` in `bin/docker-entrypoint` when the server starts. This works for a single instance. With several instances, each one runs it at boot, so prefer the job.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
    <Steps>
  <Step title="Create a project and an environment">
    Follow steps 1 and 2 of [Deploy Your First Application](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/deploy-your-first-application#step-1-create-a-project). Pick the cluster the environment runs on.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Add PostgreSQL">
    Create the database and the `DATABASE_URL` variable as described in [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the application">
    In the environment, click **New Service** › **Create application**, select **Git Repository**, then your repository and branch. Leave **Root Application Path** empty unless the Dockerfile is in a subfolder.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Set the port">
    Add port <code>3000</code> with the protocol **HTTP**, and turn on **Publicly Accessible**. Qovery serves it over HTTPS on port 443.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Set the health checks">
    Set the readiness and liveness probes to type **HTTP**, path <code>/up</code>, port <code>3000</code>. See [Service Health Checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-health-checks).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Add the variables">
    Click **Create**, without deploying yet. Then open the **Variables** section of the environment and add the other variables listed in [Set the variables](#set-the-variables) at the environment scope, so the migration job gets them too. `DATABASE_URL` already exists from the previous step. Mark keys and passwords as secrets.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the migration job">
    Click **New Service** › **Create lifecycle job**, select the same repository, branch and Dockerfile, and trigger it on the **Deploy** event (`START`) with the CMD arguments <code>["./bin/rails", "db:migrate"]</code>. Set the number of restarts to 0. See [Run the migrations](#run-the-migrations).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Deploy">
    Deploy the environment. Qovery deploys the database, then the job, then the application, builds the image from your Dockerfile and gives the application a URL on `qovery.io`. Follow the progress in the **Deployment logs** tab.
  </Step>
</Steps>
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="With a coding agent">
    Install the Qovery skills once:

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://skill.qovery.com/install.sh | bash
    ```

    Open your agent in the repository and paste:

    Deploy this Rails application with Qovery, with a PostgreSQL database and a lifecycle job that runs the migrations.

    The agent writes the Dockerfile if there is none, creates the database, the variables, the job and the application, and gives you the URL. It asks you for the `RAILS_MASTER_KEY`. See [Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills).
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Troubleshooting

The CLI commands below use the organization and project selected with `qovery context set`. Run it first, or add `--organization` and `--project` to each command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Deployment fails on the health check">
    The port in Qovery does not match the server: `3000` for Puma, `80` with Thruster in the Rails 8 Dockerfile. Check that Puma binds to `0.0.0.0`. Read the error lines with `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Blocked hosts error or 403">
    `config.hosts` does not include the domain. Set `APP_HOST` to the `qovery.io` domain shown in the Console, add your custom domains, and keep `/up` excluded from host authorization.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Missing secret_key_base or ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor::InvalidMessage">
    `RAILS_MASTER_KEY` is missing or does not match `config/credentials.yml.enc`. Set it as a secret at the environment scope, so the application and the migration job both get it.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="PendingMigrationError or missing tables">
    The migrations did not run against this database. Check that the job and the application read the same `DATABASE_URL`, and read the job output with `qovery log --job "<job name>"`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Assets return 404">
    `assets:precompile` did not run at build time, or `config.public_file_server.enabled` is `false` in production. Rails 7.1 and later serve `public/` by default; an application generated with an older version may still read `RAILS_SERVE_STATIC_FILES` in `config/environments/production.rb`, so set that variable to `1` or remove the condition. Check the build logs for the precompile step.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

For other errors, see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment).

# Deploy a Node.js Express Application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/frameworks/nodejs-express

> Deploy a Node.js Express API with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes in your own cloud account with Qovery: production Dockerfile, port and health check, migrations as a lifecycle job, static files.

This guide deploys a Node.js application built with Express, with a PostgreSQL database and migrations that run before each release. Qovery builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it on a Kubernetes cluster in your own cloud account.

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Prerequisites

- An Express application in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, with a `package-lock.json`.
- A Qovery account and a cluster: [create one in your cloud account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cloud), [connect your own cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/kubernetes), or [try it on your laptop](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/try-with-an-agent).
- The `pg` package, and a migration tool (Knex, Prisma, node-pg-migrate or another) listed in `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`, so it is in the production image.

## Prepare the server

Listen on `0.0.0.0` and on the port from `PORT`, answer a health check, and read the database URL from the environment:

```js server.js
const express = require("express");
const path = require("path");
const { Pool } = require("pg");

const app = express();
const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

app.set("trust proxy", 1);
app.use(express.static(path.join(__dirname, "public")));

app.get("/healthz", (req, res) => res.send("ok"));

const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(port, "0.0.0.0", () => console.log(`Listening on ${port}`));
```

`trust proxy` set to `1` trusts one hop, the cluster's ingress, so `req.protocol` and `req.ip` reflect what the ingress saw, and a client cannot spoof them with its own `X-Forwarded-*` headers. `path.join(__dirname, "public")` resolves the static folder from the file location, not from the working directory.

Add a `migrate` script to `package.json` that runs your migration tool, for example `"migrate": "knex migrate:latest"`, `"migrate": "prisma migrate deploy"` or `"migrate": "node-pg-migrate up"`.

## Add a production Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile Dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim

ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    PORT=3000

WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .

USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

- `node:24-slim` is the official Node.js image on Debian, on a long-term support (LTS) release. Match it to the version you develop with.
- Copying `package.json` and `package-lock.json` before the code keeps the dependency layer cached when only the code changes. `npm ci` installs the exact versions from the lock file, and `--omit=dev` leaves out the development dependencies.
- `NODE_ENV=production` turns on the production behavior of Express and many libraries.
- The `node` user comes with the image, so the server runs without root.
- `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` starts Node directly rather than through `npm start`, so Node receives the stop signal and shuts down cleanly.

If your project compiles TypeScript or bundles front-end assets, run the build in a first stage and copy only the output into this image. Add a `.dockerignore` with at least `node_modules` and `.git`.

## Port and health check

The application listens on port `3000` and answers `GET /healthz` with `200`. Use both values when you create the application in Qovery.

## Connect PostgreSQL

The application and the migration job read the connection string from `DATABASE_URL`. Create PostgreSQL, then expose its connection string under that name at the environment scope, so every service of the environment gets it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Qovery database (development)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** and pick **PostgreSQL**. Keep the visibility private, then create and deploy it. See [Create a Database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/connect-database).
    2. Open the **Variables** section of the environment, find the built-in variable `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z<ID>_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL`, select **Create alias**, and name it `DATABASE_URL`.

    From the CLI, once the application exists:

    ```bash
    # Copy the exact name of the ..._DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL variable
    qovery application env list -n my-app

    qovery application env alias create -n my-app \
      -k "QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z1234ABCD_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL" \
      --alias DATABASE_URL --scope ENVIRONMENT
    ```

    This database runs as a container on your cluster, with no automated backups. Use it for development and testing.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Blueprint (production)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** › **Blueprint** and pick a managed PostgreSQL, such as [Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/aws-rds-postgresql) or [Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/scaleway-managed-postgresql). Deploy it.
    2. The Blueprint publishes its outputs as variables named `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z<ID>_<OUTPUT>`, and by default Qovery also creates an alias for each output, named `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>` after the Blueprint name. See [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs) for the naming rules and the cases where no alias is created. Copy the prefix from the **Variables** section, then create an environment secret `DATABASE_URL` that composes the outputs with `{{...}}` interpolation. The output names differ per Blueprint.

    Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_ADDRESS}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_IP}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Interpolation inserts the values as they are, without URL encoding. Leave the Blueprint's `db_password` input empty so Qovery generates the password, or set one made of letters and digits only: characters such as `#`, `?`, `%` or `:` break the URL.

    Make sure the Blueprint is deployed in a [deployment stage](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline) that runs before the migration job.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) and [Variable Interpolation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#variable-interpolation) for the rules.

Most PostgreSQL clients for Node.js, including `pg`, Knex, Prisma and node-pg-migrate, accept the `postgresql://` URL as is.

## Set the variables

| Variable | Value | Secret |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | The alias or secret from [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql) | Yes |

Add the other variables your application reads, and mark keys and passwords as secrets.

## Run the migrations

Run the `migrate` script in a [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) built from the same repository and Dockerfile, triggered on the **Deploy** event, with these CMD arguments:

```json
["npm", "run", "migrate"]
```

The job runs once per deployment. In the default [deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline), jobs run after the databases and before the applications, so the schema is up to date when the new code starts.

Running the migrations in the start command instead works for a single instance, but every instance then runs them at boot, and a failed migration leaves the application crashing in a loop.

## Troubleshooting

The CLI commands below use the organization and project selected with `qovery context set`. Run it first, or add `--organization` and `--project` to each command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Deployment fails on the health check">
    The server listens on another port than the one set in Qovery, or on `localhost`. Pass `"0.0.0.0"` to `app.listen` and check that the port in Qovery is `3000`. Read the error lines with `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Cannot find module at startup">
    A package the server needs at runtime is in `devDependencies`, so `npm ci --omit=dev` left it out. Move it to `dependencies`. The same applies to the migration tool, which the job runs from the same image.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="relation does not exist">
    The migrations did not run against this database. Check that the job and the application read the same `DATABASE_URL` at the environment scope, and read the job output with `qovery log --job "<job name>"`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Static files return 404">
    The folder is missing from the image, because `.dockerignore` excludes it or the front-end build did not run, or `express.static` points at a path relative to the working directory. Use `path.join(__dirname, "public")`.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

For other errors, see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment).

# Deploy a Next.js Application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/frameworks/nextjs

> Deploy a Next.js application with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes in your own cloud account with Qovery: standalone output, production Dockerfile, port and health check, build-time variables, migrations as a lifecycle job.

This guide deploys a Next.js application as a Node.js server, with a PostgreSQL database and migrations that run before each release. Qovery builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it on a Kubernetes cluster in your own cloud account. Server components, API routes and server actions all work, because the full Next.js server runs in the container.

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Prerequisites

- A Next.js application in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, with a `package-lock.json`.
- A Qovery account and a cluster: [create one in your cloud account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cloud), [connect your own cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/kubernetes), or [try it on your laptop](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/try-with-an-agent).
- A migration tool if you use one (Prisma, Drizzle Kit, Knex or another), with a `migrate` script in `package.json`, for example `"migrate": "prisma migrate deploy"`. Without one, skip [Run the migrations](#run-the-migrations) and the migration job step of the deployment.

## Prepare the application

Turn on the standalone output in `next.config.js` (or `next.config.ts`). `next build` then writes a self-contained `server.js` with only the dependencies it needs:

```js next.config.js
module.exports = {
  output: "standalone",
};
```

Add a health check route that does not render a page:

```ts app/api/healthz/route.ts
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

export function GET() {
  return new Response("ok");
}
```

## Add a production Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile Dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:24-slim AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 \
    PORT=3000
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/public ./public
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/.next/static ./.next/static
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["sh", "-c", "HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 exec node server.js"]
```

- `node:24-slim` is the official Node.js image on Debian, on a long-term support (LTS) release.
- Three stages keep the final image small: `deps` installs every package, `build` runs `next build`, and `runner` gets only the standalone server, the static files and `public`.
- `ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` passes a variable of the same name to the build. Next.js writes `NEXT_PUBLIC_` values into the JavaScript bundle at build time, so they must exist during the build, not only at runtime. Add one `ARG` line per `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable.
- `.next/static` and `public` are copied next to `server.js`, because the standalone output does not include them.
- The standalone server reads `HOSTNAME` to choose the address it listens on. Kubernetes sets `HOSTNAME` to the pod name, so the start command sets it to `0.0.0.0`.
- The `node` user comes with the image, so the server runs without root.

If the project has no `public` folder, remove that `COPY` line. Add a `.dockerignore` with at least `node_modules`, `.next` and `.git`.

## Port and health check

The application listens on port `3000` and answers `GET /api/healthz` with `200`. Use both values when you create the application in Qovery.

## Connect PostgreSQL

The application and the migration job read the connection string from `DATABASE_URL`. Create PostgreSQL, then expose its connection string under that name at the environment scope, so every service of the environment gets it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Qovery database (development)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** and pick **PostgreSQL**. Keep the visibility private, then create and deploy it. See [Create a Database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/connect-database).
    2. Open the **Variables** section of the environment, find the built-in variable `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z<ID>_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL`, select **Create alias**, and name it `DATABASE_URL`.

    From the CLI, once the application exists:

    ```bash
    # Copy the exact name of the ..._DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL variable
    qovery application env list -n my-app

    qovery application env alias create -n my-app \
      -k "QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z1234ABCD_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL" \
      --alias DATABASE_URL --scope ENVIRONMENT
    ```

    This database runs as a container on your cluster, with no automated backups. Use it for development and testing.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Blueprint (production)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** › **Blueprint** and pick a managed PostgreSQL, such as [Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/aws-rds-postgresql) or [Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/scaleway-managed-postgresql). Deploy it.
    2. The Blueprint publishes its outputs as variables named `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z<ID>_<OUTPUT>`, and by default Qovery also creates an alias for each output, named `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>` after the Blueprint name. See [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs) for the naming rules and the cases where no alias is created. Copy the prefix from the **Variables** section, then create an environment secret `DATABASE_URL` that composes the outputs with `{{...}}` interpolation. The output names differ per Blueprint.

    Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_ADDRESS}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_IP}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Interpolation inserts the values as they are, without URL encoding. Leave the Blueprint's `db_password` input empty so Qovery generates the password, or set one made of letters and digits only: characters such as `#`, `?`, `%` or `:` break the URL.

    Make sure the Blueprint is deployed in a [deployment stage](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline) that runs before the migration job.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) and [Variable Interpolation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#variable-interpolation) for the rules.

Read `process.env.DATABASE_URL` only in server code: route handlers, server components and server actions. A variable without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix never reaches the browser.

## Set the variables

| Variable | Value | Secret |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | The alias or secret from [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql) | Yes |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` | An example of a public, build-time value. Declare it as an `ARG` in the Dockerfile | No |

See [Passing a value as a build argument](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#passing-a-value-as-a-build-argument). Never put a secret in a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable: it ends up in the bundle that browsers download.

## Run the migrations

Run the `migrate` script in a [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) built from the same repository and Dockerfile, triggered on the **Deploy** event, with these CMD arguments:

```json
["npm", "run", "migrate"]
```

Set the job's **target stage** to `build`. The `runner` image holds only what `server.js` needs, while the `build` stage has every package, the migration files and `package.json`. The job runs once per deployment. In the default [deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline), jobs run after the databases and before the applications, so the schema is up to date when the new code starts.

## Deploy

  <Tab title="Console">

  <Step title="Create a project and an environment">

  </Step>

## Troubleshooting

The CLI commands below use the organization and project selected with `qovery context set`. Run it first, or add `--organization` and `--project` to each command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Deployment fails on the health check">
    The server listens on the pod name instead of `0.0.0.0`, or on another port. Keep `HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0` in the start command and check that the port in Qovery is `3000`. Read the error lines with `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Build fails on COPY /app/.next/standalone">
    `output: "standalone"` is missing from the Next.js config, so `next build` did not write the folder.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="A NEXT_PUBLIC_ value is undefined in the browser">
    The value was not set when the image was built. Declare it with `ARG` in the `build` stage, create the variable in Qovery, and redeploy so the image is rebuilt.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="CSS, JavaScript or images return 404">
    `.next/static` or `public` was not copied into the `runner` stage. The standalone output leaves both out.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="relation does not exist">
    The migrations did not run against this database. Check that the job and the application read the same `DATABASE_URL`, and read the job output with `qovery log --job "<job name>"`.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

For other errors, see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment).
