# Deploy a FastAPI Application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/frameworks/fastapi

> Deploy a FastAPI application with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes in your own cloud account with Qovery: production Dockerfile, Uvicorn, health check, Alembic migrations as a lifecycle job, static files.

This guide deploys a FastAPI application served by Uvicorn, with a PostgreSQL database and Alembic migrations that run before each release. Qovery builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it on a Kubernetes cluster in your own cloud account.

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Prerequisites

- A FastAPI application in a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, with a `requirements.txt`.
- A Qovery account and a cluster: [create one in your cloud account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cloud), [connect your own cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/kubernetes), or [try it on your laptop](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/try-with-an-agent).
- These packages in `requirements.txt`: `fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `sqlalchemy`, `psycopg2-binary` and `alembic`.

## Prepare the application

Add a health check and read the database URL from the environment, in `app/main.py`:

```python app/main.py
import os
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine = create_engine(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"], pool_pre_ping=True)

app = FastAPI()
app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory=Path(__file__).parent / "static"), name="static")

@app.get("/healthz")
def healthz():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

SQLAlchemy opens a `postgresql://` URL with the `psycopg2` driver. `pool_pre_ping=True` replaces connections the database closed while they were idle. The static folder is resolved from the file location, not from the working directory. Leave out the `mount` line if the application serves no static files.

In Alembic's `migrations/env.py`, take the URL from the same variable:

```python migrations/env.py
import os
from alembic import context

config = context.config
# ConfigParser treats % as interpolation, so escape it
config.set_main_option("sqlalchemy.url", os.environ["DATABASE_URL"].replace("%", "%%"))
```

## Add a production Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` at the root of the repository:

```dockerfile Dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PORT=8000

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT} --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*'"]
```

- `python:3.13-slim` is the official Python image without build tools. `psycopg2-binary` ships its own PostgreSQL client library, so no system package is needed.
- `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` sends logs straight to stdout, where Qovery reads them.
- Copying `requirements.txt` before the code keeps the dependency layer cached when only the code changes.
- The container runs as a non-root user.
- Uvicorn binds to `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`, so Kubernetes can reach it. `--proxy-headers` with `--forwarded-allow-ips` makes the application see the `https` scheme and the client address set by the cluster's ingress, so the URLs it generates start with `https://`. `'*'` trusts these headers from any peer, which is fine when only the ingress can reach the pod. If the application uses the client address for access control or rate limiting, replace `'*'` with the IP range of your cluster's pods.
- `exec` makes Uvicorn the main process, so it receives the stop signal and shuts down cleanly.

To use several CPU cores, raise the number of instances in Qovery rather than the number of Uvicorn workers. Add a `.dockerignore` with at least `.git`, `.venv` and `__pycache__`.

## Port and health check

The application listens on port `8000` and answers `GET /healthz` with `200`. Use both values when you create the application in Qovery.

## Connect PostgreSQL

The application and the migration job read the connection string from `DATABASE_URL`. Create PostgreSQL, then expose its connection string under that name at the environment scope, so every service of the environment gets it.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Qovery database (development)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** and pick **PostgreSQL**. Keep the visibility private, then create and deploy it. See [Create a Database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/connect-database).
    2. Open the **Variables** section of the environment, find the built-in variable `QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z<ID>_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL`, select **Create alias**, and name it `DATABASE_URL`.

    From the CLI, once the application exists:

    ```bash
    # Copy the exact name of the ..._DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL variable
    qovery application env list -n my-app

    qovery application env alias create -n my-app \
      -k "QOVERY_POSTGRESQL_Z1234ABCD_DATABASE_URL_INTERNAL" \
      --alias DATABASE_URL --scope ENVIRONMENT
    ```

    This database runs as a container on your cluster, with no automated backups. Use it for development and testing.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Blueprint (production)">
    1. In the environment, click **New Service** › **Blueprint** and pick a managed PostgreSQL, such as [Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/aws-rds-postgresql) or [Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/scaleway-managed-postgresql). Deploy it.
    2. The Blueprint publishes its outputs as variables named `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z<ID>_<OUTPUT>`, and by default Qovery also creates an alias for each output, named `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>` after the Blueprint name. See [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs) for the naming rules and the cases where no alias is created. Copy the prefix from the **Variables** section, then create an environment secret `DATABASE_URL` that composes the outputs with `{{...}}` interpolation. The output names differ per Blueprint.

    Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_ADDRESS}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Scaleway Managed PostgreSQL:

    ```text
    postgresql://{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_USERNAME}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_PASSWORD}}@{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_IP}}:{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_ENDPOINT_PORT}}/{{QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z1234ABCD_DB_NAME}}
    ```

    Interpolation inserts the values as they are, without URL encoding. Leave the Blueprint's `db_password` input empty so Qovery generates the password, or set one made of letters and digits only: characters such as `#`, `?`, `%` or `:` break the URL.

    Make sure the Blueprint is deployed in a [deployment stage](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline) that runs before the migration job.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

See [Aliases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) and [Variable Interpolation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#variable-interpolation) for the rules.

## Set the variables

| Variable | Value | Secret |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | The alias or secret from [Connect PostgreSQL](#connect-postgresql) | Yes |

Add the other variables your application reads, and mark keys and passwords as secrets.

## Run the migrations

Run Alembic in a [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) built from the same repository and Dockerfile, triggered on the **Deploy** event, with these CMD arguments:

```json
["alembic", "upgrade", "head"]
```

The job runs once per deployment. In the default [deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline), jobs run after the databases and before the applications, so the schema is up to date when the new code starts.

Running the migrations in the start command instead works for a single instance, but every instance then runs them at boot, and a failed migration leaves the application crashing in a loop.

## Troubleshooting

The CLI commands below use the organization and project selected with `qovery context set`. Run it first, or add `--organization` and `--project` to each command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Deployment fails on the health check">
    Uvicorn listens on another port than the one set in Qovery, or on `127.0.0.1`, its default. Keep `--host 0.0.0.0` and check that the port in Qovery is `8000`. Read the error lines with `qovery environment deployment logs --environment "<env>" --service "<app>" --errors-only`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="400 Invalid host header">
    `TrustedHostMiddleware` rejects the request. Add the exact `qovery.io` domain shown in the Console (or the wildcard `*.qovery.io`) and your custom domains to `allowed_hosts`. Kubernetes probes call the pod by its IP address, so if the middleware blocks them, switch the probes to type **TCP** on port `8000`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="relation does not exist or KeyError: 'DATABASE_URL'">
    The migrations did not run, or the variable is missing. Check that the job and the application read the same `DATABASE_URL` at the environment scope, and read the job output with `qovery log --job "<job name>"`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Directory 'static' does not exist">
    The folder is missing from the image, because `.dockerignore` excludes it, or the path is relative to the working directory. Resolve it from `__file__` as in the example.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

For other errors, see [Diagnose a Failed Build or Deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#diagnose-a-failed-build-or-deployment).

# Use AWS IAM Roles with Qovery
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/aws-iam-roles

> Grant AWS IAM permissions to applications without managing credentials

This tutorial demonstrates how to grant AWS IAM permissions to applications, containers, or jobs deployed through Qovery, using IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). This approach eliminates credential management by automatically rotating tokens through AWS's identity service.

Everything deploys through Qovery services from the [create_service_account](https://github.com/Qovery/create_service_account) repository:

1. A **Terraform service** creates the IAM role (and the OIDC identity provider if needed)
2. A **Helm service** creates the Kubernetes ServiceAccount annotated with the role ARN
3. Your application picks up the ServiceAccount through the **Service account** advanced setting

The Terraform outputs flow into the Helm values automatically, so nothing is hardcoded. If you prefer to create the IAM resources by hand, the manual AWS Console path is kept as an alternative in step 2.

## Prerequisites

- A Qovery cluster running on AWS EKS
- Basic knowledge of AWS IAM and Kubernetes
- AWS credentials allowed to manage IAM (for the Terraform service or the Console)

## Step 1: Create an Application Requiring S3 Permissions

First, deploy a simple Debian container that will need S3 access:

- Deploy a Debian container with 1 instance and 128MB memory
- You can also use existing applications, containers, or jobs

### Get Kubernetes Namespace Name

1. Access your container variables and locate `QOVERY_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE_NAME`
2. This value represents the namespace where the container runs

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/debian_namespace.png"
    alt="Get Kubernetes namespace from container variables"
  />
</Frame>

---

## Step 2: Create the OIDC Provider and IAM Role

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Terraform service (recommended)">
    Add a **Terraform service** to the same environment:

    - Source: Git repository `https://github.com/Qovery/create_service_account`
    - Root path: `terraform/`

    Set these variables on the service:

    | Variable | Value |
    |----------|-------|
    | `TF_VAR_cluster_name` | Alias of the built-in `QOVERY_KUBERNETES_CLUSTER_NAME` |
    | `TF_VAR_role_name` | Name for the IAM role, e.g. `my-s3-role` |
    | `TF_VAR_service_account_name` | ServiceAccount name, e.g. `my-app-sa` |
    | `TF_VAR_policy_arns` | e.g. `["arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess"]` |
    | `TF_VAR_namespace` | Alias of `QOVERY_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE_NAME` to scope the role to this environment, or empty for a cluster-scoped role (required for Preview/Clone) |
    | `TF_VAR_create_oidc_provider` | `true` the first time, if the cluster's OIDC provider is not registered in IAM yet |
    | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` / `AWS_REGION` | Credentials allowed to manage IAM (mark the secret as such) |

    Deploy the service. The module creates the trust policy for you (namespace-scoped `StringEquals`, or cluster-scoped `StringLike` on `system:serviceaccount:z*:<service_account_name>` when `TF_VAR_namespace` is empty).

    The module outputs `role_arn`. Qovery exposes it to the environment as a variable named `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_<service short id>_ROLE_ARN`; check the exact name in your environment variables after the first deployment. You will reference it in step 3.

  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Manually (AWS Console)">
    ### Get Cluster OIDC Provider URL

    1. Navigate to your AWS EKS cluster Overview section
    2. Copy the OpenID Connect provider URL

    <Frame>
      <img
        src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/eks_oidc.png"
        alt="EKS OIDC provider URL"
      />
    </Frame>

    ### Create Identity Provider

    1. In AWS IAM, access the **Identity providers** section
    2. Select **OpenID Connect** provider type
    3. Paste the provider URL
    4. Click **Get thumbprint**
    5. Add `sts.amazonaws.com` as **Audience**
    6. Create the provider

    <Frame>
      <img
        src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/oidc_connect.png"
        alt="Create OIDC identity provider"
      />
    </Frame>

    ### Create a Role

    1. In IAM Roles section, select **Create role**
    2. Choose **Web identity** as Trusted entity type
    3. Set **Identity provider** and **Audience** to `sts.amazonaws.com`

    <Frame>
      <img
        src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/role_create_step1.png"
        alt="Create IAM role step 1"
      />
    </Frame>

    ### Add Role Permissions

    1. Select the desired policy (example uses `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess`)
    2. Set role name and description
    3. Proceed to creation

    ### Configure Trusted Entities

    For a role scoped to one environment, update the trust policy from:

    ```json
    "oidc.eks.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/id/xxxxxxx:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
    ```

    To:

    ```json
    "oidc.eks.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/id/xxxxxxx:sub":
    "system:serviceaccount:kubernetes_namespace:service_account_name"
    ```

    Replace placeholders:
    - `kubernetes_namespace`: Your Qovery environment namespace
    - `service_account_name`: Define a service account name (e.g., `my-app-sa`)

    For a cluster-scoped role (required by On-demand/Clone features), use `StringLike` with a wildcard:

    ```json
    "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
            "oidc.eks.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/id/xxxxxxx:sub":
            "system:serviceaccount:z*:service_account_name"
        }
    }
    ```

    This allows the service account to be used across all namespaces starting with `z`.

    <Frame>
      <img
        src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/role_trusted_entities_default.png"
        alt="Configure trusted entities"
      />
    </Frame>

    Save the **role ARN** for step 3.

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Step 3: Create the Service Account

A Helm chart creates the ServiceAccount annotated for IRSA:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: <service_account_name>
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: <role_arn>
```

Add a **Helm service** to the same environment:

**Repository Details:**

1. Repository name: `Qovery Service Account Helper`
2. Kind: `HTTPS`
3. URL: `https://qovery.github.io/create_service_account/`

**Chart Configuration:**

- Helm source: Helm repository
- Chart name: `qovery-sa-helper`
- Version: `0.2.0`

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/create_sa.png"
    alt="Create service account"
  />
</Frame>

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/helm_sa_1.png"
    alt="Helm service configuration"
  />
</Frame>

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/aws-iam-assume-role/set-helm-repo.png"

## Key Concepts

- **OIDC Integration**: Enables Kubernetes service accounts to assume AWS roles
- **Token Rotation**: Automatic credential rotation without manual management
- **Namespace Scoping**: Restricts role access to specific Kubernetes namespaces
- **Everything as Qovery services**: The IAM role and the ServiceAccount are regular services in your environment, so they are versioned, visible in the Console, replicated with Clone/Preview, and cleaned up with the environment

## Conclusion

With the Terraform and Helm services in place, granting a role to a new application comes down to setting one advanced setting. The IAM side lives in your environment like any other service, without credential management overhead.

# Certificate Management for Multi-Tenant Applications
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/certificate-management-multi-tenant

> Implement robust SSL/TLS certificate management for multi-tenant SaaS applications

Learn how to implement robust SSL/TLS certificate management for multi-tenant SaaS applications using dedicated ingresses per tenant on Qovery.

## The Challenge

Single ingress controller approach creates problems:
- Certificate generation failures affecting all domains if one validation fails
- Entire deployment risks from misconfigured domains
- Privacy issues: customers see other tenants' domains in SSL certificates
- Let's Encrypt rate limit concerns with many domains

---

## The Solution: Dedicated Ingresses Per Tenant

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/archi_overview.png" alt="Architecture overview" />
</Frame>

### Benefits

- **Isolation**: Tenant certificate/ingress separation
- **Reliability**: One tenant's issues won't cascade to others
- **Privacy**: Certificates contain only specific tenant domains
- **Scalability**: Improved rate limit and renewal management

---

## Prerequisites

- Qovery account with configured cluster
- DNS management access
- Basic understanding of Kubernetes ingress

---

## Implementation Guide

### Step 1: Organize Your Platform (Optional)

Create separate environments for better organization:

1. **Core Environment** – Main application components (frontend, API, database)
2. **Tenants Environment** – Tenant-specific ingress configurations

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/environment_structure.png" alt="Environment structure" />
</Frame>

<Info>
Separating core and tenant environments makes it easier to manage and scale your multi-tenant architecture.
</Info>

---

### Step 2: Deploy Your Main Application

<Steps>
  <Step title="Deploy Container">
    Deploy your application via UI, CLI, Terraform, or REST API to the Core environment.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Application Port">
    1. Go to **Settings** → **Ports**
    2. Add your application port

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/edit_port.png" alt="Configure application port" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add Main Domain">
    1. Go to **Settings** → **Domains**
    2. Add your main application domain
  </Step>

  <Step title="Note Environment Variables">
    Your application will have these built-in environment variables:
    - `QOVERY_CONTAINER_XXXXXXX_HOST_INTERNAL`: Internal hostname
    - `QOVERY_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE_NAME`: Kubernetes namespace

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/list_variables.png" alt="Environment variables" />
    </Frame>

    Save these values for the next steps.
  </Step>
</Steps>

---

### Step 3: Create Tenant-Specific Ingresses

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/implementation_flow.png" alt="Implementation flow" />
</Frame>

<Steps>
  <Step title="Switch to Tenants Environment">
    Navigate to your Tenants environment in Qovery Console.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create New Helm Service">
    1. Create a new Helm service
    2. Use an empty chart template (or create a minimal chart)
    3. Name it after your tenant (e.g., `tenant-acme-corp`)
    4. Be sure to select the option `Allow cluster-wide resources`
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Ingress Port">
    1. Go to **Settings** → **Ports**
    2. Configure:
       - **Service name**: Internal hostname from core application
       - **Service port**: Core application's port number
       - **Namespace**: Kubernetes namespace from core application

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/tenant_port.png" alt="Configure tenant port" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add Tenant Custom Domain">
    1. Go to **Settings** → **Domains**
    2. Add the tenant's custom domain (e.g., `acme-corp.example.com`)

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/certificate_management_for_multi_tenant_infrastructure/custom_domain.png" alt="Add custom domain" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Deploy">
    Click **Deploy**. Qovery will:
    - Create a dedicated ingress for this tenant
    - Generate an SSL certificate for the tenant's domain
    - Route traffic from the tenant domain to your core application
  </Step>
</Steps>

---

### Step 4: Scale to Multiple Tenants

**Options for adding more tenants:**

1. **Clone Existing Configuration**:
   - Clone the tenant Helm service
   - Update the custom domain
   - Deploy

2. **Create from Scratch**:
   - Repeat Step 3 for each new tenant
   - Each tenant gets isolated ingress and certificate

<Tip>
Consider automating tenant provisioning using the Qovery API or Terraform for large-scale deployments.
</Tip>

---

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Certificate Generation Issues">
    **Problem:** SSL certificate not generating for tenant domain

    **Solutions:**
    - Check DNS propagation: `dig _acme-challenge.tenant-domain.com CNAME`
    - Verify CNAME record points to Qovery cluster
    - Check ingress configuration in deployment logs
    - Monitor cert-manager logs for certificate generation details
    - Ensure domain is not behind CDN (or configure properly)
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Routing Issues">
    **Problem:** Traffic not reaching the application

    **Solutions:**
    - Verify internal service name matches application hostname
    - Confirm namespace configuration for multi-environment setups
    - Check that core application is running and healthy
    - Review ingress logs for routing errors
    - Test internal connectivity between namespaces
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Rate Limiting">
    **Problem:** Hit Let's Encrypt rate limits

    **Solutions:**
    - Use Let's Encrypt staging environment for testing
    - Implement certificate caching
    - Stagger tenant onboarding to spread certificate requests
    - Consider using wildcard certificates for subdomains
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Performance Issues">
    **Problem:** Slow response times for tenant requests

    **Solutions:**
    - Check ingress controller resource allocation
    - Monitor core application performance
    - Review network policies
    - Consider scaling ingress controller replicas
    - Implement caching at CDN or application level
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Advanced Configurations

### Wildcard Certificates

For subdomains under a single domain:

```yaml
# In tenant Helm values
domains:
  - "*.tenants.example.com"
```

### Custom Certificate Providers

Use custom certificate issuers:

```yaml
annotations:
  cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "custom-issuer"
```

### Automatic Tenant Provisioning

Use Qovery API to automate tenant creation:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.qovery.com/environment/xxx/helm \
  -H "Authorization: Token YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "name": "tenant-' + TENANT_ID + '",
    "chart": "empty-chart",
    "values_override": {...}
  }'
```

## Security Considerations

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Tenant Isolation">
    - Each tenant has dedicated ingress
    - SSL certificates are tenant-specific
    - No cross-tenant certificate exposure
    - Network policies can further isolate traffic
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Certificate Management">
    - Automatic renewal before expiration
    - Failed renewals don't affect other tenants
    - Certificate rotation without downtime
    - Private keys never shared between tenants
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Access Control">
    - Use RBAC to control who can add tenants
    - Audit logs track tenant creation
    - Separate environments limit blast radius
    - API tokens for automated provisioning
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Monitoring and Maintenance

### Key Metrics to Monitor

- Certificate expiration dates
- Certificate generation success rate
- Ingress response times
- Error rates per tenant
- SSL/TLS handshake failures

### Automated Alerts

Set up alerts for:
- Certificate generation failures
- Certificates expiring within 30 days
- Ingress health check failures
- High error rates for specific tenants

---

## Conclusion

Dedicated ingresses create a robust, scalable, and secure multi-tenant architecture with:
- Better tenant isolation
- Easier troubleshooting
- Improved customer privacy
- Reduced rate limit concerns
- Independent certificate lifecycle management

# Integrate Application Logs to CloudWatch
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/cloudwatch-integration

> Stream Kubernetes pod logs to AWS CloudWatch for full-text search

This tutorial explains how to stream Kubernetes pod logs to AWS CloudWatch for full-text search capabilities. While Qovery provides log access through its Console and CLI using Loki, that solution has limitations for direct querying and full-text search functionality.

<Info>
Loki is not a full-text search engine. It is a log aggregation system designed for Qovery's interface rather than direct queries.
</Info>

## Prerequisites

- Qovery cluster running on AWS EKS
- Access to AWS IAM Console
- Basic knowledge of Helm charts

## Step 1: AWS Permissions Setup

### Create IAM Policy

Create an IAM policy named `fluent-bit-write-policy` with these permissions:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "logs:CreateLogGroup",
        "logs:CreateLogStream",
        "logs:DescribeLogStreams",
        "logs:PutRetentionPolicy",
        "logs:PutLogEvents"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/aws-cloudwatch/fluent-bit-policy-create.png" alt="Create IAM policy" />
</Frame>

### Create IAM User

1. Create an IAM user
2. Attach the `fluent-bit-write-policy` to the user
3. Generate access credentials for later use

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/aws-cloudwatch/fluent-bit-user-create.png" alt="Create IAM user" />
</Frame>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/aws-cloudwatch/fluent-bit-cloudwatch-permissions.png" alt="Attach CloudWatch permissions" />
</Frame>

---

## Step 2: Deploy Fluent Bit with Helm

### Add AWS EKS Helm Repository

1. In Qovery Console, navigate to your environment
2. Add a new Helm repository:
   - **Name**: `eks`
   - **Kind**: `HTTPS`
   - **URL**: `https://aws.github.io/eks-charts`

### Create Helm Service

Configure the Helm service with the following settings:

**Basic Configuration:**
- **Chart**: `aws-for-fluent-bit`
- **Version**: `0.1.21`
- **Enable cluster-wide resources**: Yes

**Values Override:**

```yaml
cloudWatch:
  enabled: true
  region: us-east-1  # Change to your region
  logGroupName: /aws/eks/fluent-bit

env:
  - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: fluent-bit-secrets
        key: AWS_ACCESS_KEY
  - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: fluent-bit-secrets
        key: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

---

## Step 3: Store AWS Secrets

Add two service-scoped secret variables:

1. **AWS_ACCESS_KEY**: Your IAM user access key ID
2. **AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY**: Your IAM user secret access key

<Warning>
Always use secret variables (not regular environment variables) for AWS credentials to ensure they are encrypted.
</Warning>

## Step 4: Deploy

2. Click the **Play button** to trigger deployment

4. Verify the pods are running successfully

## Step 5: Access CloudWatch Logs

### Using CloudWatch Logs Insight

1. Navigate to AWS CloudWatch Console
2. Go to **Logs** → **Insights**
3. Select the `fluent-bit` log group
4. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights query syntax to filter and search logs

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/aws-cloudwatch/cloudwatch-search.png" alt="CloudWatch Logs Insights" />
</Frame>

### Example Queries

**Find all error logs:**
```
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
```

**Search by application name:**
```
fields @timestamp, kubernetes.pod_name, @message
| filter kubernetes.namespace_name = "your-namespace"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
```

**Count logs by pod:**
```
stats count() by kubernetes.pod_name
| sort count desc
```

# Deploy a DaemonSet in a Karpenter Context
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/deploy-daemonset-karpenter

> Schedule a DaemonSet on all Qovery Karpenter node pools: use the Qovery PriorityClass, tolerate the stable and cronjob taints, and skip Fargate nodes.

Karpenter is a great way to cut your AWS bill. However, there is some specificity when deploying DaemonSets.

## What is a DaemonSet?

A DaemonSet in Kubernetes is a specialized controller used to ensure that a copy of a particular pod runs on all nodes in a cluster.

**Automatic Scheduling**: When new nodes are added to the cluster, the DaemonSet controller automatically schedules a pod on each of those nodes.

**Cleanup**: When nodes are removed from the cluster, the pods are also automatically removed from those nodes.

DaemonSets are particularly useful for deploying background tasks or system-level services that need to run on every node, such as log collectors, monitoring agents, or network-related components.

## Priority Classes

### What is a PriorityClass?

A PriorityClass in Kubernetes is a resource used to assign priority levels to pods. When scheduling pods, Kubernetes uses these priorities to determine the order in which pods are scheduled. Here are the key features and uses of PriorityClasses:

- **Priority Scheduling**: Pods with higher priority values are scheduled before pods with lower priority values. This helps ensure that critical workloads get the necessary resources first.
- **Preemption**: If there are insufficient resources to schedule a high-priority pod, Kubernetes can preempt (evict) lower-priority pods to make room for the higher-priority one.
- **Resource Allocation**: PriorityClasses help in managing resource allocation more effectively by ensuring that essential services and critical applications receive the resources they need, even during periods of high demand.

### Use Qovery's dedicated PriorityClass

There is a known issue with Karpenter and DaemonSets when scaling nodes. This is because DaemonSets consume resources that Karpenter doesn't fully account for, leading to potential under-provisioning of nodes. Using a PriorityClass attached to DaemonSets can help mitigate this issue.

Many Helm charts include a built-in value for PriorityClass. For instance, have a look at our guides on how to deploy [Datadog](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/observability/datadog) or [JupyterHub](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/deploy-jupyterhub).

When you deploy Qovery, a PriorityClass named `qovery-standard-priority` is created. You can leverage it to deploy your Helm chart or DaemonSet with.

## Targeting all nodes

### Nodepool Default Taints

When you deploy Qovery, two nodepools are deployed by default: `default` and `stable`. The `stable` nodepool includes a taint with the key `nodepool/stable` on it. This taint restricts pod scheduling to only those pods that have the corresponding toleration.

If the optional cronjob nodepool is enabled on your cluster, a third nodepool named `cronjob` is created with a taint `nodepool/cronjob: NoSchedule`. Your DaemonSet must also tolerate this taint to be scheduled on cronjob nodes.

### How to target every node

To target all nodes and properly deploy your DaemonSet or Helm chart, add the following tolerations and affinity to your pods:

```yaml
tolerations:
  - operator: Exists

affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
          - key: eks.amazonaws.com/compute-type
            operator: NotIn
            values:
              - fargate
```

- **Tolerations**: The `Exists` operator allows the pod to tolerate all taints. This ensures that the pod can be scheduled on nodes with any taint, including the `stable` nodepool.
- **Affinity**: The node affinity rule ensures that the pod is not scheduled on Fargate nodes, which are not suitable for running DaemonSets.

# HPA vs KEDA: Choosing an Autoscaling Mode
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/hpa-vs-keda-autoscaling

> When to scale on CPU and memory with HPA, when to scale on events with KEDA, and how to configure each on Qovery

Qovery gives every application three autoscaling modes: a fixed number of instances, HPA (CPU and memory), and KEDA (event-driven). This guide explains what each mode reacts to, which workloads fit which mode, and how to set them up and switch between them.

For the full field reference, see [Application configuration: Instances & Autoscaling](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#instances-%26-autoscaling).

## What each mode reacts to

**HPA** ([Horizontal Pod Autoscaler](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)) watches the CPU and memory usage of your pods through the Kubernetes metrics-server. When average usage goes above a threshold, it adds pods. When usage stays below the threshold, it removes them.

**KEDA** ([Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling](https://keda.sh)) watches a source outside your pods: the number of messages in an SQS queue, the length of a Redis list, consumer lag on a Kafka topic, a Prometheus query, a cron schedule. It computes how many instances that backlog needs and scales to that number. Under the hood, KEDA still drives a Kubernetes HPA, but it feeds it external metrics instead of CPU.

The difference matters most for background workers. A worker waiting on I/O (an external API, a database, a slow upstream) can sit at 10% CPU while 20,000 messages pile up in its queue. HPA sees an idle pod and does nothing. KEDA sees 20,000 messages and scales out.

## Side-by-side

| | No autoscaling | HPA (CPU/Memory) | KEDA (Event-Driven) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scales on | Nothing | CPU, or CPU + memory | Queue depth, stream lag, metrics, schedules |
| Minimum instances | Fixed | 1 or more | 0 or more (scale-to-zero) |
| Scale-up delay | n/a | 15 seconds above threshold | From 0: polling interval (default 30 seconds). Above 1: Kubernetes HPA |
| Scale-down delay | n/a | 5 minutes below threshold | To 0: cooldown period (default 300 seconds). Above 1: Kubernetes HPA |
| Cloud providers | All | All | AWS and GCP |
| Cluster prerequisite | None | None | KEDA add-on enabled on the cluster |
| Setup effort | None | Two numbers and a threshold | Scaler YAML, often IAM or credentials |

## Choose HPA when

- The service handles HTTP or gRPC requests and its CPU goes up with traffic: REST APIs, web frontends, server-side rendering.
- You want autoscaling that works on any cluster with no extra setup.
- The service must always keep instances running to answer requests.

HPA scales on CPU alone or on CPU and memory together. Memory-only scaling is not supported.

## Choose KEDA when

- The service consumes a queue or a stream (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, Kinesis, Redis lists) and the backlog tells you whether it keeps up.
- The workload is sporadic and you want it to cost nothing while idle. KEDA is the only mode that accepts **0** minimum instances.
- You already expose a business metric in Prometheus (pending jobs, active sessions) that predicts load better than CPU.
- Load follows a known schedule and you want to scale up before it arrives, with the cron scaler.

KEDA requires a cluster on AWS or GCP, and Qovery supports KEDA's [built-in scalers](https://keda.sh/docs/latest/scalers/) only. External scalers are not supported.

## Choose no autoscaling when

The service is a development environment, a proof of concept, or a test. For production, run at least 2 instances, or 3 if your app needs several instances to handle normal traffic, so a node maintenance or a pod crash does not take it down.

## A typical setup

A common architecture uses both modes in the same environment:

- `api` (receives requests, pushes jobs to SQS): **HPA**, 2 to 10 instances, CPU threshold 60%.
- `worker` (consumes the SQS queue): **KEDA**, 0 to 20 instances, scaler `aws-sqs-queue` with `queueLength: "5"`.

The API scales with incoming traffic. The worker follows the queue and drops to zero when the queue is empty.

## Configure HPA

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the application resources">
    In the Qovery Console, open your application and go to **Settings** → **Resources**. Scroll to **Instances & Autoscaling**.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/getting-started/guides/hpa-vs-keda/autoscaling-mode-dropdown.png" alt="Autoscaling mode dropdown in application resources" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select HPA">
    In **Autoscaling mode**, select **HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler)**. Pick **CPU only** or **CPU + Memory**.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Set instances and thresholds">
    Set the minimum and maximum number of instances. The CPU threshold defaults to 60%. If you selected **CPU + Memory**, set the memory threshold too.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/getting-started/guides/hpa-vs-keda/hpa-settings.png" alt="HPA settings with min and max instances, autoscaling metric and CPU threshold" />
    </Frame>

    The thresholds are also available as the advanced settings [`hpa.cpu.average_utilization_percent`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#hpa-cpu-average-utilization-percent) and [`hpa.memory.average_utilization_percent`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#hpa-memory-average-utilization-percent).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Save and redeploy">
    Save, then redeploy the application to apply the new autoscaling policy.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
HPA computes usage as a percentage of the CPU and memory **requests** you set on the application. If the requests are far from real usage, the thresholds will trigger too early or too late. Right-size the resources before tuning the threshold.
</Tip>

## Configure KEDA

<Steps>
  <Step title="Enable KEDA on the cluster">
    Open your cluster settings, go to the **Add-ons** tab and enable **KEDA**. Redeploy the cluster: the add-on is only installed after the cluster deployment.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/application/cluster-keda-activation.png" alt="Enable KEDA in cluster add-ons" />
    </Frame>

    You only do this once per cluster.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select KEDA on the application">
    Open your application, go to **Settings** → **Resources** → **Instances & Autoscaling** and select **Event-driven autoscaling (KEDA)** in **Autoscaling mode**.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Set instances, polling interval and cooldown">
    - **Minimum instances**: 0 to scale to zero, or 1 or more to keep warm instances.
    - **Maximum instances**: the upper limit. Keep it low for your first test.
    - **Polling interval**: how often KEDA reads the event source while the application runs 0 instances. Default 30 seconds.
    - **Cooldown period**: how long KEDA waits after the last event before scaling back to 0. Default 300 seconds.

    Both timers only apply to scaling between 0 and 1 instance. Between 1 and the maximum, KEDA feeds its metrics to a Kubernetes HPA, which applies its own timing. See [`pollingInterval`](https://keda.sh/docs/latest/reference/scaledobject-spec/#pollinginterval) and [`cooldownPeriod`](https://keda.sh/docs/latest/reference/scaledobject-spec/#cooldownperiod) in the KEDA reference.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/getting-started/guides/hpa-vs-keda/keda-general-settings.png" alt="KEDA general settings" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add a scaler">
    Click **Add scaler**, enter the scaler type and paste its configuration YAML. Parameters go under `metadata`. Example for a Redis list, with one instance per 2 waiting items:

    ```yaml
    metadata:
      address: <redis-service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:6379
      passwordFromEnv: REDIS_PASSWORD
      listName: optimizer
      listLength: "2"
      databaseIndex: "0"
    ```

    `passwordFromEnv` reads the `REDIS_PASSWORD` environment variable from your application container. Use the full in-cluster address, as explained in [Pitfalls](#pitfalls).

    Each scaler type has its own parameters. See the [KEDA scalers reference](https://keda.sh/docs/latest/scalers/).

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/getting-started/guides/hpa-vs-keda/keda-scaler-redis.png" alt="KEDA Redis scaler configuration" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add authentication if the source needs it">
    Paste the credentials setup in **Trigger Authentication (YAML) - Optional**. Two options:

    - `podIdentity`, for cloud IAM. On AWS, `identityOwner: workload` makes KEDA reuse your application's IAM role:

      ```yaml
      podIdentity:
        provider: aws
        identityOwner: workload
      ```

    - `secretTargetRef`, to read a Qovery environment variable or secret with `qovery.env.VARIABLE_NAME`:

      ```yaml
      secretTargetRef:
        - parameter: password
          key: qovery.env.REDIS_PASSWORD
      ```

    For the IAM role and trust policy on SQS, follow the [AWS SQS example](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#instances-%26-autoscaling) in the application reference.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Save and redeploy">
    Save, then redeploy the application.
  </Step>
</Steps>

### Multiple scalers

You can add several scalers to one application. KEDA computes a target number of instances for each scaler and applies the highest one. For example, with a queue of 15 messages at 1 message per instance and another of 50 messages at 10 messages per instance, KEDA runs 15 instances.

## Migrate from HPA to KEDA

Select **Event-driven autoscaling (KEDA)** in **Autoscaling mode**, configure your scalers, save and redeploy. HPA and KEDA's `ScaledObject` both control the replica count of the same Deployment, so the deployment removes the HPA before it creates the `ScaledObject`. The application keeps its current number of instances, brought within the KEDA minimum and maximum, then KEDA scales it from its scalers.

To go from KEDA back to HPA, select **HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler)**, save and redeploy.

## Pitfalls

{/* reviewer: the "short hostnames" and "metadata" items were observed in a real environment and are not yet documented in application.mdx */}

- **Scale-to-zero on a service that receives requests.** With 0 minimum instances, nothing answers until KEDA polls the source and starts a pod. Use 0 for queue consumers and batch workers, not for APIs.
- **Short hostnames in scaler YAML.** The KEDA operator runs in the `kube-system` namespace, not in your application's namespace. A short service name like `redis-queue:6379` does not resolve from there. Use the full in-cluster name: `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:6379`. When the address does not resolve, KEDA does not scale and the application shows no error.
- **Scaler parameters outside `metadata`.** Put scaler parameters under the `metadata:` key. With parameters at the root of the YAML, the Console shows the scaler configuration as empty.
- **Memory-only HPA.** Not supported. If memory is your only signal, use CPU + Memory, or a KEDA scaler on a metric that tracks the real load.

## Check that scaling works

1. Start with a low maximum (3 or 5 instances) and a low target, such as `listLength: "1"` for Redis or `queueLength: "1"` for SQS.
2. Push a batch of messages to the queue, or generate traffic for HPA.
3. Watch the instance count on the application overview in the Console.
4. If nothing moves, read the application logs and the KEDA operator logs (`keda-operator` in `kube-system`). Authentication and address errors show up there.

The demo below runs the Redis scaler from this guide (`listLength: "2"`, 0 to 20 instances). About 120 jobs land in the queue at once, and KEDA adds workers until it reaches the 20-instance maximum, while the queue drains.

<Frame caption="Demo application dashboard: Redis queue depth and worker pods during a load test">
  <img src="/images/getting-started/guides/hpa-vs-keda/scaling-test-instances.png" alt="Redis queue depth falling while the number of KEDA-scaled worker pods rises to 20" />
</Frame>

Once scaling behaves as expected, raise the maximum to its production value.

# Minimize downtime while upgrading RDS instances
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/upgrading-rds-instance

> Upgrade an RDS PostgreSQL or MySQL instance with AWS Blue/Green deployments to reduce downtime, then align the database configuration in Qovery.

Managed RDS instances deployed with Qovery have by default a maintenance window configured, applying database updates only during the specified timeframe (see more [information here](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/database#applying-changes-to-a-managed-database)).

During the maintenance window, a downtime has to be expected on your service since the upgrade might takes a few minutes to take effect.

If this is not acceptable for your business, AWS allows you to deploy changes via the [Blue/Green Deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/blue-green-deployments.html).

This basically allows you to create a copy of your database with the new configuration (called "Green group") and then switch over to the new database by removing the old instance ("Blue group").

Blue/Green deployments on RDS are not natively supported by Qovery but you can follow this guide to upgrade your RDS instances.

# How to configure

To better explain the process, we will try to upgrade an RDS PostgreSQL instance from the version 14 to the version 15. The same procedure applies to MySQL, with the prerequisite differences called out below.

## Activate the logical replication (PostgreSQL only)

<Info>

This section applies to **PostgreSQL only**. For MySQL, RDS has no equivalent configuration to activate, the only prerequisite is that automated backups are enabled on the instance, which is the default on Qovery-managed databases. You can skip directly to the "Launch the Blue/Green deployment" section below.

</Info>

<Info>

This part has to be done only once for each database. If you have already activated the logical replication, go to the next section.

</Info>

Logical replication is necessary to use the RDS Blue/Green deployment feature.

To enable the logical replication you have to:

1. Create a Custom DB Parameter group. Make sure it targets your current engine type (PostgreSQL) and version (Parameter group family = postgres14), let's call it `parameter-group-14`. (Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithParamGroups.Creating.html))
2. Edit the DB parameter group `parameter-group-14` and activate the logical replication by setting `rds.logical_replication` to `1` (Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_MultiAZDBCluster_LogicalRepl.html#multi-az-db-clusters-logical-replication))
3. Associate the DB Parameter group `parameter-group-14` to your database. If you have read replicas, associate the parameter group to the replicas as well. (Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithParamGroups.Associating.html))
4. Reboot your database to apply the changes or wait for the next maintenance window for applying these changes.

## Enable logical replication for the "Green" database (PostgreSQL only)

We will create a separate DB Parameter group for our "Green group" so that we will ensure that the  you won't have to do the previous step the next time.
    
1. Create a Custom DB Parameter group. Make sure it targets your **next** engine type and version (Parameter group family), let's call it `parameter-group-15` Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithParamGroups.Creating.html))
2. Edit the DB parameter group `parameter-group-15` and activate the logical replication by setting `rds.logical_replication` to `1` (Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_MultiAZDBCluster_LogicalRepl.html#multi-az-db-clusters-logical-replication))

## Launch the Blue/Green deployment

### Create the Blue/Green Deployment

1. Go on the Database list on the AWS console, select the database and press the "Create new Blue/Green Deployment" button.
2. Define a name for the deployment (blue-green-upgrade), ensure you select the right engine version (PostgreSQL 15) and the right DB parameter group (parameter-group-15) and create the Blue/Green deployment.
3. Wait for all the instances to be `Available`.

AWS Documentation [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/blue-green-deployments-creating.html)

### Apply the switch over

1. From the Database list on the AWS console, select the Blue/Green deployment `blue-green-upgrade`
2. From the action list, select "Switch over"
3. Verify that everything is fine on the configuration and confirm the switch over. This will make the "Green group" the new production environment.

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/blue-green-rds/switch-over.png" alt="Switch over" />
</Frame>

4. Wait for the switch over to be completed. 

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/blue-green-rds/switch-done.png" alt="Switch over completed" />
</Frame>

### Delete the blue/green deployment
1. From the Database list on the AWS console, select the Blue/Green deployment `blue-green-upgrade`
2. From the action list, select "Delete"
3. Once completed, from the Database list on the AWS console, select the database in version 14 (note it should be renamed with a suffix `old`)
4. From the action list, select "Delete"
5. Wait for the delete operation to be completed before moving to the next step

<Warning>

For [legacy managed databases](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/database#legacy-managed-databases), do not update the version in the Qovery console until the `old` instance has actually been deleted on AWS. Qovery manages your DB parameter group through Terraform, and switching the version triggers Terraform to replace the old parameter group (targeting the previous engine family, e.g. `postgres14`/`mysql8.0`) with a new one (e.g. `postgres15`/`mysql8.4`). AWS refuses to delete a parameter group that still has an instance attached to it — and the `old` instance is still attached to it. If you re-deploy from Qovery while the `old` instance still exists, the deployment will fail with a `TERRAFORM_UNKNOWN_ERROR` and no RDS event will be emitted, since the failure happens at the Terraform plan/apply stage before any AWS API call is made against the instance. If this happens, delete the `old` instance first, then re-deploy from Qovery again.

</Warning>

## Align the configuration on Qovery (legacy managed databases)

1. Go on the Qovery console and align the database configuration by setting the version to `15`

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/blue-green-rds/update-version.png" alt="Update the database version" />
</Frame>

2. Re-deploy your database.

<Warning>

After the deployment completes, check the parameter group's apply status on AWS (`ParameterApplyStatus`). It can be reported as `pending-reboot`, meaning the new parameter group is attached, but the engine is still running with the previous group's values until the instance is rebooted. This is a silent failure mode: nothing breaks immediately, but any custom parameter you rely on (e.g. `log_bin_trust_function_creators` on MySQL) is not actually active yet, and the failure only surfaces later, for example `CREATE FUNCTION`/`CREATE TRIGGER` failing with `ERROR 1419` the next time a routine or trigger is created, possibly weeks after the migration. If the status is `pending-reboot`, reboot the instance from the AWS console to apply the new parameter values immediately.

</Warning>

## Align the configuration on Qovery (blueprint databases)

If the database was created from a [database blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints), align it with the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview) instead of the console.

1. Wait until the `old` instance has been deleted on AWS.
2. List the majors the blueprint can move to, and what moving to each one would do:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major -n <service name>
```

3. Move the blueprint to the new major, here `15`:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major -n <service name> --major 15
```

Since the database already runs that version, the command only updates Qovery's records so the console shows the right version. The database itself is not touched.

<Info>

PostgreSQL blueprints do not manage the DB parameter group: they keep the one attached to the instance, including the custom group created for logical replication. The parameter group warning above only applies to legacy managed databases.

MySQL blueprints cover both 8.0 and 8.4 with the same blueprint major, so there is nothing to align after a MySQL upgrade done on AWS.

</Info>

# Restore an RDS PostgreSQL blueprint to a point in time
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/restoring-rds-point-in-time

> Recover deleted or overwritten data from an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL blueprint with a point-in-time restore, then copy it back or replace the database.

The [Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints/aws-rds-postgresql) blueprint keeps automated backups, so AWS can restore the database as it was at any second of the retention window. The blueprint has no restore setting, and AWS always restores to a **new** instance. This guide restores a temporary copy next to your database with the AWS CLI, then copies back the data you need. Copying back changes nothing on your blueprint service, its Terraform state or its outputs.

You can run this guide on your own. Contact us first in the cases listed under [When to contact us](#when-to-contact-us).

## Before you start

- **Point-in-time recovery is on.** `backup_retention_period` is above `0` (default `14`). The restore window goes back that many days. The latest restorable time trails real time by about 5 to 7 minutes.
- **AWS CLI access** to the account and region of the environment's cluster, with permission to describe RDS instances and their automated backups, to restore an instance to a point in time, and to modify, reboot and delete the temporary copy and its automated backups.
- **A PostgreSQL client inside the cluster network.** The restored copy is private, so use [`qovery shell`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/shell) on a running container that has a PostgreSQL client, or create a temporary container from the `postgres:<major>` image with its command set to `sleep infinity`, then delete it afterwards. Use a client of the database's major version or newer.
- **The database details**, from the blueprint's outputs. Each output is a variable `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_Z<id>_<OUTPUT>`, and Qovery also gives it a short alias named after the blueprint service, `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>` (see [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs)). This guide uses the aliases: `<PREFIX>_DB_IDENTIFIER` (the RDS identifier, called `<primary>` below), `<PREFIX>_DB_ADDRESS`, `<PREFIX>_DB_PORT`, `<PREFIX>_DB_NAME`, `<PREFIX>_DB_USERNAME` and `<PREFIX>_DB_PASSWORD`. Check the actual names in your environment's variables: they carry a `_1`, `_2`... suffix when the name was already taken, keep the former name of a blueprint service renamed after its first deployment, and a database [migrated from a Qovery managed database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints#migrating-a-managed-database-to-a-blueprint) gets no alias, so use the `QOVERY_OUTPUT_TERRAFORM_...` variables or its [built-in database variables](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#database-connection-variables) instead. The password is a secret: read it from the environment of a container in the same environment.

## Choose the approach

| | Copy back (recommended) | Replace with a new service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **When** | Rows deleted or overwritten, the database is otherwise healthy | The database is unusable, or you want to roll back the whole database |
| **What changes for your applications** | Nothing | New endpoint and password, every application redeployed |
| **Data written since the restore time** | Kept | Lost |

Both start with the same two steps. Copy back is described in steps 3 and 4; replacing in [Replace the database with a new service](#replace-the-database-with-a-new-service).

## Step 1: Check the restore time

Convert the time you want to restore to UTC, then check it falls inside the window and read the settings the copy needs:

```bash
aws rds describe-db-instance-automated-backups --region <region> \
  --db-instance-identifier <primary> \
  --query "DBInstanceAutomatedBackups[?Status=='active'].RestoreWindow"
aws rds describe-db-instances --region <region> --db-instance-identifier <primary> \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].{latest:LatestRestorableTime,engine:EngineVersion,class:DBInstanceClass,subnet:DBSubnetGroup.DBSubnetGroupName,sgs:VpcSecurityGroups[].VpcSecurityGroupId}'
```

If the time is a few minutes old and after `latest`, wait a few minutes and run it again.

## Step 2: Restore a temporary copy

```bash
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --region <region> \
  --source-db-instance-identifier <primary> \
  --target-db-instance-identifier <primary>-pitr-<YYYYMMDDHHMM> \
  --restore-time <restore time, e.g. 2026-11-09T14:00:00Z> \
  --db-subnet-group-name <subnet> \
  --vpc-security-group-ids <sgs, space separated> \
  --db-parameter-group-name default.postgres<major> \
  --no-publicly-accessible --no-multi-az --no-deletion-protection
aws rds wait db-instance-available --region <region> \
  --db-instance-identifier <primary>-pitr-<YYYYMMDDHHMM>
aws rds describe-db-instances --region <region> \
  --db-instance-identifier <primary>-pitr-<YYYYMMDDHHMM> \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].[DBInstanceStatus,Endpoint.Address,DBParameterGroups[0].DBParameterGroupName,DBParameterGroups[0].ParameterApplyStatus]' --output text
```

`<major>` is the major of `engine` from step 1, for example `default.postgres17` for `17.9`. The last command must show `default.postgres<major>`. While the copy is being created, AWS can still list your database's parameter group: it switches at the end of the restore. The last column should read `in-sync`. If it still shows `<primary>-params-...` once the copy is available, run `aws rds modify-db-instance --region <region> --db-instance-identifier <primary>-pitr-<YYYYMMDDHHMM> --db-parameter-group-name default.postgres<major> --apply-immediately`, then, once the copy is available again, reboot it with `aws rds reboot-db-instance` (the copy only, never your database): the status reads `pending-reboot` until then. The restore took 12 to 19 minutes for a small database in our tests and takes longer for larger ones. The copy is billed like an instance of its class until you delete it.

<Warning>
These rules keep the copy invisible to the blueprint. Breaking one makes a later deployment of your blueprint service fail.

- **Keep `--db-parameter-group-name default.postgres<major>`.** Without it, AWS gives the copy your database's own parameter group, `<primary>-params-...`, when `db_parameters` is set. That group belongs to the blueprint, and a deployment that replaces or deletes it (a major upgrade, clearing `db_parameters`) fails while the copy still uses it.
- **Name the copy differently from your database.** Never use `<primary>` or `<primary>-replica-<N>`: the blueprint looks up instances by those names. The identifier is limited to 63 characters.
- **Do not swap the copy in place of your database** by renaming instances. The blueprint keeps tracking the original instance, and the next deployment tries to rename it back and fails. To move to the restored data, copy it back, or [replace the database with a new service](#replace-the-database-with-a-new-service).
</Warning>

## Step 3: Copy the data back

Connect from inside the cluster network. `SIDE` is the copy and `PRIMARY` your database:

```bash
SIDE="host=<copy endpoint> port=<port> dbname=<database> user=<username> sslmode=require"
PRIMARY="host=$<PREFIX>_DB_ADDRESS port=<port> dbname=<database> user=<username> sslmode=require"
export PGPASSWORD="$<PREFIX>_DB_PASSWORD"
```

The port, database and username are the values of `<PREFIX>_DB_PORT`, `<PREFIX>_DB_NAME` and `<PREFIX>_DB_USERNAME`; the copy uses the same ones. It accepts the password that was valid at the restore time.

Before writing anything, query the copy to confirm it predates the incident: overwritten values must be absent there, and deleted rows must still be present. If not, the restore time is wrong.

### Deleted rows: put them back

Rows that still exist are skipped, so rows written since the incident stay as they are. This needs a primary key or a unique constraint on the table.

First check whether the delete also changed other tables, through foreign keys with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, `SET NULL` or `SET DEFAULT`. Run this again for every table it returns:

```bash
psql "$PRIMARY" -c "select conrelid::regclass as child_table, confdeltype from pg_constraint where contype = 'f' and confdeltype in ('c', 'n', 'd') and confrelid = 'public.<table>'::regclass"
```

Tables with `c` need the same re-insert, after their parent. Tables with `n` or `d` need their reference column repaired as below. Then re-insert:

```bash
pg_dump "$SIDE" --data-only --table='public.<table>' --column-inserts --on-conflict-do-nothing \
    -f restore-<table>.raw.sql \
  && grep -v '^SELECT pg_catalog.setval' restore-<table>.raw.sql > restore-<table>.sql \
  && grep -c '^INSERT INTO' restore-<table>.sql \
  && { psql "$PRIMARY" --single-transaction -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f restore-<table>.sql \
         > restore-<table>.log 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"; }
grep -c '^INSERT 0 1' restore-<table>.log
```

- Each command runs only if the previous one succeeded, so a failed dump never reaches your database, and a count of `0` (no rows in the copy) stops it too. The first count is the rows in the copy, the second the rows re-inserted. An `exit` other than `0` means nothing was applied: the end of `restore-<table>.log` says why.
- The `grep -v` drops the sequence reset, which would move your id sequence back in time and make the next inserts collide.
- This brings back **every** row the table had at the restore time and no longer has, including rows your application deleted on purpose since then. To bring back only some rows, use the staging approach below.
- Restore parent tables before the tables that reference them. Triggers on the table fire for every re-inserted row.
- Rows created between the restore time and the incident, then deleted by it, are not in the copy. With a numeric key, list the ids still missing above the copy's highest id and check them against your application logs. A second copy at a later time is possible while that time is still in the window.

### Overwritten rows: stage, compare, repair

Copy the table into a separate `pitr_restore` schema of your database, then merge what you need with SQL:

```bash
psql "$SIDE" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  -c 'CREATE SCHEMA pitr_restore' -c 'ALTER TABLE public.<table> SET SCHEMA pitr_restore'
pg_dump "$SIDE" --schema=pitr_restore --no-owner --no-privileges -Fc -f pitr_restore.dump
pg_restore --section=pre-data --section=data --no-owner --no-privileges -d "$PRIMARY" pitr_restore.dump
```

Moving the table on the copy is harmless, since the copy is deleted afterwards. If `ALTER TABLE` fails with `must be owner of table`, run `GRANT <owner role> TO <username>` on the copy first.

Then, in an interactive `psql "$PRIMARY"` session, repair only the rows that still hold the bad value, so changes made since the restore time are kept:

```sql
-- preview
SELECT t.id, t.<column> AS now, r.<column> AS at_restore_time
FROM public.<table> t JOIN pitr_restore.<table> r ON r.id = t.id
WHERE <condition that matches only the damaged rows> LIMIT 20;

BEGIN;
UPDATE public.<table> t SET <column> = r.<column>
FROM pitr_restore.<table> r
WHERE r.id = t.id AND <condition that matches only the damaged rows>;
-- check the UPDATE count, then COMMIT; or ROLLBACK;
```

When done, run `DROP SCHEMA pitr_restore CASCADE;`, then delete the dump files (`restore-<table>.raw.sql`, `restore-<table>.sql`, `restore-<table>.log`, `pitr_restore.dump`): they contain your data.

## Step 4: Delete the temporary copy

```bash
aws rds delete-db-instance --region <region> \
  --db-instance-identifier <primary>-pitr-<YYYYMMDDHHMM> \
  --skip-final-snapshot --delete-automated-backups
```

The copy takes its own automated backups while it runs. `--delete-automated-backups` removes them, and billing stops once the instance is gone. A last automated snapshot can stay listed for a few minutes after the delete.

## Replace the database with a new service

Use this when the database cannot be repaired in place. Everything written after the restore time is lost.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Restore a temporary copy">
    Follow steps 1 and 2 above.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create a new blueprint service">
    [Create](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints#creating-a-blueprint-service) an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL service in the same environment, with the same major, a new service name, a new `db_name` and the other values of the current service, but leave `db_password` empty so Qovery generates a new password. For a database [migrated from a Qovery managed database](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints#migrating-a-managed-database-to-a-blueprint), stop here and [contact us](#when-to-contact-us). The RDS identifier is derived from `db_name`, so reusing it collides with the current instance. The new service gets its own aliases, `<NEW_PREFIX>_*`.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Copy the whole database">
    Redeploy a container that has a PostgreSQL client, so it receives the new service's variables, and build `NEW` from them. Recreate first the roles your applications use, other than the master user: list them with `pg_dumpall --dbname="$SIDE" --roles-only --no-role-passwords` and create them on the new instance with their memberships. Then:

    ```bash
    PGPASSWORD="$<PREFIX>_DB_PASSWORD" pg_dump "$SIDE" -Fc --no-owner -f full.dump
    PGPASSWORD="$<NEW_PREFIX>_DB_PASSWORD" pg_restore --no-owner -j 4 -d "$NEW" full.dump
    ```

    The two databases have different passwords, so each command sets its own.

    Compare row counts on both sides. If `pg_restore` ends with `errors ignored on restore: N`, read the messages before it. Delete `full.dump` afterwards.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Point the aliases at the new service">
    For each alias of the current service, `<PREFIX>_<OUTPUT>`, change its target from the current service's output to the new service's output of the same name, with the API call in [Changing the target of an alias](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#changing-the-target-of-an-alias). Your applications keep reading the same variable names.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Redeploy your applications">
    Redeploy every service that uses the database. Until then it keeps the old values, even though the Console shows it up to date.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Clean up">
    Delete the temporary copy (step 4). Once everything runs on the new service, delete the old blueprint service. Deleting it removes its outputs and any alias still pointing at them, so only delete it after the aliases point at the new service. Its final snapshot and automated backups are kept or deleted according to its `skip_final_snapshot` and `delete_automated_backups` values.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## When to contact us

Contact Qovery Support through your usual channel (in-app chat, shared Slack channel, or email) before acting when:

- **The database instance was deleted.** Do not deploy the blueprint service: it would create a new, empty instance under the same name. Automated backups survive the instance only when `delete_automated_backups` was `false`.
- **The database was migrated from a Qovery managed database** and you need to replace it. Its applications read the managed database's variables, which a new blueprint service does not take over. Copying data back works as described above.
- **The restore time is outside the window**, or `backup_retention_period` is `0`.
- **You would rather be guided.**

Include the organization, environment and service, the restore time with its time zone, the tables affected and their primary keys, and whether your application itself deletes or overwrites those rows.

## After the restore

- Raise `backup_retention_period` if the window was short. It goes up to 35 days.
- Test this procedure regularly, as part of your [disaster recovery plan](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/disaster-recovery#testing-your-dr-plan).

# Setting Up Cloudflare and Custom Domain on Qovery
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/cloudflare-custom-domain

> Configure Cloudflare as a domain provider for your Qovery applications

This tutorial guides you through configuring Cloudflare as a domain provider for applications deployed on Qovery. The process involves adding a custom domain and establishing proper DNS and SSL/TLS settings.

## Prerequisites

- Active Qovery application
- Domain ownership on Cloudflare or registrar
- Access to Cloudflare DNS settings

## Step 1: Add a Custom Domain

1. Access your application settings in Qovery Console
2. Navigate to the **Domains** section
3. Enter your Cloudflare-managed domain
4. **Critical**: Enable the **"Domain behind a CDN"** toggle

<Info>
Enabling "Domain behind a CDN" automatically disables certificate generation since Cloudflare handles SSL/TLS management.
</Info>

<Note>
If you keep the Cloudflare record in **DNS only** mode instead, leave "Domain behind a CDN" disabled and enable "Generate certificate": Qovery then issues a Let's Encrypt certificate for the hostname. This only works for single hostnames such as `app.example.com`. For a wildcard domain such as `*.app.example.com`, Let's Encrypt requires a DNS-01 challenge that Qovery cannot answer on your Cloudflare zone (unless the zone is connected to the cluster through the [Cloudflare DNS integration](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#cloudflare-setup)), so the certificate is never issued. Use the proxied setup described in this guide for wildcard domains.
</Note>

<Warning>
Cloudflare's free Universal SSL certificate covers your apex domain and one level of subdomains (`*.example.com`). A deeper wildcard such as `*.app.example.com` needs an Advanced Certificate (Advanced Certificate Manager) or a custom certificate uploaded to Cloudflare.
</Warning>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/1.png" alt="Add custom domain" />
</Frame>

## Step 2: Configure Cloudflare DNS

### Add CNAME Entry

1. Go to Cloudflare DNS settings
2. Add a CNAME entry using values provided by the Qovery Console
3. The proxy mode can remain enabled

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/2.png" alt="Cloudflare CNAME configuration" />
</Frame>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/3.png" alt="CNAME record details" />
</Frame>

## Step 3: Configure SSL/TLS Settings

The last step to configure the domain Cloudflare side properly is to use the **Full** TLS encryption for proper custom domain functionality.

1. Navigate to **SSL/TLS** settings in Cloudflare
2. Select **Full** encryption mode

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/4.png" alt="SSL/TLS Full encryption" />
</Frame>

<Warning>
Using "Flexible" encryption mode will not work properly with Qovery. Always use "Full" or "Full (strict)" mode.
</Warning>

## Step 4: Access Restriction Options

You have two options for restricting access to your application:

### Option 1: IP Whitelisting

Add Cloudflare IP ranges to Qovery's advanced settings to allow only Cloudflare traffic.

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/5.png" alt="IP whitelisting configuration" />
</Frame>

### Option 2: Cloudflared Tunnel

Cloudflared establishes outbound tunnels between resources and Cloudflare's network, enabling tunnel-based access without public exposure.

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/6.png" alt="Cloudflared tunnel setup" />
</Frame>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/cloudflare/7.png" alt="Tunnel configuration" />
</Frame>

## Verification

Once configured, your application should be accessible via your custom domain through Cloudflare's network.

  <img src="/images/cloudflare/8.png" alt="Domain verification" />
</Frame>

  <img src="/images/cloudflare/9.png" alt="SSL certificate verification" />

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Domain not resolving">
    - Verify CNAME record is correct
    - Check DNS propagation (can take up to 48 hours)
    - Ensure proxy mode is enabled in Cloudflare
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="SSL/TLS errors">
    - Confirm "Full" encryption mode is selected
    - Wait for SSL certificate provisioning (5-10 minutes)
    - Check that "Domain behind a CDN" toggle is enabled in Qovery
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Wildcard domain shows an error and serves the wrong certificate">
    - "Generate certificate" is enabled on a wildcard domain (`*.app.example.com`). Qovery cannot issue wildcard certificates on a Cloudflare zone, so the certificate stays pending and the service shows an error.
    - Disable "Generate certificate", enable "Domain behind a CDN", redeploy the service and switch the Cloudflare record to Proxied.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="502 Bad Gateway errors">
    - Verify application is running in Qovery
    - Check that the CNAME points to the correct Qovery domain
    - Ensure Cloudflare IP ranges are whitelisted if using IP restriction
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
