# 502 Bad Gateway: recv() failed (104: Connection reset by peer)
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/nginx-502-connection-reset

> Fix random 502 errors from the NGINX ingress when your service resets the connection: keep-alive timeouts, single instances, restarts and load balancer health checks.

Clients get a `502 Bad Gateway` from time to time, and the NGINX logs of the service show this line at the same moment:

```text
[error] 164#164: *108859 recv() failed (104: Connection reset by peer) while reading response header from upstream, client: 203.0.113.10, server: api.example.com, request: "POST /data HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://10.0.18.128:5000/data"
```

The same request usually works when it is sent again a few seconds later.

## What the error means

NGINX forwarded the request to a pod of your service, and the pod closed the TCP connection (it sent a TCP reset) before it returned any response header. NGINX cannot give the client an answer, so it returns `502`.

The reset comes from the pod side: your application, its runtime, or the pod being stopped. NGINX only reports it. To confirm, open the service **Logs** in the Console and look at the [NGINX logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/logs#nginx-logs): the access line for the failed request shows the `502` status and the upstream address of the pod.

## Cause 1: the application closes idle connections before NGINX does

This is the most common cause when the errors look random and grow with traffic.

NGINX keeps connections to your pods open and reuses them for the next requests. The ingress-nginx controller keeps an idle upstream connection for 60 seconds by default. Many application servers close idle connections much sooner:

| Server | Default idle keep-alive timeout |
|---|---|
| Node.js `http.Server` (Express, NestJS, Fastify on Node) | 5 seconds (`keepAliveTimeout`) |
| Gunicorn | 2 seconds (`--keep-alive`) |
| Uvicorn | 5 seconds (`--timeout-keep-alive`) |

When NGINX sends a request on a connection that the application is closing at that very moment, the application answers with a reset and the request fails with `502`.

**Fix:** make the application keep idle connections open longer than NGINX does, so NGINX is always the side that closes them. Set the keep-alive timeout of your server above 60 seconds.

For Node.js, set both timeouts on the HTTP server, with `headersTimeout` higher than `keepAliveTimeout`:

```js
const server = app.listen(port);
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65000;
server.headersTimeout = 66000;
```

In NestJS, apply the same two values to `app.getHttpServer()` after `await app.listen(port)`.

For Gunicorn, start it with `--keep-alive 75`. For Uvicorn, use `--timeout-keep-alive 75`.

Redeploy the service. The `recv() failed` lines should stop.

## Cause 2: the only pod was stopped or moved

With a single instance, every restart of that pod drops the connections it holds. This happens on each deployment, when the pod is out of memory, and when the cluster moves the pod to another node to consolidate nodes.

**Fix:**

1. Run at least 2 instances: open the service **Settings**, then **Resources**, and set the minimum number of instances to 2 or more. See [Instances and autoscaling](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#instances-%26-autoscaling).
2. Configure a readiness probe so a new pod gets traffic only once it can answer. See [Health checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-health-checks).
3. Handle `SIGTERM` in your application: stop accepting new connections, finish the requests in flight, then exit. If your service needs more time to drain, raise [`deployment.termination_grace_period_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#deployment-termination-grace-period-seconds).
4. Exit code 137 means the pod received `SIGKILL`: either it ran out of memory (`Reason: OOMKilled`), or it did not stop within the termination grace period of step 3. See [SIGKILL Signal 137](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#service-runtime-issues).

## Cause 3: the load balancer has no healthy target (AWS)

On AWS, traffic goes from the cloud load balancer to the NGINX ingress pods. If the load balancer sends traffic to nodes, a node without an NGINX pod fails the health check, and requests can hang or fail while NGINX pods move between nodes.

With the AWS Load Balancer Controller, the load balancer sends traffic directly to the IP addresses of the NGINX pods, so node health no longer matters. It is controlled by the cluster advanced setting [`aws.eks.enable_alb_controller`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#aws-eks-enable-alb-controller), which defaults to `true`. If an older cluster still has it set to `false`, enable it and redeploy the cluster.

<Warning>
Switching `aws.eks.enable_alb_controller` replaces the load balancer: public access to your services is cut for up to 10 minutes while the new load balancer and its DNS propagate. Plan a maintenance window.
</Warning>

Also keep at least 2 NGINX replicas with [`nginx.hpa.min_number_instances`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#nginx-hpa-min-number-instances) (default `2`).

## Check the service without NGINX

To find out whether the application or the path in front of it is at fault, send the same requests to the service directly with [`qovery port-forward`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/port-forward). The traffic skips NGINX and the load balancer:

```bash
qovery port-forward "<console-url-of-the-service>" --port 8080:<service-port>
curl -v http://localhost:8080/your/endpoint
```

If the errors also happen through the port-forward, the cause is in the application.

## Related errors

- `client intended to send too large body`: the request body is above the limit of 100 MB. Raise [`network.ingress.proxy_body_size_mb`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-ingress-proxy-body-size-mb) on the service.
- A `502` or `504` after exactly 60 seconds is a timeout, not a reset. See [NGINX timeout: increase the 60 second limit](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/nginx-timeout).

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# NGINX timeout: increase the 60 second limit
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/nginx-timeout

> Slow requests fail with 504 or 502 when the NGINX ingress gets no response data for 60 seconds. Raise the proxy read, send and connect timeouts of the service, or set the Gateway API request timeout.

A slow request fails when your service sends no response data for 60 seconds, even though the same call works when you run the application locally. The client gets a `504 Gateway Time-out` (sometimes a `502`), and the NGINX logs of the service show:

```text
upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream
```

WebSocket and server-sent event connections that stay quiet for 60 seconds are closed for the same reason.

## Cause

Requests to a public port go through the ingress of the cluster before they reach your service. By default, the NGINX ingress waits at most 60 seconds between two reads of the response from your service, then gives up. This is an inactivity limit, not a limit on the total duration: a response that keeps sending data, such as a stream, can last longer. Your application keeps running, but the client has already received an error.

There is no single "request timeout" field: NGINX has one timeout per step, and each is an advanced setting of the service.

| Advanced setting | What it limits | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`network.ingress.proxy_read_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-ingress-proxy-read-timeout-seconds) | Time to wait between two reads of the response from your service, including the first byte. This is the one that ends slow requests. | `60` |
| [`network.ingress.proxy_send_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-ingress-proxy-send-timeout-seconds) | Time to transmit the request to your service, for large uploads. | `60` |
| [`network.ingress.send_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-ingress-send-timeout-seconds) | Time to transmit the response to a slow client. | `60` |
| [`network.ingress.proxy_connect_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-ingress-proxy-connect-timeout-seconds) | Time to open a connection to your service. Rarely needs a change. | `60` |

## Fix on the NGINX ingress

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the advanced settings of the service">
    In the Console, open the application, container or Helm service, go to **Settings**, then **Advanced Settings**.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Raise the timeouts">
    Set `network.ingress.proxy_read_timeout_seconds` to a value above the duration of your longest request, for example `120` or `300`. For long uploads, raise `network.ingress.proxy_send_timeout_seconds` too. For large downloads to slow clients, raise `network.ingress.send_timeout_seconds`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Redeploy the service">
    The new values apply only after the service is redeployed. Saving the settings is not enough.
  </Step>
</Steps>

With the API or Terraform, set the same keys in the advanced settings of the service:

```json
{
  "network.ingress.proxy_read_timeout_seconds": 300,
  "network.ingress.proxy_send_timeout_seconds": 300
}
```

## Fix on the Gateway API

When the cluster advanced setting [`k8s.use_api_gateway`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#k8s.use_api_gateway) is `true`, new services are exposed through the Gateway API instead of NGINX. Services created before the switch can still route through NGINX, where the `network.ingress.*` settings above apply. Check how your own service is exposed before changing settings. For a service exposed through the Gateway API, the `network.ingress.*` settings do not apply. Use these instead, then redeploy the service:

- [`network.gateway_api.http_request_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#network-gateway-api-http-request-timeout-seconds): maximum time to wait for the complete response. Requests that take longer end with `504 Gateway Timeout`.
- [`envoy.gateway_api.http_request_timeout_seconds`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#envoy-gateway-api-http-request-timeout-seconds): the cluster-wide default, used by services that do not set their own value.

## Before raising the timeout

A longer timeout keeps a connection and a worker busy for the whole request. For work that takes minutes, consider answering at once and processing in the background: put the job in a queue, return `202 Accepted` with an ID, and let the client poll for the result. A [lifecycle job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job) or a [cron job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cronjob) can also run long tasks outside the request path.

If requests fail with `502` well before 60 seconds, the cause is not a timeout. See [502 Bad Gateway: recv() failed (104: Connection reset by peer)](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/nginx-502-connection-reset).

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# default backend - 404
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/default-backend-404

> Your domain answers default backend - 404 or a plain 404 from NGINX. The request reached the cluster but matched no route: check the domain, the public port and the last deployment.

Opening the URL of your service returns a bare page with:

```text
default backend - 404
```

or a plain `404 Not Found` page served by NGINX, while your application has no such page.

## What the error means

The request reached the ingress of your cluster, but no route matched its host name and path, so the ingress answered with its fallback page. Your application never saw the request.

A route exists only for a service that has a publicly accessible port, for each domain attached to that service, once the service is deployed. Check those three things in order.

## 1. The domain is attached to the right service

If you use a custom domain, its DNS record points to the cluster, but the cluster only routes it if the domain is also declared on the service.

1. Open the service **Settings**, then **Domains**, and check that the exact host name is listed. `www.example.com` and `example.com` are two different domains.
2. Check that the DNS record is the CNAME given by Qovery for this service. See [Custom domains](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#custom-domains).
3. Redeploy the service after adding or changing a domain.

To rule out the custom domain, open the domain Qovery assigned to the service (shown in the Console). If that URL works, the problem is the custom domain setup.

## 2. The port is publicly accessible

Open the service **Settings**, then **Ports**:

- At least one port must have **Publicly Accessible** enabled.
- The **Internal Port** must be the port your application listens on. If your application reads the port from a `PORT` variable, make sure the variable and the internal port match.
- Your application must listen on `0.0.0.0`, not on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`.

See [Ports](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#ports).

## 3. The last deployment succeeded

The route is created when the service deploys. If the deployment failed, for example because the application crashed at startup, the route may not exist yet.

Open the deployment logs of the service and fix the first error. Application crashes at startup, such as an unhandled exception or a missing environment variable, show in the service logs. See [Application is crashing](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#service-deployment-issues) and [Debugging rapidly crashing applications](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#service-runtime-issues).

## For Helm services

A Helm chart creates its own Kubernetes Services, with names the chart decides. A public port of the Helm service must point to one of them, by its exact name (or its selectors) and the port it exposes. The name is often prefixed with the release name, so it differs from the short name in the chart values. List the Services with `kubectl get svc -n <environment-namespace>` (see [Connect to your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/connect-to-cluster)).

## Custom 404 page

The NGINX fallback page is the expected answer for unknown hosts. To serve your own page instead, the cluster advanced settings [`nginx.default_backend.enabled`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#nginx-default-backend-enabled), `nginx.default_backend.image_repository` and `nginx.default_backend.image_tag` let you run a custom default backend.

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# Image pull errors: 401 Unauthorized from ECR, 429 Too Many Requests from Docker Hub
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/image-pull-errors

> Fix builds and deployments that cannot pull an image: 401 Unauthorized from a private AWS ECR registry, and the Docker Hub pull rate limit (429 toomanyrequests).

This page covers the two most common errors when Qovery pulls a container image, either for the `FROM` line of your Dockerfile during the build, or for a service deployed from a container registry.

## 401 Unauthorized from a private ECR registry

```text
ERROR: unexpected status from HEAD request to https://123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v2/my-base-image/manifests/1.2.3: 401 Unauthorized
```

### Cause

Qovery tried to read an image from a private registry without valid credentials for it. It happens most often when the `FROM` line of a Dockerfile points to a private ECR repository: the build only logs in to the registries declared in your organization, so a registry that is not declared is pulled anonymously and refused.

### Fix

<Steps>
  <Step title="Declare the registry in your organization">
    Go to **Organization Settings**, then **Container Registries**, and click **Add Registry**. Choose **ECR** and set the registry URL to the host used in your image reference, with the protocol:

    ```text
    https://123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
    ```

    The account ID and the region must be the ones of the repository, not of your cluster. During the build, Qovery logs in to the registries of your organization that your Dockerfile uses, so the `FROM` line can pull from it.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Give the credentials read access">
    Use **Assume role via STS** (recommended) or static access keys. Either way, the identity needs `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` on `*` and the read actions (`ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer`, `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`) on the repositories. The full policy is in [AWS ECR with STS assume role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/container-registry#aws-ecr-with-sts-assume-role).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Cross-account repositories">
    If the repository is in another AWS account than the role or the access keys, the IAM policy is not enough: the policy of each repository must also allow that role or user for the same actions.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Check the external ID condition">
    With STS, if the trust policy of the role has an `sts:ExternalId` condition, it must list the Qovery ID of the registry and the all-zeros value `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`. Without the registry ID, every deployment that pulls from this registry fails, even though the Console can validate the registry. Without the all-zeros value, the Console cannot validate the registry or list your images. See [Trust policy](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/container-registry#trust-policy).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Deploy again">
    The deployment logs show a login to the registry before the build pulls the image.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The same steps apply to any private registry (GCP Artifact Registry, ACR, GitHub, GitLab, a generic registry): declare it under **Container Registries** with the URL used in the image reference, and give the credentials read access.

## 429 Too Many Requests from Docker Hub

```text
429 Too Many Requests - Server message: toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. You may increase the limit by authenticating and upgrading: https://www.docker.com/increase-rate-limit
```

### Cause

Docker Hub limits anonymous pulls per source IP address. Your builds and nodes reach the internet through a small number of IP addresses (the NAT gateways of the cluster, for example), so all your services share one anonymous quota. Busy days, many services using public base images such as `node` or `python`, or preview environments, use it up quickly. The limit can also be reached by other traffic from the same IP addresses.

### Fix

Authenticate to Docker Hub so that pulls count against your own account:

1. Create a Docker Hub access token (Docker Hub **Account Settings**, then **Security**, then **New Access Token**).
2. In Qovery, go to **Organization Settings**, then **Container Registries**, click **Add Registry**, choose **Docker Hub**, and enter your Docker Hub username and the token. See [Docker Hub](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/container-registries/docker-hub).
3. Deploy again. Builds log in to Docker Hub before pulling the `FROM` images. Services deployed from a Docker Hub image must use this registry.

A paid Docker Hub plan raises the limit further. See [Docker Hub usage and limits](https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/usage/).

Other ways to stop depending on Docker Hub limits:

- Pull official images from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery mirror, for example `FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/node:20` instead of `FROM node:20`.
- Copy the base images you use to your own registry and reference them from there.

<Info>
On Qovery-managed EKS clusters that use Karpenter, the cluster advanced setting [`aws.ecr.enable_pull_through_cache`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings#aws-ecr-enable-pull-through-cache) caches the public ECR images used by Qovery components. It does not cache your own images or Docker Hub images.
</Info>

## Related

- [Image mirroring](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring): how Qovery copies the image of each service to the registry of the cluster before deploying it.
- [Container registries](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/container-registry)

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# BackoffLimitExceeded: Job has reached the specified backoff limit
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/job-backoff-limit-exceeded

> A Qovery cron job or lifecycle job fails with BackoffLimitExceeded, often with no error in the logs. Find why the container exited and set the number of restarts and max duration.

A cron job or a lifecycle job is marked as failed, and its events or deployment logs show:

```text
BackoffLimitExceeded: Job has reached the specified backoff limit
```

Sometimes the job logs show nothing wrong, or nothing at all.

## What the error means

Qovery runs cron jobs and lifecycle jobs as Kubernetes Jobs. Each time the container of the job exits with a non-zero code, or is killed, Kubernetes counts one failure. When the number of failures goes above the backoff limit, Kubernetes stops retrying and marks the Job as failed with `BackoffLimitExceeded`.

The backoff limit is the **Number of restarts** of the job in Qovery (`max_nb_restart` in the API). Its default is `0`: a single failed run fails the job.

`BackoffLimitExceeded` is only the final status. The real error is the reason the container stopped, so look for that.

## Find why the container stopped

<Steps>
  <Step title="Read the job logs">
    Open the job in the Console and go to **Logs**. Look at the last lines before the end of the run: an exception, a stack trace, `Killed`, or an exit message. Logs are kept for a limited time, so check a failed run soon after it happens.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Check the exit code">
    If the logs are empty or end abruptly, connect to the cluster (see [Connect to your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/connect-to-cluster)) and inspect the pod of the failed run:

    ```bash
    kubectl get pods -n <environment-namespace>
    kubectl describe pod <job-pod-name> -n <environment-namespace>
    ```

    Look under `State` for the container that ran, or under `Last State` if it restarted. `Reason: OOMKilled` means the job ran out of memory. `Exit Code: 137` alone is only a hint: it means the container received `SIGKILL`, which also happens when the job is stopped from outside or reaches its maximum duration. Another non-zero exit code comes from your program. A command that cannot be found usually gives `Exit Code: 127` or a `StartError`.

    By default only the last failed run of a cron job is kept ([`cronjob.failed_jobs_history_limit`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#cronjob-failed-jobs-history-limit) is `1`). Raise it to keep more failed runs to inspect.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Common causes and fixes

### The command is wrong

The job starts, the command fails at once, and nothing useful is printed. This is the most frequent cause when there is no log at all.

In the job **Settings**, Qovery has two fields: **Entrypoint**, which replaces the `ENTRYPOINT` of the image, and **CMD Arguments**, which are passed to it. Putting the full command in **Entrypoint** when the image already has an entrypoint (or the reverse) runs something other than what you expect. Check them against the image:

- Leave **Entrypoint** empty to keep the entrypoint of the image, and put your command in **CMD Arguments** as a JSON array, for example `["npm", "run", "report"]`.
- To run a shell command, set **Entrypoint** to `/bin/sh` and **CMD Arguments** to `["-c", "./run.sh && echo done"]`.

Run the same command locally with `docker run <image> <arguments>` to confirm it works.

### The job ran out of memory

`Reason: OOMKilled` means the container used more memory than its limit. Exit code `137` without that reason can have another cause, as described above. Raise the memory of the job in its **Resources** settings, or process the data in smaller batches.

### The job ran longer than its max duration

When a run takes longer than the **Max Duration** of the job (`max_duration_seconds` in the API), Kubernetes stops it and the run counts as failed. Raise **Max Duration** in the job settings, or make the job do less per run.

### The job fails sometimes and should retry

For jobs that call external systems that can fail for a moment, set **Number of restarts** above `0` so Kubernetes retries a failed run before giving up. Make sure the job is safe to run twice.

### Two runs overlap

If a run is still going when the next schedule starts, [`cronjob.concurrency_policy`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#cronjob-concurrency-policy) decides what happens. With `Replace`, the running job is stopped. Keep the default `Forbidden` unless your job is built for it.

## Make failures visible

A job that fails without logs is hard to fix the next time. Make your job:

- log a line when it starts and when it ends, with the outcome,
- catch errors at the top level, log them, and exit with a non-zero code,
- report the failure to the tool your team already watches (error tracker, chat, monitoring).

See also [Lifecycle Jobs and Cronjobs execution failed](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#service-deployment-issues), [Cron jobs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cronjob) and [Lifecycle jobs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/lifecycle-job).

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu. No preemption victims found
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/insufficient-cpu

> Pods stay Pending with Insufficient cpu or Insufficient memory on Qovery. Learn how Kubernetes places pods on nodes, then size your services and node pools to fit.

A deployment fails or hangs, and the deployment logs show a scheduling error like this one, sometimes repeated many times (`x44`):

```text
0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu. preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```

The same message exists with `Insufficient memory`, and with more nodes (`0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory`).

## What the error means

Kubernetes could not find a node with enough free CPU (or memory) for the new pod, and it found no lower-priority pod it could evict to make room. The pod stays `Pending` until room appears. If none appears before the deployment times out, the deployment fails.

To fix it, you need to know how Kubernetes counts resources.

## How CPU and memory are allocated

- **Requests, not usage.** Each pod reserves the vCPU and memory set in the **Resources** settings of its service. Kubernetes places pods by adding up these reservations, not by looking at real usage. A node at 10% CPU usage can still be full.
- **A pod must fit on one node.** Resources are not pooled across nodes. A cluster of three nodes with 2 vCPU each cannot run a pod that asks for 3 vCPU.
- **Part of each node is reserved.** The operating system, the kubelet and the system pods (ingress, logging, metrics, DNS) take some CPU and memory on every node. What remains for your pods, the allocatable capacity, is lower than the instance size. On a small instance with 2 vCPU and 4 GiB, plan for about 1.5 to 1.9 vCPU and around 3 GiB for your own services.
- **Every instance counts.** A service with 3 instances of 1 vCPU reserves 3 vCPU, on one or more nodes. During a rolling deployment, new pods start before old ones stop, so the service needs room for extra pods for a while.
- **Instance size matters per dimension.** Changing to an instance with more memory but the same number of vCPU does not help with `Insufficient cpu`. For example, `t3a.medium` and `t3a.large` both have 2 vCPU.

<Info>
An environment is not a node. All the services of an environment run in one Kubernetes namespace of the cluster, and their pods are spread over the nodes of the cluster.
</Info>

## See what is reserved

- In the Console, open the cluster and go to the **Workloads** tab. It shows the CPU and memory requested per environment and per service, against the capacity of the cluster. See [Workloads](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#workloads).
- With kubectl (see [Connect to your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/connect-to-cluster)), check the allocatable capacity and the requests of a node:

  ```bash
  kubectl describe node <node-name>
  ```

  The `Allocatable` section gives what pods can use, and `Allocated resources` gives what is already reserved.

## Fix

Pick the option that matches what you found.

### Lower the requests of your services

Services often ask for more than they use. Open the service **Settings**, then **Resources**, and reduce **vCPU** or **Memory** to what the service needs, with some headroom, then redeploy. Compare with real usage in the monitoring of the service first.

### Give the cluster more room

On AWS clusters with Karpenter, Karpenter adds nodes when pods are pending. If it does not:

- The pod may be larger than the biggest instance type allowed. Check the **Instance types** of the node pools in the cluster settings, and allow larger sizes. See [Settings for node pools](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/eks/managed#resources).
- The node pool may have reached its **Node pool limits** for CPU or memory. Raise them.

On clusters with a fixed node range (GKE, AKS, Scaleway Kapsule, or AWS without Karpenter), raise the maximum number of nodes in the cluster settings, or pick an instance type with more vCPU or memory, then update the cluster.

### Run more, smaller instances

A service that needs 2 vCPU in one pod needs a node with at least 2 vCPU of allocatable capacity free. Two instances of 1 vCPU fit in more places. With autoscaling, set a minimum and a maximum number of instances so the service grows with the load instead of reserving its peak all the time. See [Instances and autoscaling](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#instances-%26-autoscaling).

## Cluster updates fail for the same reason

A cluster update also needs free room: Qovery components are upgraded one by one, and their new pods must be scheduled while the old ones still run. On a cluster that is full and cannot add nodes, the update can fail with a Helm timeout, for example `Helm timed out for release vertical-pod-autoscaler`. Allow more nodes, then update the cluster again. See [Helm upgrade failed: context deadline exceeded](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/helm-timed-out).

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# Deployment stuck on Queued
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/deployment-stuck-queued

> A Qovery deployment stays in the Queued status and never starts building. Find what it waits for in the deployment history, cancel what blocks it, and avoid long queues.

You deploy a service, and its deployment status stays on:

```text
QUEUED
```

for a long time, without moving to `BUILDING` or `DEPLOYING`. Deploying again does not help.

## What Queued means

`QUEUED` means the deployment request is accepted and waits for its turn. Qovery processes one deployment action at a time per environment. A new request waits while another deployment of the same environment is running, and starts when that one ends. See [Queueing and merging](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/actions#queueing-and-merging).

So a deployment that stays queued is almost always waiting for another one: a long build, a deployment stuck on a step, or a chain of requests in front of it.

## Find what the deployment waits for

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the deployment history">
    Open the environment and go to its **Deployments** tab. See [Deployment History](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/history). Look for a deployment in progress above your queued one, and for other queued requests.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Check the running deployment">
    Open the logs of the running deployment. A build that takes very long, a service that never becomes healthy, or a Helm release that waits for its pods will hold the queue until it finishes or times out.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Count the queued requests">
    With auto-deploy, each push to the branch creates a deployment request. Many pushes in a short time, with long builds, create a queue. Requests from the same user with the same action are merged, but requests from different users or actions are not.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Unblock the queue

Cancel the deployment that blocks the queue, or the queued requests you no longer need. In the deployment history, click the cancel icon next to the deployment. Deployments in **Queued** or **In Progress** status can be cancelled.

From the CLI, after selecting the organization and project with `qovery context set` (or with `--organization` and `--project`):

```bash
qovery environment cancel --environment "<environment-name>" --watch
```

To force the cancellation, add `--force`. With the API, call `POST /environment/{environmentId}/cancelDeployment`.

Once the queue is empty, deploy the service again. Cancelling a deployment in the middle can leave some services partly updated, so redeploy the environment if several services were involved.

<Warning>
For lifecycle jobs, the Console asks you to confirm a forced cancellation, because the job may already have made changes (for example a database migration).
</Warning>

## Avoid long queues

- Fix the deployment that blocks: a service that fails its health checks keeps the deployment running until the timeout. See [Health checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-health-checks).
- Make builds faster so each deployment holds the queue for less time. Build parallelism and resources are described in [Deployment pipeline](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/pipeline).
- Use [deployment restrictions](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#deployment-restrictions) on file paths so that a push only deploys the services it changes.
- If you push often to the same branch, deploy from a branch that receives merged changes, not every commit.

If a deployment stays queued while the deployment history shows nothing running, contact support with the environment URL: the request may be stuck on the Qovery side.

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# Helm upgrade failed: context deadline exceeded
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/helm-timed-out

> A cluster update or a Helm service fails with Helm timed out, UPGRADE FAILED or context deadline exceeded. Find the resource that never became ready, then fix it or raise the timeout.

A cluster update or the deployment of a Helm service fails with an error like:

```text
Helm timed out for release vertical-pod-autoscaler during helm UPGRADE: Error: UPGRADE FAILED: an error occurred while rolling back the release. original upgrade error: context deadline exceeded
```

For your own charts, the release name is the one of your Helm service, and the error can also read `INSTALL FAILED` or `timed out waiting for the condition`.

## What the error means

Helm installed or upgraded the release, then waited for its pods and jobs to become ready. They did not become ready before the timeout, so Helm stopped and rolled the release back. The timeout is the symptom: the cause is a pod that could not be scheduled, could not start, or never passed its readiness check.

## During a cluster update

When the release is a Qovery component (for example `vertical-pod-autoscaler`, `ingress-nginx`, `cert-manager`), the cluster update could not start the new version of that component. The most common reason is a full cluster: the new pods cannot be scheduled because no node has room, and the cluster cannot add nodes.

1. Open the cluster **Logs** and look, a few lines before the timeout, for a scheduling message such as `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory`.
2. Give the cluster room: raise the maximum number of nodes, allow larger instance types, or raise the node pool limits. See [Insufficient cpu or memory](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/insufficient-cpu).
3. Update the cluster again.

A cluster with a fixed number of nodes (same minimum and maximum) cannot add a node during the update. If its nodes are full, the extra pods the update needs have no room. Allow at least one more node than you run day to day.

## During the deployment of a Helm service

<Steps>
  <Step title="Find the resource that is not ready">
    Connect to the cluster (see [Connect to your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/connect-to-cluster)) and watch the namespace of the environment while you deploy:

    ```bash
    kubectl get pods -n <environment-namespace> --watch
    kubectl get events -n <environment-namespace> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
    ```

    A pod in `Pending` cannot be scheduled. A pod in `ImagePullBackOff` cannot pull its image. A pod in `CrashLoopBackOff` starts and crashes: read its logs with `kubectl logs <pod> -n <namespace> --previous`. A pod `Running` but not `Ready` fails its readiness probe.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Check the values">
    Every `qovery.env.<NAME>` in your values override must match a variable available to the Helm service, with the same case. A value that is not replaced, or a chart key with a typo, often leaves a pod unable to connect to its database. See [Environment variables in values](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/helm#environment-variables-in-values).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Raise the timeout if the chart is slow">
    Some charts need more time on first install, for example to create CRDs or run database migrations. Raise the timeout of the Helm service in its general settings (default 300 seconds), or add a Helm argument such as `--timeout 15m0s` in the **Arguments** field. See [Helm](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/helm).
  </Step>
</Steps>

### Charts that wait for their own hooks (Apache Airflow)

Some charts run a job as a Helm hook, for example database migrations, and start pods that wait for that job to finish. If Helm waits for those pods to be ready before it runs the hook, neither side can progress, and the release times out however long the timeout is.

The Apache Airflow chart is the most common case: its pods wait in `wait-for-airflow-migrations` and the migration job never starts. Turn off Helm hooks for its jobs in your values override, so they run as normal jobs:

```yaml
createUserJob:
  useHelmHooks: false
  applyCustomEnv: false
migrateDatabaseJob:
  useHelmHooks: false
  applyCustomEnv: false
```

Check the documentation of your chart for an equivalent option.

### The chart deploys, but the Console shows it as not running

Qovery finds the pods of a Helm service through its labels and annotations. If your chart does not set them, the deployment can succeed while the Console shows no pods and no logs. Add the `qovery.labels.service` and `qovery.annotations.service` macros to the templates of your chart. See [Helm service logging limitations](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/overview#service-runtime-issues).

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# VpcLimitExceeded: The maximum number of VPCs has been reached
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/vpc-limit-exceeded

> Creating an AWS cluster on Qovery fails because the region has reached its VPC quota. Raise the quota, delete unused VPCs, or deploy the cluster on an existing VPC.

Creating a cluster on AWS fails, and the cluster logs show:

```text
Error: creating EC2 VPC: operation error EC2: CreateVpc, https response error StatusCode: 400, api error VpcLimitExceeded: The maximum number of VPCs has been reached.
```

The preflight report of the cluster can also show `[FAIL] VPC quota`.

## Cause

By default, a cluster managed by Qovery gets its own VPC. AWS limits the number of VPCs per region and per account, with a default quota of 5. When the region already holds as many VPCs as the quota allows, AWS refuses to create one more. The default VPC of the region counts too, as do VPCs left behind by deleted clusters or other tools.

## Fix

Pick one of the three options.

### Raise the VPC quota

1. Open the [AWS Service Quotas console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/servicequotas/) in the region of the cluster.
2. Go to **Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC)**, then **VPCs per Region**.
3. Request a higher value. Small increases are often approved automatically within minutes.
4. Deploy the cluster again from the Qovery Console.

### Delete unused VPCs

In the AWS VPC console, list the VPCs of the region and delete the ones nothing uses any more. Check first that a VPC has no running instances, load balancers, NAT gateways or databases. VPCs created by Qovery for deleted clusters carry the tags described in [AWS account cleanup](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#aws-account-cleanup).

### Deploy the cluster on an existing VPC

When you create the cluster, choose **Deploy on my existing VPC** in the network settings and give the VPC ID and the subnet IDs. Qovery then creates no new VPC. The VPC must have DNS hostnames enabled and the subnets must carry the tags Qovery needs. See [Use your existing VPC](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/eks/managed#use-your-existing-vpc) and the [VPC configuration checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/eks/preflight-checks#vpc-configuration-checks-custom-vpc-mode-only).

<Info>
The existing VPC option is set when the cluster is created and cannot be changed afterwards.
</Info>

## Check quotas before you create a cluster

Qovery runs [preflight checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/eks/preflight-checks) before it creates an AWS cluster, including the VPC, Elastic IP and EKS quotas of the region. Add the `servicequotas:GetServiceQuota` permission to the IAM policy used by Qovery so the checks read your real quotas instead of the AWS defaults.

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# Environment variable is undefined in a React, Vite or Next.js frontend
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/frontend-env-vars-undefined

> process.env.REACT_APP_API_URL is undefined in the browser after deploying on Qovery. Frontend variables are read at build time: declare them as Dockerfile build arguments.

You set a variable such as `REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL` in Qovery, but in the browser your frontend reads:

```text
undefined
```

or calls a wrong URL, such as the backend host name appended to the frontend URL (`https://frontend.example.com/backend.example.com/api`).

## Cause

The code of a React (Create React App), Vite or Next.js frontend that runs in the browser does not run in your container. Its build tool replaces `process.env.REACT_APP_*`, `import.meta.env.VITE_*` or `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_*` with fixed values when you run `npm run build`. After that, the files served to the browser no longer read any environment variable.

Qovery injects your variables into the running container, which is too late for these frameworks. A variable reaches the build only if the Dockerfile declares it. See [Build-time variables](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#build-time-variables).

## Fix

<Steps>
  <Step title="Declare the variable as a build argument">
    In the build stage of your Dockerfile, add an `ARG` with the same name as the Qovery variable, before the build command:

    ```dockerfile
    FROM node:20 AS build
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY package*.json ./
    RUN npm ci
    COPY . .

    ARG REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL
    RUN npm run build

    FROM nginx:alpine
    COPY --from=build /app/build /usr/share/nginx/html
    ```

    In a multi-stage Dockerfile, declare the `ARG` in the stage that runs the build. An `ARG` declared in another stage is not visible there.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create the variable in Qovery">
    Create `REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL` on the frontend service, or at environment level. To point at another service of the environment, create an [alias](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases) on the built-in variable of the backend that ends in `_HOST_EXTERNAL`, named the way your frontend expects. The browser cannot reach the `_HOST_INTERNAL` host; see [Use the public host name of the backend](#use-the-public-host-name-of-the-backend).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add the protocol">
    The built-in host variables hold a host name only, without `https://`. Used as is, the browser treats the value as a relative path, which gives URLs like `https://frontend.example.com/backend.example.com`. Add the protocol where you build the URL:

    ```js
    const apiUrl = `https://${process.env.REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL}`;
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Redeploy the frontend">
    Changing the value of a variable declared as an `ARG` changes the image tag, so Qovery builds the frontend again with the new value.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Use the public host name of the backend

The browser calls your backend over the internet, so it needs the public host name of the backend, not its internal one. Use the variable ending in `_HOST_EXTERNAL`, which exists only when the backend has a publicly accessible port. A value ending in `_HOST_INTERNAL` only resolves inside the cluster. See [Linking services together](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/linking-services).

If the backend uses a custom domain, set the variable to that domain instead.

<Warning>
Build arguments are written into the image and into the JavaScript files sent to every visitor. Never pass secrets to a frontend this way. Keep API keys and tokens on the backend.
</Warning>

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# Datadog on Qovery: service tags, log annotations and uninstalling the agent
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/troubleshoot/datadog

> Find Qovery services by name in Datadog, fix Datadog autodiscovery annotations that break a deployment, and remove the Datadog agent from a cluster.

This page covers three questions that come up once the Datadog agent runs on a Qovery cluster. To install the agent, follow [Datadog](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/observability/datadog) first.

## Services show up as app-z1234abcd in Datadog

In Datadog, `kube_service`, `container_name` and similar tags carry the Kubernetes names Qovery generates, such as `app-z1a2b3c4d`, not the names you gave your services. Dashboards are hard to read, and filtering by team or environment is not possible.

### Fix: add Unified Service Tagging labels

Attach the Datadog standard labels to your services with [Labels & Annotations](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/labels-annotations):

1. Go to **Organization Settings**, then **Labels & Annotations**, and add a label group with:

   | Label | Example value |
   |---|---|
   | `tags.datadoghq.com/service` | `checkout-api` |
   | `tags.datadoghq.com/env` | `production` |
   | `tags.datadoghq.com/version` | `1.4.2` |

   Add your own labels too, for example `team: payments`.
2. Assign the label group to the service.
3. Redeploy the service. Labels are applied at deployment.

Datadog then sets the `service`, `env` and `version` tags on the metrics, logs and traces of the service. See [Unified Service Tagging](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/observability/datadog#unified-service-tagging).

Label groups apply to applications, cron jobs, lifecycle jobs and databases. For a Helm service, set the labels in the values of the chart.

### Alternative: turn environment variables into tags

The Datadog agent can also copy environment variables of a container into tags. This was the usual workaround before labels were available, and it still works. In the values of your Datadog Helm service:

```yaml
agents:
  useConfigMap: true
  customAgentConfig:
    container_env_as_tags:
      SERVICE_DISPLAY_NAME: "service_name"
      TEAM: "team"
```

Create the `SERVICE_DISPLAY_NAME` and `TEAM` variables on your services, redeploy them, then redeploy the Datadog service. These tags are attached to containers, not to pods, so pod-level views in Datadog do not show them.

## Logs are missing or the deployment fails after adding a Datadog log annotation

You added a Datadog autodiscovery annotation to a service, for example:

```text
ad.datadoghq.com/my-container.logs: [{"source": "nodejs", "service": "checkout-api"}]
```

and Datadog does not collect the logs as configured, or the service no longer deploys.

### Logs are missing or untagged

The Datadog agent reads the annotation after the pod starts. A mistake in it changes what the agent collects, not how the pod is scheduled or becomes ready. Check these points in the annotation group:

- **The key names the container.** The part between `ad.datadoghq.com/` and `.logs` must be the name of the container in the pod, not the name of the service in Qovery. Get it with `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'`.
- **The value is valid JSON.** It must be a JSON array, with double quotes around every key and string. A trailing comma or single quotes make it invalid.
- **The scope is right.** Datadog reads autodiscovery annotations on pods. Set the scope of the annotation group to pods.

Then redeploy the service. See [Datadog Autodiscovery Annotations](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/observability/datadog#datadog-autodiscovery-annotations).

### The deployment fails

The agent does not take part in the rollout, so look for the cause in the deployment itself. Open the deployment logs and the Kubernetes events of the service, and read the first error line. If it mentions the annotation, Kubernetes rejected its key: a key is an optional prefix, a `/`, and a name of at most 63 characters made of letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`.

## Uninstall the Datadog agent

How you remove the agent depends on how it was installed.

**Installed as a Qovery Helm service** (the method in the [Datadog guide](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/observability/datadog)): stop the Datadog Helm service, then delete it (three-dot menu, **Remove helm**). Deleting a Helm service removes all the Kubernetes resources created by the chart. From the CLI: `qovery helm stop -n <datadog-service> --watch`, then `qovery helm delete -n <datadog-service> --watch`. These commands use the organization, project and environment selected with `qovery context set`; run it first, or add `--organization`, `--project` and `--environment`. See [Delete a Helm service](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/helm#delete-service).

**Installed by hand with Helm or kubectl:** connect to the cluster (see [Connect to your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/connect-to-cluster)) and remove it the same way:

```bash
# Find the release and its namespace
helm list --all-namespaces | grep -i datadog

# Uninstall it
helm uninstall <release-name> -n <namespace>
```

If the release is gone but agent pods remain, and the namespace contains nothing else, delete the namespace:

```bash
kubectl delete namespace <datadog-namespace>
```

After removing the agent, remove the Datadog labels and annotations you no longer need, and the `DD_*` variables of your services, then redeploy them.

## Still stuck?

Contact Qovery support from the Console: click the help button at the bottom right, then **Contact Support**. You can also post in your dedicated Slack channel. Include the Console URL of the service, the deployment ID or the time of the error, and the error line from the logs. See [Help and Support](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support).

# FAQ
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/faq

> Answers to common questions about projects and environments, databases, Git providers, cluster access, Kubernetes upgrades and how Qovery works.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the difference between a Project, an Application, and an Environment?">
    A **project** is the site that you're working on. Each project can contain multiple **applications** and be deployed in multiple **environments**. An environment is a standalone copy of your site, including apps, databases, storage, data, and all other services. By default, `main` branch is the production environment, while all other branches can be set up as identical copies of the prod environment for testing purposes.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How does Qovery manage databases?">
    Databases created from the Console run in `container` mode, directly on your Kubernetes cluster. They are well suited for development and testing. For production, provision a cloud provider managed database with a [Blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints): e.g. on AWS, the **Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL** blueprint provides an [AWS RDS](https://aws.amazon.com/rds) instance. Existing databases in `managed` mode keep working. Please check out our [database section](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/database) for further details.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Qovery replace Kubernetes?">
    Behind the scene, Qovery uses [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/). Qovery extends Kubernetes to make it accessible to any developer teams.

    **Important**: Qovery does not modify Kubernetes. It only deploys his services in a `qovery` Kubernetes namespace.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Qovery support mono repository?">
    Yes, absolutely! Check out our monorepo guide.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Qovery support microservices?">
    Yes, absolutely! Check out our microservices guide.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What Git providers do you support?">
    GitHub, GitLab, BitBucket.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do you support GitHub Enterprise or Gitlab Self-hosted?">
    Not at the moment, but you can upvote for this feature in [our roadmap](https://roadmap.qovery.com/roadmap).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Qovery support private Git repository?">
    Yes, absolutely!
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which IP address does my cluster use to communicate externally over the Internet?">
    There isn't just one public cluster IP address dedicated to external communication. However, worker nodes inside your cluster each have a public IP automatically attached to them. You can view those default public IPs in the details of your worker nodes (EC2 instances for AWS users) which belong to the node group in your cluster.

    For improved security and control, the `Static IP` feature allows you to ensure that outbound traffic from your cluster uses specific IP addresses. For more information on the `Static IP` feature and how to enable it at cluster creation, see [Static IP on EKS](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/eks/managed#static-ip) or [Static IP on GKE](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/gke/managed#static-ip). GKE clusters can enable stable Cloud NAT IPs through the NAT Gateway feature's `staticIpsEnabled` option.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="If I have N custom domains under the same root domain, do I need to create N CNAME records, or just creating one for the root domain is enough?">
    You have to create N CNAME, one per custom domain.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do you support new Kubernetes version?">
    The Qovery team manages your Kubernetes cluster's upgrade, and you don't have to think about it. Upgrades from one minor Kubernetes version to another require a good amount of tests to make sure everything goes smoothly with zero interruptions for your app. This is why Qovery always provides 1 or 2 minor versions below the last one offered by the cloud provider. Our goal is to guarantee you the maximum uptime.

    More details on this dedicated section: [how does Qovery handle Kubernetes version upgrades](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#faq).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I upgrade my cluster myself?">
    NO and you SHOULDN'T!

    More details on this dedicated section: [how does Qovery handle Kubernetes version upgrades](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#faq).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I have access to my Kubernetes cluster?">
    Absolutely, you can follow this guide to connect to your cluster with kubectl.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I have access to my application with a shell?">
    Absolutely, you can connect directly to your application with a shell by clicking on the Qovery cloud shell button:

    <img src="/images/qovery_cloud_shell.png" alt="Qovery Cloud Shell" />

    Then you just have to select the pod and the container.

    You can also check out our [CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/shell) and the `qovery shell` command.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How application auto-scaling works?">
    Take a look at [our application documentation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/application#instances-%26-autoscaling).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why you should use Qovery?">
    ### The power of Kubernetes
    Under the hood, Qovery uses **containers** and **Kubernetes** to run applications. With us, your applications scale accordingly to your traffic and needs. We rely on major cloud providers to provide reliable infrastructure to make your applications highly available.

    ### Reliable infrastructure
    What's more, we took on our shoulders the complexity of providing and managing other infrastructure requirements you need (like databases or message brokers), so you can focus merely on developing business features.

    ### Simple and Powerful
    With Qovery, the cloud is simple again. Get all the benefits of using cloud and Kubernetes without dealing with its complexity. You don't need to hire infrastructure experts - configuring continuous integration, deployment, databases, message brokers, storage, DNS, SSL/TLS, VPCs, and many others - we do it all for you. On Qovery, you can spin up a set of microservices, databases, and other cloud services in minutes with a single Git push!

    ### Built for all developers
    Qovery is designed by developers for developers. Our goal is to make your life easier and allow you to move faster. Developer experience is at our heart. Building cloud-native applications was never that fast and simple!

    ### Fully customizable for advanced business use cases
    Create teams, split responsibilities, manage privileges, enforce company-wide rules, deploy to multiple clouds, plug in your own CI solutions. Qovery Business allows you to bring your organization to the next level with ease.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How Qovery works under the hood?">
    [Here](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/basic-concepts) is a detailed explanation on how Qovery works under the hood.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How can I contact you?">
    Contact us by email at hello (at) qovery.com or via Pylon directly in the Qovery console (existing customers).
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Help and Support
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/useful-resources/help-and-support

> Get help from the AI Copilot, contact Qovery support through Pylon in the Console or your Slack channel, and read the shared responsibility model.

## Qovery support

If you need any help, you can:

1. Check the [troubleshooting section](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/logs) for common issues and solutions.
2. Use the **AI Copilot** built into Qovery for instant assistance.
3. Contact support via **Pylon** within the console by clicking on the **help button** on the bottom right, then select **Contact Support**.
4. Reach out directly in your **dedicated Slack channel**.

There, you can discuss directly with our fantastic team as well as our wonderful community!

## Shared responsibility model

Qovery is responsible for deployed elements on your cloud provider made and maintained by Qovery. We are not responsible for the cloud provider itself nor for the applications you deploy via Qovery. While our support team is always here to help, please note that we may have limited ability to assist with issues that are fully managed by you or your cloud provider.

The following RACI Matrix clarifies who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed at each layer of the stack:

<div className="raci-legend">
  <div><strong className="role-r-text">R</strong> = Responsible (performs the work)</div>
  <div><strong className="role-a-text">A</strong> = Accountable (ultimately answerable)</div>
  <div><strong className="role-c-text">C</strong> = Consulted (provides input)</div>
  <div><strong className="role-i-text">I</strong> = Informed (kept up-to-date)</div>
</div>

# Configuration Overview
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/overview

## Configuration Hierarchy

Qovery uses a hierarchical structure to organize your infrastructure:

```mermaid
graph TB
    O[Organization] --> P[Projects]
    P --> E[Environments]
    E --> S[Services]
    S --> A[Applications]
    S --> D[Databases]
    S --> H[Helm Charts]
    S --> J[Jobs]
    S --> T[Terraform]
    E --> C[Clusters]

    style O fill:#642DFF,color:#fff
    style P fill:#7C3FFF,color:#fff
    style E fill:#965FFF,color:#fff
    style S fill:#B080FF,color:#fff
```

# User Account
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/user-account

> Manage your personal account settings and preferences

Your user account settings allow you to manage your personal information and communication preferences in Qovery.

## Accessing Your Account Settings

To access your user account settings:

1. Click on the **user icon** in the top right corner of the Qovery Console
2. Select **Profile settings** from the menu

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/configuration/user-account/access_user_account.png"
    alt="Access user account settings"
  />
</Frame>

## Theme

Qovery supports **light**, **dark**, and **system** themes. To switch, click your avatar in the top-right corner and select your preferred option under **Theme**:

- **System** — follows your OS/browser preference
- **Light** — always use the light theme
- **Dark** — always use the dark theme

## Account Information

### Name Fields

Your **first name** and **last name** are retrieved from your Git account and cannot be changed directly in Qovery.

<Info>
  To update your name, you need to modify it in your Git provider (GitHub,
  GitLab, or Bitbucket) settings.
</Info>

### Account Email

Your **account email** is sourced from your Git credentials and cannot be modified within Qovery. This email is used for authentication and account identification.

<Info>
  To change your account email, update it in your Git provider settings. The
  change will be reflected in Qovery after your next login.
</Info>

### Communication Email

The **communication email** is a customizable field where you designate your preferred contact address for product updates, announcements, and important notifications.

<Warning>
  Qovery uses your communication email to share important updates about the
  product. Please provide a valid, professional business email address that you
  check regularly.
</Warning>

**To update your communication email:**

1. Navigate to your user account settings
2. Locate the **Communication Email** field
3. Enter your preferred email address
4. Click **Save** to update

**Best practices:**

- Use a business email address
- Ensure the email is monitored regularly
- Don't use temporary or disposable email addresses
- Keep this email up-to-date to receive important notifications

### Timezone

Your **timezone** is automatically synced with your browser settings to display dates and times correctly throughout the Qovery Console.

This ensures that:

- Deployment times are shown in your local timezone
- Logs timestamps match your local time
- Scheduled tasks display correctly
- Activity history is accurately represented

<Tip>
  The timezone is automatically detected and updated based on your browser. No
  manual configuration is needed.
</Tip>

## Why Account Settings Matter

### Stay Informed

By maintaining accurate communication email settings, you'll receive:

- **Product updates** - New features and improvements
- **Service notifications** - Important system announcements
- **Security alerts** - Account and security-related updates
- **Best practices** - Tips and guides for using Qovery effectively

### Accurate Timestamps

Proper timezone configuration ensures:

- Deployment schedules align with your team's working hours
- Log analysis uses correct timestamps
- Collaboration across distributed teams is easier
- Audit trails are accurate

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I change my name?">
    Your name is synced from your Git provider (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket). To update it:

    1. Log into your Git provider
    2. Update your profile name
    3. Log out and back into Qovery
    4. Your updated name will be reflected

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I change my account email?">
    Your account email is tied to your Git provider authentication. To change it:

    1. Update your email in your Git provider settings
    2. Ensure the new email is verified
    3. Log out and back into Qovery
    4. The new email will be used for your account

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="I'm not receiving communication emails">
    If you're not receiving emails:

    1. Check your spam/junk folder
    2. Verify your communication email is correct
    3. Ensure your email server isn't blocking emails from Qovery
    4. Add Qovery's email domain to your safe senders list
    5. Contact support if the issue persists

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="My timezone is incorrect">
    The timezone is automatically detected from your browser. If it's incorrect:

    1. Check your computer's system timezone settings
    2. Ensure your browser has correct timezone settings
    3. Try clearing your browser cache
    4. Refresh the Qovery Console

    The timezone should update automatically when you refresh the page.

  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Organization
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization

> Create, switch and delete Qovery organizations, and manage billing and organization settings. Only the organization owner can delete it.

An organization is a shared account where developers can collaborate across many projects. Organization owners and admins can manage all aspects of the organization, from clusters to member access.

## Prerequisites

To follow this section, you must have [created an account](https://console.qovery.com/signup).

## Creating an Organization

### When Signing Up

When you sign up for Qovery, you will be asked to create your first organization and project. You will need to:

1. Sign in through your Git provider (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket), Google or Microsoft
2. Fill in your profile: full name, a work email (personal email domains are rejected), and company name. Submitting creates your organization and a first project automatically
3. Choose how to set up your first cluster: connect your own cloud account if you have cloud admin access, or set up a local demo cluster otherwise

You start on the Scale plan during your trial. For more information on available plans, visit the [pricing page](https://www.qovery.com/pricing).

Qovery also has a Free plan, with no time limit and no credit card: 3 users plus unlimited AI agents, 1 cluster of your own, and 1,000 deployment minutes a month with a hard stop: at the limit, new deployments pause until next month or until you upgrade, and Free never bills overage. It includes preview environments and environment cloning, with community support. See the [pricing page](https://www.qovery.com/pricing) for the current plans and limits.

### After Signing Up

You can create multiple organizations to separate concerns. To create a new organization:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Access Organization Menu">
    Click on your current organization dropdown menu in the header
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create New Organization">
    Click the `+` button in the bottom of the dropdown menu

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/organization/create_organization_after_signing_up.png" alt="Create organization after signing up" />
    </Frame>

  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Organization">
    Fill in the required information and select your plan
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Change an Organization

If you have access to multiple organizations, you can switch between them:

1. Locate the organization dropdown in the header
2. Click on the dropdown to see all available organizations
3. Select the organization you want to switch to

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/configuration/organization/change_organization.png"
    alt="Change organization"
  />
</Frame>

## Delete an Organization

<Warning>
  Deleting an organization is **irreversible**. All data associated with the
  organization will be permanently deleted.
</Warning>

To delete an organization:

1. Navigate to Organization Settings
2. Scroll to the "Danger Zone" section
3. Click "Delete Organization"
4. Confirm the deletion by typing the organization name

## Billing

Manage your organization's billing and subscription:

- **View Invoices**: Access all past and current invoices
- **Payment Methods**: Add or update credit cards and payment details
- **Subscription**: Upgrade or downgrade your plan
- **Usage**: Monitor resource usage and costs

During the trial, add a credit card to activate your organization on one of the **Starter**, **Growth**, or **Scale** plans, billed monthly once the trial ends. You can switch between these plans until the trial ends.

<Info>
When you create an organization or add a payment card, you must provide your billing details, including a billing address. A **VAT number** is required for billing addresses in EU countries and optional elsewhere. Postal codes are validated against the expected format for the selected country.
</Info>

For pricing details, visit the [pricing page](https://www.qovery.com/pricing).

### General Information

Configure basic organization details:

- **Company name**: Your organization's official name
- **Description**: Brief description of your organization
- **Website**: Your company website URL
- **Admin contact emails**: Enter one or multiple email addresses separated by commas

<Info>
  Admin contact emails are used for communications about infrastructure outages,
  maintenance updates, and weekly and monthly usage reports.
</Info>

Click **Update** to save your changes.

### Agent

<Info>
Agent Tasks is available to all organizations. Capabilities and configuration may evolve.
</Info>

The **Agent** section manages what's shared with every [Agent Task](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/agent-tasks/overview) in the organization: AI provider tokens under **Agent > Token**, and MCP servers under **Agent > MCP**.

**Token**: create and manage the AI provider tokens used by agent tasks. Qovery currently supports [Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/) (Anthropic), [AWS Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/), and Anthropic-compatible gateways as providers. See [Choose a Provider and Model](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/agent-tasks/overview#creating-an-agent) for the Anthropic-compatible Base URL and limits. A token created here, or created on the fly from an agent task's **Choose a Provider** step, is saved to this list and can be reused by any other agent task in the organization instead of re-entering credentials each time.

**MCP**: connect any remote HTTPS MCP server here (name, URL, and headers) to make it available when configuring an individual agent.

<Info>
Qovery's own MCP server is added here automatically, organization-scoped and read-only, as soon as any agent task adds a Qovery service as Context, see [Add MCP Servers](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/agent-tasks/overview#creating-an-agent). To add it yourself instead, for example with write access, use `https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp` and authenticate with an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) (a regular API token works too).
</Info>
