# Members & RBAC
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac

> Manage organization members and role-based access control

## Organization Members

You can invite someone to join your organization by email. Once they accept the invitation, they will have access to the organization and all its projects based on their assigned role.

### Accessing Members Settings

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open Organization Settings">
    Click the Settings tab while you are on your organization overview.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/organization/access_settings.png" alt="How to access your organization settings" />
    </Frame>

  </Step>

  <Step title="Navigate to Members Section">
    Open the **Members** section within the organization settings

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/organization/members.png" alt="Qovery - List all members within an organization" />
    </Frame>

  </Step>
</Steps>

### Inviting Members

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
1. Click the **Invite Member** button
2. Enter the member's email address
3. Select a role (see Default Roles below)
4. Click **Send Invitation**

The invited member will receive an email with instructions to join the organization.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="CLI and API">
    You need the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), signed in with `qovery auth`. The `qovery api` command sends authenticated requests to the [Qovery API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/introduction).

    Get the ID of the role to give, built-in or custom:

    ```bash
    ORGANIZATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"  # from qovery organization list --json

    qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/availableRole"
    ```

    Send the invitation with `POST /organization/{organizationId}/inviteMember`. `email` is required, and `role_id` sets the role:

    ```bash
    ROLE_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ROLE_ID"  # id of the role from the list above

    qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/inviteMember" \
      --field email=dev@example.com \
      --field role_id="$ROLE_ID"
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Terraform">
    Use the [`qovery_organization_member`](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/Qovery/qovery/latest/docs/resources/organization_member) resource. Terraform sends the invitation, and the invitee becomes a member once they accept it with the invited email address:

    ```hcl
    resource "qovery_organization_member" "dev" {
      organization_id = "<organizationId>"
      email           = "dev@example.com"
      role_id         = "<roleId>"
    }
    ```

    The read-only `invitation_status` attribute is `PENDING`, `EXPIRED` or `ACCEPTED`.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

#### Check it worked

List the pending invitations:

```bash
ORGANIZATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"  # from qovery organization list --json

qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/inviteMember"
```

The invitation appears with `invitation_status` set to `PENDING` and its `role_name`. Once the person accepts it, they appear in `GET /organization/{organizationId}/member` instead.

<Info>
  Each user can only hold **one** role at a time. Changing the role of a member requires the user to logout/login to make the changes effective or wait a few minutes (max 1 hour).
</Info>

## Default Roles

Qovery provides 5 built-in roles with predefined permissions that apply across the entire organization.

### Owner

Full access to the organization. Only one user can be the owner, and ownership can be transferred (see below).

### Admin

Same as Owner except cannot delete the organization or transfer ownership.

### DevOps

Can manage organization infrastructure (clusters, registries, webhooks, API tokens) and has full access to all projects and environments across the organization. Cannot manage members, roles, or billing.

### Billing Manager

Can manage billing only. Has read-only access to cluster information but no access to any project.

### Viewer

Read-only access to all organization resources, clusters, and projects.

## Default Roles - Permissions Matrix

| Action | Owner | Admin | DevOps | Billing Manager | Viewer |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Read organization data (registries, clusters, label groups) | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Edit organization settings | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| Delete organization | yes | no | no | no | no |
| Transfer ownership | yes | no | no | no | no |
| Manage billing | yes | yes | no | yes | no |
| Manage members & roles | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| Manage clusters & container registries | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Manage organization setup (API tokens, webhooks, SSO) | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Create project | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Read any project & environment | yes | yes | yes | no | yes |
| Deploy, manage, and configure any environment | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Open a shell and port-forward on any service | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| Read cluster info | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |

## Custom Roles

Custom roles let you grant access scoped to specific projects and clusters, instead of applying permissions across the entire organization. This is useful when you want to give a user access to only certain projects or restrict what they can do within a project.

To manage custom roles as code, use the [`qovery_custom_role`](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/Qovery/qovery/latest/docs/resources/custom_role) Terraform resource, or the `/organization/{organizationId}/customRole` API endpoints.

<Tip>
Giving an AI agent or a script access? A custom role applies to whole projects and environment types. To limit a token to exactly what it needs, for example deploying the staging environment and nothing else, use an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token).
</Tip>

### Scope and limitations

Custom roles are configured through **cluster-level** and **project-level** permissions only. They always inherit the ability to read organization data (registries, clusters, label groups).

**Custom roles cannot:**
- Generate API tokens
- Manage organization settings (webhooks, SSO)
- Manage members & roles
- Manage billing

<Info>
  If a user with a custom role needs to generate an API token (e.g. for the CLI or Terraform provider), an org admin or DevOps user must generate it for them.
</Info>

### Cluster Level Permissions

Set individually for each cluster. A cluster created after the role is configured starts with **Read-Only** access:

| Level | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| **Read-Only** | View cluster information (name, region, status). |
| **Create Environment** | Create and manage environments on this cluster. Cluster settings (nodes, instance type) remain read-only. |
| **Full Access** | Everything in Create Environment, plus manage cluster settings (start/stop, node scaling, configuration). |

### Project Level Permissions

Set per project, independently for each environment type (Development, Preview, Staging, Production):

| Level | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| **No Access** | No visibility or interaction with this environment type. |
| **Read-Only** | View environments, services, logs, and variables. No write access. |
| **Deploy** | Everything in Read-Only, plus trigger deployments and stop services. Cannot modify service configuration or environment variables. |
| **Manage** | Everything in Deploy, plus edit service configuration, manage environment variables and secrets, and create or delete services. |
| **Full Access** | Everything in Manage, plus delete environments and manage project-level settings. |

### Shell and Port-forward Permissions

Remote access to the running services is granted separately from the level, with two permissions set per project and per environment type:

| Permission | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| **Shell** | Open a shell on the services of this environment type, with [`qovery shell`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/shell) or from the **Cloud Shell** tab of a service in the console. |
| **Port-forward** | Forward a local port to the services of this environment type, with [`qovery port-forward`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/port-forward). |

- Both can be granted from **Read-Only** up, for example to let a user port-forward to a database without being able to deploy.
- Neither can be granted with **No Access**.
- **Full Access** on a project always includes both.
- They are independent: a role can deploy to Production without being able to open a shell there.

<Info>
  Custom roles created before these permissions existed have both enabled on every environment type where their level is Deploy or above, so their access did not change.
</Info>

When a permission is missing, the connection is refused.

### Custom roles vs built-in DevOps role

A custom role configured with Full Access on all clusters and Full Access on all projects covers the same day-to-day operations as the DevOps role, but with two differences: it cannot generate API tokens or manage org-level settings, and it can optionally be scoped to specific projects only.

| Capability | DevOps (built-in) | Custom role |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| Access to all projects & environments | yes | only if explicitly granted |
| Full cluster management | yes | only if explicitly granted |
| Read org data (registries, label groups) | yes | yes |
| Generate API tokens | yes | no |
| Manage org setup (webhooks, SSO) | yes | no |
| Manage members & roles | no | no |
| Manage billing | no | no |

### Example configurations

**Developer - access to a specific project**

A developer who should deploy and configure services in one project but have no visibility into other projects:

| Scope | Level |
| --- | --- |
| Cluster | Read-Only |
| Target project - Development | Manage |
| Target project - Preview | Manage |
| Target project - Staging | Read-Only |
| Target project - Production | No Access |
| Other projects | No Access |

**On-call engineer - deploy to any project, no config changes**

An engineer who needs to trigger deployments and read logs across all projects in an incident, but should not be able to modify service configuration:

| Scope | Level |
| --- | --- |
| All clusters | Read-Only |
| All projects - all environment types | Deploy |

**Deployer without shell access in production**

A developer who deploys to every environment type and can debug Production through port-forward, but cannot open a shell there:

| Scope | Level | Shell | Port-forward |
| --- | --- | :---: | :---: |
| Cluster | Read-Only | | |
| Target project - Development, Preview, Staging | Deploy | yes | yes |
| Target project - Production | Deploy | no | yes |

**Security auditor - read-only across everything**

A user who needs visibility into all environments for audit purposes:

| Scope | Level |
| --- | --- |
| All clusters | Read-Only |
| All projects - all environment types | Read-Only |

**Infrastructure-as-code operator - manage a specific environment**

A user running Terraform or similar tooling against a single environment (API token must be generated by an admin):

| Scope | Level |
| --- | --- |
| Cluster hosting the target environment | Create Environment |
| Target project - relevant environment type | Manage |
| Other environment types / projects | No Access |

## Transfer Ownership

You can transfer ownership of the organization to another member. To do so:

1. Navigate to the **Members** section in organization settings
2. Click on the member you want to transfer ownership to
3. Select **Transfer Ownership** from the menu
4. Confirm the transfer

With the API, call `POST /organization/{organizationId}/transferOwnership` with the `user_id` of the new owner: the `id` of the member in `GET /organization/{organizationId}/member`.

<Warning>
  Once ownership is transferred, you will no longer be the owner of the
  organization.
</Warning>

# SSO (SAML/OIDC)
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/sso

> Set up SAML or OIDC Single Sign-On between your Identity Provider and Qovery, configure the default role and group synchronization, and provision users.

Qovery allows you to configure a SAML or OIDC connection with your Identity Provider (IDP).

## How to Enable SSO

<Steps>
  <Step title="Contact Qovery">
    Contact your Customer Success Manager (CSM) to enable the SSO feature for your organization.

    - Qovery will provide you a unique `$CONNECTION_NAME` that you will need to configure your IDP
    - You will need to provide required information to setup the configuration on Qovery side
  </Step>

  <Step title="Validate Authentication Flow">
    When the configuration is done on your side and on Qovery side, we plan a session to validate the authentication flow.
  </Step>

  <Step title="User Provisioning">
    Once your users are provisioned using SAML or OIDC inside your organization, you will need to remove old users and transfer your organization ownership.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Configure Your IDP

<Info>
The following sections use Okta as IDP to illustrate the setup and information to share. The same principles apply to other Identity Providers.
</Info>

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="SAML">
    ### Configure Your SAML Application

    #### Create SAML Application

    Create your SAML application and check `SAML 2.0`:

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/create-app.png" alt="Create Okta Application" />
    </Frame>

    #### Qovery Authentication Information

    In **SAML Settings > General** section:

    - Set the **Single sign-on URL** to:
      ```
      https://auth.qovery.com/login/callback?connection=$CONNECTION_NAME
      ```

    - Enable the **Use this for Recipient URL and Destination URL** checkbox

    - Set the **Audience URI** to:
      ```
      urn:auth0:qovery:$CONNECTION_NAME
      ```

    Leave the other fields in this section at their default values.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/saml-settings.png" alt="SAML Settings" />
    </Frame>

    #### Configure Attribute Statements

    In **Attribute Statements** section:

    - Add attribute `email` to point to your user email property (e.g., `user.email` in Okta)
    - Add attribute `name` to point to your user full name property (e.g., `user.displayName` in Okta)

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/user-attributes.png" alt="User Attributes" />
    </Frame>

    <Info>
    You may not see the "user.displayName" populated in the Okta admin console. See this [Okta documentation](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/okta-display-name-and-group-rules?language=en_US) for more information.
    </Info>

    ##### Google SAML

    <Warning>
    **Google Workspace** does not expose a full name property. Instead of mapping the `name` attribute, you must map `firstName` and `lastName` to the **First name** and **Last name** fields in the Google Admin console attribute mapping. These two attributes are mandatory for Google SAML.
    </Warning>

    #### (Optional) Configure Group Attribute Statements

    If you want to automatically assign a Qovery role according to your users' groups (see [Configure Group Synchronization](#configure-group-synchronization)), you need to expose this information:

    - Add attribute `groups` to match the targeted IDP groups you want to expose
    - Use a regex to expose the groups you plan to use for role synchronization, i.e `.*Qovery.*`

    <Info>
    Okta recommends to [expose only group names used by the target Application](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/content/topics/apps/define-group-attribute-statements.htm?cshid=ext-define-group-attribute-statements).
    </Info>

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/group-attributes.png" alt="Group Attributes" />
    </Frame>

    #### (Optional) Enable Global Token Revocation

    In **Logout** section:

    - Set the **Endpoint URL** to:
      ```
      https://qovery.eu.auth0.com/oauth/global-token-revocation/connection/$CONNECTION_NAME
      ```
    - Set **Subject format** to "Issuer and Subject Identifier"

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/global-revocation.png" alt="Global Token Revocation" />
    </Frame>

    ### SAML Information To Share

    #### Required Information

    Go to **Sign On** tab and gather the following required information:

    - Sign on URL
    - Signing Certificate

    Go to **General** section, edit **SAML Settings** section, and click on **Preview the SAML Assertion**. This will generate an XML file that you will need to share.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/saml-assertion.png" alt="SAML Assertion" />
    </Frame>

    <Info>
    **Validate your XML**: You should see in the SAML Assertion XML file the fields that IDP will expose to Qovery inside `<saml2:AttributeStatement>`, for example:

    ```xml
    <saml2:AttributeStatement>
        <saml2:Attribute Name="email" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic">
            <saml2:AttributeValue
                xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
                xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">user@example.com
            </saml2:AttributeValue>
        </saml2:Attribute>
        <saml2:Attribute Name="name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic">
            <saml2:AttributeValue
                xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
                xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">Foo Bar
            </saml2:AttributeValue>
        </saml2:Attribute>
    </saml2:AttributeStatement>
    ```

    If you want to synchronize groups, you should see the property `groups` here as well.
    </Info>

    #### (Optional) Global Token Revocation Information

    If you want to enable global token revocation, you'll need to also share:

    - Issuer
    - Sign out URL
    - Subject (follow [these instructions](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/How-to-obtain-an-application-ID?language=en_US) for Okta)

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/saml-attributes-to-share.png" alt="SAML Attributes to Share" />
    </Frame>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="OIDC">
    ### Configure Your OIDC Application

    #### Create OIDC Application

    Create your OIDC application: choose `OIDC - OpenID Connect` and `Web Application`:

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/oidc-create-app.png" alt="Create OIDC Application" />
    </Frame>

    #### Qovery Authentication Information

    In **General** tab > **General Settings** section:

    - Set the **Sign-in redirect URIs** to:
      ```
      https://auth.qovery.com/login/callback
      ```

    - Set the **Sign-out redirect URIs** to:
      ```
      https://auth.qovery.com/v2/logout
      ```

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/oidc-uris.png" alt="OIDC URIs" />
    </Frame>

    In **General** tab > **Client Credentials** section, set the **Client authentication** to `Client secret`.

    #### (Optional) IDP-Initiated Login

    To make your application available to your users, you'll need the **Initiate Login URI**:

    ```
    https://console.qovery.com/login?connection=CONNECTION_NAME
    ```

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/oidc-idp-initiated.png" alt="OIDC IDP Initiated" />
    </Frame>

    #### (Optional) Expose Groups

    If you want to automatically assign a Qovery role according to your users' groups (see [Configure Group Synchronization](#configure-group-synchronization)), you need to expose them.

    Go to **Sign On** > **OpenID Connect ID Token**:

    - Add a `groups` claim
    - You can filter on the groups you want to expose or not (e.g., `.*` to expose all groups assigned to your users)

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/oidc-groups.png" alt="OIDC Groups" />
    </Frame>

    #### (Optional) Enable Global Token Revocation

    In **Logout** section:

    - Set the **Endpoint URL** to:
      ```
      https://qovery.eu.auth0.com/oauth/global-token-revocation/connection/$CONNECTION_NAME
      ```
    - Set **Subject format** to "Issuer and Subject Identifier"

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/configuration/sso-saml-oidc/global-revocation.png" alt="Global Token Revocation" />
    </Frame>

    ### OIDC Information To Share

    #### Required Information

    Qovery needs the following information to configure properly your OIDC application:

    - Your **Client ID**
    - Your **Client Secret**
    - Your **OIDC discovery metadata** (e.g., on Okta: `https://{yourdomain}/.well-known/openid-configuration`)
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Configuration Qovery Side

Before this step, you have validated your SAML/OIDC authentication flow with your CSM.

### Check Your Enterprise Connection

You can use the CLI to check your connection configuration:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection get
```

This should give you the following output:

```
# Connection Name: $CONNECTION_NAME

# Connection Settings
Default Role | Enforce Sync Group
viewer       | ✗ false

# Group Mappings
Qovery Role | Your IDP Groups
```

<Info>
**By default:**
- The "Default Role" is set to "viewer"
- The synchronization on IDP groups is disabled
</Info>

### Configure The Default Role

This is the Qovery role that will be associated to your IDP users when they log in to Qovery.

You can indicate either a [Qovery provided role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac) or a [custom role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac#custom-roles):

<CodeGroup>

```bash Qovery Provided Role
qovery enterprise-connection update \
  --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
  --default-role="Devops"
```

```bash Custom Role
qovery enterprise-connection update \
  --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
  --default-role="My Custom Role"
```

</CodeGroup>

<Info>
If you choose to enable the "Enforce Sync Group" parameter, the default role is used in case no mapping is found for your IDP users group.
</Info>

### Configure Group Synchronization

Group synchronization tells Qovery to always synchronize the Qovery role with your IDP users' groups. You need to configure **Group Mappings** when setting **Enforce Sync Group** to `true`.

#### Enable Group Synchronization

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection update \
  --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
  --enforce-group-sync=true
```

#### Add Group Mappings

You can create a mapping table to associate the expected Qovery role based on your user IDP group.

**Example 1**: Users with IDP groups "Administrators" or "DevSecOps" get the "admin" Qovery role:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings add \
  --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
  --qovery-role="admin" \
  --idp-group-names="Administrators,DevSecOps"
```

**Example 2**: Users with IDP group "Devs" get the "Qovery Devs" custom role:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings add \
  --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
  --qovery-role="Qovery Devs" \
  --idp-group-names="Devs"
```

The output should be:

```
Qovery Role | Your IDP Groups
Qovery Devs | Devs
admin       | Administrators ; DevSecOps
```

#### Manage Group Mappings

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="List all group mappings">
    ```bash
    qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings get \
      --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Delete a group mapping">
    ```bash
    qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings delete \
      --connection=$CONNECTION_NAME \
      --qovery-role="admin"
    ```
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

<Warning>
Do not forget to configure your IDP correctly to expose a `groups` attribute if you want to benefit from the mappings configuration.
</Warning>

## User Provisioning

Users are **not auto-provisioned** into Qovery. They need to log in at least once to Qovery using the SAML or OIDC authentication flow to be present in your organization.

Qovery defines a user according to both their email and their authentication provider. This means that when your users use the new SAML/OIDC authentication flow, they will be considered as new users in your organization. You will need to manually remove the old users that were using classic SSO login.

<Warning>
**Billing Consideration**

Qovery computes billing according to the number of users present in your organization.

During the transition from classic SSO to SAML/OIDC authentication flow, you may experience a billing increase if you don't delete old users progressively. If it happens, a refund will be done the next month.
</Warning>

## Transfer Organization Ownership

Don't forget to transfer your organization ownership to the new user that will be using SAML/OIDC authentication flow.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Identify the New Owner">
    Ensure the new owner has logged in at least once using the SAML/OIDC authentication flow.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Transfer Ownership">
    Follow the organization ownership transfer process in the Qovery console.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Remove Old Users">
    Progressively remove old users who were using classic SSO authentication.
  </Step>
</Steps>

# API Token
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-token

> Create, review, edit, and delete organization API tokens in Qovery to give CI/CD pipelines, Terraform, and scripts role-based access to the Qovery API.

An API Token is used by third-party applications or scripts to access to your organization via the Qovery API (CI/CD, Terraform, Pulumi, etc.).

You can manage API tokens attached to your organization directly from the Qovery Console or using the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/token).

<Note>
  Qovery offers a second kind of token. An **API Token** carries a
  [role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac) and is the right choice for
  CI/CD, Terraform and scripts. An
  [**API Policy Token**](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) carries no
  role but a policy evaluated on every request, and is meant for autonomous
  agents that need a narrower footprint than any role can express, for
  example an agent that may only deploy the staging environment and never
  delete anything.
</Note>

    </Frame>

  </Step>
</Steps>

## Create a New Token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
<Steps>
  <Step title="Click Add new Button">
    Press the **Add new** button to create a new API token
  </Step>

<Step title="Configure Token">
  Provide the following information: - **Name**: A descriptive name for the
  token - **Description**: Purpose or usage details - **Role**: Select a role
  managed via the [Qovery RBAC system](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac)
</Step>

  <Step title="Save Token">
    After creation, the token will be displayed once
  </Step>
</Steps>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="CLI and API">
    You need the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), signed in with `qovery auth`.

    Run `qovery token`. It asks for the organization, a name, a description and a role, then prints the token once:

    ```bash
    qovery token
    ```

    With the API, get the role ID from `GET /organization/{organizationId}/availableRole`, then call `POST /organization/{organizationId}/apiToken`. `name` and `role_id` are required:

    ```bash
    ORGANIZATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"  # from qovery organization list --json

    qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/availableRole"

    ROLE_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ROLE_ID"  # id of the role from the list above

    qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/apiToken" \
      --field name=ci-deployer \
      --field description="GitHub Actions" \
      --field role_id="$ROLE_ID"
    ```

    The response contains the token value. It is returned only once.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Terraform">
    Use the [`qovery_api_token`](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/Qovery/qovery/latest/docs/resources/api_token) resource. `organization_id`, `name` and `role_id` are required:

    ```hcl
    resource "qovery_api_token" "ci" {
      organization_id = "<organizationId>"
      name            = "ci-deployer"
      description     = "GitHub Actions"
      role_id         = "<roleId>"
    }
    ```

    The token value is in the sensitive `token` attribute. It is only known at creation and is stored in the Terraform state, so use an encrypted remote state with restricted access. Any attribute change replaces the token.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Check it worked

List the tokens of the organization:

```bash
ORGANIZATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"  # from qovery organization list --json

qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/apiToken"
```

The new token appears with its `name` and `role_name`. To confirm the token itself works, call the API with it:

```bash
QOVERY_API_TOKEN="REPLACE_WITH_THE_NEW_TOKEN"
curl -H "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_API_TOKEN" https://api.qovery.com/organization
```

The response lists the organizations the token can access.

<Warning>
  **Important**: Make sure you safely store the token returned by the UI. You
  won't be able to retrieve it again (you will have to create a new one).
</Warning>

## Review Token Usage

Each token in the Token API list shows its role, its creation date, and **Last used**, the time elapsed since the token was last used, for example "Last used 3 days ago". Hover over it to see the exact date and time in UTC. Use it to identify tokens that are no longer in use before you delete them. The **Last used** label is not displayed when no usage has been recorded for the token.

2. Click the **delete icon** (trash icon) next to the token
3. Confirm the deletion

With the API, call `DELETE /organization/{organizationId}/apiToken/{apiTokenId}`. Token IDs come from `GET /organization/{organizationId}/apiToken`.

# API Policy Token (Preview)
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token

> Give an autonomous agent programmatic access to your organization, constrained by a policy evaluated on every request

An **API Policy Token** is a second kind of organization token, intended for autonomous agents and narrowly scoped automation. Unlike a regular [API Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-token), it carries **no role**. Instead you attach an [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/) policy, written in [rego](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-language), and Qovery evaluates that policy against every API request the token makes. The policy is the token's entire authorization.

<Info>
  **Preview**: this feature and the policy input contract described below are still
  evolving and are likely to change. Expect to revisit your policies as the
  feature matures.
</Info>

<Note>
  In the Qovery Console, this feature is labelled **Policy API Token**,
  in the **Token API** section of your organization settings.
</Note>

## Why use one

A role answers "what kind of thing may this token do, across a scope". A policy answers "may *this exact request* proceed". That is what makes it a fit for an agent: you can hand out a token that reads everything in one environment, deploys that environment, may update one service, and can never delete anything - a shape no role expresses.

|                             | API Token                                              | API Policy Token                                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Authorization               | An [RBAC role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac) | A rego policy, evaluated on every request                              |
| Granularity                 | What the role allows                                   | Any condition over the HTTP request and the resource it targets        |
| Who can create it           | Depends on your role                                   | Organization **Owner** or **Admin** only                               |
| Editable after creation     | No                                                     | No                                                                     |
| Typical use                 | CI/CD, Terraform, scripts                              | AI agents, tightly scoped automation                                   |

## How it works

### What Open Policy Agent does

[Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/) (OPA) is an open source, general-purpose policy engine and a [CNCF graduated project](https://www.cncf.io/projects/open-policy-agent-opa/). Its model is deliberately narrow: it knows nothing about Qovery and holds no permission model of its own. You give it two things - a policy, and a JSON document called the **input** - and it answers a query against them. That is all it does.

That separation is the point. The rules deciding what your agent may do live in the policy rather than in Qovery's permission code, so you can express a constraint Qovery never anticipated without Qovery having to invent a role for it.

Qovery runs OPA as a sidecar next to the API, reachable only over the pod's loopback interface. Your policy and the requests it is evaluated against never leave Qovery's infrastructure, and a decision costs an in-pod round trip rather than a call out to a network service.

### How Qovery evaluates a request

The policy is evaluated at authentication time, before the request reaches the endpoint it targets. That is also why the policy sees the request's raw path rather than a route template - the route has not been matched yet.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant API as Qovery API
    participant DB as Qovery database
    participant OPA as OPA sidecar (same pod)

    Note over Agent,API: Authorization: Token sk-qov-01-...
    Agent->>API: GET /environment/{environmentId}/application
    API->>DB: Look up the token by its hash
    DB-->>API: The token and the policy it carries
    API->>DB: Resolve the IDs found in the request path
    DB-->>API: The targeted service, environment and project
    API->>OPA: Evaluate allow against the input document
    OPA-->>API: true, false or undefined
    API-->>Agent: 200 and the response, or 401 Unauthorized
```

1. **The token is recognised** by its `sk-qov-01` prefix in the `Authorization` header, which is what tells it apart from a regular API token sent under the same `Token` scheme.
2. **The token is looked up.** Only a hash of the token value is stored, so the presented value is hashed and matched against it. An unknown or expired token stops here.
3. **The target is resolved.** Qovery takes the IDs appearing in the request path and asks its own database what they are - a service, an environment, a project - and what that resource's ancestry is. This is what fills `qovery_metadata`, and it is why a policy can talk about environments while the request only names a service.
4. **The input document is built** from the request and that resolved metadata. Its exact shape is [documented below](#what-the-policy-sees).
5. **The policy is loaded.** The first time a pod handles a given token, it uploads that token's policy to its OPA sidecar as a module, under a package unique to the token. Per-token packages are what stop one token's rules from ever contributing to another token's decision, and they are the reason your policy must not declare a `package` of its own. The module is compiled once and reused for subsequent requests.
6. **The policy is evaluated** against the input, and OPA returns the value of `allow`: `true`, `false`, or undefined when no rule produced a value.
7. **The decision is applied.** `true` lets the request continue to the endpoint. Anything else - including undefined, a non-boolean value, or an OPA that could not be reached - answers `401 Unauthorized`.

### Rego, the policy language

Policies are written in [rego](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-language), OPA's language. It is declarative and derives from [Datalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datalog), extended to query nested JSON documents - which is exactly what an `input` document is. There are no statements to sequence and no control flow to trace: you declare the conditions under which something holds, and OPA searches for a way to satisfy them.

Five ideas carry almost every Qovery policy.

**A rule has a head and a body, and the body is an AND.** Every expression in the body must hold for the rule to produce its value.

```rego
# Reads as: allow, if the method is GET and the environment is that one.
allow if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"
}
```

**Rules sharing a name are an OR.** Defining `allow` twice is not a conflict, it adds an alternative. This is how a policy grants several unrelated things without collapsing into one tangled condition:

```rego
default allow := false

allow if read_only_access
allow if deploy_access

# The two alternatives, each a rule of its own.
read_only_access if input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}

deploy_access if input.request.path == ["api", "application", "5bf547f9-b445-44bc-aab8-7f341187d362", "deploy"]
```

**Anything missing is undefined, not an error.** An expression referring to a value that is not there is itself undefined, and that propagates: the surrounding rule simply does not fire. `input.request.body.key` on a request that carried no body is undefined, so the rule using it does not fire, so the request is denied. Nothing throws, and fail-closed comes out as the natural default rather than something bolted on.

**`default` supplies a value when nothing fires.** Without it, a request matching no rule leaves `allow` undefined; with it, the answer is explicitly `false`.

```rego
default allow := false
```

**`:=` assigns, `==` compares, `in` tests membership.** Membership needs no loop, which keeps a list of allowed verbs readable:

```rego
allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"

allow if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == allowed_environment_id
}
```

Rego also ships a large standard library - `startswith`, `endswith`, `count`, `regex.match`, `sprintf` and many more - listed in the [policy reference](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-reference).

<Tip>
  The [Rego Playground](https://play.openpolicyagent.org/) evaluates a policy
  against an input document in your browser, which is a fast way to get a feel
  for the language before writing a real policy. Paste one of the
  [recipes](#policy-recipes) and an `input` document from this page into it.
</Tip>

### What this means in practice

- **The policy is the only thing constraining the token.** Internally a policy token is granted organization-admin access, and the policy is what narrows it. A policy whose `allow` is unconditionally `true` therefore grants **full organization-admin access**.
- **It fails closed.** Anything other than an explicit `true` denies the request: no matching rule, a non-boolean `allow`, a request path that Qovery cannot resolve, or a policy engine that cannot be reached.
- **Only an organization Owner or Admin can create one.** Creating a policy token is equivalent to handing out organization-admin access, so it is restricted to roles that already hold it. Custom roles cannot create one.
- **Revocation is immediate.** The token is looked up on every request, with no caching.
- **Actions are attributed in the audit log** as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`, so an agent's activity is distinguishable from a regular API token's.

<Warning>
  Treat creating an API Policy Token with the same care as granting
  organization-admin. Start from a `default allow := false` policy and add only
  the rules you need.
</Warning>

## What the policy sees

Your policy is evaluated against this `input` document:

```json
{
  "request": {
    "method": "POST",
    "path": ["api", "environment", "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49", "service", "deploy"],
    "body": { "force": true }
  },
  "qovery_metadata": {
    "organization_id": "a3c8f0d2-1b44-4e9a-9c31-6f5d2e8a7b10",
    "service_id": null,
    "service_type": null,
    "environment_id": "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49",
    "project_id": "c47d1e83-9a06-4f52-8d7b-2e1a94c6f5b3",
    "cluster_id": "9f1c2b3d-4e5a-6b7c-8d9e-0f1a2b3c4d5e"
  },
  "token": {
    "id": "0198f2a1-6c3d-7b41-9e08-5a2d3c4b7e91",
    "name": "deploy-agent"
  }
}
```

| Field                                | Description                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `input.request.method`               | The HTTP verb, uppercase.                                                                                                                                                         |
| `input.request.path`                 | The path segments of the request, decoded. These are the real segments with real IDs, not a route template.                                                                        |
| `input.request.body`                 | The parsed JSON body, or `null` when the request carries none (the normal case for `GET` and `DELETE`).                                                                            |
| `input.qovery_metadata.organization_id` | The organization the token belongs to.                                                                                                                                         |
| `input.qovery_metadata.service_id`   | The service the request targets, or `null`.                                                                                                                                       |
| `input.qovery_metadata.service_type` | `APPLICATION`, `CONTAINER`, `DATABASE`, `ROUTER`, `JOB`, `HELM`, `TERRAFORM`, `ARGOCD_APP`, `AGENTIC_WORKFLOW`, or `null`.                                                         |
| `input.qovery_metadata.environment_id` | The environment the request targets, or `null`.                                                                                                                                  |
| `input.qovery_metadata.project_id`   | The project the request targets, or `null`.                                                                                                                                       |
| `input.qovery_metadata.cluster_id`   | The cluster the targeted resource runs on, or `null`.                                                                                                                             |
| `input.token.id`, `input.token.name` | The token making the request.                                                                                                                                                     |

<Note>
  The public API path is internally prefixed with `api`, so
  `POST https://api.qovery.com/environment/<id>/service/deploy` reaches your
  policy as `["api", "environment", "<id>", "service", "deploy"]`. Include that
  first segment when you match on a path.
</Note>

A few behaviours worth knowing before you write rules against these fields:

- **The `qovery_metadata` keys are always present**, set to `null` when nothing of that kind was resolved. Test `input.qovery_metadata.service_id == null`, not the absence of the key.
- **Qovery resolves one target per request**, preferring a service over an environment over a project. For `/api/environment/<env>/application/<app>`, the target is the application: `environment_id`, `project_id` and `cluster_id` are then read from *that service's* ancestry rather than from the path. So a rule on `environment_id` still holds for a request that only names the service.
- **IDs belonging to another organization are ignored**, as if they were not in the path.
- **A request whose path cannot be resolved is denied**, rather than shown with `null` fields. A rule phrased as `service_id != "<id>"` cannot be widened by a failed lookup.
- **Only JSON bodies are forwarded.** A request with a non-JSON body, a malformed JSON body, or a body larger than 1 MiB is denied outright rather than presented to the policy with `body` set to `null`. Inside a policy, `body == null` therefore always means "there was no body".
- **Query parameters, headers and the client IP are deliberately not exposed.**

## Writing the policy

<Warning>
  Do not include a `package` declaration. Qovery prepends a per-token package so
  that one token's rules can never authorize another's, and a submitted
  `package` line is rejected. Submit rule definitions only.
</Warning>

- The policy **must define an `allow` rule**, and the decision must be the boolean `true`. Anything else denies.
- Start with `default allow := false`. Without it, a request that matches no rule leaves `allow` undefined, which Qovery also treats as a denial - the default just makes the intent explicit.
- Maximum policy size: 65,536 characters.
- The policy is compiled when you create the token, so a syntax error comes back immediately as a `400` with the compiler diagnostics.
- The engine is OPA 1.19, so rego v1 syntax is available directly: `if`, `in` and `contains` need no `import` statement.

## Starter policy

This is the policy prefilled in the Console when you create a token. It grants read-only access to one environment, write access to one service in it (but never a deletion), and the right to deploy that environment.

```rego
default allow := false

allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"
allowed_application_id := "5bf547f9-b445-44bc-aab8-7f341187d362"

allow if read_only_access_on_env
allow if modify_only_allowed_service
allow if allow_deployment

# Read-only access to every endpoint that touches this environment.
read_only_access_on_env if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == allowed_environment_id
}

# Write access only when the request targets this service, and never a deletion.
modify_only_allowed_service if {
	input.request.method != "DELETE"
	input.qovery_metadata.service_id == allowed_application_id
}

# Deploy this environment.
allow_deployment if {
	input.request.path == ["api", "environment", allowed_environment_id, "service", "deploy"]
}
```

## Policy recipes

For complete use cases, with the full policy, the prompt for the agent, and what the agent can and cannot do, see the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview): incident investigation, preview environments, stopping idle environments, right-sizing, scaling, rollbacks, tests on a copy of production and security patches.

The recipes below are smaller building blocks.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Read-only access to one environment">
    Every `GET` and `HEAD` on the environment, its services and their sub-resources. Nothing else.

    ```rego
    default allow := false

    allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"

    allow if {
    	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
    	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == allowed_environment_id
    }
    ```

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Deploy, and nothing else">
    A token for a release pipeline: it can trigger deployments and cannot read or change anything else. Matching on the exact path is what keeps it that narrow.

    ```rego
    default allow := false

    allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"
    allowed_application_id := "5bf547f9-b445-44bc-aab8-7f341187d362"

    # Deploy every service of that environment.
    allow if input.request.path == ["api", "environment", allowed_environment_id, "service", "deploy"]

    # Deploy that one application.
    allow if input.request.path == ["api", "application", allowed_application_id, "deploy"]
    ```

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Change one service, but never delete it">
    Full read and write on a single service, with deletion excluded whatever the endpoint.

    ```rego
    default allow := false

    allowed_application_id := "5bf547f9-b445-44bc-aab8-7f341187d362"

    allow if {
    	input.request.method != "DELETE"
    	input.qovery_metadata.service_id == allowed_application_id
    }
    ```

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Constrain the request body">
    Because the parsed JSON body is part of the input, a rule can constrain the content of a change and not just its target. Here the agent may create environment variables on one application, but only those named `FEATURE_*`.

    ```rego
    default allow := false

    allowed_application_id := "5bf547f9-b445-44bc-aab8-7f341187d362"

    allow if {
    	input.request.method == "POST"
    	input.request.path == ["api", "application", allowed_application_id, "environmentVariable"]
    	startswith(input.request.body.key, "FEATURE_")
    }
    ```

    A request with no body leaves `input.request.body.key` undefined, so this rule denies it.

  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Create an API Policy Token

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the Token API section">
    Go to your organization settings and open the **Token API** section, the same
    page as the [API tokens](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-token). The
    **Policy API Token** section sits below the API token list.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Click Add new">
    Press the **Add new** button of the Policy API Token section.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure the token">
    Provide:

    - **Token name**: a descriptive name, unique within the organization
    - **Description**: what the token is for
    - **Policy (rego)**: your policy, prefilled with the starter policy above

  </Step>

  <Step title="Store the token value">
    The token is displayed once, in the form `sk-qov-01-...`. Copy it before
    closing the modal.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
  **Important**: Make sure you safely store the token returned by the UI. You
  won't be able to retrieve it again (you will have to create a new one).
</Warning>

## Use the token

An API Policy Token uses the same `Authorization` header scheme as a regular API token:

```bash
export QOVERY_POLICY_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."

curl -X GET "https://api.qovery.com/environment/<environmentId>/application" \
  -H "Authorization: Token ${QOVERY_POLICY_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json"
```

If the policy does not allow the request, the API answers `401 Unauthorized`.

## Inspect and revoke

In the Policy API Token list, each token shows its creator and creation date, and **Last used**, the time elapsed since the token was last used. Hover over it to see the exact date and time in UTC. **Last used** is not displayed when no usage has been recorded for the token. Each token also offers:

- **Inspect policy** (scroll icon): shows the policy attached to the token, read-only. A policy can always be reviewed after creation - only the token value is write-once.
- **Delete** (trash icon): revokes the token. Confirm the deletion, and the token stops working immediately.

Policies cannot be edited. To change one, delete the token and create a new one with the updated policy.

## Manage tokens via the API

| Operation | Endpoint |
| --------- | -------- |
| Create | `POST /organization/{organizationId}/policyApiToken` |
| List | `GET /organization/{organizationId}/policyApiToken` |
| Revoke | `DELETE /organization/{organizationId}/policyApiToken/{policyApiTokenId}` |

Creating a token, with the policy passed as a string in `opa_policy`:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.qovery.com/organization/${ORGANIZATION_ID}/policyApiToken" \
  -H "Authorization: Token ${QOVERY_API_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "deploy-agent",
    "description": "Deploys the staging environment",
    "opa_policy": "default allow := false\n\nallow if input.request.path == [\"api\", \"environment\", \"4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49\", \"service\", \"deploy\"]\n"
  }'
```

The response contains the token value in its `token` field. This is the only response that ever carries it.

The list endpoint returns each token with its `opa_policy`, never the token value. The create endpoint also accepts an optional `expires_at` (RFC 3339 date-time), after which the token stops authenticating; the Console form does not expose it yet, so set an expiration through the API if you need one.

Errors to expect when creating a token:

| Status | Cause |
| ------ | ----- |
| `400` | The policy is empty, oversized, declares a `package`, or does not compile. The response carries the OPA diagnostics. |
| `403` | The caller is not an organization owner or admin. |
| `409` | A policy token with that name already exists in the organization. |

## Test a policy before attaching it

A denied request tells you only that it was denied, so it is worth evaluating a policy locally first. Install [OPA](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs) 1.19 - the same version Qovery runs - then:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Save the policy with a temporary package line">
    Qovery adds the `package` declaration for you, so add one locally and remove
    it before submitting.

    ```rego
    # policy.rego
    package qovery.policy

    default allow := false

    allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"

    allow if {
    	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
    	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == allowed_environment_id
    }
    ```

  </Step>

  <Step title="Save the request you want to test">
    Write an `input.json` following the [input document](#what-the-policy-sees)
    shown above.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Evaluate">
    ```bash
    opa check policy.rego
    opa eval -d policy.rego -i input.json --format raw 'data.qovery.policy.allow'
    ```

    `true` means the request would be allowed. `false`, or an empty result, means
    it would be denied.

  </Step>
</Steps>

<Tip>
  Test the denials too, not just the allows. Flip the method to `DELETE`, point
  the request at another environment, and confirm the answer is `false`.
</Tip>

## Current limitations

<Warning>
  - **A denied request returns `401` with no explanation.** Which rule failed is not surfaced to you today, so test policies locally before attaching them.
  - **Policies cannot be edited.** Delete the token and create a new one.
  - **Expiration is API-only.** The Console form does not expose `expires_at`.
  - **The input contract may change.** Fields are added rather than renamed or removed, and policies may need to be updated.
</Warning>

# Agent policy examples
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview

> Ready-to-use API Policy Tokens for autonomous infrastructure agents: each example gives the use case, the full policy, the prompt, and what the agent can and cannot do.

These examples show AI agents doing real DevOps work on their own, each with an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) (Preview) that allows exactly that job and nothing else. Qovery checks the policy on every API request the agent makes, through the CLI or the API. So the agent does not need a human to approve each action, and anything outside the job is refused.

Each page gives you:

- the use case, and what the agent does step by step,
- what the policy allows and what it blocks,
- the full policy, ready to copy,
- a prompt to create the token with the `qovery-policy-token` skill,
- a prompt to give the agent its task.

## Examples

Start at the top. The first jobs only read or touch non-production environments. The last ones change production, in a narrow way.

| Example | Level | What the agent does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Investigate a production incident](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/investigate-production-incident) | Read only | Reads production status, deployment history and logs, and reports the cause. Changes nothing. |
| [Fix a bug and verify it in a preview environment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/fix-in-preview-environment) | Previews | Reads production, then deploys and checks a fix in the pull request's preview environment. |
| [Stop idle environments](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/stop-idle-environments) | Hygiene | Stops listed dev and QA environments when idle, and starts them again. |
| [Clean up preview environments](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/clean-up-preview-environments) | Hygiene | Deletes previews whose pull request is merged, closed or idle. Never production or staging. |
| [Right-size applications](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/right-size-applications) | Cost | Sets CPU and memory from real usage, within bounds, then redeploys. |
| [Scale before a traffic peak](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/scale-before-traffic-peak) | Reliability | Adds instances before a known peak and removes them after, between a floor and a ceiling. |
| [Roll back a bad release](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/roll-back-bad-release) | Reliability | Deploys the last healthy version when a release goes wrong. |
| [Test on a copy of production](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/test-on-production-clone) | Change | Clones production into a sandbox, runs tests on the copy, and deletes it. |
| [Patch a security issue](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/patch-security-issue) | Change | Tests a security fix on a copy of production, then deploys the patched commit. |

## How to use an example

<Steps>
  <Step title="Copy the policy and replace the IDs">
    Every value that starts with `REPLACE_WITH_` is an ID from your organization: organization, project, environment, application or cluster. Copy them from the Console URL or list them with the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview).
  </Step>
  <Step title="Create the token">
    In the Console, open your organization settings, then **Token API**, then **Add new** in **Policy API Token**, and paste the policy. Or ask a coding agent with the `qovery-policy-token` skill, using the prompt on the page. Only an organization Owner or Admin can create a policy token.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Give the token to the agent">
    Set it in the agent's environment, never in the prompt:

    ```bash
    export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
    ```

    The agent uses the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the Qovery CLI.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Give the agent its task">
    Use the prompt on the page, adapted to your project and environment names.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## What every policy has in common

- **Deny by default.** Each policy starts with `default allow := false`. A request is allowed only if one rule says so.
- **A rule for CLI lookups.** The Qovery CLI turns names into IDs by listing the organization, its projects and the project's environments (and its clusters, for the examples that clone). The `cli_lookup` rule allows those reads and nothing more.
- **No environment variable values.** The read rules leave out `environmentVariable` endpoints, because values can be sensitive. Remove that line if your agent needs them.
- **One scope per job.** Each rule is tied to an environment, a project, or a list of services, so the agent cannot reach anything else.

## Test a policy before you create the token

A denied request returns `401` with no detail, and a policy cannot be edited after creation. Test it first with [OPA](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs#running-opa). Add a temporary `package` line, then evaluate it against a request:

```bash
(echo "package test"; cat policy.rego) > /tmp/policy.rego

cat > /tmp/input.json <<'EOF'
{
  "request": { "method": "DELETE", "path": ["api", "environment", "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"], "body": null },
  "qovery_metadata": {
    "organization_id": "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID",
    "service_id": null, "service_type": null,
    "environment_id": "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
    "project_id": "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID",
    "cluster_id": null
  },
  "token": { "id": "test", "name": "test" }
}
EOF

opa eval -d /tmp/policy.rego -i /tmp/input.json 'data.test.allow'
```

The result must be `false` for every action the agent must not do. Do not submit the `package` line: Qovery adds its own. The [Rego Playground](https://play.openpolicyagent.org/) works too. The `qovery-policy-token` skill runs these tests for you, then checks the token against the real API.

# Investigate a production incident
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/investigate-production-incident

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that reads production status, deployment history and logs to find the cause of an incident, and cannot change anything.

An on-call agent that looks at production when something breaks. It reads the status of every service, the deployment history and the logs, and reports what changed and what it thinks the cause is. It cannot change, deploy or delete anything.

**Level:** Read only. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Finds the failing service in the production environment.
2. Reads its status, its recent deployments and the environment logs.
3. Compares the failing deployment with the last healthy one.
4. Writes a short report: what broke, when, the likely cause, and the fix it suggests to a human.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name, as the Qovery CLI does
    - Read the production environment: services, status, deployment history and logs
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Read environment variable values, even in production
    - Deploy, redeploy, restart or stop anything
    - Change any configuration, or delete anything
    - Read any other environment
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego investigate-production-incident.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_production

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read production: services, status, deployment history and logs.
# Environment variables are left out, because their values can be sensitive.
read_production if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == production_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project that holds production |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token read-only access to the production environment of my project, including logs and deployment history, but not environment variables. No writes, no deploys, no deletes.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
Our production checkout service started failing about 20 minutes ago.
Use Qovery to investigate. The project is "shop" and the environment is "production".

1. Find which services are not healthy and since when.
2. Read the deployment history and the logs of the failing services.
3. Compare the last failing deployment with the last healthy one.
4. Give me a short report: what broke, the most likely cause, and the fix you suggest.

Do not try to change or redeploy anything. Your token only allows reads.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- This is the safest place to start: the token cannot change production, so you can give it to an agent on day one.
- If you also want the agent to read logs through the [Qovery MCP Server](https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/mcp-server), use an API token with a read-only role for the MCP Server. It does not accept API Policy Tokens.

# Fix a bug and verify it in a preview environment
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/fix-in-preview-environment

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that reads production to find a bug, then deploys and checks its fix in preview environments, and cannot touch production or staging.

A triage agent that reads production to find a bug, pushes a fix on a branch, and checks it in the preview environment Qovery creates for the pull request. It can deploy, redeploy and stop previews. Production and staging are read only.

**Level:** Previews. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Reads production status, deployment history and logs to find the bug.
2. Pushes a fix on a branch and opens a pull request (in your Git provider, outside Qovery).
3. Deploys or redeploys the preview environment of that pull request and checks that it works.
4. Stops the preview when the check is done.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read every environment of the project, production included, except environment variables
    - Deploy, redeploy, restart or stop a preview environment, or one of its services
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Deploy, restart or stop production or staging
    - Change configuration or environment variables, even in a preview
    - Delete anything, or clone an environment
    - Act on another project
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego fix-in-preview-environment.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# Long-lived environments in the project that the agent must never change.
protected_environment_ids := {
	production_environment_id,
	"REPLACE_WITH_STAGING_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_project
allow if manage_preview

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read every environment of the project, production included, except environment variables.
read_project if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == project_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Deploy, redeploy, restart or stop a preview environment, or one of its services.
manage_preview if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == project_id
	not input.qovery_metadata.environment_id in protected_environment_ids
	input.request.path[count(input.request.path) - 1] in {"deploy", "redeploy", "restart", "restart-service", "stop"}
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project where previews are created |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |
| `protected_environment_ids` | every long-lived environment of the project: production, staging and any other one the agent must not touch |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token for a triage agent: read the whole project except environment variables, and deploy, redeploy, restart or stop any environment of the project except production and staging. No deletes, no config changes.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
Users report that the discount code field rejects valid codes.
The Qovery project is "shop".

1. Read the production logs and deployment history to find the error.
2. Fix the bug on a new branch and open a pull request.
3. Wait for the preview environment of the pull request, deploy it if needed,
   and check that a valid discount code is accepted.
4. Stop the preview environment when you are done, and post the result on the pull request.

You cannot deploy production. A human merges the pull request.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- The policy cannot see whether an environment is a preview. It allows every environment of the project except the ones you list in `protected_environment_ids`. Add any new long-lived environment to that list.
- To also let the agent delete previews, use the [preview cleanup](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/clean-up-preview-environments) policy, or add its delete rule to this one.

# Stop idle environments
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/stop-idle-environments

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that stops development environments when nobody uses them and starts them again in the morning, and cannot touch anything else.

A cost agent that stops development and QA environments when nobody uses them, for example at night and on weekends, and starts them again when the team needs them. It can only stop and start the environments you list.

**Level:** Hygiene. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Reads the status and the deployment history of each listed environment.
2. Decides which ones are idle, for example no deployment for 24 hours or outside working hours.
3. Stops the idle environments.
4. Starts them again at the time you choose, with a deploy.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read the status and deployment history of the listed environments
    - Stop a listed environment, or start it again with a deploy
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Stop or deploy production, staging or any environment that is not listed
    - Delete an environment or a service
    - Change any configuration
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego stop-idle-environments.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"

# The non-production environments the agent may stop and start.
idle_candidate_environment_ids := {
	"REPLACE_WITH_DEV_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
	"REPLACE_WITH_QA_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_candidates
allow if stop_or_start

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read the status and deployment history of those environments.
read_candidates if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id in idle_candidate_environment_ids
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Stop an environment, or start it again with a deploy. Nothing else.
stop_or_start if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "environment"
	input.request.path[2] in idle_candidate_environment_ids
	input.request.path[3] in {"stop", "deploy"}
	count(input.request.path) == 4
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project that holds the environments |
| `idle_candidate_environment_ids` | the development and QA environments the agent may stop |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token for a cost agent: read status and deployment history of the dev and qa environments, and stop or deploy them. Nothing else, no other environment, no deletes, no config changes.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
Check the "dev" and "qa" environments of the Qovery project "shop".

If an environment has had no deployment in the last 24 hours, or if it is
after 8 PM or a weekend in Paris time, stop it.
On weekdays at 8 AM Paris time, start the stopped ones again.

List what you stopped or started, and why.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- If a fixed schedule is enough, use [deployment rules](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment-rule) instead: they start and stop environments on a schedule with no agent at all. Use an agent when the decision depends on activity.
- Starting an environment is a deploy. The policy allows a deploy of the listed environments only.
