# Clean up preview environments
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/clean-up-preview-environments

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that deletes preview environments after the pull request is merged or idle, and can never delete production or staging.

A cleanup agent that deletes preview environments once their pull request is merged or closed, or after 7 days without activity. It can delete whole environments of one project, except the long-lived ones you protect.

**Level:** Hygiene. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Lists the environments of the project and their last deployment.
2. Checks the pull request behind each preview in your Git provider.
3. Deletes the previews whose pull request is merged or closed, or that are idle for 7 days.
4. Reports what it deleted.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read the environments of the project, except environment variables
    - Delete a whole environment of the project, unless it is protected
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Delete production, staging or any protected environment
    - Delete a single service, a database or the project
    - Delete anything in another project
    - Deploy, stop or change anything
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego clean-up-preview-environments.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"

# Long-lived environments in the project that the agent must never delete.
protected_environment_ids := {
	"REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
	"REPLACE_WITH_STAGING_ENVIRONMENT_ID",
}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_project
allow if delete_preview

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read the environments of the project, to see which previews are idle.
read_project if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == project_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Delete a whole environment of the project, unless it is protected.
delete_preview if {
	input.request.method == "DELETE"
	input.request.path[1] == "environment"
	count(input.request.path) == 3
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == project_id
	not input.qovery_metadata.environment_id in protected_environment_ids
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project where previews are created |
| `protected_environment_ids` | every long-lived environment of the project the agent must never delete |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.


The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. - Qovery can also delete a preview automatically when its pull request is closed. See [preview environments](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/use-cases/preview-environments). The agent is useful for the previews that stay open but idle.

# Right-size applications
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/right-size-applications

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that sets CPU and memory from real usage within bounds you choose, and cannot change instances, branch or anything else.

A cost agent that sets the CPU and memory of applications from their real usage over the last 30 days. It can change CPU and memory within bounds you choose, then redeploy. The number of instances and the Git branch must stay as they are.

**Level:** Cost. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Reads the usage of each listed application over the last 30 days.
2. Proposes new CPU and memory values, with some headroom.
3. Applies them, within the bounds of the policy.
4. Redeploys the application and checks that it is healthy.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read the staging environment, except environment variables
    - Change CPU and memory of the listed applications, within the bounds
    - Redeploy the listed applications
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Set CPU or memory outside the bounds
    - Change the minimum or maximum number of instances
    - Change the Git branch
    - Change or redeploy any application that is not listed
    - Read or change production, delete anything
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego right-size-applications.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
staging_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_STAGING_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# The applications the agent may resize. Instances and branch stay as they are today.
applications := {
	"REPLACE_WITH_API_APPLICATION_ID": {"min_instances": 1, "max_instances": 3, "branch": "main"},
	"REPLACE_WITH_WORKER_APPLICATION_ID": {"min_instances": 1, "max_instances": 2, "branch": "main"},
}

# Bounds for CPU (millicores) and memory (MB).
cpu_bounds := {"min": 100, "max": 2000}
memory_bounds := {"min": 128, "max": 4096}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_staging
allow if resize
allow if redeploy

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read staging: services, status, deployment history and logs.
read_staging if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == staging_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Change CPU and memory within the bounds. Instances and branch must not change.
resize if {
	input.request.method == "PUT"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	count(input.request.path) == 3
	app := applications[input.request.path[2]]
	body := input.request.body
	body.cpu >= cpu_bounds.min
	body.cpu <= cpu_bounds.max
	body.memory >= memory_bounds.min
	body.memory <= memory_bounds.max
	body.min_running_instances == app.min_instances
	body.max_running_instances == app.max_instances
	body.git_repository.branch == app.branch
}

# Redeploy a resized application so the new values apply.
redeploy if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	applications[input.request.path[2]]
	input.request.path[3] == "redeploy"
	count(input.request.path) == 4
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project |
| `staging_environment_id` | the environment the agent works on |
| `applications` | each application the agent may resize, with its current minimum and maximum instances and Git branch |
| `cpu_bounds, memory_bounds` | the lowest and highest CPU (millicores) and memory (MB) the agent may set |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

  <Tab title="With the coding agent">


    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
/qovery-optimize Right-size the "api" and "worker" applications in the
"staging" environment of the Qovery project "shop".

Use the real CPU and memory usage of the last 30 days. Keep 30% headroom
over the peak. Do not change the number of instances.
Apply the new values, redeploy each application, and check it is healthy.
Report the old and new values, and the expected saving.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- Editing an application sends its full configuration. The policy checks CPU, memory, the number of instances and the Git branch. Other fields in the same request are not checked: add a rule for any other field you want to freeze.
- Start on staging. Once you trust the results, copy the policy for production with tighter bounds.
- The `qovery-optimize` skill uses Qovery observability data when it is enabled on the cluster. See [Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills).

# Scale before a traffic peak
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/scale-before-traffic-peak

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that adds instances before a known traffic peak and removes them after, within a floor and a ceiling, and cannot change anything else.

A reliability agent that adds instances before a known traffic peak, such as a launch, a sale or a marketing email, and removes them after. It can change the number of instances of listed production applications between a floor and a ceiling. CPU, memory and branch stay as they are.

**Level:** Reliability. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Reads the current instances and the status of each listed application.
2. Before the peak, raises the minimum and maximum number of instances.
3. Redeploys the applications and checks they are healthy.
4. After the peak, sets the instances back.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read the production environment, except environment variables
    - Set the minimum and maximum instances of the listed applications, between the floor and the ceiling
    - Redeploy the listed applications
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Go above the ceiling, set an unlimited maximum, or go below the floor
    - Change CPU, memory or the Git branch
    - Deploy a new version
    - Change environment variables, delete anything, or touch other applications
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego scale-before-traffic-peak.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# The applications the agent may scale, with their current CPU, memory and branch, and the
# highest number of instances the agent may set.
applications := {
	"REPLACE_WITH_API_APPLICATION_ID": {"cpu": 1000, "memory": 2048, "branch": "main", "floor": 2, "ceiling": 12},
	"REPLACE_WITH_WEB_APPLICATION_ID": {"cpu": 500, "memory": 1024, "branch": "main", "floor": 2, "ceiling": 8},
}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_production
allow if scale
allow if redeploy

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read production: services, status, deployment history and logs.
read_production if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == production_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Change the number of instances between the floor and the ceiling.
# CPU, memory and branch must stay as they are.
scale if {
	input.request.method == "PUT"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	count(input.request.path) == 3
	app := applications[input.request.path[2]]
	body := input.request.body
	body.min_running_instances >= app.floor
	body.max_running_instances >= body.min_running_instances
	body.max_running_instances <= app.ceiling
	body.cpu == app.cpu
	body.memory == app.memory
	body.git_repository.branch == app.branch
}

# Redeploy a scaled application so the new values apply.
redeploy if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	applications[input.request.path[2]]
	input.request.path[3] == "redeploy"
	count(input.request.path) == 4
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |
| `applications` | each application the agent may scale, with its current CPU, memory and branch, and the floor and ceiling for its instances |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

# Roll back a bad release
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/roll-back-bad-release

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that reads errors after a deploy and rolls production services back to the last healthy version, and cannot change configuration or delete anything.

A reliability agent that watches production after a release. If error rates go up, it finds the last healthy version of the service and deploys it again. It can deploy a given version of the listed services, and nothing else.

**Level:** Reliability. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Reads the deployment history and the logs after a release.
2. Decides whether the new version is the cause of the errors.
3. Finds the last healthy commit or image tag in the deployment history.
4. Deploys that version, checks the service is healthy, and reports.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, project and environment by name
    - Read the production environment, except environment variables
    - Deploy a given commit of the listed applications
    - Deploy a given image tag of the listed containers
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Deploy without naming the version
    - Deploy, stop or restart anything else
    - Change configuration or environment variables
    - Delete anything
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego roll-back-bad-release.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# The production services the agent may roll back.
application_ids := {"REPLACE_WITH_API_APPLICATION_ID", "REPLACE_WITH_WEB_APPLICATION_ID"}
container_ids := {"REPLACE_WITH_WORKER_CONTAINER_ID"}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_production
allow if deploy_application_version
allow if deploy_container_version

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, project and environment by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read production: services, status, deployment history and logs.
read_production if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == production_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Deploy a given commit of an application. The commit must be named in the request.
deploy_application_version if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	input.request.path[2] in application_ids
	input.request.path[3] == "deploy"
	count(input.request.path) == 4
	count(input.request.body.git_commit_id) > 0
}

# Deploy a given image tag of a container. The tag must be named in the request.
deploy_container_version if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "container"
	input.request.path[2] in container_ids
	input.request.path[3] == "deploy"
	count(input.request.path) == 4
	count(input.request.body.image_tag) > 0
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |
| `application_ids` | the applications the agent may roll back |
| `container_ids` | the containers the agent may roll back (leave the set empty if you have none) |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token for a rollback agent on production: read production except environment variables, and deploy a named commit of the api and web applications or a named image tag of the worker container. Nothing else.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
We deployed a new version of the "api" application in the "production"
environment of the Qovery project "shop" 10 minutes ago.

Check the logs and the deployment status. If the error rate is clearly
higher than before the deployment, roll back:
find the last commit that was deployed and healthy in the deployment history,
deploy that commit, and check that the service is healthy again.

Report what you saw, what you rolled back to, and the commit that caused it.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- The policy cannot know whether a commit is older than the current one. It allows deploying any named commit or tag of the listed services, so the agent could also deploy a newer version. Keep tests and code review on your main branch.
- Qovery already rolls back automatically when new pods fail to start, with the [RollingUpdate strategy](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/strategies). This agent handles the other case: the new version starts, but behaves badly.

# Test on a copy of production
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/test-on-production-clone

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that clones production into a sandbox project, runs tests on the copy and deletes it, and cannot change production.

A test agent that clones production into a sandbox project, runs end-to-end tests on the copy, and deletes it. It can do anything inside the sandbox project. Production is read only, and the copy can only land in the sandbox, on the non-production cluster.

**Level:** Change. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Clones the production environment into the sandbox project, on the non-production cluster.
2. Deploys the copy and runs the end-to-end tests against it.
3. Reports the results.
4. Deletes the copy.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, projects, environments and clusters by name
    - Read the production environment, except environment variables
    - Clone production into the sandbox project, on the non-production cluster, as a non-production environment
    - Deploy, change, test and delete anything inside the sandbox project
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Deploy, change or delete anything in production
    - Clone production into another project, onto another cluster, or as a production environment
    - Clone or move anything from the sandbox into production
    - Read or change production environment variables
    - Delete the sandbox project itself
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego test-on-production-clone.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# A project and a cluster dedicated to test copies.
sandbox_project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_SANDBOX_PROJECT_ID"
sandbox_cluster_id := "REPLACE_WITH_NON_PRODUCTION_CLUSTER_ID"

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_production
allow if clone_production
allow if manage_sandbox

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, projects, environments and clusters by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "cluster"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
		["api", "project", sandbox_project_id],
		["api", "project", sandbox_project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read production configuration and status, except environment variables.
read_production if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == production_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Clone production, only into the sandbox project, on the non-production cluster,
# and never as a production environment.
clone_production if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path == ["api", "environment", production_environment_id, "clone"]
	input.request.body.project_id == sandbox_project_id
	input.request.body.cluster_id == sandbox_cluster_id
	input.request.body.mode != "PRODUCTION"
}

# Do anything inside the sandbox project: deploy the copy, run tests, change it, delete it.
# Cloning or moving out of the sandbox is excluded, so nothing can land in production.
manage_sandbox if {
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == sandbox_project_id
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id != null
	not "clone" in input.request.path
	not "moveToProject" in input.request.path
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project that holds production |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |
| `sandbox_project_id` | a project that holds only test copies |
| `sandbox_cluster_id` | a cluster that does not run production |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token for a test agent: read production except environment variables, clone production only into the sandbox project on the non-production cluster, and do anything inside the sandbox project. No change to production.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
Run the end-to-end tests on a copy of production.

1. Clone the "production" environment of the Qovery project "shop" into the
   project "sandbox", on the cluster "non-prod", as a DEVELOPMENT environment.
   Name it "e2e-<today's date>".
2. Deploy the copy and wait until every service is running.
3. Run `npm run test:e2e` with BASE_URL set to the copy's URL.
4. Report the results, then delete the copy.

Do not change anything in production.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- A clone copies the configuration, not the data: Qovery-managed databases in the copy start empty. Seed them in the test if you need data.
- A clone copies environment variables. Before the first run, check that no variable of the copy points to a production database or a production external service.
- The same policy works for other jobs on a copy, for example testing a database version upgrade before a human runs it in production.

# Patch a security issue
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/patch-security-issue

> An API Policy Token example for an agent that tests a security fix on a copy of production, then deploys the patched commit, and cannot change production configuration or secrets.

A security agent that fixes a vulnerable dependency or base image, tests the fix on a copy of production, and then deploys the patched commit to production. In production it can only deploy a named commit of the listed applications.

**Level:** Change. See all the [agent policy examples](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/policy-examples/overview).

## What the agent does

1. Fixes the vulnerability in the code or the Dockerfile, on a branch (in your Git provider).
2. Clones production into the sandbox project and deploys the patched branch on the copy.
3. Runs the tests on the copy, then deletes it.
4. Deploys the patched commit to production and checks the service is healthy.

## What the policy allows

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="The agent can" icon="check">
    - Find the organization, projects, environments and clusters by name
    - Read the production environment, except environment variables
    - Clone production into the sandbox project, on the non-production cluster
    - Deploy, change, test and delete anything inside the sandbox project
    - Deploy a named commit of the listed production applications
  </Card>
  <Card title="The agent cannot" icon="xmark">
    - Change production configuration or environment variables
    - Redeploy, stop or delete anything in production
    - Deploy an application that is not listed
    - Clone or move anything from the sandbox into production
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Anything the policy does not allow is refused with `401 Unauthorized`.

## The policy

Copy it, then replace each `REPLACE_WITH_...` value with a real ID from your organization.

```rego patch-security-issue.rego
default allow := false

organization_id := "REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"
project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_ID"
production_environment_id := "REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENT_ID"

# A project and a cluster dedicated to test copies.
sandbox_project_id := "REPLACE_WITH_SANDBOX_PROJECT_ID"
sandbox_cluster_id := "REPLACE_WITH_NON_PRODUCTION_CLUSTER_ID"

# The production applications the agent may patch.
application_ids := {"REPLACE_WITH_API_APPLICATION_ID", "REPLACE_WITH_WEB_APPLICATION_ID"}

allow if cli_lookup
allow if read_production
allow if clone_production
allow if manage_sandbox
allow if deploy_patched_version

# Let the Qovery CLI find the organization, projects, environments and clusters by name.
cli_lookup if {
	input.request.method == "GET"
	input.request.path in {
		["api", "organization"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "project"],
		["api", "organization", organization_id, "cluster"],
		["api", "project", project_id],
		["api", "project", project_id, "environment"],
		["api", "project", sandbox_project_id],
		["api", "project", sandbox_project_id, "environment"],
	}
}

# Read production configuration and status, except environment variables.
read_production if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == production_environment_id
	not "environmentVariable" in input.request.path
}

# Clone production, only into the sandbox project, on the non-production cluster.
clone_production if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path == ["api", "environment", production_environment_id, "clone"]
	input.request.body.project_id == sandbox_project_id
	input.request.body.cluster_id == sandbox_cluster_id
	input.request.body.mode != "PRODUCTION"
}

# Do anything inside the sandbox project: deploy the patched copy, test it, delete it.
# Cloning or moving out of the sandbox is excluded, so nothing can land in production.
manage_sandbox if {
	input.qovery_metadata.project_id == sandbox_project_id
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id != null
	not "clone" in input.request.path
	not "moveToProject" in input.request.path
}

# Deploy the patched commit of a production application. Nothing else in production.
deploy_patched_version if {
	input.request.method == "POST"
	input.request.path[1] == "application"
	input.request.path[2] in application_ids
	input.request.path[3] == "deploy"
	count(input.request.path) == 4
	count(input.request.body.git_commit_id) > 0
}
```

| Value | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| `organization_id` | your organization |
| `project_id` | the project that holds production |
| `production_environment_id` | the production environment |
| `sandbox_project_id` | a project that holds only test copies |
| `sandbox_cluster_id` | a cluster that does not run production |
| `application_ids` | the production applications the agent may patch |

You can copy the IDs from the Console URL, or list them with `qovery project list`, `qovery environment list` and `qovery application list`.

## Create the token

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="With the coding agent">
    In a session signed in as an organization Owner or Admin, ask:

    ```
    /qovery-policy-token for a security patch agent: read production except environment variables, clone production only into the sandbox project on the non-production cluster, do anything inside the sandbox project, and deploy a named commit of the api and web applications in production. No other change to production.
    ```

    The `qovery-policy-token` skill finds the IDs, writes a policy like the one above, tests it locally and against the API, then creates the token.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="In the Console">
    1. Open your organization settings, then **Token API**.
    2. In **Policy API Token**, click **Add new**.
    3. Enter a name and a description, and paste the policy with your IDs.
    4. Copy the token (`sk-qov-01-...`). It is shown once.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Prompt for the agent

The agent runs with the [Qovery Agent Skills](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/agent-skills) and the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that supports skills. Give it the token through the environment, never in the prompt:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="sk-qov-01-..."
```

Then give the agent its task:

```
The base image of the "api" application has a critical vulnerability
(CVE-2026-1234 in openssl). Fix it and ship it.

1. Update the Dockerfile to a patched base image on a new branch, and push it.
2. Clone the "production" environment of the Qovery project "shop" into the
   project "sandbox", on the cluster "non-prod". Point the copy's "api"
   application to your branch, deploy it, and run `npm test` and `npm run test:e2e`.
3. If the tests pass, delete the copy, merge the branch, and deploy the merged
   commit to the "api" application in production.
4. Check that production is healthy and report the commit you deployed.

Do not change any production setting or environment variable.
```

Every call the agent makes appears in the [audit logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/audit-logs) as `policy:<token-id>:<token-name>`.

## Good to know

- The policy allows deploying any named commit of the listed applications. Protect your main branch with code review if a human must approve the code itself.
- A clone copies environment variables. Check that the copy does not point to a production database before the first run.
- To release to a small part of production first, you need a canary setup in your application or your ingress. The policy does not change how a deploy is rolled out.

    ```hcl
    resource "qovery_aws_credentials" "my_aws_credentials" {
      organization_id = "<organizationId>"
      name            = "my-aws-credentials"
      role_arn        = "<roleArn>"

      organization_id = "<organizationId>"
      credentials_id  = qovery_aws_credentials.my_aws_credentials.id
      name            = "my-cluster"
      cloud_provider  = "AWS"
      region          = "us-east-2"
    }
    ```

#### Check it worked

List the clusters of your organization:

```bash
qovery cluster list
```

Your cluster shows the status `DEPLOYED` once the installation ends. A status that ends with `ERROR`, or `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, means it failed: see [Logs](#logs). With the API, `GET /organization/{organizationId}/cluster/{clusterId}/status` returns the same value in `status`.

### Managed Cluster by Qovery vs Self-Managed

Qovery offers two deployment models for your Kubernetes clusters:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Qovery-Managed Cluster" icon="wand-magic-sparkles">
    **Zero Configuration**

    Qovery creates and manages your Kubernetes cluster in your cloud account. Automated setup, updates, and scaling.

    ✅ Full automation
    ✅ 15-30 minute setup
    ✅ Best practices built-in
    ✅ Auto-scaling (with Karpenter on AWS)
    ✅ Automatic Kubernetes upgrades
    ✅ Monitoring and alerting included

  </Card>

  <Card title="Self-Managed Cluster (BYOK)" icon="server" href="https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok">
    **Full Control**

    Connect your existing Kubernetes cluster to Qovery. You manage the cluster infrastructure, Qovery manages your application deployments.

    ✅ Use existing clusters
    ✅ Custom configurations
    ✅ Compliance requirements
    ✅ Multi-tenant setups
    ✅ Your upgrade schedule
    ✅ Bring your own tools

  </Card>
</CardGroup>

#### Comparison

| Feature                       | Qovery-Managed                   | Self-Managed (BYOK)              |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **Setup Time**                | 15-30 minutes                    | 10-15 minutes (existing cluster) |
| **Infrastructure Management** | Fully automated by Qovery        | You manage infrastructure        |
| **Kubernetes Upgrades**       | Automatic, tested by Qovery      | You control timing and process   |
| **Auto-scaling**              | Built-in (Karpenter on AWS)      | You configure                    |
| **Monitoring**                | Included                         | You provide                      |
| **Cost**                      | Infrastructure + Qovery platform | Infrastructure + Qovery platform |
| **Customization**             | Standard configurations          | Full control                     |
| **Best For**                  | Teams wanting automation         | Teams with specific requirements |

<Info>
  For production workloads, we recommend **Qovery-Managed clusters** for their
  automated updates, built-in best practices, and reduced operational overhead.
  Choose **BYOK** if you have specific compliance requirements or existing
  cluster investments.
</Info>

### Overview

Once your cluster is created, the cluster card displays comprehensive information about your cluster's configuration and health:

**Cluster Details:**

- Deployed nodes and their current statuses
- Instance type configuration (min/max instances)
- Reserved resources: CPU, memory, and disk capacity
- Current Kubernetes version with upgrade warnings if applicable
- Last deployment timestamp and status
- Karpenter nodepool grouping (if using Karpenter)
- Per-node resource allocation

<Frame>
  <img
    src="/images/configuration/clusters/cluster-overview.png"
    alt="Cluster Overview"
  />
</Frame>

### Workloads

The **Workloads** tab of a cluster shows how much CPU and memory the pods running on the cluster have requested, per environment and per service. The data comes from the live cluster metrics: if the metrics are unavailable, the tab displays a message instead.

- **CPU and Memory bars**: each bar shows the requested resources against the cluster capacity. It is split into the top environments, the other environments, the cluster system pods, and the remaining available capacity.
- **Environments table**: lists each environment with its namespace, number of pods, and the CPU and memory it requests, along with its share of the cluster. Click the CPU or memory column header to change the sort order.
- **Services**: expand an environment row to list its services, and click a service to open its page.
- **Cluster system**: groups the pods that are not linked to a Qovery service, by namespace.

### Statuses

Qovery tracks cluster health using two status categories:

#### Cluster Statuses

| Status                                                                           | Description                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| <Icon icon="circle-check" iconType="solid" color="green" /> **Running**          | Cluster is healthy and operational        |
| <Icon icon="triangle-exclamation" iconType="solid" color="yellow" /> **Warning** | Minor issues detected, requires attention — for example an [AWS quota warning](#aws-quota-warnings) |
| <Icon icon="circle-xmark" iconType="solid" color="red" /> **Error**              | Critical issues, intervention required    |
| <Icon icon="circle" iconType="regular" color="gray" /> **Status unavailable**    | Cluster unreachable or offline            |

#### Deployment Statuses

| Status                        | Description                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **Deployment Queued**         | Deployment is waiting in the queue                |
| **Deploying**                 | Deployment is currently in progress               |
| **Last Deployment Failed**    | The most recent deployment encountered errors     |
| **Last Deployment Succeeded** | The most recent deployment completed successfully |

#### AWS Quota Warnings

On AWS clusters, when Karpenter cannot create new nodes because an AWS service quota has been reached, the cluster status becomes **Warning** and a yellow callout is shown on the cluster overview. The callout reports:

- the **quota name** (or code) that was hit,
- the **impacted resource**,
- a **message** describing the issue,
- a **suggested action** — typically requesting an AWS quota increase, then retrying or waiting for the cluster to scale again.

While the warning is active, the cluster-status indicator shown next to your services (on the service overview) reads **Quota issue** instead of the generic warning label. The warning clears automatically once new nodes can be scheduled again; it may remain visible for a short time after the last occurrence.

### Performing Actions on Clusters

Available cluster operations and their cloud provider compatibility:

| Action      | AWS | Azure | GCP | Scaleway | Description                                                  |
| ----------- | --- | ----- | --- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Update**  | ✅  | ✅    | ✅  | ✅       | Redeploy cluster after configuration changes                 |
| **Stop**    | ✅  | ✅    | ✅  | ✅       | Temporarily pause cluster (provider charges may still apply) |
| **Restart** | ✅  | ✅    | ✅  | ✅       | Resume a stopped cluster                                     |
| **Delete**  | ✅  | ✅    | ✅  | ✅       | Permanently remove cluster                                   |

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Console">
To perform an action:

1. Navigate to your cluster page
2. Click the action dropdown menu
3. Select the desired action
4. Track progress through cluster logs
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="CLI and API">
    You need the [Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview), signed in with `qovery auth`.

    ```bash
    CLUSTER_NAME="REPLACE_WITH_CLUSTER_NAME"

    # Update: redeploy the cluster after configuration changes
    qovery cluster deploy -n "$CLUSTER_NAME" --watch

    # Stop the cluster
    qovery cluster stop -n "$CLUSTER_NAME" --watch

    # Upgrade to the next Kubernetes version available for the cluster
    qovery cluster upgrade -n "$CLUSTER_NAME" --watch
    ```

    To delete a cluster, call `DELETE /organization/{organizationId}/cluster/{clusterId}`. The `deleteMode` query parameter selects the deletion option described below: `DEFAULT`, `DELETE_CLUSTER_AND_QOVERY_CONFIG` or `DELETE_QOVERY_CONFIG`:

    ```bash
    ORGANIZATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_ORGANIZATION_ID"  # from qovery organization list --json
    CLUSTER_ID="REPLACE_WITH_CLUSTER_ID"  # from qovery cluster list

    qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/cluster/$CLUSTER_ID?deleteMode=DEFAULT" --method DELETE
    ```

    Run `qovery cluster list` to follow the status of the cluster.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Terraform">
    Set the `state` attribute of `qovery_cluster`: `DEPLOYED` deploys it, `STOPPED` stops it, and `READY` does not deploy it. Run `terraform apply`. Remove the resource and apply to delete the cluster.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

#### Updating a Cluster

Redeploys your cluster after making configuration changes through the Qovery Console or API.

#### Stopping a Cluster

Temporarily pauses your cluster to reduce costs.

<Warning>
  Some cloud provider charges may continue even when the cluster is stopped
  (e.g., storage, reserved IPs, load balancers).
</Warning>

#### Restarting a Cluster

Resumes a stopped cluster and redeploys all services.

#### Deleting a Cluster

Permanently removes your cluster. You have three deletion options:

1. **Default (Recommended)**: Complete cleanup
   - Deletes all Qovery-managed resources
   - Removes cloud provider infrastructure
   - No residual costs

2. **Delete on cloud provider and Qovery configuration**: Manual database handling
   - Deletes cluster from cloud provider
   - Removes Qovery configuration
   - Requires manual database cleanup

3. **Delete Qovery configuration only**: Keep cloud resources
   - Removes Qovery management only
   - Cloud infrastructure continues running
   - Continue managing manually in cloud console

<Warning>
  Cluster deletion is **permanent and irreversible**. Ensure you have backups
  before proceeding.
</Warning>

#### Additional Actions

**Audit Logs:**

- Access complete cluster activity history
- Track configuration changes and deployments
- Available for compliance and troubleshooting

**Cluster ID:**

- Retrieve unique cluster identifier
- Required for API operations and support tickets

**Kubeconfig:**

- Download Kubernetes configuration file
- Enable direct kubectl access
- Use for advanced debugging and management

From the CLI, run `qovery cluster kubeconfig --cluster-id "<clusterId>"`. Add `--read-only` for a read-only kubeconfig.

<Warning>
  **Security Best Practice**: Kubeconfig provides cluster-admin access. Store
  securely and never commit to version control.
</Warning>

## Deployments

Each cluster has its own **Deployments** tab that lists its past deployments, most recent first — each with its status, timestamp, duration, and who or what triggered it. Select a deployment to open its logs. This is the same [deployment history](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/history) available on environments and services, applied to the cluster itself.

A cluster deployment run with the **Dry-run** option enabled — a checkbox in the cluster update dialog that previews the changes without applying them — is tagged with a **Dry run** badge in the list.

<Info>
Bookmarked links to the previous cluster logs URL are automatically redirected to the **Deployments** tab.
</Info>

## Custom Domain and Wildcard TLS

By default, Qovery assigns a subdomain under one of its managed domains (randomly assigned) to your cluster services. However, Let's Encrypt rate limits may affect certificate issuance.

To use your own custom domain with wildcard TLS certificates, Qovery supports **Cloudflare** and **AWS Route53** integration.

### Cloudflare Setup

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create Cloudflare API Token">
    1. Log into your Cloudflare account
    2. Go to **My Profile** → **API Tokens**
    3. Click **Create Token**
    4. Use the **Edit zone DNS** template or create a custom token
    5. Grant these permissions:
       - Zone → DNS → Edit
       - Zone → Zone → Read
    6. Set Zone Resources to include your domain
    7. Create and copy the token
  </Step>

  <Step title="Contact Qovery Support">
    Contact Qovery Support via your usual channel (in-app chat, Slack, or email) with the following information:
    - Your cluster ID
    - Your domain name (e.g., `example.com`)
    - Your Cloudflare API token
    - Your Cloudflare account email

    The Qovery team will configure the integration for you.

  </Step>

  <Step title="Verify DNS">
    Once configured, Qovery will automatically manage DNS records in your Cloudflare account
  </Step>
</Steps>

### AWS Route53 Setup

<Steps>
  <Step title="Create AWS IAM Credentials">
    1. Log into your AWS Console
    2. Navigate to **IAM** → **Users**
    3. Create a new user or select an existing one
    4. Attach the policy with these permissions:
       ```json
        {
          "Version": "2012-10-17",
          "Statement": [
            {
              "Effect": "Allow",
              "Action": [
                "route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets",
                "route53:ListResourceRecordSets",
                "route53:ListTagsForResources"
              ],
              "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/*"
              ]
            },
            {
              "Effect": "Allow",
              "Action": [
                "route53:ListHostedZones",
                "route53:ListHostedZonesByName"
              ],
              "Resource": [
                "*"
              ]
            },
            {
              "Effect": "Allow",
              "Action": "route53:GetChange",
              "Resource": "arn:aws:route53:::change/*"
            }
          ]
        }
       ```
    5. Create and save the **Access Key ID** and **Secret Access Key**
  </Step>

  <Step title="Get Hosted Zone ID (Optional)">
    1. In AWS Console, go to **Route53** → **Hosted zones**
    2. Select your domain
    3. Copy the **Hosted Zone ID** (format: `Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ`)

    <Info>
    The Hosted Zone ID is optional. If not provided, Qovery will auto-detect it.
    </Info>

  </Step>

  <Step title="Contact Qovery Support">
    Contact Qovery Support via your usual channel (in-app chat, Slack, or email) with the following information:
    - Your cluster ID
    - Your domain name (e.g., `example.com`)
    - Your AWS Access Key ID
    - Your AWS Secret Access Key
    - Your AWS region (e.g., `us-east-1`)
    - Your Hosted Zone ID (optional)

    The Qovery team will configure the integration for you.

  </Step>

  <Step title="Verify DNS">
    Once configured, Qovery will automatically create and manage DNS records in your Route53 hosted zone
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
  The interface and configuration options may evolve. Both **Cloudflare** and **AWS Route53**
  are supported. Additional DNS providers will be added in future releases.
</Info>

## AWS Account Cleanup

If cluster deletion fails or leaves resources behind, you can manually clean up using AWS Console tags.

### Manual Cleanup Steps

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open AWS Console">

  </Step>

<Step title="Search for Qovery Resources">
  1. Select **All supported resource types** 2. Add tag filter: `ClusterId` or
  `QoveryCluster` 3. Search for resources
</Step>

  <Step title="Review and Delete">
    1. Review the list of tagged resources
    2. Manually delete each resource through AWS Console
    3. Common resources to check:
       - EC2 instances
       - EKS clusters
       - VPCs and networking components
       - Load balancers
       - EBS volumes
       - Security groups
  </Step>
</Steps>

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is a cluster?">
    A cluster is a group of computing resources (nodes) that work together to run your applications. Learn more in our [Basic Concepts](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/basic-concepts) guide.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do I need a cluster?">
    Clusters provide several key benefits:

    - **Kubernetes orchestration**: Automatic container management, scaling, and healing
    - **Disaster recovery**: Built-in redundancy and failover capabilities
    - **Auto-scaling**: Automatically adjust resources based on demand
    - **Environment isolation**: Separate development, staging, and production workloads
    - **Multi-region deployment**: Deploy applications closer to your users

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What instance types are available?">
    Instance availability varies by cloud provider:

    **AWS**: 400+ instance types available
    - General purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, storage optimized, GPU instances
    - Supports both x86_64 and ARM architectures (Graviton)

    **Scaleway**: Multiple instance ranges
    - From cost-effective shared instances to dedicated high-performance options
    - x86_64 architecture

    **GCP**: GKE auto-pilot
    - Fully managed node provisioning
    - Automatic optimization based on workload requirements
    - x86_64 architecture

    **Azure**: Various VM series
    - Multiple performance tiers and specialized workloads
    - x86_64 architecture

    <Info>
    Architecture compatibility: Ensure your container images support your chosen architecture (x86_64 or ARM).
    </Info>

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How does Qovery handle Kubernetes upgrades?">
    Qovery follows a careful upgrade process:

    1. **Testing period**: Each new Kubernetes version undergoes 1 month of internal testing
    2. **Rollout**: After testing, updates roll out to customers over 3 weeks
    3. **Manual upgrades**: Option available for customers who want to upgrade immediately

    <Warning>
    **Never upgrade Kubernetes manually** through your cloud provider console. This can cause incompatibilities with Qovery components. Always use Qovery-managed upgrades.
    </Warning>

    You'll receive notifications when new versions are available for your clusters.

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What happens when vulnerabilities are discovered?">
    Security is our main concern. When vulnerabilities surface:

    1. **Rapid identification**: Continuous monitoring of security databases
    2. **Impact assessment**: Evaluate severity and affected systems
    3. **Mitigation solutions**: Develop and test patches
    4. **Customer communication**: Transparent notifications with recommended actions
    5. **Deployment assistance**: Guided remediation process

    Critical security patches may be applied automatically after customer notification.

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What is a mirroring registry?">
    A mirroring registry is a private container registry that caches images from public registries, providing:

    - Faster image pulls (cached locally)
    - Protection against rate limits
    - Improved reliability and availability
    - Better control over image versions

    Learn more in our [Image Mirroring documentation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring).

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why does my cluster show 'unavailable' status?">
    An unavailable status can occur due to:

    **Common Causes:**
    - Cluster manually stopped through cloud provider
    - Cloud provider outage or service disruption
    - Network connectivity issues
    - Accidental deletion of critical resources
    - Control plane issues

    **Troubleshooting Steps:**
    1. Check cloud provider status page for outages
    2. Verify cluster hasn't been manually stopped in cloud console
    3. Review Qovery cluster logs for error messages
    4. Check cloud credentials are still valid
    5. Contact Qovery support if issue persists

    <Warning>
    Always manage clusters through Qovery Console to avoid status inconsistencies. Manual changes in cloud provider consoles can cause unexpected behavior.
    </Warning>

  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Cluster Advanced Settings
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/cluster-advanced-settings

> Fine-tune your Kubernetes cluster infrastructure with advanced configuration options

## Overview

Cluster Advanced Settings allow you to fine-tune infrastructure-level parameters for your Qovery-managed Kubernetes clusters. These settings provide granular control over networking, logging, security, resource allocation, and cloud provider-specific features.

## Cloud Provider Availability

Settings are tagged with their supported cloud providers:

<CardGroup cols={4}>
  <Card title="AWS" icon="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg">
    Amazon Web Services
  </Card>
  <Card title="GCP" icon="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg">
    Google Cloud Platform
  </Card>
  <Card title="Azure" icon="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg">
    Microsoft Azure
  </Card>
  <Card title="Scaleway" icon="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg">

## Configuring Cluster Advanced Settings

### Via Qovery Console (Recommended)

The easiest way to configure cluster advanced settings is directly from the Qovery Console:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Navigate to Cluster Settings">
    Go to your cluster page and click on **Settings**
  </Step>

  <Step title="Open Advanced Settings">
    In the settings menu, select **Advanced Settings**
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Settings">
    Browse and configure the advanced settings you need. Settings are organized by category for easy navigation.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Save and Redeploy">
    Click **Save** and redeploy your cluster for changes to take effect
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/configuration/clusters/cluster-advanced-settings-console.png" alt="Cluster Advanced Settings in Console" />
</Frame>

<Tip>
Use the **"Show only overridden settings"** toggle to filter and view only the settings you've customized from their default values.
</Tip>

<Warning>
After updating cluster advanced settings, you must **redeploy the cluster** for changes to take effect.
</Warning>

### Via Qovery API

You can also configure advanced settings using the Qovery API:

```bash
curl -X PATCH "https://api.qovery.com/cluster/{cluster_id}/advancedSettings" \
  -H "Authorization: Token YOUR_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "loki.log_retention_in_week": 24,
    "nginx.hpa.min_number_instances": 3,
    "database.postgresql.deny_any_access": false,
    "database.postgresql.allowed_cidrs": ["10.0.0.0/16"]
  }'
```

### Via Terraform

Use the [Qovery Terraform Provider](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview) to manage cluster advanced settings as code, with the `advanced_settings_json` attribute of the `qovery_cluster` resource:

```hcl
resource "qovery_cluster" "my_cluster" {
  organization_id = var.organization_id
  credentials_id  = var.aws_credentials_id
  name            = "production-cluster"
  cloud_provider  = "AWS"
  region          = "us-east-1"

  advanced_settings_json = jsonencode({
    "loki.log_retention_in_week"          = 24
    "nginx.hpa.min_number_instances"      = 3
    "nginx.controller.enable_client_ip"   = true
    "database.postgresql.deny_any_access" = false
    "database.postgresql.allowed_cidrs"   = ["10.0.0.0/16"]
  })
}
```

Only list the settings you override. Removing a key from `advanced_settings_json` does not reset the setting: set it to its default value instead.

## Cluster sizing

<a id="cluster-profile"></a>

### cluster.profile

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg" alt="GCP" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `string`

**Description:** Defines the cluster sizing profile, which determines the default resource allocation and performance characteristics of the cluster.

<Info>
  Choosing a larger profile may incur higher costs but provides better performance and capacity for workloads.
  Here are detailed insights to help you choose the right profile:
  - `Small`: Suitable for development, testing, or small-scale applications with low resource demands.
    * 3-5 nodes | 12-20 vCPUs | 24-40 GB RAM | ~50-100 pods
    * Node size: 2-4 vCPUs, 4-8 GB RAM per node
    * Use cases: Development, staging, small internal tools
  - `Medium`: A balanced option for moderate workloads, suitable for most production applications.
    * 6-10 nodes | 48-80 vCPUs | 96-160 GB RAM | ~200-400 pods
    * Node size: 4-8 vCPUs, 8-16 GB RAM per node
    * Use cases: Small to medium production apps, multi-tenant dev environments
  - `Large`: Designed for high-traffic applications or workloads requiring significant resources.
    * 11-20 nodes | 176-320 vCPUs | 352-640 GB RAM | ~500-1000 pods
    * Node size: 8-16 vCPUs, 16-32 GB RAM per node
    * Use cases: Enterprise production applications, microservices architectures
  - `ExtraLarge`: Ideal for enterprise-level applications with intensive resource needs and 
    high availability requirements.
    * 20+ nodes | 400+ vCPUs | 800+ GB RAM | 1000+ pods
    * Node size: 16-32+ vCPUs, 32-64+ GB RAM per node
    * Use cases: Large-scale production, ML/AI workloads, intensive data processing
</Info>

**Valid values:** `Small`, `Medium`, `Large`, `ExtraLarge`

**Default Value:** `Medium`

## Logs

<a id="aws-cloudwatch-eks-logs-types"></a>

### aws.cloudwatch.eks_logs_types

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `array of strings`

**Description:** EKS control plane log types exported to CloudWatch. Select any subset of the valid values, or use an empty list (`[]`) to disable exports. Redeploy the cluster for changes to take effect.

**Valid values:** `api`, `audit`, `authenticator`, `controllerManager`, `scheduler`

**Default Value:** `["api", "audit", "authenticator", "controllerManager", "scheduler"]`

<a id="aws-cloudwatch-eks-logs-retention-days"></a>

### aws.cloudwatch.eks_logs_retention_days

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

**Description:** Maximum retention days in CloudWatch for EKS logs.

**Valid values:** 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 14, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922, 3288, 3653

**Default Value:** `90`

<a id="aws-vpc-enable-s3-flow-logs"></a>

### aws.vpc.enable_s3_flow_logs

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `boolean`

**Description:** Enable flow logs on the cluster VPC and store them in an S3 bucket. VPC flow logs capture information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in your VPC.

**Use Case:** Required for compliance frameworks (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, HIPAA) that mandate network traffic logging. Also useful for security investigations and troubleshooting connectivity issues.

**Default Value:** `false`

<a id="aws-vpc-flow-logs-retention-days"></a>

### aws.vpc.flow_logs_retention_days

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

**Description:** Set the number of retention days for flow logs. Set to `0` for unlimited retention.

**Default Value:** `365`

<a id="aws-vpc-enable-nat-gateway-secondary-eip"></a>

### aws.vpc.enable_nat_gateway_secondary_eip

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `boolean`

**Description:** Enable a secondary Elastic IP (EIP) per NAT Gateway. When enabled, each of the 3 NAT Gateways in your VPC receives an additional EIP, doubling the number of outbound public IP addresses from 3 to 6. This is useful when your workloads interact with external services that have IP-based rate limits — more IPs means higher aggregate limits.

**Default Value:** `false`

<Warning>
Enabling this setting creates 3 additional Elastic IPs in your AWS account. Each EIP incurs standard AWS charges. This setting only takes effect when the cluster uses NAT Gateways. Before enabling, verify that your AWS account has sufficient EIP quota (default is 5 per region). You can check and request an increase in the AWS Service Quotas console.
</Warning>

<a id="loki-log-retention-in-week"></a>

### loki.log_retention_in_week

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg" alt="GCP" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

**Description:** Maximum retention period (in weeks) for application logs collected by Loki and displayed in the Qovery console log viewer. Retention is enforced both at the Loki compactor level and via object storage lifecycle policies.

**Use Case:** Increase for compliance requirements or debugging long-running issues. Decrease to save storage costs on the underlying object storage bucket.

**Default Value:** `12` (84 days)

<a id="loki-deployment-mode"></a>

### loki.deployment_mode

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg" alt="GCP" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `enum (single_binary, simple_scalable)`

**Description:** Loki deployment topology. `single_binary` runs Loki as a single pod; `simple_scalable` splits it into separate write, read, and backend components for larger clusters.

**Use Case:** Switch to `simple_scalable` when the cluster ingests more logs than a single Loki pod can handle. Keep the default for small to medium clusters.

**Default Value:** `single_binary`

<a id="loki-single-binary-cpu-request-m"></a>

### loki.single_binary.cpu_request_m

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg" alt="GCP" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

## DNS

<a id="dns-coredns-extra-config"></a>

### dns.coredns.extra_config

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `string`

**Description:** Additional configuration to add to CoreDNS. This can be used to customize DNS resolution rules on the cluster. The value is appended to the default CoreDNS Corefile.

**Use Case:** Forward specific domains to internal DNS servers (split-horizon DNS), resolve private hosted zones, or add custom caching rules.

**Default Value:** `null`

**Examples:**

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Forward to internal DNS">
    Route queries for your internal domain to a private DNS server:

    ```corefile
    corp.internal:53 {
        errors
        cache 30
        forward . 10.0.0.2
    }
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Forward to public resolver">
    Use Google Public DNS for a specific domain:

    ```corefile
    example.com:53 {
        errors
        cache 30
        forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
    }
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Image Registry

<a id="registry-image-retention-time"></a>

### registry.image_retention_time

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

**Description:** Allows you to specify an amount in seconds after which images in the default registry are deleted.

<Info>
Changing this setting will only affect new ECR repositories created after the change. Existing repositories will not be affected.
</Info>

**Default Value:** `31536000` (1 year)

<a id="aws-ecr-enable-pull-through-cache"></a>

### aws.ecr.enable_pull_through_cache

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `boolean`

**Description:** Cache the public ECR images used by Qovery-managed infrastructure components in the private ECR registry of the cluster's AWS account and region. This reduces NAT Gateway traffic generated when nodes pull system images from `public.ecr.aws`.

When enabled, Qovery:

- Configures an Amazon ECR pull through cache rule for `public.ecr.aws` under the `qovery-ecr-public` repository prefix.
- Rewrites public ECR image references in Qovery-managed infrastructure Helm charts to use the private regional ECR registry.
- Grants EKS worker and Karpenter node roles the permissions required to populate the cache on the first pull.
- On a VPC managed by Qovery, creates the `ecr.api` and `ecr.dkr` interface VPC endpoints. Image layers use the S3 gateway endpoint.
- On your existing VPC, checks at each cluster deployment that the VPC endpoints you created are in place (see below).

<Warning>
This setting is available only for Qovery-managed EKS clusters that use Karpenter. On a VPC managed by Qovery, the cluster must use NAT Gateways: the setting is not supported for clusters without NAT Gateways.
</Warning>

#### Clusters deployed on your existing VPC

When the cluster uses your existing VPC, you own its network, so Qovery does not create the VPC endpoints. Without them, the cache still works but image pulls keep going through your NAT Gateway, so they cost as much as before. Create the following in the cluster VPC:

- `ecr.api` and `ecr.dkr` interface endpoints with private DNS enabled, whose security groups accept TCP 443 from the node subnets.
- An S3 gateway endpoint attached to the route tables of the node subnets. Image layers are served from Amazon S3.

The node subnets are the EKS subnets of the cluster, plus its private subnets when nodes are created in private subnets. Follow [Use the ECR Pull Through Cache on Your Existing VPC](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/aws/ecr-pull-through-cache-existing-vpc) for the step-by-step setup.

These prerequisites can only be checked when the cluster is deployed, not when the setting is saved. Qovery checks them at each cluster deployment. If one is missing, the deployment goes through every step and then ends in error, listing what is missing. Qovery components still use the cache, but their traffic goes through the NAT Gateway until the endpoints are in place.

<Info>
Cached images expire 90 days after they are imported into the private ECR registry. If an expired image is requested again, Amazon ECR imports it again from the public registry. Enabling this setting adds private ECR storage and VPC interface endpoint charges to the AWS account, while reducing NAT Gateway processing charges for public ECR pulls.
</Info>

See [Amazon ECR pull through cache rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/pull-through-cache.html) for details about how Amazon ECR populates and refreshes cached images.

**Default Value:** `false`

<a id="registry-mirroring-mode"></a>

### registry.mirroring_mode

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `string`

**Description:** Allows you to specify the [image mirroring mode](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring) to be used for each image deployed on this cluster.

**Valid values:**
- `Service` — each service gets its own mirror repository (`qovery-mirror-{service_id}`). Provides better isolation but creates more repositories. Works on **all** cluster types.
- `Cluster` — all services in the cluster share a single mirror repository (`qovery-mirror-cluster-{cluster_id}`). Fewer repositories, but requires registry lifecycle policy support for automated image cleanup.
- `Disabled` — images are not mirrored: pods pull them directly from the registry of each container or job, with its credentials. Only available on **Scaleway Kapsule**. See [Disable Mirroring on Scaleway Kapsule](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring#disable-mirroring-on-scaleway-kapsule) for requirements and limits.

<Warning>
`Cluster` mode is only available on cluster types that support registry lifecycle policies: **EKS**, **GKE**, **AKS** (and their self-managed variants). It is not supported on DOKS, Scaleway Kapsule, or full self-managed clusters.
</Warning>

<Note>
A change to `registry.mirroring_mode` applies to each service on its next deployment. Redeploying the cluster is not required.
</Note>

**Default Value:** `Service`

<a id="cloud-provider-container-registry-tags"></a>

### cloud_provider.container_registry.tags

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/scaleway-icon.svg" alt="Scaleway" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/gcp-icon.svg" alt="GCP" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} /> <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/azure-icon.svg" alt="Azure" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `Map<String, String>`

**Description:** Add additional tags on the cluster dedicated registry.

**Default Value:** `{}`

**Example:**
```json
{
  "cloud_provider.container_registry.tags": {
    "Environment": "Production",
    "Team": "Platform"
  }
}
```

## Network - Load Balancer

<a id="aws-eks-enable-alb-controller"></a>

### aws.eks.enable_alb_controller

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20"  style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `boolean`

**Description:** Enable the AWS ALB controller to manage the load balancer for the cluster.

<Warning>
Enabling this feature will create a 10 min max downtime on your application's public access (time to delete, replace and propagate DNS of the new load balancer).
</Warning>

**Use Case:** For custom VPCs (Qovery Managed VPC does not require these), you need to add labels to subnets: `kubernetes.io/role/elb=1` on public subnets, `kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1` on private subnets, and `kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>=shared` on all subnets.

**Default Value:** `true`

<a id="aws-eks-alb-controller-replicas"></a>

### aws.eks.alb_controller.replicas

**Cloud Provider:** <img src="/images/logos/cloud-providers/aws-icon.svg" alt="AWS" width="20" style={{display: "inline", verticalAlign: "middle", marginRight: "4px"}} />

**Type:** `integer`

**Description:** Sets AWS ALB controller number of replicas. For production clusters, it's recommended to have at least 2 replicas for high availability.

**Default Value:** `2`

<a id="aws-eks-alb-controller-vpa-vcpu-min-in-milli-cpu"></a>
