# Qovery-Managed Scaleway Kapsule
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/scaleway/managed

> Connect your Scaleway account and create a Kapsule cluster managed by Qovery, then edit its settings, network and static IP for egress traffic.

## Creating a Scaleway Kapsule Cluster

### Connect Your Scaleway Account

Qovery needs API credentials to manage resources in your Scaleway account. We use a secure API key approach with granular permissions.

### Generate API Key

<Steps>
  <Step title="Access IAM Console">
    1. Log into [Scaleway Console](https://console.scaleway.com)
    2. Click your profile/organization name in the top-right
    3. Select **Identity and Access Management (IAM)**

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/scaleway-credentials/iam-menu.png" alt="Scaleway IAM menu" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create Application">
    1. Navigate to **Applications** tab
    2. Click **+ Create application**
    3. Name it: `qovery-manager` or similar
    4. Description: "Qovery cluster management"
    5. Click **Create application**

    <Tip>
    Applications help organize API keys by purpose. You can reuse this application for multiple clusters.
    </Tip>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Generate API Key">
    1. Click on your newly created application
    2. Go to **API keys** tab
    3. Click **+ Generate API key**
    4. Description: "Qovery cluster access"
    5. Select **Object Storage preferred Project** (your main project)
    6. Click **Generate API key**

    <Warning>
    **Save these credentials immediately!** The secret key is only shown once and cannot be retrieved later.
    </Warning>

    You'll see:
    - **Access key ID**: `SCWxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`
    - **Secret access key**: `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`

    Copy both to a secure location.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Permissions">
    1. Go to **Policies** tab in IAM
    2. Click **+ Create policy**
    3. Name it: `qovery-permissions`
    4. Click **Add rule** for each of these permission sets:

    **Required Permissions:**
    - **Containers** - Full access (for Kapsule management)
    - **Network Services** - Full access (for VPC, Load Balancers)
    - **Compute** - Full access (for instances)
    - **Storage** - Full access (for persistent volumes)
    - **VPC** - Full access (for networking)
    - **IAM** - Read only (`IAMReadOnly`, to check the permissions of the API key before deploying a cluster)

    **Optional Permissions:**
    - **VPC Gateway** - Full access (required if you want to use the [Static IP for egress traffic](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/scaleway/managed#static-ip-for-egress-traffic) feature)

    5. Under **Principal**, attach this policy to your application
    6. Click **Create policy**

    <Info>
    These permissions allow Qovery to fully manage your Kubernetes infrastructure, including creating instances, configuring networking, and managing storage.
    </Info>

    <Info>
    **Why IAM read access?** Before deploying a cluster, Qovery reads the policies attached to its API key to check that they grant the permission sets required by the features enabled on the cluster, for example **VPC Gateway** full access when Static IP for egress traffic is enabled. A missing permission is reported when the deployment starts, instead of failing midway through the infrastructure provisioning. `IAMReadOnly` gives list and read access to the users, groups, applications, policies, and API keys of your Organization. It does not allow Qovery to create, modify, or delete any of them.
    </Info>

    <Tip>
    `IAMReadOnly` is an Organization-level permission set, while the other permission sets apply to your project. Add it in a separate rule and select it under **Organization management** instead of **Resource management**.
    </Tip>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Gather Required IDs">
    You'll need these identifiers:

    **Organization ID:**
    1. Go to **Organization Settings**
    2. Copy the **Organization ID** (format: `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`)

    **Project ID:**
    1. Go to your **Project Dashboard**
    2. Click **Project settings**
    3. Copy the **Project ID** (format: `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`)

    <Tip>
    Keep these IDs handy - you'll need them when configuring Qovery.
    </Tip>
  </Step>
</Steps>

### Add Credentials to Qovery

<Steps>
  <Step title="Start Cluster Creation">
    1. Go to [Qovery Console](https://console.qovery.com)
    2. Go to your organization overview and click on the **Clusters** tab
    3. Click **Create Cluster**
    4. Select **Scaleway** as the cloud provider
  </Step>

  <Step title="Enter Credentials">
    Provide the information you gathered:
    - **Access Key ID**: Your Scaleway access key
    - **Secret Access Key**: Your Scaleway secret key
    - **Organization ID**: Your Scaleway organization ID
    - **Project ID**: Your Scaleway project ID

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/scaleway-credentials/create-credentials.png" alt="Enter Scaleway credentials in Qovery Console" />
    </Frame>

    Click **Next** to validate the credentials.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Verify Connection">
    Qovery will test the credentials and verify it can access your Scaleway account.

    <Info>
    If validation fails, double-check your API key has all required permissions attached via the policy.
    </Info>
  </Step>
</Steps>

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What permissions does Qovery need?">
    Qovery requires these Scaleway permissions to manage your infrastructure:
    - **Containers**: Create and manage Kapsule Kubernetes clusters
    - **Network Services**: Configure Load Balancers, DNS, and Public Gateways
    - **Compute**: Provision and manage instances for node pools
    - **Storage**: Create and manage Block Storage volumes for persistent data
    - **VPC**: Configure Private Networks, Security Groups, and network routing
    - **IAM** (read only): Check that the API key has the permissions required by your cluster before deploying it

    One additional permission is needed for optional features:
    - **VPC Gateway**: Required only if you enable the [Static IP for egress traffic](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/scaleway/managed#static-ip-for-egress-traffic) feature

    These permissions are applied via IAM policies attached to your API key's application.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use a custom IAM policy?">
    Yes! You can create a custom IAM policy with more restrictive permissions. However, ensure it includes all the resource types needed for managing Kapsule, networking, compute, and storage. Missing permissions may cause deployment failures.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I rotate credentials?">
    To rotate Scaleway credentials:
    1. In Scaleway Console, go to **IAM** → **Applications**
    2. Find your application (e.g., `qovery-manager`)
    3. Go to **API keys** tab
    4. Click **+ Generate API key** to create a new key
    5. Update credentials in Qovery Console
    6. Wait 24 hours to ensure all systems use new keys
    7. Delete the old API key in Scaleway Console
    8. Set a reminder to rotate again in 90 days
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What are the credential formats?">
    - **Access Key ID**: Starts with `SCW` followed by alphanumeric characters
    - **Secret Access Key**: UUID format (xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx)
    - **Organization ID**: UUID format
    - **Project ID**: UUID format

    All UUIDs use the standard 8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal format.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

### Create the Cluster

<Steps>
  <Step title="Select Scaleway as Hosting Mode">
    Click on `Scaleway` as hosting mode and then `Qovery Managed` option.

    In the `Create Cluster` window enter:

    * **Cluster name**: enter the name of your choice for your cluster.
    * **Description**: enter a description to identify better your cluster.
    * **Production cluster**: select this option if your cluster will be used for production.
    * **Region**: select the geographical area in which you want your cluster to be hosted.
    * **Credentials**: select one of the existing cloud provider credentials or [create new credentials](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/scaleway#step-1-create-scaleway-credentials).

    To confirm, click `Next`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Set Resources">
    In the `Set Resources` window, select:

    * **Instance type**: select the type of [worker nodes](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#what-is-a-cluster) you want to deploy to your cluster.
    * **Node auto-scaling**: define the minimum and the maximum number of worker nodes that your cluster can run. The lowest number is the number of worker nodes running on your infrastructure at any time, while the highest number is the maximum number of worker nodes that can automatically be deployed as traffic grows. Please note that a minimum of 3 worker nodes is required to deploy your Kapsule cluster.
    * **Control plane type**: select the type of control plane managing your cluster. [Click here to know more](https://www.scaleway.com/en/docs/kubernetes/reference-content/kubernetes-control-plane-offers/)

    <Warning>
    Instance type selection from your Qovery Console has direct consequences on your cloud provider's bill. While Qovery allows you to switch to a different instance type whenever you want, it is your sole responsibility to keep an eye on your infrastructure costs, especially when you want to upsize.

    Please be aware that changing the instance type or disk size might cause a downtime for your service.

    For an overview of the instance types each cloud provider offers, see **What instance types are available?** in the [Clusters FAQ](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#faq).

    Also, before downsizing, you need to ensure that your applications will still have enough resources to run correctly.
    </Warning>

    To confirm, click `Next`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure Network">
    In the `Configure Network` window, configure your cluster networking options:

    * **Static IP for egress traffic**: Enable this option if your applications need to connect to external services that require IP allowlisting. When enabled, your cluster will use a fixed public IP address for all outbound traffic.
    * **NAT Gateway type**: Select the appropriate gateway size based on your expected outbound traffic requirements:
      - **VPC-GW-S** (Up to 100 Mbps): Small development environments, low traffic
      - **VPC-GW-M** (Up to 1 Gbps): Standard production workloads
      - **VPC-GW-L** (Up to 3 Gbps): High-traffic applications
      - **VPC-GW-XL** (Up to 10 Gbps): Very high-traffic, enterprise workloads

    <Info>
    The Static IP feature is useful when connecting to external databases, third-party APIs, or enterprise services that require IP allowlisting. See [Scaleway Public Gateway documentation](https://www.scaleway.com/en/docs/network/vpc/concepts/#public-gateways) for more details.
    </Info>

    To confirm, click `Next`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Create and Install">
    In the `Ready to install your cluster` window, check that the services needed to install your cluster are correct.

    You can now press the `Create and Install` button.

    Your cluster is now displayed in your organization settings, featuring the `Installing...` status (orange status). Once your cluster is properly installed, its status turns to green and you will be able to deploy your applications on it.

    You can follow the execution of the action via the cluster status and/or by accessing the [Cluster Logs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#logs)
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Managing your Cluster Settings

To manage the settings of an existing cluster:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open Qovery Console">
    Open your [Qovery Console](https://console.qovery.com).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Navigate to Cluster Page">
    On your organization overview, go to the **Clusters** tab.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Access Cluster Settings">
    Click on your cluster card and go to the **Settings** tab.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Below you can find a description of each section

### General

The `General` tab allows you to define high-level information on your cluster:

|Item|Description|
|--------------|---------------------------|
|Cluster Name|To edit the name of your cluster.|
|Description|To enter or edit the description of your cluster.|
|Production Cluster|To enter or edit the production flag of your cluster.|

### Credentials

Here you can manage here the cloud provider credentials associated with your cluster.

If you need to change the credentials:
- generate a new set of credentials on your cloud provider ([Procedure for Scaleway account](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/scaleway#step-1-create-scaleway-credentials))
- create the new credential on the Qovery by opening the drop-down and selecting "New Credentials"

Once created and associated, you need to [update your cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/clusters#updating-a-cluster) to apply the change.

### Mirroring registry

In this tab, you will see that a container registry already exist (called `registry-{$UIID}`).
This is your cloud provider container registry used by Qovery to manage the deployment of your applications by mirroring the docker images.

The credentials configured on this registry are the one used to create the cluster. But you can still update them if you prefer to manage them separately (dedicated pair of creds just to access the registry).

Check [this link](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring) for more information.

To have pods pull images directly from the registry they are stored in (for example GitHub Container Registry) instead of this registry, see [Disable Mirroring on Scaleway Kapsule](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/deployment/image-mirroring#disable-mirroring-on-scaleway-kapsule).

### Network

In the **Network** tab, you can configure advanced networking options for your Scaleway Kapsule cluster.

#### Static IP for Egress Traffic

By default, Scaleway clusters use random public IPs for outbound traffic. Enable the **Static IP for egress traffic** option if your applications need to connect to external services that require IP allowlisting.

<Warning>
  This feature requires the **VPCGatewayFullAccess** IAM permission set in addition to the standard Qovery permissions. Make sure it is added to your Qovery IAM policy before enabling this option. See the [Scaleway IAM Permissions Reference](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/security-and-compliance/scaleway-iam-permissions#vpcgatewayfullaccess-%E2%80%94-static-ip-for-egress-traffic) for details.
</Warning>

**When to use:**
- External databases with IP-based authentication
- Third-party APIs requiring IP allowlisting
- Enterprise services with strict security policies
- Partner integrations that need stable source IPs

**To enable:**
1. Navigate to the **Network** tab in your cluster settings
2. Enable **Static IP for egress traffic**
3. Select the appropriate NAT Gateway type based on your traffic requirements
4. Click **Update** to apply the changes

**NAT Gateway Types:**

| Gateway Type | Bandwidth | Use Case |
|--------------|-----------|----------|
| **VPC-GW-S** | Up to 100 Mbps | Small development environments, low traffic |
| **VPC-GW-M** | Up to 1 Gbps | Standard production workloads |
| **VPC-GW-L** | Up to 3 Gbps | High-traffic applications |
| **VPC-GW-XL** | Up to 10 Gbps | Very high-traffic, enterprise workloads |

<Info>
Once enabled, all outbound traffic from your cluster will use the assigned static IP address instead of random IPs. Choose the gateway size that matches your expected outbound traffic volume. For detailed specifications and pricing, see [Scaleway Public Gateway documentation](https://www.scaleway.com/en/docs/network/vpc/concepts/#public-gateways) and [pricing](https://www.scaleway.com/en/pricing/network/).
</Info>

# Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK)
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok

> Connect an EKS, GKE or Kapsule cluster with the Qovery Operator, or try it on local k3s with qovery demo up. Other clusters you run use the Qovery CLI.

The Qovery Operator connects a Kubernetes cluster you already run to Qovery. You create the cluster in the Qovery Console, install the Operator once with Helm, and Qovery then installs and updates the Qovery stack on the cluster from a platform profile.

<Info>
The Qovery Operator installation is in Preview and available on every Qovery plan, including Free. [Current limitations](#current-limitations) lists what the Preview does not cover yet. It supports EKS, GKE and Scaleway Kapsule. Every other cluster you run, such as Azure AKS, k3s or an on-premise cluster, uses the [installation with the Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy). See [Which installation to use](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups#which-installation-to-use).
</Info>

<Tip>
Want to try Qovery before you connect a real cluster? Run `qovery demo up`. It creates a local k3s cluster with Docker and installs the Qovery Operator on it in a few minutes. This local demo is the only k3s setup that uses the Operator. See [Local cluster for development](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/docker).
</Tip>

## How it works

- Qovery never stores the kubeconfig of your cluster. You install the Operator yourself, with your own `kubectl` and `helm` access.
- The Operator runs in the `qovery` namespace. It opens an outbound connection to Qovery and runs the Qovery deployments as Kubernetes Jobs inside your cluster. These Jobs run with `cluster-admin` rights.
- The platform profile of the cluster lists the components Qovery installs and their settings. The list can grow as Qovery adds components, and the profile page of the cluster always shows the current one. Today, the profile holds:
  - **Qovery stack**: the Qovery agent, the shell agent, the Qovery priority classes and the Qovery StorageClasses used by container databases and service storage (for example `aws-ebs-gp3-0`, `gcp-pd-ssd`, `scw-sbv-ssd-0`). A StorageClass that already exists with the same name is kept as it is, and Qovery does not change the default StorageClass of the cluster.
  - **Log infra**: Loki and Alloy, for application logs.
  - **Gateway API**: Envoy Gateway, which exposes your applications.
  - **DNS and certificates**: cert-manager and ExternalDNS, for the Qovery-provided domain and its TLS certificates.
- Application images are built inside your cluster and pushed to a registry Qovery creates from your cloud credential: Amazon ECR on AWS, Artifact Registry on GCP, Scaleway Container Registry on Scaleway.

## Prerequisites

<Check>A Qovery organization, on any plan including Free</Check>
<Check>A running Kubernetes cluster on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) or Scaleway (Kapsule), with Kubernetes 1.31 or later</Check>
<Check>`kubectl` access to the cluster with `cluster-admin` rights and `helm` on your machine, only to install the Operator once. Later Operator updates go through Qovery.</Check>
<Check>At least one node with 4 vCPU and 8 GiB of memory free, for example an 8 vCPU node. Each build runs in a builder pod that requests the CPU and RAM of the service [build settings](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#build-settings), 4000m and 8 GiB by default, so a 4 vCPU node cannot host it.</Check>
<Check>A cluster that does not already run cert-manager, ExternalDNS or Envoy Gateway</Check>
<Check>A default StorageClass (`kubectl get storageclass`), unless Loki stores logs in object storage. Since EKS 1.30, EKS creates `gp2` without marking it as the default.</Check>
<Check>On EKS, the Amazon EBS CSI driver add-on with its IAM role. The Loki `pvc` storage, container databases and service storage all use it. GKE and Kapsule include their CSI driver.</Check>
<Check>The cluster can create a public load balancer for a Service of type `LoadBalancer`, which Envoy Gateway uses to expose your applications. On EKS, the public subnets must carry the `kubernetes.io/role/elb=1` tag.</Check>
<Check>For services with autoscaling, metrics-server (`kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io`). GKE and Kapsule include it. On EKS, add the `metrics-server` add-on.</Check>
<Check>A working cluster DNS (CoreDNS) that resolves public names</Check>
<Check>Outbound internet access from the cluster to Qovery and to public container registries</Check>
<Check>A Qovery cloud credential for the provider of the cluster. You can create it during the installation.</Check>

Before you install, run `qovery cluster preflight` with your kubeconfig pointing to the cluster. It checks most of these prerequisites and the components that must not already run on the cluster, changes nothing, and tells you how to fix each problem. If Loki will store logs in object storage (`s3`, `gcs` or `s3Compatible`), add `--loki-object-storage`, since the default check expects a default StorageClass for the `pvc` storage. See [Supported cluster setups](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups).

The [preflight checks](#preflight-checks) verify several of these prerequisites again at each deployment of the cluster.

### Credential permissions

The cloud credential lets Qovery create the cluster registry, push the images it builds and clean them up. It does not need access to the Kubernetes cluster itself.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="AWS">
    The credential only needs Amazon ECR. Do not use the Qovery CloudFormation stack offered in the credential form, because it grants the permissions of a cluster managed by Qovery.

    **Recommended: an IAM role that Qovery assumes through STS**

    1. Create an IAM role with this trust policy, where `<ORGANIZATION_ID>` is the ID of your Qovery organization, shown in the Console URL (`console.qovery.com/organization/<ORGANIZATION_ID>/…`):

       ```json
       {
         "Version": "2012-10-17",
         "Statement": [
           {
             "Effect": "Allow",
             "Principal": {
               "AWS": [
                 "arn:aws:iam::283389881690:role/qovery-deployer",
                 "arn:aws:iam::283389881690:user/qovery-deployer"
               ]
             },
             "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
             "Condition": {
               "StringLike": {
                 "sts:ExternalId": "<ORGANIZATION_ID>:*"
               }
             }
           }
         ]
       }
       ```

       Qovery sends the external ID `<organization id>:<cluster id>`, and `<organization id>:00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` when it checks the credential. The `<ORGANIZATION_ID>:*` condition accepts both.

    2. Attach this permissions policy to the role, where `<ACCOUNT_ID>` is your AWS account ID and `<CLUSTER_REGION>` the region of the cluster. Keep the `us-east-1` statement even if the cluster runs in another region, because Qovery checks the credential there. The `ClusterRegistry` statement only covers repositories whose names start with `z` or `qovery-mirror-`, the prefixes Qovery uses (`z<first 8 characters of the cluster ID>-…`). Do not give your own repositories in that region these prefixes.

       ```json
       {
         "Version": "2012-10-17",
         "Statement": [
           {
             "Sid": "EcrLogin",
             "Effect": "Allow",
             "Action": "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
             "Resource": "*"
           },
           {
             "Sid": "CredentialCheck",
             "Effect": "Allow",
             "Action": "ecr:DescribeRepositories",
             "Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-1:<ACCOUNT_ID>:repository/*"
           },
           {
             "Sid": "ClusterRegistry",
             "Effect": "Allow",
             "Action": [
               "ecr:DescribeRepositories",
               "ecr:CreateRepository",
               "ecr:PutLifecyclePolicy",
               "ecr:TagResource",
               "ecr:ListTagsForResource",
               "ecr:DescribeImages",
               "ecr:BatchDeleteImage",
               "ecr:DeleteRepository",
               "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
               "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload",
               "ecr:UploadLayerPart",
               "ecr:CompleteLayerUpload",
               "ecr:PutImage",
               "ecr:BatchGetImage",
               "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer"
             ],
             "Resource": [
               "arn:aws:ecr:<CLUSTER_REGION>:<ACCOUNT_ID>:repository/z*",
               "arn:aws:ecr:<CLUSTER_REGION>:<ACCOUNT_ID>:repository/qovery-mirror-*"
             ]
           }
         ]
       }
       ```

    3. Set the maximum session duration of the role to at least 4 hours, for example 8 hours. Qovery requests 4-hour sessions, and with the default of 1 hour the credential check fails with `DurationSeconds exceeds the MaxSessionDuration`.

       ```bash
       aws iam update-role --role-name <ROLE_NAME> --max-session-duration 28800
       ```

    4. In the credential form, set **Authentication type** to **Assume role via STS**, skip the CloudFormation step, then fill in **Name** and **Role ARN**.

    **Alternative: access keys**

    Create an IAM user with the same permissions policy, then set **Authentication type** to **Static credentials** in the credential form and paste its access key and secret key.

    **For both**

    - The EKS node role must be able to pull from ECR in the same account, for example with the `AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly` managed policy.
    - The policy above covers only ECR. If Terraform services use the cluster credentials, add the permissions they need to the same role or user.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="GCP">
    Qovery creates, reads and deletes Artifact Registry repositories and images in the project of the credential, in the cluster region. The setup commands shown in the credential form grant the permissions of a cluster managed by Qovery. For BYOK, grant only the roles below.

    - Grant the service account the **Artifact Registry Administrator** role (`roles/artifactregistry.admin`) on the project.
    - With a JSON key, Qovery checks the key by listing the Cloud Storage buckets of the project, so also grant a role with the `storage.buckets.list` permission, for example **Storage Bucket Viewer** (`roles/storage.bucketViewer`). A Workload Identity Federation credential does not need it.
    - With Workload Identity Federation, run the setup command of the credential form (see the [GCP cluster credentials](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/installation/gcp)), then replace the Qovery custom role it binds by the Artifact Registry role:

      ```bash
      gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding <PROJECT_ID> --member serviceAccount:<SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL> --role projects/<PROJECT_ID>/roles/qovery_role
      gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <PROJECT_ID> --member serviceAccount:<SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL> --role roles/artifactregistry.admin
      ```

      The setup command also lets the service account through the organization policy `constraints/iam.allowServiceAccountCredentialLifetimeExtension`. Keep that exception, because Qovery requests 4-hour tokens.
    - Qovery creates no image pull secret for Artifact Registry. The GKE node service account must be able to pull from Artifact Registry in the project of the credential, for example with the `roles/artifactregistry.reader` role.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Scaleway">
    Qovery creates, reads and deletes Container Registry namespaces and images in the project of the API key, in the cluster region.

    - Give the API key the **ContainerRegistryFullAccess** permission set on the project.
    - Qovery checks the key by listing the Container Registry namespaces of the `fr-par` region, whatever the cluster region.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Loki object storage

Skip this section if Loki stores logs in a persistent volume, the default.

<Warning>
Create the bucket and its identity **before you deploy the profile**, then fill in their fields on the Loki page of the profile. Choose the storage before the first deployment, because changing it later does not move the logs already stored.
</Warning>

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="AWS: S3 bucket and IAM role">
    Create the bucket in the region of the cluster, since Loki uses that region. Loki reaches the bucket through IRSA, so your EKS cluster needs an IAM OIDC provider. Create an IAM role with this permissions policy:

    ```json
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<BUCKET_NAME>"
        },
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"],
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<BUCKET_NAME>/*"
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

    And this trust policy, for the `loki` service account of the `qovery` namespace:

    ```json
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:oidc-provider/<OIDC_PROVIDER>" },
          "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
          "Condition": {
            "StringEquals": {
              "<OIDC_PROVIDER>:sub": "system:serviceaccount:qovery:loki",
              "<OIDC_PROVIDER>:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
            }
          }
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

    `<OIDC_PROVIDER>` is the OIDC issuer of the cluster without `https://`, for example `oidc.eks.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLE`. On the profile, fill in **S3 bucket name** and **Loki IAM role ARN**.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="GCP: GCS bucket and service account">
    Loki reaches the bucket through GKE Workload Identity. Enable it on the cluster and its node pools.

    1. Create the bucket and a GCP service account, and grant the service account the `roles/storage.objectAdmin` role on the bucket.
    2. Let the `loki` service account of the `qovery` namespace act as it:

       ```bash
       gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding <SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL> --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member "serviceAccount:<PROJECT_ID>.svc.id.goog[qovery/loki]"
       ```

    3. On the profile, fill in **GCS bucket name** and **GCP service account email**.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Scaleway: S3-compatible bucket">
    1. Create the bucket and an API key that can read and write it.
    2. Create the credentials Secret in the `qovery` namespace, with the keys `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. The credentials stay in your cluster and never reach Qovery.

       ```bash
       read -r -p "Access key: " S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID
       read -r -s -p "Secret key: " S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; echo
       kubectl -n qovery create secret generic loki-s3-credentials --from-literal=S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID="$S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID" --from-literal=S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="$S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
       unset S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
       ```

       Create the namespace first if the Operator is not installed yet: `kubectl create namespace qovery`.
    3. On the profile, fill in **S3-compatible bucket name**, **S3-compatible endpoint** (an `https://` URL, for example `https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud`), **S3-compatible region** (for example `fr-par`) and **S3-compatible credentials Secret** (`loki-s3-credentials`).
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Create the cluster

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the cluster creation page">
    In the Qovery Console, go to **Clusters** and create a new cluster. Under **Connect existing cluster (BYOK)**, select **AWS**, **GCP** or **Scaleway**.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/byok-operator/add-cluster.png" alt="Add cluster page with the Connect existing cluster (BYOK) section" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Fill in the general information">
    - **Cluster name**: the name of the cluster in Qovery.
    - **Production cluster**: off by default. Turn it on for a production cluster.
    - **Credentials**: select a cloud credential of the provider, or create one.
    - **Region**: the region of your cluster. On Scaleway, the list shows zones. Select a zone of the cluster region, for example `fr-par-1` for a cluster in `fr-par`.

    Click **Continue**.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/byok-operator/general-information.png" alt="Connect AWS cluster step" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure the Qovery Operator">
    Leave the settings as they are, unless you want the Operator and its Jobs pinned to specific nodes. To pin them, fill in **Node group label key** and **Node group label value** with the label of your node group or node pool. The default key is the EKS one. Use the key of your cluster:

    | Cluster | Node label key |
    | --- | --- |
    | EKS managed node group | `eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup` |
    | EKS with Karpenter | `karpenter.sh/nodepool` |
    | GKE | `cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool` |
    | Scaleway Kapsule | `k8s.scaleway.com/pool-name` |

    If those nodes are tainted, add their taints under **Node group taints to tolerate**. These settings place only the Operator and its Jobs, not the platform components. You cannot use `kubernetes.io/arch` as a key, because Qovery sets the architecture of each build itself.

    Click **Continue** and Qovery creates the cluster. It creates the registry repositories in your cloud account at the first deployment that needs them.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/byok-operator/configure-operator.png" alt="Configure Qovery Operator step" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Install the Qovery Operator">
    1. With a kubeconfig pointing to your cluster, run `qovery cluster preflight` and fix the failed checks. See [Check your cluster before you install](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups#check-your-cluster-before-you-install).
    2. Download the Helm values file `values.yaml`. It contains the credential of the cluster, so keep it private and delete it once the Operator is installed.
    3. From the folder of the values file, with a kubeconfig pointing to your cluster, run the Helm command shown in the Console.

    Keep the page open. Once the Operator connects to Qovery, the Console opens the profile of the cluster and shows the Operator status at the bottom of the profile sidebar.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/byok-operator/install-operator.png" alt="Install Qovery Operator step with the Helm values file and command" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure and deploy the platform profile">
    On the profile page, review the settings of each component. If you change a setting, click **Save and deploy**. To keep the defaults, open the **Manage deployment** menu of the cluster and click **Deploy**. Qovery installs the components of the profile through the Operator. Follow the progress in the cluster logs.

    <Tip>
    Choose the Loki storage before the first deployment. The default, `pvc`, needs a default StorageClass. Object storage (`s3` on AWS, `gcs` on GCP, `s3Compatible` on Scaleway) needs a bucket and an identity you create, see [Loki object storage](#loki-object-storage), and is required for high availability. Changing the storage later does not move the logs already stored.
    </Tip>

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/byok-operator/cluster-profile.png" alt="Profile page of a cluster connected with the Qovery Operator" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>
</Steps>

Once the deployment succeeds, you can deploy your applications on the cluster.

## Preflight checks

To check the cluster before the Operator is installed, use `qovery cluster preflight`, described in [Supported cluster setups](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups).

Before each deployment of the cluster, Qovery checks your configuration and the cluster itself. The results appear in the cluster deployment logs, under **Control-plane preflight** and **In-cluster preflight checks**, with a recommended action for each check that fails.

The checks cover:

- the Operator connection, the platform profile and its required inputs, and the DNS provider configuration;
- access to the Kubernetes API, the Kubernetes permissions of the deployment Jobs, and target namespaces still being deleted;
- the cluster DNS, and access from the cluster to Qovery, to the Helm chart registries and to the container registries;
- Helm releases, CRDs or a cert-manager installation that conflict with the profile;
- a default StorageClass, when a component of the profile needs one.

A blocking check that fails stops the deployment before Qovery changes anything in the cluster. The other checks only add a warning to the logs, and the deployment continues. Today, the checks on the Operator connection, the platform profile, its inputs and the DNS provider block, and so do Kubernetes API access and target namespaces still being deleted. The other in-cluster checks only warn.

## Current limitations

- **DNS**: applications are exposed on the domain provided by Qovery. The DNS provider of the cluster cannot be changed.
- **Observe and metrics**: Observe and the Monitoring graphs of the cluster and its services are not available on BYOK clusters yet, and Qovery installs no metrics stack on them. If you need them, tell us, since we prioritize BYOK features from customer requests.
- **Existing installations**: Qovery does not adopt an existing cert-manager, ExternalDNS or Envoy Gateway installation. Use a cluster without them. See [Components that must not already run on the cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups#components-that-must-not-already-run-on-the-cluster).
- **Removal**: deleting the cluster in Qovery does not uninstall anything from the cluster. See [Remove the cluster](#remove-the-cluster).

Need a component, a DNS provider or a cloud provider that is not covered yet? Contact Qovery Support through your usual channel: in-app chat, shared Slack or Microsoft Teams channel, or email.

## Remove the cluster

<Warning>
Deleting the cluster in Qovery removes only its Qovery configuration. The Operator and the platform keep running in your cluster, and the Envoy load balancer keeps its public IP and keeps incurring cloud costs until you uninstall the gateway releases (step 2).
</Warning>

1. In Qovery, delete the environments of the cluster, then delete the cluster.
2. Uninstall the gateway releases while `envoy-gateway` still runs:

   ```bash
   helm -n qovery uninstall qovery-cluster-gateway qovery-gateway-class
   ```

   If `envoy-gateway` is already gone, the GatewayClass keeps its finalizer. Remove it with:

   ```bash
   kubectl patch gatewayclass qovery-public-gateway --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
   ```

3. List the other releases of the `qovery` namespace with `helm -n qovery list` and uninstall each one with `helm -n qovery uninstall <release>`, `qovery-operator` last. Then delete the namespace with `kubectl delete namespace qovery`.
4. Delete the CRDs that the platform installed (Gateway API, Envoy Gateway and cert-manager), if nothing else uses them.
5. Delete the registry repositories Qovery created in your cloud account: the `z<first 8 characters of the cluster ID>-…` and `qovery-mirror-…` ECR repositories, the Artifact Registry repositories or the Scaleway Container Registry namespaces. Mirror repositories of deleted services can remain, so check for them too.
6. If Loki used object storage, delete the bucket and its identity.

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="The Operator does not connect">
    - Check that the Operator pod is running: `kubectl -n qovery get pods`.
    - Read its logs: `kubectl -n qovery logs deployment/qovery-operator --tail=100`.
    - A `gateway communication error` or `transport error` at startup is often a cluster DNS issue. Check that a Pod resolves the Qovery endpoint:

      ```bash
      kubectl -n default run qovery-dns-preflight --rm -i --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup engine.qovery.com
      ```

      The lookup must return an address. A timeout or `no servers could be reached` means the cluster DNS must be fixed first.
    - Check that the cluster can reach the internet.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Loki stays Pending">
    With the `pvc` storage, the Loki volume needs a default StorageClass and, on EKS, the EBS CSI driver. Check `kubectl get storageclass` and, on EKS, `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=aws-ebs-csi-driver`. To mark a class as default, run `kubectl annotate storageclass <NAME> storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true`, then deploy the cluster again. With object storage, Loki has no volume. Check the bucket and identity fields of the Loki page against [Loki object storage](#loki-object-storage).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="A build stays on Provisioning builder">
    No node has enough free CPU and memory for the builder pod. `kubectl -n qovery get pods` shows a `build-…` pod in `Pending`, and `kubectl -n qovery describe pod <pod>` reports `Insufficient cpu` or `Insufficient memory`. Add a node with at least 4 vCPU and 8 GiB free, or lower **CPU** and **RAM** in the [build settings](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/service-advanced-settings#build-settings) of the service.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="The credential is refused when the cluster is created">
    Qovery checks that the credential can use the registry of the provider in the cluster region before it creates anything. Compare the credential with [Credential permissions](#credential-permissions).
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Supported cluster setups for your own cluster
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups

> Qovery runs on any Kubernetes cluster: the Qovery Operator for EKS, GKE and Kapsule, the Qovery CLI for others. Check version, prerequisites and conflicts.

Qovery runs on any Kubernetes cluster. There are two ways to install it on a cluster you already run, and the provider of your cluster decides which one to use. Both are available on every Qovery plan, including Free.

To try Qovery before you connect a real cluster, run `qovery demo up`. It creates a local k3s cluster with Docker and installs the Qovery Operator on it. The table below applies to clusters you run yourself: the local demo is the only k3s setup that uses the Operator. See [Local cluster for development](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/docker).

## Which installation to use

| Your cluster | Installation | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon EKS (AWS), Google GKE (GCP) or Scaleway Kapsule | [Qovery Operator installation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok) (Preview) | You create the cluster in the Qovery Console and install the Operator once with Helm. Qovery then installs and updates its stack on the cluster. |
| Any other cluster: Azure AKS, k3s, OpenShift, Rancher, on-premise or another provider | [Installation with the Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy) | You run `qovery cluster install` with your kubeconfig pointing to the cluster. |

Both installations need **Kubernetes 1.31 or later**.

The rest of this page covers the Qovery Operator installation: the checks to run before you install, its prerequisites and the components that must not already run on the cluster.

Most failed installations come from a component that already exists on the cluster, such as cert-manager, or from a missing default StorageClass. Run the preflight first: it takes a few seconds and changes nothing on the cluster.

## Check your cluster before you install

The preflight reads your cluster with your current kubeconfig context and reports each check as `PASS`, `WARN`, `FAIL` or `SKIP`, with the fix for each problem. It needs no Qovery account and is available from Qovery CLI 1.180.0.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install the Qovery CLI">
    <Tabs>
  <Tab title="Linux">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="*nix">
        To download and install Qovery CLI on any Linux distribution:

        ```bash
        curl -s https://get.qovery.com | bash
        ```

        <Warning>
        The install script does not verify the binary's integrity. For security-sensitive environments, use the **Manual** tab to download a pinned release and verify its checksum against the official [checksums.txt](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) published with each release.
        </Warning>
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Arch Linux">
        Qovery is part of [AUR](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages) packages, so you can install it with [yay](https://github.com/Jguer/yay):

        ```bash
        yay qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on Linux manually from a [pinned release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) to ensure you control what version is installed.

        Replace `X.Y.Z` with the version you want to install:

        ```bash
        VERSION=1.180.0  # version number without the 'v' prefix
        ARCH=amd64      # use arm64 for ARM64
        ARCHIVE="qovery-cli_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"

        # Download the binary and checksums for your platform
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ARCHIVE}" -o "${ARCHIVE}"
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" -o checksums.txt

        # Verify the checksum of the downloaded file only (fails if tampered)
        grep "${ARCHIVE}" checksums.txt | sha256sum --check

        # Extract and install
        tar -xzf "${ARCHIVE}"
        mv qovery /usr/local/bin/qovery
        chmod +x /usr/local/bin/qovery
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="MacOS">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Homebrew">
        The common solution to install a command line binary on the MacOS is to use [Homebrew](https://brew.sh).

        ```bash
        # Add Qovery brew repository
        brew tap Qovery/qovery-cli

        # Install the CLI
        brew install qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Script">
        To download and install Qovery CLI from the command line:

        ```bash
        curl -s https://get.qovery.com | bash
        ```

        <Warning>
        The install script does not verify the binary's integrity. For security-sensitive environments, use the **Manual** tab to download a pinned release and verify its checksum against the official [checksums.txt](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) published with each release.
        </Warning>
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on macOS manually from a [pinned release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) to ensure you control what version is installed.

        Replace `X.Y.Z` with the version you want to install:

        ```bash
        VERSION=1.180.0  # version number without the 'v' prefix
        ARCH=amd64      # use arm64 for Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)
        ARCHIVE="qovery-cli_${VERSION}_darwin_${ARCH}.tar.gz"

        # Download the binary and checksums for your platform
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ARCHIVE}" -o "${ARCHIVE}"
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" -o checksums.txt

        # Verify the checksum of the downloaded file only (fails if tampered)
        grep "${ARCHIVE}" checksums.txt | shasum -a 256 --check

        # Extract and install
        tar -xzf "${ARCHIVE}"
        mv qovery /usr/local/bin/qovery
        chmod +x /usr/local/bin/qovery
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Windows">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Scoop">
        The classic way to install binaries on Windows is to use [Scoop](https://scoop.sh).

        ```bash
        # Add Qovery bucket
        scoop bucket add qovery https://github.com/Qovery/scoop-qovery-cli

        # Install the CLI
        scoop install qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on Windows manually by downloading the [latest release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases), and uncompress its content to `C:\Windows`.
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Docker">
    Install Docker on your local machine and run the following command:

    ```bash
    # Pull and Run the latest Qovery CLI
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:latest help
    ```

    Change `latest` by the version you want to use. For example, to use the version 0.58.4, run:

    ```bash
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:0.58.4 help
    ```

    <Info>
    `ghcr.io` is the [GitHub Container Registry](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/pkgs/container/qovery-cli).
    </Info>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Point kubectl to your cluster">
    ```bash
    kubectl config current-context
    ```

    The preflight checks this context. To check another one, pass `--context <name>` and, if needed, `--kubeconfig <path>`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Run the preflight">
    ```bash
    qovery cluster preflight
    ```

    If Loki will store logs in object storage (`s3`, `gcs` or `s3Compatible`) instead of the default `pvc` storage, add `--loki-object-storage`. Add `--json` for a machine-readable report.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Fix the failed checks">
    The command exits with status `1` when at least one check fails. A failed check would make the installation or the first deployment of the cluster fail, so fix it and run the preflight again. A warning does not block the installation but can break a feature, for example autoscaling without metrics-server.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The preflight only sends read requests and one permission review to the Kubernetes API. It creates, changes and deletes nothing, and it reads no Secret content.

### What the preflight checks

| Check | Fails when | Warns when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kubernetes API and version | The API is unreachable, or Kubernetes is older than 1.30 | Kubernetes is 1.30, or newer than 1.36 |
| cluster-admin permissions | Your kubeconfig user is not cluster-admin | |
| Node OS and architecture | No Ready Linux node with an `amd64` or `arm64` CPU | Some nodes cannot run Qovery, for example Windows nodes |
| Node size for builds | | No schedulable node has 4 vCPU and 8 GiB allocatable |
| Namespace `qovery` | The namespace is being deleted | |
| Existing Qovery CLI installation | The Helm release `qovery` of an installation with the Qovery CLI exists | |
| Existing cert-manager | cert-manager or its CRDs exist outside the Qovery installation | |
| Existing ExternalDNS | ExternalDNS runs outside the Qovery installation | |
| Existing Envoy Gateway | Envoy Gateway or its CRDs exist outside the Qovery installation | |
| Existing Gateway API CRDs | | The Gateway API CRDs were installed by another tool |
| Default StorageClass | No default StorageClass and Loki uses `pvc` storage | Several StorageClasses are marked as default |
| Amazon EBS CSI driver (AWS only) | The driver is missing and Loki uses `pvc` storage | The driver is missing and Loki uses object storage |
| Cluster DNS | The `kube-dns` Service has no ready endpoint | The `kube-dns` Service does not exist, so DNS could not be verified |
| LoadBalancer Services | | A LoadBalancer Service has no address |
| metrics-server | | The `metrics.k8s.io` API is not available |

The table describes the checks for the Qovery Operator installation. When the preflight picks the installation with the Qovery CLI (any cluster other than EKS, GKE or Kapsule, or `--install-path cli`):

- An existing cert-manager, ExternalDNS or Envoy Gateway is a warning, not a failure. `qovery cluster install` installs these components too: turn off the Qovery copy in the Helm values file it generates, or remove the existing one.
- An existing Helm release `qovery` is your CLI installation, so it passes.
- The cloud provider result tells you which installation to use and never fails.

The preflight also reports the provider of your nodes and the installation to use. This result is informational and never fails the preflight: on EKS, GKE or Kapsule it confirms the Qovery Operator installation, and on any other cluster it recommends the [installation with the Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy).

### What the preflight does not check

Some prerequisites cannot be verified without creating a resource on the cluster. Check them yourself:

- **Outbound access and public DNS from a Pod.** The lookup must return an address:

  ```bash
  kubectl -n default run qovery-dns-preflight --rm -i --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup engine.qovery.com
  ```

  This command creates a temporary Pod and deletes it when it ends.
- **Public load balancers.** The preflight only looks at LoadBalancer Services that already exist. If there are none, it reports `SKIP`. The Qovery gateway needs the cluster to create a public load balancer.
- **Free capacity.** The preflight compares the allocatable CPU and memory of each node with what a build needs. It does not know what your workloads already use.

Once the Operator is installed, Qovery runs more checks before each deployment of the cluster. See [Preflight checks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok#preflight-checks).

## Operator installation: providers and versions

| | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| Providers | Amazon EKS (AWS), Google GKE (GCP), Scaleway Kapsule |
| Kubernetes versions | 1.31 or later |
| Node operating system | Linux |
| Node CPU architectures | `amd64` and `arm64` |
| Node autoscaling | Managed node groups, node pools and Karpenter. See the node label keys in [Create the cluster](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok#create-the-cluster). |

Kubernetes 1.30 can reject part of the Gateway API CRDs that Qovery installs, and older versions lack an API they use. The preflight fails below 1.30 and warns on 1.30.

For any other cluster, such as Azure AKS, k3s or an on-premise cluster, use the [installation with the Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy).

## Operator installation: prerequisites

The full list, with the cloud credential permissions, is in [Prerequisites](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok#prerequisites). In short, the cluster needs:

- `kubectl` access with `cluster-admin` rights and `helm` on your machine, only to install the Operator once.
- At least one Linux node with 4 vCPU and 8 GiB of memory free, for the builder pods.
- A default StorageClass, unless Loki stores logs in object storage. On EKS, the Amazon EBS CSI driver add-on with its IAM role.
- The ability to create a public load balancer for a Service of type `LoadBalancer`. On EKS, the public subnets must carry the `kubernetes.io/role/elb=1` tag.
- A working cluster DNS (CoreDNS) that resolves public names.
- Outbound internet access to Qovery and to public container registries.
- metrics-server, for services with autoscaling.

## Components that must not already run on the cluster

Qovery installs these components in the `qovery` namespace and manages them. It does not take over an installation that already exists.

| Component | What Qovery installs | If it already runs on the cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cert-manager | cert-manager v1.20, Helm release `cert-manager` | Use a cluster without cert-manager, or uninstall it and its CRDs if nothing else uses it. |
| ExternalDNS | ExternalDNS for the domain provided by Qovery, Helm release `external-dns` | Use a cluster without ExternalDNS, or uninstall it if nothing else uses it. |
| Envoy Gateway | Envoy Gateway v1.9, Helm releases `envoy-gateway-crd` and `envoy-gateway`, plus the Qovery GatewayClass and Gateway in the releases `qovery-gateway-class` and `qovery-cluster-gateway` | Use a cluster without Envoy Gateway, or uninstall it and its CRDs if nothing else uses it. |
| Gateway API CRDs | The experimental channel of the Gateway API CRDs, bundle v1.6.1, from release `envoy-gateway-crd` | CRDs installed and kept up to date by another tool, such as the GKE Gateway API, a service mesh or a load balancer controller, can conflict with Qovery. On GKE, disable the Gateway API of the cluster if nothing uses it. Otherwise, contact Qovery Support before you install. |
| Existing Qovery CLI installation | | A cluster installed with `qovery cluster install` holds the Helm release `qovery`. The Qovery Operator does not take it over. Uninstall it with `helm -n qovery uninstall qovery` and remove its cert-manager, ExternalDNS and Gateway resources, or use another cluster. |

<Warning>
Uninstalling cert-manager, ExternalDNS or Envoy Gateway removes the certificates, DNS records or routes they manage. Check what depends on them before you remove them, or use a dedicated cluster for Qovery.
</Warning>

## Get help

If the preflight reports a problem you cannot fix, or you are not sure which installation fits your cluster, contact Qovery Support through your usual channel: in-app chat, shared Slack or Microsoft Teams channel, or email. Include the output of `qovery cluster preflight --json`. It contains no credential.

# Install Qovery on other Kubernetes clusters with the CLI
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy

> Install Qovery with qovery cluster install on any Kubernetes cluster other than EKS, GKE and Kapsule, such as AKS, k3s, OpenShift or an on-premise cluster.

## Overview

Qovery runs on any Kubernetes cluster. The `qovery cluster install` command of the Qovery CLI installs Qovery on a cluster you already run, such as Azure AKS, k3s, OpenShift or an on-premise cluster. You keep control of your cluster infrastructure, and Qovery manages application deployments on it.

<Info>
Use this installation for any cluster other than Amazon EKS, Google GKE and Scaleway Kapsule, for example Azure AKS, k3s or an on-premise cluster. For an EKS, GKE or Kapsule cluster, use the [Qovery Operator installation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok). See [Which installation to use](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups#which-installation-to-use).

This installation is available on every Qovery plan, including Free.
</Info>

## What Qovery Installs

`qovery cluster install` generates a Helm values file and the Helm commands that install the `qovery` chart.

<Warning>
The values file holds the credential your cluster uses to connect to Qovery. Do not commit it to version control or share it, and delete it once the installation is done.
</Warning>

The values file enables:

**Qovery components**:
- Qovery engine and cluster agent (run and track deployments)
- Qovery shell agent (terminal access to your services)

**Platform components**:
- Envoy Gateway, with the Gateway API CRDs and the Qovery GatewayClass and Gateway (exposes your applications)
- cert-manager (TLS certificates)
- ExternalDNS (domain management)
- metrics-server (autoscaling)
- Loki and Alloy (application logs)

To keep a component you already run, such as cert-manager, turn off the Qovery copy in the values file before you run the Helm commands.

## Networking Requirements

### Inbound

- **Port 443**: HTTPS traffic to applications
- **Port 80**: HTTP traffic (redirects to 443)

### Outbound

- **Qovery API**: `https://api.qovery.com`
- **Container Registries**: ECR, Docker Hub, GCR, etc.
- **Git Providers**: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket

### Load Balancer

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Cloud Load Balancer">
    Automatically provisioned by cloud provider:
    - AWS: ALB/NLB
    - GCP: Google Cloud Load Balancer
    - Azure: Azure Load Balancer
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="MetalLB (On-Premise)">
    Install MetalLB for bare metal:
    ```bash
    kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.13.12/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml

    # Configure IP pool
    cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
    apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
    kind: IPAddressPool
    metadata:
      name: first-pool
      namespace: metallb-system
    spec:
      addresses:
      - 192.168.1.240-192.168.1.250
    ---
    apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
    kind: L2Advertisement
    metadata:
      name: first-pool
      namespace: metallb-system
    spec:
      ipAddressPools:
      - first-pool
    EOF
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Storage Configuration

Ensure default storage class exists:

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: standard
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd  # Change based on your provider
parameters:
  type: pd-standard
```

For on-premise, consider:
- **NFS**: Network File System
- **Ceph**: Distributed storage
- **Local Path**: Local storage (not recommended for production)

## Troubleshooting

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Agent Not Connecting">
    **Check**:
    - Agent pods running: `kubectl get pods -n qovery`
    - Agent logs: `kubectl logs -n qovery -l app=qovery-agent`
    - Outbound internet access from cluster
    - API token is correct
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Load Balancer Pending">
    **For Cloud**: Check cloud provider quotas and permissions
    
    **For On-Premise**: Install MetalLB and configure IP pool
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Storage Issues">
    **Check**:
    - Storage class exists: `kubectl get sc`
    - Default storage class set
    - Provisioner is working
    - Sufficient storage capacity
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Local Cluster for Development
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/docker

> Run Qovery on your machine with Docker and a local k3s cluster for development and testing: prerequisites, installation, usage, limitations, and cleanup.

## Overview

Run Qovery on your local machine using Docker and k3s (lightweight Kubernetes). Perfect for development, testing, and learning without cloud costs or Docker Desktop requirements.

<Warning>
**Demo Environment Only**: This local installation is designed for demonstration and testing purposes only. It is **not intended for production use**.
</Warning>

## Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

**System Requirements:**
- **Operating System**: Linux, macOS, or Windows (WSL only)
- **CPU & Memory**: Minimum 4 CPU cores and 8GB RAM for Docker
- **Software**: Docker daemon running (Docker Desktop not required, especially on Linux), `k3d`, `helm` and `kubectl`. `qovery demo up` checks that they are installed before it starts.

<Note>
**Linux Users**: You only need Docker Engine running on your machine. Docker Desktop is not required.
</Note>

        ```bash
        ARCH=amd64      # use arm64 for Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)
        ARCHIVE="qovery-cli_${VERSION}_darwin_${ARCH}.tar.gz"

        # Download the binary and checksums for your platform
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ARCHIVE}" -o "${ARCHIVE}"
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" -o checksums.txt

        # Verify the checksum of the downloaded file only (fails if tampered)
        grep "${ARCHIVE}" checksums.txt | shasum -a 256 --check

        # Extract and install
        tar -xzf "${ARCHIVE}"
        mv qovery /usr/local/bin/qovery
        chmod +x /usr/local/bin/qovery
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Windows">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Scoop">
        The classic way to install binaries on Windows is to use [Scoop](https://scoop.sh).

        ```bash
        # Add Qovery bucket
        scoop bucket add qovery https://github.com/Qovery/scoop-qovery-cli

        # Install the CLI
        scoop install qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on Windows manually by downloading the [latest release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases), and uncompress its content to `C:\Windows`.
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Docker">
    Install Docker on your local machine and run the following command:

    ```bash
    # Pull and Run the latest Qovery CLI
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:latest help
    ```

    Change `latest` by the version you want to use. For example, to use the version 0.58.4, run:

    ```bash
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:0.58.4 help
    ```

    <Info>
    `ghcr.io` is the [GitHub Container Registry](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/pkgs/container/qovery-cli).
    </Info>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Authenticate">
    Sign in to your Qovery account (or create one if you haven't already):

    ```bash
    qovery auth
    ```

    This will open your browser to complete the authentication process.

    <Tip>
    **Running in a terminal without browser access?** Use `qovery auth --headless` instead.
    </Tip>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Set Context">
    Configure your CLI context:

    ```bash
    qovery context set
    ```

    Select your organization when prompted.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Deploy Local Cluster">
    Install a local k3s Kubernetes cluster with Qovery:

    ```bash
    qovery demo up
    ```

    This command:
    - Creates a local k3s cluster with k3d (lightweight Kubernetes in Docker)
    - Installs the Qovery Operator and Engine v2 on it and connects the cluster to your organization
    - Lets Qovery deploy its stack on the cluster, including networking and ingress
    - Checks that the Operator and the engine are running before it finishes
    - Takes approximately 5-10 minutes to complete, and shows each step with its duration

    <Warning>
    On macOS and WSL, you may be prompted for your password (`sudo`). It adds the local address `172.42.0.3` so that traffic from your machine reaches the applications on the cluster. If the address is already set, the prompt is skipped.
    </Warning>

    If the command fails, it prints an error code and a diagnostic ID. See [Troubleshooting](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/demo#troubleshooting).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Access the Console">
    Once the installation is complete, navigate to [console.qovery.com](https://console.qovery.com)

    You should see your demo cluster connected and ready to use. You can now start deploying applications!
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Using Your Local Cluster

Once your local cluster is running, you can:

- **Deploy applications** via the [Qovery Console](https://console.qovery.com)
- **Use kubectl** to interact with your local k3s cluster directly
- **Use k9s** for a terminal-based Kubernetes dashboard
- **Follow tutorials** to deploy applications locally

<Tip>
The local cluster runs entirely on your machine, making it perfect for testing and development without cloud costs.
</Tip>

## Limitations

<Warning>
Local Kubernetes is **NOT for production**:
- Single node (no high availability)
- Limited resources
- Runs only while Docker runs on your machine
- Performance limitations
</Warning>

## Cleanup

When you're finished testing, remove the local cluster:

```bash
qovery demo destroy
```

This command removes the local k3s cluster and all Qovery components from your machine.
