## Reference

From the Blueprint's [README](https://github.com/Qovery/service-catalog/blob/AWS/valkey-serverless/9/1.2.1/AWS/valkey-serverless/9/README.md).

Creates an AWS ElastiCache Serverless cache on Valkey 9. There is no node type or shard count to pick: AWS scales the cache with the load and bills the data stored and the ECPUs consumed. Traffic is encrypted in transit, data is encrypted at rest, and access goes through a password-protected user.

For a cache with a fixed node type, use the `aws-elasticache-valkey` blueprint instead.

### Connecting

Three things differ from the node-based blueprint:

- **Use a cluster-mode client.** A serverless cache always runs in cluster mode, and AWS only supports clients that speak the cluster protocol. Multi-key commands only work on keys that share a hash slot; across slots they fail with `CROSSSLOT`.
- **Two ports.** The cache serves writes and consistent reads on `6379` and replica reads on `6380`, on the same hostname. Many clients open connections to both, so the security group opens both.
- **A user name is required.** Applications authenticate as the `app` user with `valkey_password`. There is no auth token and no usable `default` user.

The `valkey_url` output carries all of it: `rediss://app:<password>@<host>:6379`. The `rediss://` scheme is correct: Valkey speaks the Redis protocol, and TLS is always on.

### Variables

#### Required

| Name | Type | Sensitive | Description |
| ---- | ---- | --------- | ----------- |
| `valkey_name` | string | | Cache name, lowercased by AWS. Must start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, and use single hyphens between them; max 32 chars. Underscores are not allowed. |

The limit is 32 characters to leave room for the suffixes of the user id (`<name>-app`) and the user group id (`<name>-users`), which ElastiCache caps at 40.

#### Credentials

| Name | Type | Sensitive | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | --------- | ------- | ----------- |
| `valkey_password` | string | yes | _generated_ | Omit and Qovery generates a 32-character alphanumeric password. To set your own: 16–128 chars, must not contain a comma, /, @, ", or spaces. |

In the Console, leaving the field blank omits it. Through the API or Terraform, omit the variable rather than sending an empty string: the platform rejects an empty variable value.

Changing `valkey_password` replaces the password in place, without touching the cache or its data. AWS takes a few minutes to apply it (close to four in testing). Applications still holding the old one must be redeployed with the new value.

#### Usage limits

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `data_storage_max_gb` | number | `0` | Most data the cache may store, in whole GB (1–5000). `0` = the AWS maximum, 5000 GB. |
| `ecpu_per_second_max` | number | `0` | Most ECPUs per second the cache may use, a whole number (1000–15000000). `0` = the AWS maximum, 15000000. |

With both at `0`, the cache scales as far as AWS allows. A cap bounds the bill as well as the capacity.

The blueprint always sends both limits, with `0` translated to the AWS maximum. A cache whose limits are removed altogether cannot be updated: AWS rejects the call with `No modifications were requested`.

#### Network

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `subnet_ids` | string | | Leave empty — derived from the Qovery cluster's ElastiCache subnet group. Set it (comma-separated, one per Availability Zone) only on a cluster with a user-provided VPC, where that lookup finds nothing. Read at creation only. |
| `security_group_ids` | string | | Leave empty for the blueprint's own security group. Set it (comma-separated ids) to attach existing groups instead; they must open 6379 and 6380 to the cluster. |
| `allowed_cidrs` | string | | Leave empty to allow the whole VPC, which covers every pod of the cluster. Set it (comma-separated IPv4 network addresses, such as `10.0.0.0/24`) to narrow the blueprint's security group. Ignored when `security_group_ids` is set. |

By default the cache is attached to the Qovery cluster network. The subnets come from the ElastiCache subnet group created at cluster bootstrap (`elasticache-<cluster vpc id>`): one subnet per Availability Zone, three at most. The security group is created by the blueprint, named `qovery-valkey-serverless-<name>`, and opens 6379–6380 to every CIDR of the VPC. It does not reuse the cluster workers security group, which opens 6379 only.

ElastiCache cannot move a serverless cache to other subnets, so `subnet_ids` is read once. A later change to the variable or to the cluster's subnet group leaves the cache where it is.

#### Backups

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `backup_retention_period` | number | `14` | Whole days to retain daily automatic snapshots (0–35). `0` disables. |
| `daily_snapshot_time` | string | `00:00` | Time of the daily snapshot (UTC), `hh24:mi`. Only used when `backup_retention_period > 0`. |

**Deleting the service deletes the cache without a final snapshot.** The AWS Terraform provider has no argument for one on a serverless cache. To keep the data, take a manual snapshot in AWS before deleting the service.

#### IAM role

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `role_arn` | string | — | Unset = use the cluster credentials directly. Set an IAM role ARN of the cluster's AWS account to assume it; cross-account roles are not supported. |

### Outputs

| Name | Sensitive | Description |
| ---- | --------- | ----------- |
| `valkey_identifier` | | ElastiCache serverless cache name |
| `valkey_host` | | Hostname to connect to, for cluster-mode clients |
| `valkey_port` | | Port of the primary endpoint (`6379`), for writes and consistent reads |
| `valkey_reader_port` | | Port of the reader endpoint (`6380`), on the same hostname |
| `valkey_username` | | Valkey user applications authenticate as (`app`) |
| `valkey_password` | yes | Password of that user (generated when the input was left empty) |
| `valkey_url` | yes | `rediss://app:<password>@<host>:<port>` on the primary endpoint |
| `valkey_arn` | | Serverless cache ARN |
| `valkey_engine_version_actual` | | Engine version actually running (incl. AWS-chosen patch) |
| `valkey_security_group_id` | | Security group created for the cache (empty when `security_group_ids` is set) |

### Access control

The blueprint creates one ElastiCache user and one user group, both on the `valkey` engine, and attaches the group to the cache:

- user `<name>-app`, user name `app`, access string `on ~* &* +@all` (every key, every pub/sub channel, every command), authenticated by password;
- user group `<name>-users`, holding that user.

Terraform manages the membership list of the group: a user added to it outside the blueprint is removed on the next deployment.

### Lifecycle ignore_changes

- `subnet_ids` — set at creation; see [Network](#network).

### Assuming an IAM role

Optional. Set the `role_arn` variable to make the blueprint assume an IAM role instead of using the configured credentials directly; leave it unset to use them as is.

- Format: `arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<name>`, with an optional path (`role/<path>/<name>`). The `aws-cn`, `aws-us-gov` and `aws-iso*` partitions are accepted too.
- The role must be in the **same AWS account** as the credentials; cross-account roles are not supported.
- The role's trust policy must allow the deploy credentials' IAM principal to assume it.
- The role itself must carry the permissions listed in [Required AWS IAM permissions](#required-aws-iam-permissions).

### Required AWS IAM permissions

> When `role_arn` is set, Terraform makes these AWS calls as the assumed role, so the permissions below belong to that role. Access to a user-provided Terraform backend, if you use one, is not covered by `role_arn`: it keeps using the deploy credentials.

Unless `role_arn` is set, the credentials used to deploy this blueprint must allow the actions below. The EC2 read actions let Terraform look up the cluster VPC and its subnets. `ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint`, the `ec2:CreateTags` that goes with it and `iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole` are the ones the AWS managed policy `AmazonElastiCacheFullAccess` grants for serverless caches: ElastiCache places a VPC endpoint in the chosen subnets.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "elasticache:CreateServerlessCache",
        "elasticache:ModifyServerlessCache",
        "elasticache:DeleteServerlessCache",
        "elasticache:DescribeServerlessCaches",
        "elasticache:CreateUser",
        "elasticache:ModifyUser",
        "elasticache:DeleteUser",
        "elasticache:DescribeUsers",
        "elasticache:CreateUserGroup",
        "elasticache:ModifyUserGroup",
        "elasticache:DeleteUserGroup",
        "elasticache:DescribeUserGroups",
        "elasticache:DescribeCacheSubnetGroups",
        "elasticache:AddTagsToResource",
        "elasticache:RemoveTagsFromResource",
        "elasticache:ListTagsForResource"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:DescribeVpcs",
        "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
        "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups",
        "ec2:DescribeAvailabilityZones",
        "ec2:CreateSecurityGroup",
        "ec2:DeleteSecurityGroup",
        "ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress",
        "ec2:RevokeSecurityGroupIngress",
        "ec2:RevokeSecurityGroupEgress",
        "ec2:CreateTags",
        "ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-service-role/elasticache.amazonaws.com/AWSServiceRoleForElastiCache",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": { "iam:AWSServiceName": "elasticache.amazonaws.com" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

| `dedicated_log_volume` | bool |  | `false` |  | Provision a dedicated EBS volume for database logs (RDS feature) |
| `role_arn` | string |  |  |  | Unset = use the cluster credentials directly. Set an IAM role ARN of the cluster's AWS account to assume it; cross-account roles are not supported. |

</Accordion>

Outputs become environment variables that other services in the environment can use. By default Qovery also creates an alias for each output, prefixed with the Blueprint's name; see [Aliases Qovery creates for outputs](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#aliases-qovery-creates-for-outputs) for the naming rules and the cases where no alias is created.

<Warning>
Secret variables and outputs are encrypted and masked in Qovery, but Terraform can also keep their values, and values derived from them, in its state. With the Qovery-managed state backend (the default), Qovery stores the state. If you use your own backend, protect it and keep state files out of version control.
</Warning>

## Reference

From the Blueprint's [README](https://github.com/Qovery/service-catalog/blob/AWS/mysql/8/3.8.1/AWS/mysql/8/README.md).

Creates an AWS RDS MySQL 8.4 instance with configurable instance class, storage, backups, maintenance window, monitoring, and network settings. Storage is encrypted by default.

A dedicated parameter group is attached with `log_bin_trust_function_creators = 1` so the master user can create triggers/stored procedures without superuser privileges.

The RDS identifier is derived from `db_name` by lowercasing and replacing underscores with hyphens (AWS requirement). The actual MySQL database name is kept as provided.

### Variables

#### Required

| Name          | Type   | Sensitive | Description                                                                                                              |
| ------------- | ------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `db_name`     | string |           | MySQL database name. Letters, digits, underscores only; must start with a letter; max 64 chars. Hyphens are not allowed. |
| `instance_class`    | string |           | RDS instance class. Default suggestion: `db.t3.micro`.                                             |
| `allocated_storage` | number |           | Allocated storage in GiB (min 20; max 65536 for gp3/io1/io2, but gp2 caps at 16384) |

Available instance classes: every RDS instance class Qovery offers for native managed PostgreSQL and MySQL — the `db.t3`, `db.t4g`, `db.m5`–`db.m8g`, `db.r5`–`db.r8g` (including `db.r5b`), `db.x2g`, `db.x2idn` and `db.x2iedn` families, with their Graviton (`g`), Intel (`i`), local-storage (`d`) and network-optimized (`n`) variants. `db.c6gd` is left out because RDS offers it only for Multi-AZ DB clusters. The full list is in `qbm.yml`.

#### Credentials

Both are optional — omit them and Qovery supplies the values, the way native managed
databases did. In the console, leaving the field blank omits it. Through the API or
Terraform, omit the variable rather than sending an empty string: the platform rejects an
empty variable value.

| Name | Type | Sensitive | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | --------- | ------- | ----------- |
| `db_username` | string |  | `qoveryadmin` | Leave empty to use qoveryadmin, the login used by native managed databases. To set your own: letters, digits, underscores; must start with a letter; max 32 chars (MySQL limit). Reserved names not allowed: admin, rdsadmin, mysql. |
| `db_password` | string | yes | _generated_ | Leave empty when creating a database and Qovery generates a 32-character alphanumeric password; when adopting an existing instance this must carry the current master password of that instance, because RDS never returns it. To set your own: 8–128 chars, must not contain /, @, ", or spaces. Changing it rotates the master password on the live instance (adopted instances: only once `manage_db_password` is true). |
| `manage_db_password` | bool |  | `false` | Adopted instances only, and one-way: once true, leave it true. Switching it on applies `db_password` to the instance, so confirm that value is the one the instance already has. Changing `db_password` then rotates it. An instance this blueprint created always owns its password. |

Changing `db_password` rotates the live instance's master password: the value is sent as a
write-only argument, triggered by a version derived from the password itself, so a change
reaches RDS and an unchanged password sends nothing.

An adopted instance does not take part until `manage_db_password` is set to true. That keeps
its import plan clean, and it has a consequence worth stating plainly: **while the flag is
false, editing `db_password` changes what the blueprint publishes without changing anything on
the instance.** Consumers pick up a credential RDS will reject. On an adopted instance, either
set the flag before touching the password, or do not touch the password at all.

Setting the flag is itself a write. Until then the version that triggers the send is null in
state, so switching it to true moves that value and applies `db_password` to the instance —
harmless when the two already agree, and an overwrite of the live password when they do not.
Confirm the stored password is the one the instance actually has before opting in.

A rotation also obeys `apply_changes_now`. Left false, RDS defers the password change to the
maintenance window while the new value is published immediately — consumers redeployed in
between cannot connect. Set `apply_changes_now` when you rotate.

Adoption (`import_identifier` set) requires both explicitly. `username` is `ForceNew` on
`aws_db_instance`, so a defaulted value would plan a replacement and destroy the live
database; and RDS never returns the master password, so a generated one would be published
as the credential without ever being applied.

#### Instance & storage

| Name                | Type   | Default       | Description                                                    |
| ------------------- | ------ | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `port`              | number | `3306`        | Database port                                                  |
| `storage_type`      | string | `gp3`         | EBS storage type: `gp2`, `gp3`, `io1`, `io2`                   |
| `storage_encrypted` | bool   | `true`        | Encrypt storage at rest                                        |
| `disk_iops`         | number | `0`           | Provisioned IOPS. Only meaningful with io1/io2 (always) or gp3 (≥400 GiB). 0 lets AWS choose the default. |

#### Network

| Name                   | Type   | Default | Description                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ------ | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `multi_az`             | bool   | `false` | Enable Multi-AZ deployment                                                                               |
| `publicly_accessible`  | bool   | `false` | Expose the database to the public internet                                                               |
| `db_subnet_group_name` | string |         | Leave empty — derived from the Qovery cluster's DB subnet group. Set it only on a cluster with a user-provided VPC, where that lookup finds nothing. |
| `security_group_ids`   | string |         | Leave empty — derived from the Qovery cluster's workers security group. Set it (comma-separated ids) only on a cluster with a user-provided VPC, where that lookup finds nothing. |

By default the instance is attached to the Qovery cluster network: the DB subnet group created at cluster bootstrap (named after the cluster VPC id) and the cluster workers security group, so pods in the cluster can reach the database out of the box. On clusters deployed into an existing VPC (user-provided network), the `ClusterId` tag lookup may not resolve; set `db_subnet_group_name` and `security_group_ids` explicitly in that case.

#### Maintenance & upgrades

| Name                           | Type   | Default               | Description                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `apply_changes_now`            | bool   | `false`               | Apply changes immediately                            |
| `allow_major_version_upgrade`  | bool   | `false`               | Allow major engine version upgrades on apply         |
| `auto_minor_version_upgrade`   | bool   | `true`                | Auto-apply minor version upgrades during maintenance |
| `preferred_maintenance_window` | string | `Tue:02:00-Tue:04:00` | Maintenance window (UTC), `ddd:hh24:mi-ddd:hh24:mi`  |

#### Backups

| Name                       | Type   | Default       | Description                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------ | ------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `preferred_backup_window`  | string | `00:00-01:00` | Daily backup window (UTC), `hh24:mi-hh24:mi` |
| `backup_retention_period`  | number | `7`           | Days to retain backups (0–35). `0` disables. |
| `skip_final_snapshot`      | bool   | `false`       | Skip final snapshot on deletion              |
| `delete_automated_backups` | bool   | `false`       | Delete automated backups when the instance is deleted. Default keeps them for `backup_retention_period` days; set true for throwaway instances |
| `copy_tags_to_snapshot`    | bool   | `true`        | Propagate instance tags to snapshots         |

Deleting the service keeps a final snapshot and the automated backups by default, and both keep
costing storage until deleted by hand: the snapshot indefinitely, the backups for
`backup_retention_period` days. For a throwaway or test instance, set both `skip_final_snapshot` and
`delete_automated_backups` to `true`. The final snapshot is named
`<cluster name>-<db name>-<YYYYMMDDhhmmss>`: `db_name` lowercased with `_` turned into `-`, the
UTC time the name was stamped, and any character AWS rejects removed (prefixed `snap-` if the
result does not start with a letter). It is stamped once at creation, so successive
create/destroy cycles of the same name do not collide.

| `monitoring_interval`                   | number | `0`                 | Enhanced monitoring interval in seconds (0 disables). Allowed values: 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60. |
| `monitoring_role_arn`                   | string |                     | IAM role ARN for enhanced monitoring. Required when `monitoring_interval > 0`. |
| `ca_cert_identifier`                    | string | `rds-ca-rsa2048-g1` | CA certificate identifier                                                      |

#### Upgrading from an earlier blueprint version

Read this before repointing a deployment at this version.

- An adopted instance now keeps running its exact live version (for example `8.0.x`) instead of
  having `engine_version` ignored. Nothing is sent to AWS for an instance whose version is unchanged.
- Deleting now keeps a final snapshot and the automated backups for services **created** on this
  version. An existing service does not change behaviour: Qovery stores every variable default when
  the service is created, so repointing it here keeps `skip_final_snapshot = true` and
  `delete_automated_backups = true`. To keep a snapshot and backups on delete, set both to `false`
  on the service. The upgrade itself adds `time_static.created` and, with those set to `false`,
  updates `skip_final_snapshot`, `delete_automated_backups` and `final_snapshot_identifier` in
  place — Terraform-only arguments, nothing is sent to AWS and the instance is not rebooted.
- For an instance this blueprint created, and for an adopted instance already opted in with
  `manage_db_password`, the first apply writes the master password once. Old state carries no record of
  what was last sent, so the value Qovery holds is applied. An instance whose password was rotated
  outside Terraform — which earlier versions of this document told you to do — is reset to the
  Qovery-held value, and applications using the out-of-band password stop connecting. Make the two agree
  before you upgrade. An adopted instance left at `manage_db_password = false` is not touched: nothing is
  sent, and an out-of-band rotation survives.
- `manage_db_password` is one-way. Setting it back to false after an adopted instance has been handed
  over leaves Terraform with a change AWS rejects as "no modifications were requested".
- Terraform moves from 1.9.7 to 1.13.3, and `1.9.7` is no longer an accepted override. State written by
  1.13.3 cannot be read by 1.9.7, so a deployment cannot be repointed at an earlier blueprint version
  once it has applied.
- From 3.6.0 the parameter group name no longer depends on the Qovery cluster name. Up to 3.5.1, renaming
  the cluster made the next apply create a new group and then fail to delete the old one, still attached
  to the instance. An existing group keeps its name and is not touched by the upgrade.

### Lifecycle ignore_changes

On the primary instance, `engine_version` is no longer ignored. Terraform requests the exact
version held in the internal `engine_version` variable, which Qovery sets on every deploy to the
live version, so an adopted `8.0.x` instance stays on `8.0.x`. With `auto_minor_version_upgrade`
enabled, AWS may still move the running minor forward; the next deploy then requests that newer
version, so Terraform never tries to go back. Read replicas inherit the primary's version.

A bare `"8.4"` is never sent to a live instance, because AWS resolves it to the region's default
minor, which upgrades an older minor and is refused on a newer one. Without the variable, an
existing instance keeps its live version (read through the `aws_db_instance` data source) and only
a new instance gets `8.4`.

A few attributes remain ignored:

- `password` — the master password moved to the write-only `password_wo`; ignoring the plain attribute stops the value left in older state reading as a removal.
- `enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports` — list type, not yet supported by the qbm.yml schema.
- `max_allocated_storage` — will turn into a managed input when the storage autoscale feature is added.

- `parameter_group_name` — an adopted instance keeps its live parameter group; the blueprint's group is applied on create.
- `name_prefix` on the parameter group — groups created before 3.6.0 were prefixed with the cluster name. Ignoring it means a cluster rename, or the upgrade to 3.6.0, never replaces the group. New groups are prefixed with the database name only.

### Assuming an IAM role

Optional. Set the `role_arn` variable to make the blueprint assume an IAM role instead of using the configured credentials directly; leave it unset to use them as is.

- Format: `arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<name>`, with an optional path (`role/<path>/<name>`). The `aws-cn`, `aws-us-gov` and `aws-iso*` partitions are accepted too.
- The role must be in the **same AWS account** as the credentials; cross-account roles are not supported.
- The role's trust policy must allow the deploy credentials' IAM principal to assume it.
- The role itself must carry the permissions listed in [Required AWS IAM permissions](#required-aws-iam-permissions).

### Required AWS IAM permissions

> When `role_arn` is set, Terraform makes these AWS calls as the assumed role, so the permissions below belong to that role. Access to a user-provided Terraform backend, if you use one, is not covered by `role_arn`: it keeps using the deploy credentials.

Unless `role_arn` is set, the credentials used to deploy this blueprint must allow the actions below. The RDS actions target instances in any region you deploy to; EC2 read actions are needed so Terraform can look up the default VPC, subnets, and security groups when none are explicitly configured.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "rds:CreateDBInstance",
        "rds:DeleteDBInstance",
        "rds:ModifyDBInstance",
        "rds:DescribeDBInstances",
        "rds:CreateDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:DeleteDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:ModifyDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:DescribeDBParameterGroups",
        "rds:DescribeDBParameters",
        "rds:DescribeDBSubnetGroups",
        "rds:DescribeDBSecurityGroups",
        "rds:AddTagsToResource",
        "rds:RemoveTagsFromResource",
        "rds:ListTagsForResource"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:DescribeVpcs",
        "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
        "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups",
        "ec2:DescribeAvailabilityZones"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

When `monitoring_interval > 0`, the supplied `monitoring_role_arn` must be assumable by RDS (`monitoring.rds.amazonaws.com` trust relationship) and grant the `AmazonRDSEnhancedMonitoringRole` managed policy. The identity that applies the blueprint (the assumed role when `role_arn` is set) also needs `iam:PassRole` on that role, to hand it to RDS. It is not in the policy above because it only applies when monitoring is enabled; add this statement, with the resource set to your `monitoring_role_arn`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "iam:PassRole",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<monitoring-role-name>"
}
```

| `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled` | bool |  | `false` |  | Off keeps the current CloudWatch log exports. On also exports the PostgreSQL log, replicas included; turning it off again does not stop it. |
| `option_group_name` | string |  |  |  | Empty = AWS default. |
| `db_parameters` | string |  |  |  | Empty = keep the current group (one this blueprint made is deleted). Else JSON, e.g. \{"log_connections":"1"\}; static params need apply_method pending-reboot. |
| `deletion_protection` | bool |  | `false` |  | Prevent the database from being deleted via TF or the API |
| `iam_database_authentication_enabled` | bool |  | `false` |  | Enable IAM database authentication |
| `dedicated_log_volume` | bool |  | `false` |  | Provision a dedicated EBS volume for database logs (RDS feature) |
| `read_replica_count` | number |  | `0` |  | Same-region read replicas (0 disables; max 15), e.g. for analytics tools. Requires backup_retention_period &gt; 0. |
| `read_replica_instance_class` | string |  |  |  | Empty = same as the primary. Analytics workloads often want a larger class. |
| `read_replica_publicly_accessible` | bool |  | `false` |  | Expose read replicas to the public internet. Keep false unless an external analytics tool must reach them directly. |
| `read_replica_allowed_cidrs` | string |  |  |  | Empty = the primary's security groups. Else up to 50 network CIDRs (10.0.0.0/24, not 10.0.0.5/24); public ones need read_replica_publicly_accessible. |
| `read_replica_multi_az` | bool |  | `false` |  | Enable Multi-AZ for read replicas (higher availability, roughly doubles their cost). |
| `role_arn` | string |  |  |  | Unset = use the cluster credentials directly. Set an IAM role ARN of the cluster's AWS account to assume it; cross-account roles are not supported. |

</Accordion>

<Warning>
Secret variables and outputs are encrypted and masked in Qovery, but Terraform can also keep their values, and values derived from them, in its state. With the Qovery-managed state backend (the default), Qovery stores the state. If you use your own backend, protect it and keep state files out of version control.
</Warning>

## Reference

From the Blueprint's [README](https://github.com/Qovery/service-catalog/blob/AWS/postgres/18/1.10.1/AWS/postgres/18/README.md).

Creates an AWS RDS PostgreSQL 18 instance with configurable instance class, storage, backups, maintenance window, monitoring, and network settings. Storage is encrypted by default.

When the blueprint creates the instance, the RDS identifier is derived from `db_name`: lowercased, each run of underscores turned into one hyphen, and a trailing hyphen dropped (AWS requirement). An adopted instance keeps its existing identifier (`import_identifier`), which can differ from `db_name`. The actual PostgreSQL database name is kept as provided.

### Variables

#### Required

| Name          | Type   | Sensitive | Description                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | ------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `db_name`     | string |           | PostgreSQL database name. Letters, digits, underscores only; must start with a letter; max 63 chars. Hyphens are not allowed. |
| `instance_class`    | string |           | RDS instance class. Default suggestion: `db.t3.micro`.                                             |
| `allocated_storage` | number |           | Allocated storage in GiB (min 20; max 65536 for gp3/io1/io2, 16384 for gp2). A value below the instance's current disk size is a no-op: RDS cannot shrink storage. Default suggestion: `20`. |

Available instance classes: every RDS instance class Qovery offers for native managed PostgreSQL and MySQL — the `db.t3`, `db.t4g`, `db.m5`–`db.m8g`, `db.r5`–`db.r8g` (including `db.r5b`), `db.x2g`, `db.x2idn` and `db.x2iedn` families, with their Graviton (`g`), Intel (`i`), local-storage (`d`) and network-optimized (`n`) variants. `db.c6gd` is left out because RDS offers it only for Multi-AZ DB clusters. The full list is in `qbm.yml`.

#### Credentials

Both are optional — omit them and Qovery supplies the values, the way native managed
databases did. In the console, leaving the field blank omits it. Through the API or
Terraform, omit the variable rather than sending an empty string: the platform rejects an
empty variable value.

| Name | Type | Sensitive | Default | Description |
| ---- | ---- | --------- | ------- | ----------- |
| `db_username` | string |  | `qoveryadmin` | Leave empty to use qoveryadmin, the login used by native managed databases. To set your own: letters, digits, underscores; must start with a letter; max 63 chars. Reserved names not allowed: admin, rdsadmin, rdsrepladmin, rdstopmgr, or any name starting with 'pg_'. |
| `db_password` | string | yes | _generated_ | Leave empty when creating a database and Qovery generates a 32-character alphanumeric password; when adopting an existing instance this must carry the current master password of that instance, because RDS never returns it. To set your own: 8–128 chars, must not contain /, @, ", or spaces. Changing it rotates the master password on the live instance (adopted instances: only once `manage_db_password` is true). |
| `manage_db_password` | bool |  | `false` | Adopted instances only, and one-way: once true, leave it true. Switching it on applies `db_password` to the instance, so confirm that value is the one the instance already has. Changing `db_password` then rotates it. An instance this blueprint created always owns its password. |

Changing `db_password` rotates the live instance's master password: the value is sent as a
write-only argument, triggered by a version derived from the password itself, so a change
reaches RDS and an unchanged password sends nothing.

An adopted instance does not take part until `manage_db_password` is set to true. That keeps
its import plan clean, and it has a consequence worth stating plainly: **while the flag is
false, editing `db_password` changes what the blueprint publishes without changing anything on
the instance.** Consumers pick up a credential RDS will reject. On an adopted instance, either
set the flag before touching the password, or do not touch the password at all.

Setting the flag is itself a write. Until then the version that triggers the send is null in
state, so switching it to true moves that value and applies `db_password` to the instance —
harmless when the two already agree, and an overwrite of the live password when they do not.
Confirm the stored password is the one the instance actually has before opting in.

A rotation also obeys `apply_changes_now`. Left false, RDS defers the password change to the
maintenance window while the new value is published immediately — consumers redeployed in
between cannot connect. Set `apply_changes_now` when you rotate.

Adoption (`import_identifier` set) requires both explicitly. `username` is `ForceNew` on
`aws_db_instance`, so a defaulted value would plan a replacement and destroy the live
database; and RDS never returns the master password, so a generated one would be published
as the credential without ever being applied.

#### Instance & storage

| Name                 | Type   | Default | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------- | ------ | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `port`               | number | `5432`  | Database port                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `max_allocated_storage` | number |      | Leave empty to keep the current storage autoscaling setting: off on a new database, the primary's on a new read replica. `0` turns autoscaling off. Otherwise the ceiling in GiB RDS may grow the disk to: at least 10% above the current disk (the larger of `allocated_storage` and the live size; on a replica, its own disk; AWS recommends 26%), at most 65536 (16384 for gp2). Takes effect immediately, whatever `apply_changes_now` says. |
| `storage_type`       | string | `gp3`   | EBS storage type: `gp2`, `gp3`, `io1`, `io2`                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `storage_encrypted`  | bool   | `true`  | Encrypt storage at rest                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `disk_iops`          | number | `0`     | Provisioned IOPS. Only meaningful with io1/io2 (always) or gp3 (≥400 GiB). 0 lets AWS choose the default. |
| `storage_throughput` | number | `0`     | 0 = AWS baseline on a new instance; an existing one keeps its current value. Otherwise provisioned storage throughput in MiB/s, 500-4000, gp3 with `allocated_storage` ≥400 GiB only (below that AWS fixes it at 125 MiB/s). Needs `disk_iops` set too, 12000 or more (on an existing instance, its current IOPS): AWS rejects a throughput without IOPS. Max 0.25 × `disk_iops`. To return throughput to baseline, set 500 and keep `disk_iops` at the instance's current IOPS (12000 at the gp3 baseline). |

**Storage autoscaling.** With `max_allocated_storage` set, RDS grows the disk on its own when free
space stays at or below 10% for 5 minutes, up to that ceiling. It waits until the previous
storage change has finished optimizing, and grows a disk at most four times in 24 hours. Left
empty, the blueprint keeps whatever the instance has, including a ceiling set in the AWS console.

- **The ceiling must be at least 10% above the current disk**, not only above `allocated_storage`,
  and on each read replica above that replica's own disk. Once autoscaling has grown a disk, the
  deploy fails before changing anything if the ceiling is too close to it, and names the minimum.
  An unchanged ceiling is not checked, except when `allocated_storage` raises the disk or a new
  replica is about to be created with it. A replacement that keeps the identifier is not caught:
  if its disk sits within 10% of the ceiling, AWS refuses it at apply, so raise the ceiling first.
- **It applies immediately**, without a reboot, whatever `apply_changes_now` says: RDS ignores the
  apply-immediately flag for a ceiling change.
- **A disk never shrinks.** The blueprint asks for the larger of `allocated_storage` and the live
  disk size, so a grown disk does not show as a change, and setting `0` after a growth turns
  autoscaling off at the current size.
- With io1/io2 storage, AWS also requires the IOPS-to-ceiling ratio to stay within a range, and
  rejects a ceiling outside it when the deploy applies.

#### Network

| Name                   | Type   | Default | Description                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ------ | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `multi_az`             | bool   | `true`  | Enable Multi-AZ deployment                                                                               |
| `publicly_accessible`  | bool   | `false` | Expose the database to the public internet                                                               |
| `db_subnet_group_name` | string |         | Leave empty — derived from the Qovery cluster's DB subnet group. Set it only on a cluster with a user-provided VPC, where that lookup finds nothing. |
| `security_group_ids`   | string |         | Leave empty — derived from the Qovery cluster's workers security group. Set it (comma-separated ids) only on a cluster with a user-provided VPC, where that lookup finds nothing. |

By default the instance is attached to the Qovery cluster network: the DB subnet group created at cluster bootstrap (named after the cluster VPC id) and the cluster workers security group, so pods in the cluster can reach the database out of the box. On clusters deployed into an existing VPC (user-provided network), the `ClusterId` tag lookup may not resolve; set `db_subnet_group_name` and `security_group_ids` explicitly in that case.

#### Read replicas

| Name                               | Type   | Default | Description                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `read_replica_count`               | number | `0`     | Number of same-region read replicas (0 disables; max 15). Point analytics tools (Metabase, BI dashboards) at the replica endpoints to offload reads. Requires `backup_retention_period` > 0. |
| `read_replica_instance_class`      | string |         | Instance class for read replicas. Empty = same as the primary. Analytics workloads often want a larger class here. |
| `read_replica_publicly_accessible` | bool   | `false` | Expose replicas to the public internet.                                                |
| `read_replica_allowed_cidrs`       | string |         | Empty = replicas use the primary's security groups. Comma-separated IPv4 network CIDRs, max 50 (e.g. Metabase Cloud IPs; 10.0.0.0/24, not 10.0.0.5/24): replicas then accept only these and the VPC on the database `port`. Needs `read_replica_count` > 0; public addresses also need `read_replica_publicly_accessible` = true. |
| `read_replica_multi_az`            | bool   | `false` | Enable Multi-AZ for replicas.                                                           |

Read replicas are asynchronous read-only copies of the primary — point analytics/BI tools (Metabase, Superset, dashboards, ad-hoc reporting) at their endpoints to keep heavy read traffic off the primary. They inherit the primary's engine version, storage size, storage type, and encryption, and share its database name, master username, and password; connect with the same credentials at the replica endpoint. `max_allocated_storage` and `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled` apply to every replica too: left unset, an existing replica keeps its own autoscaling ceiling and log exports, and a new one starts from the primary's. Because replication is asynchronous, replicas are eventually consistent (fine for analytics, not for read-after-write). Creating replicas requires automated backups on the primary (`backup_retention_period > 0`, the default). Replica endpoints are exposed via the `read_replica_endpoints` output. Analytics tools running inside the cluster can reach them over the cluster network out of the box; set `read_replica_publicly_accessible = true` only for tools that live outside the VPC. To let such a tool in without opening the primary, set `read_replica_publicly_accessible = true` and list its egress IPs in `read_replica_allowed_cidrs` (e.g. the Metabase Cloud IPs for your region): the blueprint creates a dedicated security group allowing those CIDRs plus the VPC's own CIDRs on the database port, and attaches it to the replicas **instead of** the primary's groups. Replacing rather than adding is deliberate: on a Qovery-managed network the cluster workers group also carries the cluster-wide `database.postgresql.allowed_cidrs` rule (`0.0.0.0/0` by default), which would otherwise leave a public replica reachable from anywhere. Clients inside the VPC keep access through the VPC CIDR rule. With the variable unset, replicas carry the primary's security groups, including on an adopted instance.

#### Maintenance & upgrades

| Name                           | Type   | Default               | Description                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `apply_changes_now`            | bool   | `false`               | Apply changes immediately                            |
| `allow_major_version_upgrade`  | bool   | `true`                | Allow major engine version upgrades on apply         |
| `auto_minor_version_upgrade`   | bool   | `true`                | Auto-apply minor version upgrades during maintenance |
| `preferred_maintenance_window` | string | `Tue:02:00-Tue:04:00` | Maintenance window (UTC), `ddd:hh24:mi-ddd:hh24:mi`  |

#### Backups

| Name                       | Type   | Default       | Description                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------ | ------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `preferred_backup_window`  | string | `00:00-01:00` | Daily backup window (UTC), `hh24:mi-hh24:mi` |
| `backup_retention_period`  | number | `14`          | Days to retain backups (0–35). `0` disables. |
| `skip_final_snapshot`      | bool   | `false`       | Skip final snapshot on deletion              |
| `delete_automated_backups` | bool   | `false`       | Delete automated backups when the instance is deleted. Default keeps them for `backup_retention_period` days; set true for throwaway instances |
| `copy_tags_to_snapshot`    | bool   | `true`        | Propagate instance tags to snapshots         |

Deleting the service keeps a final snapshot and the automated backups by default, and both keep
costing storage until deleted by hand: the snapshot indefinitely, the backups for
`backup_retention_period` days. For a throwaway or test instance, set both `skip_final_snapshot` and
`delete_automated_backups` to `true`. The final snapshot is named
`<cluster name>-<db name>-<YYYYMMDDhhmmss>`: `db_name` slugged as for the identifier, the UTC
time the name was stamped. The cluster name is cleaned in this order: any character AWS rejects is
removed, hyphen runs are collapsed, it is cut to 160 characters to stay within the 255-character
limit, then leading and trailing hyphens are dropped. The whole name is prefixed `snap-` if it does
not start with a letter. It is stamped once at creation, so successive create/destroy cycles of the
same name do not collide.

#### Monitoring

| Name                                    | Type   | Default             | Description                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `performance_insights_enabled`          | bool   | `true`              | Enable RDS Performance Insights                                                |
| `performance_insights_retention_period` | number | `7`                 | Performance Insights retention in days. Only used when `performance_insights_enabled` is true. Valid: 7, 731, or a multiple of 31. |
| `monitoring_interval`                   | number | `0`                 | Enhanced monitoring interval in seconds (0 disables). Allowed values: 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60. |
| `monitoring_role_arn`                   | string |                     | IAM role ARN for enhanced monitoring. Required when `monitoring_interval > 0`. |
| `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled`        | bool   | `false`             | Off keeps the current CloudWatch log exports: none on a new database, the primary's on a new read replica. On also exports the PostgreSQL log to CloudWatch Logs, on the primary and every read replica, immediately. Turning it back off does not stop an export. |
| `ca_cert_identifier`                    | string | `rds-ca-rsa2048-g1` | CA certificate identifier                                                      |

**CloudWatch log export.** `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled = true` adds the `postgresql` log to
what the instance already exports; RDS publishes it to the log group
`/aws/rds/instance/<identifier>/postgresql`. `false` does not remove anything: the instance keeps
the exports it has, so an export set in the AWS console (`upgrade`, for instance) survives every
deploy.

- **To stop the export, disable it in the AWS console** and keep the input `false`. With `true`,
  the next deploy turns it back on.
- **The log group is not managed by the blueprint.** RDS creates it; the blueprint neither sets its
  retention (CloudWatch defaults to never expire) nor deletes it with the instance.
- **What gets logged follows the parameter group.** The RDS default logs errors, failed logins and
  deadlocks; set `log_min_duration_statement` or `auto_explain` through `db_parameters` for more.

| Name                                  | Type   | Default | Description                                        |
| ------------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `option_group_name`                   | string |         | Optional option group name. Empty = AWS default. |
| `deletion_protection`                 | bool   | `false` | Prevent deletion via TF/API                        |
| `iam_database_authentication_enabled` | bool   | `false` | Enable IAM DB authentication                       |
| `dedicated_log_volume`                | bool   | `false` | Provision a dedicated EBS volume for database logs |
| `role_arn`                            | string |         | Unset = use the cluster credentials directly. Set an IAM role ARN of the cluster's AWS account to assume it; cross-account roles are not supported. |

#### Parameters

| Name            | Type   | Default | Description |
| --------------- | ------ | ------- | ----------- |
| `db_parameters` | string |         | Empty = the instance keeps its current parameter group, except one this blueprint created: that one is deleted and the instance and its read replicas return to the family default. JSON object of PostgreSQL parameters, e.g. \{"log_connections":"1","shared_preload_libraries":\{"value":"pg_stat_statements,auto_explain","apply_method":"pending-reboot"\}\}: the blueprint creates a parameter group with them and attaches it to the instance and its read replicas. Static parameters need apply_method pending-reboot and take effect at the next reboot. |

Each value is either the parameter value, or an object carrying `apply_method` too. RDS applies a
dynamic parameter with `immediate` (the default here) and refuses it for a static one, which needs
`pending-reboot`:

```json
{
  "log_connections": "1",
  "max_wal_size": "16384",
  "checkpoint_timeout": "1800",
  "idle_in_transaction_session_timeout": "600000",
  "shared_preload_libraries": { "value": "pg_stat_statements,auto_explain", "apply_method": "pending-reboot" },
  "auto_explain.log_min_duration": "5000"
}
```

- **Write values the way RDS stores them** — plain integers in the parameter's own unit (`max_wal_size` in MB, `checkpoint_timeout` in seconds). Anything else is
  normalised by AWS and shows up as a change on every deploy. JSON `true`/`false` are sent as
  `1`/`0`.
- **Overriding `shared_preload_libraries` replaces the RDS default**, `pg_stat_statements`. Keep it
  in the list, or Performance Insights' SQL statistics stop.
- **The blueprint never reboots the instance to apply parameters.** A new instance starts on the group. On an existing
  one, attaching the group for the first time, and every change to a `pending-reboot` parameter,
  waits for a reboot: the instance shows `pending-reboot` in the AWS console until you reboot it
  there. Changes to dynamic parameters apply without one.
- The group is named `<identifier>-params-<suffix>` and its family follows the engine major
  (`postgres18`). With `db_parameters` set, a major upgrade creates a group of the new family with
  the same parameters and moves the instance onto it along with the engine. RDS upgrades the read
  replicas as part of the primary's upgrade, so they move onto the new group in the same deploy, and
  only then is the old group deleted: it is never sent a parameter its version may not know.
- **A major upgrade with `db_parameters` set, or being cleared, needs `apply_changes_now = true`**,
  and the deploy fails before changing anything otherwise. Deferred to the maintenance window, the
  upgrade would keep the old group attached, and it could not be deleted. Either apply the upgrade
  now, or upgrade first and set `db_parameters` afterwards.
- Clearing `db_parameters` moves the instance and replicas back to `default.postgres18` and deletes
  the group; dynamic parameters revert straight away, static ones at the next reboot. Left unset, the
  blueprint does not touch the parameter group, so a group attached by other means stays in place.
  The blueprint recognises its own group by name, `<identifier>-params-` followed by 26 hex
  characters: do not give a group of your own a name of that shape.

#### Upgrading from an earlier blueprint version

Read this before repointing a deployment at this version.

- **Repointing a service from an older PostgreSQL major upgrades its engine in place.** Qovery
  sets `engine_version` to the highest 18.x that RDS lists as a valid upgrade target from the
  running version, and Terraform runs the major upgrade (downtime; with `apply_changes_now = false`,
  in the next maintenance window). An instance already upgraded through RDS to 18 is only
  relabelled. An instance on a custom parameter group needs a group of the new family first: RDS
  refuses the upgrade otherwise. From a newer major, do not repoint here: RDS cannot downgrade.

- Deleting now keeps a final snapshot and the automated backups for services **created** on this
  version. An existing service does not change behaviour: Qovery stores every variable default when
  the service is created, so repointing it here keeps `skip_final_snapshot = true` and
  `delete_automated_backups = true`. To keep a snapshot and backups on delete, set both to `false`
  on the service. The upgrade itself adds `time_static.created` and, with those set to `false`,
  updates `skip_final_snapshot`, `delete_automated_backups` and `final_snapshot_identifier` in
  place — Terraform-only arguments, nothing is sent to AWS and the instance is not rebooted.
- For an instance this blueprint created, and for an adopted instance already opted in with
  `manage_db_password`, the first apply writes the master password once. Old state carries no record of
  what was last sent, so the value Qovery holds is applied. An instance whose password was rotated
  outside Terraform — which earlier versions of this document told you to do — is reset to the
  Qovery-held value, and applications using the out-of-band password stop connecting. Make the two agree
  before you upgrade. An adopted instance left at `manage_db_password = false` is not touched: nothing is
  sent, and an out-of-band rotation survives.
- `manage_db_password` is one-way. Setting it back to false after an adopted instance has been handed
  over leaves Terraform with a change AWS rejects as "no modifications were requested".
- Terraform moves from 1.9.7 to 1.13.3, and `1.9.7` is no longer an accepted override. State written by
  1.13.3 cannot be read by 1.9.7, so a deployment cannot be repointed at an earlier blueprint version
  once it has applied.
- `parameter_group_name` is no longer ignored. Left unset (`db_parameters` empty), nothing changes:
  Terraform sends no value and a group attached in the AWS console stays. Setting `db_parameters`
  replaces that group with the blueprint's, so copy any parameters you still need into it first.
- On an **adopted** instance with read replicas, the replicas are now given the primary's security
  groups explicitly, even with `read_replica_allowed_cidrs` unset. If they currently carry other
  groups (typically the VPC default group), the first apply swaps them in place: no replacement,
  no reboot. An instance this blueprint created is unaffected; its replicas already had these groups.
- `max_allocated_storage` and `enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports` are no longer ignored, and nothing
  changes until you set the new inputs: repointing leaves `max_allocated_storage` empty and
  `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled` false, and both keep what the primary and each replica have,
  including autoscaling and exports set in the AWS console. `allocated_storage` now follows the live
  disk when that is larger, so a disk grown by autoscaling no longer shows as a change. Qovery can
  turn the log export on but not off; disable it in the AWS console.

### Lifecycle ignore_changes

On the primary instance, `engine_version` is no longer ignored. Terraform requests the exact
version held in the internal `engine_version` variable, which Qovery sets on every deploy:

- the live version, while the service stays on this major
- the highest valid upgrade target, when the service moves here from an older major.

With `auto_minor_version_upgrade` enabled, AWS may still move the running minor forward; the next
deploy then requests that newer version, so Terraform never tries to go back. Read replicas inherit
the primary's version.

A bare major such as `"18"` is never sent to a live instance, because AWS resolves it to the
region's default minor, which upgrades an older minor and is refused on a newer one. Without the
variable, an existing instance keeps its live version (read through the `aws_db_instance` data
source) and only a new instance gets the bare major.

`enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports` and `max_allocated_storage` are managed, on the primary and on
the read replicas, but an unset input keeps the live value instead of clearing it: the blueprint
reads each instance through the `aws_db_instance` data source on every plan, so an empty
`max_allocated_storage` keeps the live ceiling and `cloudwatch_logs_export_enabled = false` keeps
the live exports. A replacement that changes the identifier (a `db_name` change on an instance this
blueprint created) finds no live instance and starts from the inputs alone. One that keeps it (an
adopted instance, whose identifier is `import_identifier`, or a `storage_encrypted` toggle) reads
the old instance, so the new one inherits its disk size, autoscaling ceiling and log exports.

Two attributes remain ignored on the primary:

- `password` — the master password moved to the write-only `password_wo`; ignoring the plain attribute stops the value left in older state reading as a removal.
- `tags` — ignored on the primary and every read replica, so tag changes from the blueprint never reach an existing database. The reason is adoption: the native path tags managed RDS with `cluster_id`, which the YACE CloudWatch exporter filters DB metrics on.

### Assuming an IAM role

Optional. Set the `role_arn` variable to make the blueprint assume an IAM role instead of using the configured credentials directly; leave it unset to use them as is.

- Format: `arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<name>`, with an optional path (`role/<path>/<name>`). The `aws-cn`, `aws-us-gov` and `aws-iso*` partitions are accepted too.
- The role must be in the **same AWS account** as the credentials; cross-account roles are not supported.
- The role's trust policy must allow the deploy credentials' IAM principal to assume it.
- The role itself must carry the permissions listed in [Required AWS IAM permissions](#required-aws-iam-permissions).

### Required AWS IAM permissions

> When `role_arn` is set, Terraform makes these AWS calls as the assumed role, so the permissions below belong to that role. Access to a user-provided Terraform backend, if you use one, is not covered by `role_arn`: it keeps using the deploy credentials.

Unless `role_arn` is set, the credentials used to deploy this blueprint must allow the actions below. The RDS actions target instances in any region you deploy to; EC2 read actions are needed so Terraform can look up the default VPC, subnets, and security groups when none are explicitly configured. The EC2 write actions are used while `read_replica_allowed_cidrs` is set, and on the apply that clears it (Terraform revokes the rules and deletes the group), so keep them until that apply has run.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "rds:CreateDBInstance",
        "rds:CreateDBInstanceReadReplica",
        "rds:DeleteDBInstance",
        "rds:ModifyDBInstance",
        "rds:DescribeDBInstances",
        "rds:DescribeDBParameters",
        "rds:CreateDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:ModifyDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:DeleteDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:DescribeDBParameterGroups",
        "rds:ResetDBParameterGroup",
        "rds:DescribeDBSubnetGroups",
        "rds:DescribeDBSecurityGroups",
        "rds:AddTagsToResource",
        "rds:RemoveTagsFromResource",
        "rds:ListTagsForResource"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:DescribeVpcs",
        "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
        "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups",
        "ec2:DescribeAvailabilityZones"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:CreateSecurityGroup",
        "ec2:DeleteSecurityGroup",
        "ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress",
        "ec2:RevokeSecurityGroupIngress",
        "ec2:RevokeSecurityGroupEgress",
        "ec2:ModifySecurityGroupRules",
        "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroupRules",
        "ec2:CreateTags"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

When `monitoring_interval > 0`, the supplied `monitoring_role_arn` must be assumable by RDS (`monitoring.rds.amazonaws.com` trust relationship) and grant the `AmazonRDSEnhancedMonitoringRole` managed policy. The identity that applies the blueprint (the assumed role when `role_arn` is set) also needs `iam:PassRole` on that role, to hand it to RDS. It is not in the policy above because it only applies when monitoring is enabled; add this statement, with the resource set to your `monitoring_role_arn`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "iam:PassRole",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<monitoring-role-name>"
}
```

## Reference

From the Blueprint's [README](https://github.com/Qovery/service-catalog/blob/GCP/redis/7/1.0.8/GCP/redis/7/README.md).

Creates a GCP Memorystore for Redis 7 instance with configurable tier, memory size, auth, TLS, persistence, maintenance window, and optional cross-zone read replicas. There is no user-supplied password: when `auth_enabled` is true, GCP generates an AUTH string that is published via the `redis_auth_string` output.

### Variables

#### Required

| Name             | Type   | Sensitive | Description                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `redis_name`     | string |           | Memorystore instance ID. Lowercase letters, digits, hyphens; must start with a letter and not end with a hyphen; max 40 chars. |
| `tier`            | string |           | Service `tier`. BASIC is a single node with no failover. STANDARD_HA adds cross-zone replication and automatic failover. |
| `memory_size_gb`  | number |           | Instance memory size in GiB (min 1, max 300). Default suggestion: `1`.                                            |

#### Engine & sizing

| Name             | Type   | Default     | Description                                                                              |
| ---------------- | ------ | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `redis_version`  | string | `REDIS_7_2` | Redis version: `REDIS_7_2`, `REDIS_7_0`                                                   |
| `maxmemory_policy` | string | `noeviction` | Redis eviction policy applied once `memory_size_gb` is full                             |

#### Auth & network

| Name                      | Type   | Default          | Description                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `auth_enabled`            | bool   | `true`           | Require an AUTH string to connect                                                                                |
| `transit_encryption_mode` | string | `DISABLED`       | In-transit (TLS) encryption. Defaults to DISABLED, meaning cache traffic and (if `auth_enabled`) the AUTH string travel unencrypted over the VPC. SERVER_AUTHENTICATION requires clients to trust the CA certificate published via the redis_server_ca_certs output. |
| `authorized_network`      | string |                  | VPC network self-link the instance connects to. Empty = the project's default network. Set this to your Qovery cluster's VPC self-link so pods in the cluster can reach the instance. |
| `connect_mode`            | string | `DIRECT_PEERING` | How the instance connects to `authorized_network`. PRIVATE_SERVICE_ACCESS requires a pre-existing private services access connection on that network. |
| `reserved_ip_range`       | string |                  | CIDR /29 (DIRECT_PEERING) or named allocated range (PRIVATE_SERVICE_ACCESS) reserved for the instance. Empty = GCP picks an unused range automatically. |

By default the instance attaches to the project's **default** VPC network, which is usually *not* the Qovery cluster's VPC. Set `authorized_network` to the cluster's VPC self-link (and `connect_mode`/`reserved_ip_range` as required by that network's setup) so pods in the cluster can reach the instance without extra peering.

**Security note — plaintext by default:** `transit_encryption_mode` defaults to `DISABLED`. Since `auth_enabled` also defaults to `true`, the generated AUTH string and all cache traffic (including the data itself) travel **unencrypted** over the VPC on every connection — anyone able to observe traffic on that network path can capture both. Memorystore instances are never reachable from the public internet, but this offers no protection against other workloads sharing the same VPC. Set `transit_encryption_mode = SERVER_AUTHENTICATION` for anything beyond a trusted, fully isolated environment; clients then need to trust the CA certificate published via `redis_server_ca_certs` and connect over TLS (e.g. `rediss://`), which most Redis client libraries support but require explicit configuration for.

#### Persistence

| Name                  | Type   | Default             | Description                                                     |
| --------------------- | ------ | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `persistence_mode`    | string | `DISABLED`          | `DISABLED` or `RDB`                                               |
| `rdb_snapshot_period` | string | `TWENTY_FOUR_HOURS` | Snapshot interval. Only used when `persistence_mode` is `RDB`.   |

#### Maintenance

| Name                     | Type   | Default | Description                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ------ | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `maintenance_day`        | string |         | Day of week for the scheduled maintenance window. Empty disables a fixed window (GCP may perform maintenance at any time). |
| `maintenance_start_hour` | number | `2`     | Maintenance window start hour, UTC 24h (0-23). Only used when `maintenance_day` is set. |

#### Read replicas

| Name            | Type   | Default | Description                                                                                                        |
| --------------- | ------ | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `replica_count` | number | `0`     | Number of exposed cross-zone read replicas (0-5). Only supported when `tier` is STANDARD_HA; read traffic can be pointed at the redis_read_endpoint output. STANDARD_HA always allocates a standby node for failover regardless of this value; 0 just means that node isn't exposed as a readable replica. |

Replicas are asynchronous, cross-zone, read-only copies of the primary; point analytics/BI tools at the `redis_read_endpoint` output to keep read traffic off the primary. Setting `replica_count > 0` requires `tier = STANDARD_HA`.

`STANDARD_HA` always allocates a standby node for automatic failover, independent of `replica_count` — GCP requires at least one such node once `STANDARD_HA` is selected. `replica_count = 0` (the default) just means that standby isn't exposed as a readable replica; the blueprint sends GCP the required minimum under the hood. Set `replica_count` to 1-5 to also expose it (or additional nodes) via `redis_read_endpoint`.

#### Misc

| Name             | Type   | Default | Description                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------ | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gcp_project_id` | string |         | Leave empty — inferred from the credentials used to deploy (cluster credentials or the env-mode service account). Set it only to target a different GCP project. |

### Outputs

| Name                        | Sensitive | Description                                                                                  |
| --------------------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `redis_id`                  |           | Memorystore instance ID                                                                       |
| `redis_host`                |           | Primary endpoint hostname                                                                      |
| `redis_port`                |           | Primary endpoint port                                                                          |
| `redis_current_location_id` |           | Zone the primary node currently runs in                                                       |
| `redis_auth_string`         | yes       | AUTH string for authenticating (set only when `auth_enabled` is true)                         |
| `redis_server_ca_certs`     |           | Server CA certificates (PEM) for TLS verification when `transit_encryption_mode` is `SERVER_AUTHENTICATION` |
| `redis_read_endpoint`       |           | Read replica endpoint hostname (empty when `replica_count` is 0)                              |
| `redis_read_endpoint_port`  |           | Read replica endpoint port (empty when `replica_count` is 0)                                  |

### Required GCP IAM permissions

The credentials used to deploy this blueprint must be able to manage Memorystore Redis instances in the target project:

```json
{
  "bindings": [
    {
      "role": "roles/redis.admin",
      "members": ["<the deploying principal>"]
    }
  ]
}
```

`roles/redis.admin` (or the underlying `redis.instances.*` permissions) is sufficient for create, read, update, and delete. If `authorized_network` points at a network in a different (Shared VPC host) project, grant `roles/compute.networkUser` on that network to the Memorystore Redis service agent of *this* project — the one hosting the instance (`service-PROJECT_NUMBER@cloud-redis.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, where `PROJECT_NUMBER` is `gcp_project_id`'s project, or the deploy credentials' default project when `gcp_project_id` is empty) — not a service agent from the network's project.
