# MCP Server
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/mcp-server

> Set up the Qovery MCP Server so Claude, ChatGPT, or another MCP-compatible client can manage your existing Qovery infrastructure in natural language.

## Overview

The Qovery MCP Server lets you interact with your Qovery infrastructure from any MCP-compatible client (Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, etc.) using natural language.

<Info>
**What is MCP?** The Model Context Protocol is an open standard developed by Anthropic that allows AI assistants to interact with external tools and systems. [Learn more →](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
</Info>

<Tip>
**Want to deploy a new application from source code?** The MCP Server is for managing *existing* infrastructure. To deploy a new application from your codebase using an AI agent, install the [Qovery Agent Skill](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/ai-agent) instead — it works with Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and 30+ AI coding tools. The skill and MCP Server complement each other: use the skill to deploy, then the MCP Server to manage.
</Tip>

## Prerequisites

- **MCP-Compatible Client**: Any MCP-compatible application
- **Qovery Account**: Active account with infrastructure

## Setup

The Qovery MCP Server is accessible at `https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp`. You can find this URL and manage your MCP access in the Console under **Settings > MCP Server**. Choose one of the two authentication methods below to connect your MCP client.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="OAuth (recommended)">

    If your MCP client supports OAuth, this is the easiest option — no token generation required. The client will handle authentication automatically.

    **Example with Claude Code:**

    ```bash
    # Read-only (default)
    claude mcp add --transport http qovery https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp --callback-port 4242

    # Read/write
    claude mcp add --transport http qovery "https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp?read_write=true" --callback-port 4242
    ```

    Refer to your MCP client's documentation for how to configure OAuth with a custom server URL.

  </Tab>

  <Tab title="API Token">

    If your MCP client doesn't support OAuth, generate a Qovery API token and send it in the `Authorization` header. Never put a token in the MCP URL: URLs end up in client configuration files, shell history, and proxy logs.

    <Tip>
    Give an agent the least-privileged token that does the job, such as an API token with a read-only role. Avoid giving an agent a long-lived admin token. For agents that act through the CLI or the API, an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) (Preview) scopes access request by request.
    </Tip>

    **Step 1 - Generate a token:**

    <Steps>
      <Step title="Open Qovery Console">
        Go to [console.qovery.com](https://console.qovery.com)
      </Step>

      <Step title="Navigate to Settings">
        Click on the settings icon in your organization
      </Step>

      <Step title="Access API Tokens">
        Go to **API Tokens** section
      </Step>

      <Step title="Generate Token">
        Click "Generate Token" and copy it

        <Warning>
        Save this token securely. You won't be able to see it again!
        </Warning>
      </Step>
    </Steps>

    **Step 2 - Configure your MCP client:**

    Point the client at `https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp` and add this HTTP header:

    ```
    Authorization: Token your_qovery_token
    ```

    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Claude Code (CI and headless runs)">

        Claude Code supports OAuth, so on a workstation use the **OAuth** tab instead. Use a token only where the browser sign-in cannot run, such as CI or a remote container, and prefer a short-lived, least-privileged token.

        ```bash
        # Read-only (default)
        claude mcp add --transport http qovery https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_TOKEN"

        # Read/write
        claude mcp add --transport http qovery "https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp?read_write=true" --header "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_TOKEN"
        ```

        Claude Code stores the header, token included, in its configuration (`~/.claude.json`, or `.mcp.json` with `--scope project`). Do not commit that file with a token in it.

      </Tab>
    </Tabs>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

<Info>
The Qovery MCP Server is also available through the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0.1/servers?search=io.github.Qovery).
</Info>

## Access Modes

| Mode | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| Read-only | Yes | Can query and list resources (environments, services, deployments, etc.) |
| Read/write | No (`read_write=true`) | Can also trigger deployments, update configurations, and perform write operations |

<Info>
The `devops_copilot` tool depends on two settings in your Qovery Console:

1. **Copilot must be enabled** — if disabled, the tool will not be accessible at all, regardless of your MCP configuration
2. **Write access must be enabled** — required to use the tool in read/write mode (in addition to the `read_write=true` URL parameter)
</Info>

<Warning>
Enable write mode only when needed. Prefer read-only mode to limit the blast radius of unintended AI actions.
</Warning>

## Usage Examples

Once connected, you can interact with your infrastructure naturally:

```
"Show me all my environments"
"What services are running in production?"
"List projects in my organization"
```

## Troubleshooting

### MCP Server Not Connecting

**Issue**: Client doesn't show Qovery tools or cannot connect

**Solutions**:
1. Verify the MCP Server URL is correct: `https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp`
2. Check your internet connection
3. Restart your MCP client
4. Contact Qovery Support if the issue persists

### Authentication Errors

**Issue**: "Authentication failed" or "Invalid token" errors

**Solutions**:
1. Verify your API token is correct (check for copy-paste errors)
2. Ensure the token hasn't been revoked or expired
3. Generate a new API token if needed from Qovery Console

## Security Best Practices

<Warning>
**API Token Security**:
- Never share your API tokens publicly
- Don't commit tokens to version control
- Revoke tokens you no longer need from Qovery Console
- Use tokens with the minimum required permissions
- Rotate tokens regularly
</Warning>

### Token Permissions

The API token has the same permissions as the role you selected during creation:
- Can only access resources within your organization
- Respects organization RBAC policies
- All actions are audited in Qovery Console

# Securing AI Agent Access
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/securing-ai-access

> Grant AI agents safe, read-only access to your Qovery infrastructure for troubleshooting and investigation

## Overview

When you let an AI agent (Claude Code, Cursor, the Qovery Agent Skill, etc.) interact with your infrastructure, you want it to **investigate freely but never mutate or leak anything**. Approving each generated command one by one creates decision fatigue, and a single misread `curl` or `qovery api ... --method DELETE` can exfiltrate data or change production state.

<Note>
The classifications and the permission template on this page are a **recommendation, not an absolute rule** - adapt them to suit your team's needs. In all cases, these guardrails sit **on top of** the permissions granted by the token used to authenticate: a command can never do more than the token allows, so a read-only token remains your strongest safeguard regardless of what the allowlist contains.
</Note>

This page describes the recommended ways to give an agent a safe, read-only footprint:

1. **[MCP Server in read-only mode](#option-1-mcp-server-read-only)** - the native, recommended option. No allowlist to maintain.
2. **[A CLI permission allowlist](#option-2-cli-permission-allowlist)** - for agents driving the `qovery` CLI directly (e.g. Claude Code with the Qovery Agent Skill).
3. **[An API Policy Token](#option-3-api-policy-token-preview)** - enforced by Qovery rather than by the agent's own configuration.

<Tip>
These approaches complement each other. The MCP Server is the simplest guardrail; the CLI allowlist is for workflows where the agent runs `qovery` commands in a shell; an API Policy Token constrains the credential itself, so it holds no matter which client the agent uses.
</Tip>

---

## Option 1 - MCP Server (read-only)

The [Qovery MCP Server](https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/mcp-server) is **read-only by default**. It can query and list resources but cannot deploy, update, or delete anything unless you explicitly opt into write mode with `read_write=true`.

```bash
# Read-only (default) - safe for troubleshooting
claude mcp add --transport http qovery https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp --callback-port 4242

# Read/write - only when you intend to make changes
claude mcp add --transport http qovery "https://mcp.qovery.com/mcp?read_write=true" --callback-port 4242
```

For an extra layer, generate a **read-only API token** in the Console (**Settings > API Tokens**) and pass it to the MCP Server. Even if write mode were requested, the token's permissions would block any destructive action.

<Warning>
Enable write mode only when needed. Prefer read-only mode to limit the blast radius of unintended AI actions.
</Warning>

---

## Option 2 - CLI permission allowlist

If your agent drives the `qovery` CLI directly, you can constrain it at the tool-permission level. The example below is a Claude Code `.claude/settings.json` that you can commit to your repo and share across your team.

The policy follows three tiers:

| Tier | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **allow** | Read-only commands, safe to run without confirmation |
| **ask** | Reads that could expose sensitive data or commands that can mutate depending on flags - require confirmation |
| **deny** | Mutating commands and commands that return credentials/tokens in clear text - never run |

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(qovery status:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment statuses:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment deployment list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment deployment explain:*)",

      "Bash(qovery application list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery container list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery database list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery project list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery service list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery helm list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cronjob list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery lifecycle list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster list-nodes:*)",
      "Bash(qovery terraform list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery webhook list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery webhook list-event:*)",

      "Bash(qovery application env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery container env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery project env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery helm env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cronjob env list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery lifecycle env list:*)",

      "Bash(qovery application domain list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery container domain list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery helm domain list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery container registry list:*)",
      "Bash(qovery environment stage list:*)",

      "Bash(qovery log:*)",

      "Bash(qovery version:*)",
      "Bash(qovery list-commands:*)",
      "Bash(qovery console:*)"
    ],

    "ask": [
      "Bash(qovery api:*)",
      "Bash(qovery shell:*)",
      "Bash(qovery port-forward:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster kubeconfig:*)",
      "Bash(qovery env import:*)",
      "Bash(qovery env parse:*)",
      "Bash(qovery context set:*)",
      "Bash(curl:*)",
      "Bash(wget:*)"
    ],

    "deny": [
      "Bash(qovery token:*)",
      "Bash(qovery auth token:*)",

      "Bash(qovery * deploy:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * redeploy:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * stop:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * cancel:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * delete:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * update:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * create:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * clone:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * edit:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster install:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster upgrade:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster lock:*)",
      "Bash(qovery cluster unlock:*)",

      "Bash(qovery * env create:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * env update:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * env delete:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * env alias:*)",
      "Bash(qovery * env override:*)",

      "Bash(qovery terraform plan-and-apply:*)",
      "Bash(qovery terraform delete:*)",
      "Bash(qovery terraform force-unlock:*)",
      "Bash(qovery terraform migrate-state:*)",

      "Bash(qovery api * --method POST:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * --method PUT:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * --method PATCH:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * --method DELETE:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * -X POST:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * -X PUT:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * -X PATCH:*)",
      "Bash(qovery api * -X DELETE:*)"
    ]
  }
}
```

<Info>
The `Bash(...:*)` syntax is Claude Code's current permission format. Other agents use their own permission files but follow the same allow / ask / deny model - adapt the command patterns accordingly.
</Info>

### Why `qovery api` is in `ask`, not `allow`

`qovery api` is a raw passthrough to the Qovery API. It defaults to `GET`, **but** it switches to `POST` as soon as you pass `--field` or `--input`, and it accepts `--method DELETE` / `PUT` / `PATCH`. It can also reach endpoints that return secrets. Because permission patterns are glob-based (not regex with negation), there is no clean way to allow "`qovery api` in GET only." The safe compromise is to **ask** for every `qovery api` call and **deny** the explicitly mutating method flags as a backstop.

---

## Option 3 - API Policy Token (Preview)

The two options above are enforced on the agent's side: they depend on the agent using the MCP Server, or on its permission file being respected. An [**API Policy Token**](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) is enforced by Qovery instead. The token carries no role - it carries an Open Policy Agent (rego) policy that Qovery evaluates on every API request made with it, whatever client sends it.

That makes it the right tool when the constraint has to hold regardless of the agent's own configuration, or when it is finer than "read-only":

```rego
default allow := false

allowed_environment_id := "4a9dc488-df2b-4544-9c5f-4eb0428fda49"

# This token can read that environment, and do nothing else anywhere.
allow if {
	input.request.method in {"GET", "HEAD"}
	input.qovery_metadata.environment_id == allowed_environment_id
}
```

<Warning>
A policy token is only as narrow as its policy: it authenticates as organization-admin and the policy is the sole constraint, so a policy that allows everything grants everything. Only an organization owner or admin can create one.
</Warning>

See [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token) for the full input contract, more policy recipes, and the current limitations.

---

## Command reference

### Safe (read-only)

These only read and display data. They never return secret values - environment-variable and secret commands return **names only**.

| Area | Commands |
|------|----------|
| Status | `status`, `environment statuses`, `environment deployment list`, `environment deployment explain` |
| Listings | `<service> list`, `cluster list`, `cluster list-nodes`, `project list`, `terraform list`, `webhook list`, `webhook list-event` |
| Variables (names only) | `<service> env list` |
| Domains / stages / registries | `<service> domain list`, `environment stage list`, `container registry list` |
| Logs | `log` |
| Meta | `version`, `list-commands`, `console` |

### Confirm before running

| Command | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| `qovery api` | Mutates when `--field`/`--input`/`--method` is used; can reach sensitive endpoints |
| `qovery shell`, `qovery port-forward` | Interactive access - can modify container state |
| `qovery cluster kubeconfig` | Returns a cluster access token |
| `qovery env import`, `qovery env parse` | Reads/writes variable values (including secrets) locally |
| `curl`, `wget` | Raw HTTP - can exfiltrate to arbitrary domains |

### Never run

| Command | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| `qovery token`, `qovery auth token` | Print an API/access token in clear text |
| `deploy`, `redeploy`, `stop`, `cancel`, `delete`, `update`, `create`, `clone`, `edit` (any service) | Mutate platform state |
| `cluster install` / `upgrade` / `lock` / `unlock` | Mutate cluster state |
| `<service> env create` / `update` / `delete` / `alias` / `override` | Mutate variables and secrets |
| `terraform plan-and-apply` / `delete` / `force-unlock` / `migrate-state` | Mutate infrastructure and Terraform state |

### API endpoints that return secrets

Even though they are `GET` requests, these endpoints return credentials in clear text. Block them in any read-only setup (they are covered by the `qovery api` rules above, but list them explicitly if you allow `curl`):

| Endpoint | Exposes |
|----------|---------|
| `GET /database/{databaseId}/masterCredentials` | Database master password |
| `GET /organization/{organizationId}/{aws,gcp,scaleway,onPremise}/credentials` | Cloud provider credentials |
| `GET /organization/{organizationId}/cluster/{clusterId}/cloudProviderInfo` | Cloud provider credentials |
| `GET /cluster/{clusterId}/token` | Cluster token |
| `GET /cluster/{clusterId}/argoCdConfig` | ArgoCD token |

<Warning>
Secret **values** are never returned by standard `env list` commands or service endpoints - but **tokens and cloud credentials** are returned by the endpoints above and by `qovery token`. Keep those in the deny list.
</Warning>

---

## Best practices

<Steps>
  <Step title="Prefer read-only mode end to end">
    Use the MCP Server in its default read-only mode, and/or back the agent with a read-only API token created in **Settings > API Tokens**. When read-only is not granular enough, or the guardrail must not depend on the agent's own configuration, use an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Commit the permission policy">
    Check the `.claude/settings.json` (or equivalent) into your repository so the whole team inherits the same guardrails.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Keep secrets out of logs">
    `qovery log` is safe to allow, but logs reflect whatever your application writes. Avoid logging PII or credentials in the first place.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Review the deny list when the CLI updates">
    New mutating commands may be added over time. The verb-based deny patterns (`deploy`, `delete`, etc.) cover most cases, but review periodically.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Skill reference

The install command installs all eleven skills. Your agent picks the skill from your prompt, or you can call it with its slash command (for example `/qovery-signup`).

| Skill | What it does | Example prompt |
|-------|--------------|----------------|
| `qovery` | Entry point. Routes your request to the right skill and handles quick operations: list, status, stop, restart, logs, clone, scale, custom domains, deployment history. | "List my Qovery environments" |
| `qovery-signup` | Creates a Qovery account from your terminal: installs the Qovery CLI if needed, authenticates with `qovery auth --headless` (the first login creates the account), creates your first organization, then hands off to qovery-onboard. Never handles raw tokens. | "Create a Qovery account and log me in" |
| `qovery-onboard` | Guided setup. Understands your role, experience, and constraints, then recommends and sets up the Qovery configuration: cloud provider, cluster, environments, RBAC, security, and cost defaults. Handles BYOK and platform migrations. | "I'm new to Qovery, help me get started" |
| `qovery-deploy` | From source code to a running app: analyzes the codebase, creates a Dockerfile if missing, provisions databases, and deploys with the CLI and API or with Terraform. | "Deploy my application with Qovery" |
| `qovery-troubleshoot` | Diagnoses and fixes deployment failures, crashes, connectivity and performance issues: 8-layer diagnosis, 20+ error patterns, MCP Server integration, and runbook generation. | "My deployment is failing" |
| `qovery-optimize` | Optimizes costs and right-sizes resources from historical consumption, estimates cloud costs, and generates reports with CSV export. | "Optimize my Qovery costs" |
| `qovery-speedup` | Measures the deployment pipeline timeline, finds bottlenecks (build, startup, health check, scheduling), and proposes Dockerfile and configuration fixes. | "My deployments are slow" |
| `qovery-preview` | Creates a preview environment per pull request: detects or creates a blueprint environment, clones it for each PR, switches the branch, configures auto-shutdown (stop, delete, or recycle), and cleans up. | "Set up preview environments for my project" |
| `qovery-terraform` | Generates Terraform manifests (qovery/qovery provider) from an existing Qovery setup, imports resources into state, and validates them in a test clone. Never applies to the original without confirmation. | "Convert my environment to Terraform" |
| `qovery-policy-token` | Creates a scoped, least-privilege API Policy Token: turns your intent into an OPA/Rego policy, tests it locally and against the API, creates the token, and verifies it allows exactly what you want and denies everything else. | "I need a scoped token for an AI agent limited to the staging environment" |
| `qovery-assess` | Read-only assessment of a whole organization: inventories clusters, environments and services, runs 147 best-practice checks across reliability, security, performance, delivery, cost and disaster recovery, and writes a shareable gap analysis. Modifies nothing. | "Is my setup production-ready?" |

Source: [github.com/Qovery/qovery-skills](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-skills).

## Why Qovery for AI agents?

  <Card title="Your cloud, your control" icon="server">
    Deploys to your own AWS, GCP, Azure, or Scaleway. Direct billing, no shared infra.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Full audit trail" icon="list-check">
    Every agent action logged — what changed, when, by which agent.
  </Card>
  <Card title="RBAC for agents" icon="shield-check">
    Agents respect your permission model. Scope an agent's credential with an [API Policy Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-policy-token).
  </Card>
  <Card title="Ephemeral by design" icon="clock">
    Environments up and down in minutes. Sleep mode and TTL handle cleanup.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Self-healing" icon="rotate">

# Build Optimizer
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/capabilities/build-optimizer

> Analyze the latest build of a service with AI to find why it is slow, mostly Docker layer cache misses, and get fixes, a reworked Dockerfile when one applies, and a prompt for your coding agent.

## Overview

<Note>
The Build Optimizer is in preview. The API below works for every organization with AI features enabled, as long as build analysis is available on its Qovery instance (otherwise starting an analysis returns `503`, see [Start Errors](#start-errors)); the Console entry point is not available to every organization yet. The result format and the analysis itself may still change.
</Note>

The Build Optimizer analyzes the latest Docker build of an application or job and explains how to make it faster. It reads the Dockerfile, the build logs and the cache history of earlier builds, finds the steps that re-ran instead of being cached, and tells you what invalidated their cache.

Use it when a build takes longer than it should, for example when a dependency install (`npm ci`, `pip install`, `go mod download`) runs on every deployment although your dependencies did not change. Typical causes are `COPY . .` placed before the dependency install, or a build argument declared before the install whose value changes between builds.

The analysis runs on demand, on one build, from the API or the Console. It is not a Copilot chat command. It never changes your Dockerfile, your build settings or your image: it returns suggestions for you to review and apply.

<Tip>
For a scheduled agent that reviews build **and** deployment times and opens pull requests with the changes, see the [Build & Deployment Optimizer](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/agent-tasks/build-deployment-optimizer) Agent Task.
</Tip>

## Requirements

| Requirement | Details |
|-------------|---------|
| AI features enabled | The organization must have AI features enabled (`ai_features_enabled` on the organization). Otherwise starting an analysis returns `403`. An organization admin can change it with [Edit the organization's AI features opt-in](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/organization-main-calls/edit-the-organizations-ai-features-opt-in). |
| Supported services | Applications built from a git repository with a Dockerfile, and cron or lifecycle jobs built from a Dockerfile, either stored in the git repository or written inline on the job. Services deployed from a container image have no build to analyze. |
| A build to analyze | Only the **latest build** of the service can be analyzed: its most recent deployment that ran a build, successful or failed (a failed build only through the API). A deployment that reused an existing image did not build anything and does not count. `latest_build_execution_id` is `null` when no deployment in the kept history ran a build. |
| A readable Dockerfile | Qovery reads the Dockerfile from the repository at the commit of that build, or the job's inline Dockerfile. It must not be empty and must be at most about 100 KB (102,400 characters). Otherwise starting an analysis returns `422`. |
| Permissions | Starting an analysis needs the **Deploy** permission or higher on the service's environment. Reading the result needs **Read-Only**. See [Members & RBAC](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac#project-level-permissions). |
| One at a time | A service runs one analysis at a time. Starting another while one is running returns `409`. |

## Run an Analysis

### From the Console

Where the Console entry point is available for your organization:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the logs of the latest build">
    Open the service, go to **Deployments**, and open the logs of its latest deployment that ran a build. In the Console, the build must have succeeded; to analyze a failed build, use the API.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Start the analysis">
    On the **Build** step, click **Optimize**. The button shows **Analyzing** while the analysis runs; hover it to see the current step.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/build-optimizer/deployment-logs-optimize.png" alt="Build step of the deployment logs, with the Optimize button next to the step name" />
    </Frame>

    **Optimize** is disabled, with the reason on hover, when the build did not succeed, when the deployment is not the service's latest build, or when the build analysis is unavailable. If the previous analysis failed, hovering **Optimize** shows why, and clicking it starts a new one.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Read the result">
    The result opens by itself when the analysis you started is done. If it fails, an error message shows the reason. Later, the button reads **Open analysis** and opens the same result.

    The result shows the review confidence, the estimated time saved (when there is one), the assets reviewed, the summary and the **Improvements target**. Below them, **Prompt for AI agents** and **Reworked Dockerfile** (when the analysis returns one) are collapsed, each with a **Copy** button. Values hidden from the analysis appear as `<redacted>` in the reworked Dockerfile: put them back before using it.

    <Frame>
      <img src="/images/build-optimizer/analysis-modal.png" alt="Build optimization analysis with High review confidence, an estimated time saved of 1min 30s – 1min 50s, the assets reviewed and the summary" />
    </Frame>
  </Step>
</Steps>

### From the API

The examples use an application. For a cron or lifecycle job, set `URL` to `https://api.qovery.com/job/$JOB_ID/buildAnalysis`.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Get the latest build">
    Read the build analysis of the service. `latest_build_execution_id` is the only build you can analyze, and `analysis` holds the previous analysis, if any.

    ```bash
    QOVERY_API_TOKEN="REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_API_TOKEN"
    APPLICATION_ID="REPLACE_WITH_APPLICATION_ID"
    URL="https://api.qovery.com/application/$APPLICATION_ID/buildAnalysis"

    RESPONSE=$(curl -sS --fail-with-body "$URL" -H "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_API_TOKEN")
    echo "$RESPONSE"
    EXECUTION_ID=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r '.latest_build_execution_id')
    ```

    ```json
    {
      "latest_build_execution_id": "6e5c1d3a-6b6f-4c35-9a2f-8f1d2c3b4a5e-42",
      "analysis": null
    }
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Start the analysis">
    Send that execution ID. The API answers `202` with the new analysis in `PENDING`, and the analysis continues in the background. Any other status means the analysis did not start: see [Start Errors](#start-errors), and do not wait for a result.

    ```bash
    curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST "$URL" \
      -H "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_API_TOKEN" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d "{\"execution_id\": \"$EXECUTION_ID\"}"
    ```

    Starting an analysis replaces the previous one of the service.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Wait for the result">
    Read the build analysis again until `analysis.status` is `DONE` or `FAILED`. The loop prints each status. It also stops, and prints the error, when a request fails (for example an invalid token), and it stops on `null` when the service has no analysis.

    ```bash
    while :; do
      RESPONSE=$(curl -sS --fail-with-body "$URL" \
        -H "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_API_TOKEN") || { echo "$RESPONSE"; break; }
      STATUS=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r '.analysis.status')
      echo "$STATUS"
      case "$STATUS" in DONE|FAILED|null) break ;; esac
      sleep 10
    done
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Read the result">
    ```bash
    curl -sS --fail-with-body "$URL" -H "Authorization: Token $QOVERY_API_TOKEN" | jq '.analysis'
    ```

    See [What You Get Back](#what-you-get-back) for the fields.
  </Step>
</Steps>

API reference: [Get the build analysis of an application](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/application-build-analysis/get-the-build-analysis-of-an-application), [Analyse the latest build of an application](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/application-build-analysis/analyse-the-latest-build-of-an-application), and the same calls [for a job](https://www.qovery.com/docs/api-reference/job-build-analysis/analyse-the-latest-build-of-a-job).

### Start Errors

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `400` | `execution_id` is missing or blank. |
| `403` | You lack the Deploy permission, or AI features are disabled for the organization. |
| `404` | The service does not exist. |
| `409` | The execution is not the latest build, the service has no build, or an analysis is already running. Read the build analysis again to get the current `latest_build_execution_id`. |
| `422` | Qovery cannot read the Dockerfile of this build, for example a path that does not exist at the build commit. |
| `500` | Qovery could not load the build or the service's secret values, which it needs to keep them out of the analysis. Retry later. |
| `503` | Build analysis is not available on this Qovery instance. Retrying does not help. |

### Progress

| Status | Step | What happens |
|--------|------|--------------|
| `PENDING` | Starting | The analysis is accepted. The Dockerfile was already read when the API answered `202`. |
| `COLLECTING` | Reading build logs and cache history | Qovery gathers what the analysis reviews (see below). |
| `ANALYSING` | Analysing with AI | The AI model works on the build. |
| `DONE` | Done | `analysis.result` holds the result. |
| `FAILED` | Failed, or Timed out | `failure_code` and `failure_reason` say why. |

| Failure code | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `MODEL_ERROR` | The AI model failed or returned an unusable result. |
| `TIMEOUT` | The analysis took too long, for example the AI model did not answer within 4 minutes. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR` | Any other error. |

If Qovery restarts cleanly during an analysis, the analysis fails with `INTERNAL_ERROR` and `failure_reason` says so: start it again. If the Qovery process stops without warning, the analysis keeps its last status (`COLLECTING` or `ANALYSING`) for up to 11 minutes, then reads as `FAILED` with `TIMEOUT`. During those 11 minutes, starting a new analysis returns `409`.

<Accordion title="Follow progress live with the websocket route">
  Progress is also streamed on the websocket route `/build/analysis` of `wss://ws.qovery.com`, with the query parameters `organization`, `cluster`, `project`, `environment` and `service` (all IDs). It needs the same access as the service logs.

  Each frame is one progress event:

  ```json
  {
    "status": "COLLECTING",
    "step": "Reading build logs and cache history",
    "message": null,
    "terminal": false
  }
  ```

  Past events are replayed first, then new ones as they come. `message` explains a failure. The connection closes with code `1000` after the event with `"terminal": true` (`DONE` or `FAILED`). Without that event, it closes with `1011` when the progress is unavailable, or `1001` after 15 minutes. Read the build analysis to get the result.
</Accordion>

## What the Analysis Reviews

| Asset | What Qovery reads |
|-------|-------------------|
| `DOCKERFILE` | The Dockerfile of the build: from the repository at the build commit (`dockerfile_source: GIT`), or the job's inline Dockerfile (`INLINE`). |
| `DOCKERIGNORE` | Whether a `.dockerignore` file exists in the root path of the repository at the build commit. Only for a Dockerfile from git. |
| `BUILD_SETTINGS` | The root path, the Dockerfile path, the target build stage, and the names of the build arguments. |
| `BUILD_LOGS` | For each BuildKit step: its instruction, its duration, and whether it was cached or re-ran. Also the base image digests, the build context size, and, when reported, the CPU and memory used by the builder and any out-of-memory kill. |

The analysis also reads the **cache history**: up to 10 earlier builds that can have written the cache this build started from. The layer cache is shared by every build of the same repository, root path, Dockerfile and target stage on the same cluster, whatever the branch or environment. The history only includes builds of your own organization. So the history includes earlier builds of the service and builds of other services built from the same repository, for example the same application in another environment. When those builds alternate, each one can start from a cache the other overwrote.

For each build argument, the analysis learns whether its value differs from the build that last wrote the cache, and how many distinct values it has across the services sharing the cache. Qovery compares the values itself and sends only the result.

`assets_reviewed` in the result lists what was available for this analysis.

## What You Get Back

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `summary` | Two to four sentences on what slows the build and why, with the evidence: the step, its seconds, what invalidated its cache. Says so when the build is already efficient. |
| `confidence` | `HIGH`, `MEDIUM` or `LOW`. See the table below. |
| `estimated_time_saved` | Seconds saved on each build once every improvement is applied, as `min_seconds` and `max_seconds`. `null` when there is nothing to save or no timing to base it on. |
| `improvements` | The changes to make, one sentence each, highest impact first. Empty when the build is already efficient. An improvement can also be a Qovery setting, for example moving a variable from a build argument to a runtime variable. |
| `dockerfile` | The reworked Dockerfile, made of targeted edits to your original file, never a full rewrite. `null` when no improvement is a Dockerfile change, or when the edits cannot be applied cleanly to your file. |
| `dockerfile_rationale` | Why the reworked Dockerfile builds faster. `null` when there is no reworked Dockerfile. |
| `agent_prompt` | A ready-to-paste prompt for your AI coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) to apply the changes in your repository. |
| `assets_reviewed` | What the analysis read. See [What the Analysis Reviews](#what-the-analysis-reviews). |

The analysis itself also carries `execution_id` (the analyzed build) and `stale`, which is `true` once the service has a newer build than the analyzed one.

### Confidence

The confidence says how sure the analysis is that applying the improvements saves the estimated time.

| Confidence | When |
|------------|------|
| `HIGH` | The build logs, the cache history or the builder metrics show both the cause (for example a build argument value that changed, or an out-of-memory kill) and the seconds it costs. |
| `MEDIUM` | One of the two, the cause or the time, is inferred. |
| `LOW` | Only the Dockerfile suggests the issue, or there are improvements but no time range. |

When there is no improvement, the confidence says how sure the analysis is that the build has nothing left to gain.

## Apply the Result

<Steps>
  <Step title="Review the analysis">
    Read the summary and the improvements. The analysis is a suggestion: check that each change keeps your image behaving the same way.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Apply the changes">
    Use either:

    - **Copy the reworked Dockerfile** from `dockerfile`, when the analysis returns one. Values hidden from the analysis appear as `<redacted>`: put back the values of your original file before you commit.
    - **Paste `agent_prompt` into your coding agent.** It names the files and the exact changes, asks the agent to keep the image behavior identical, to put back any `<redacted>` value, to build twice locally and check the second build hits the cache, and to stop for your review before committing or deploying.

    Improvements that are Qovery settings, such as [build-time variables](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment-variables#build-time-variables), are changed in the Console or the API.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Deploy and compare">
    Commit, then deploy. The first build after a Dockerfile change re-runs the changed steps, so compare the build time on the builds after it. You can run a new analysis on the latest build to check what is left.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Limits and Data Handling

- **Suggestions only.** Qovery never changes your Dockerfile, your build settings or your image. Starting an analysis never triggers a build.
- **Latest build only.** Only the latest build of a service can be analyzed. Qovery keeps one analysis per service: a new analysis replaces the previous one, and the kept one is marked `stale` once a newer build exists.
- **AI model.** The analysis runs on an Anthropic Claude model through Amazon Bedrock, called by Qovery.
- **Dockerfile values are hidden.** Before the Dockerfile is sent, every literal `ARG` and `ENV` value is replaced with `<redacted>` (references such as `$NODE_ENV` are kept). So are credential-like strings: AWS access key IDs, GitHub, GitLab and Slack tokens, npm auth tokens, private keys, credentials in URLs and `Authorization` header values.
- **Secret values are masked.** The values of the service's secret variables are masked in the Dockerfile and the build logs before they are sent, and in the stored result. Values shorter than 6 characters are not masked.
- **Build arguments are compared, not sent.** The analysis receives their names and whether their values changed between builds. Non-secret values can still appear in the build log lines that are sent, where BuildKit prints them.

### Rollback Deployment

## Tips for Effective Use

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Be Specific When Needed">
    **Good**: "Deploy my-api version 2.0 to production"

    **Less Clear**: "Deploy something"

    Copilot will ask for clarification if needed
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Use Context">
    **Build on Previous**:
    - "Show production"
    - "Deploy latest there"
    - "Now check if it's healthy"
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Combine Operations">
    **Single Request**: "Deploy to staging, wait for health check, then promote to production"

    Copilot handles the entire workflow
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Ask for Explanations">
    - "Why did that fail?"
    - "What does this error mean?"
    - "How do I fix this?"

    Copilot provides context and guidance
  </Accordion>

# Advanced Workflows
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/examples/advanced-workflows

> Complex multi-step automation scenarios with Qovery AI Copilot

## Multi-Step Deployments

### Progressive Deployment Pipeline

```
You: "Deploy the new version to dev, then staging, then production - but only if tests pass at each stage"

Copilot:
1. Deploys to dev environment
2. Runs automated tests
3. If tests pass, deploys to staging
4. Runs staging tests
5. Waits for approval before production
6. Deploys to production
7. Monitors production health
```

### Blue-Green Deployment

```
You: "Set up a blue-green deployment for my-api in production"

Copilot:
1. Creates green environment (copy of blue)
2. Deploys new version to green
3. Runs health checks on green
4. Switches traffic to green
5. Monitors for issues
6. Keeps blue as backup
```

### Canary Deployment

```
You: "Deploy version 2.0 as a canary to 10% of production traffic"

Copilot:
1. Deploys new version alongside current
2. Configures traffic split (90% old, 10% new)
3. Monitors error rates
4. Gradually increases traffic if healthy
5. Rolls back if errors spike
```

### Maintenance Windows

```
You: "Every Sunday from 2 AM to 4 AM, perform maintenance on staging: update all services, run database optimization, clear caches"

Copilot:
1. Creates weekly maintenance window (Sun 2-4 AM)
2. Schedules sequential tasks:
   - 2:00 AM: Deploy latest versions to all services
   - 2:30 AM: Run database optimization scripts
   - 3:00 AM: Clear application caches
   - 3:30 AM: Run health checks
3. Monitors each task completion
4. Sends maintenance report at 4 AM
5. Alerts if any task fails
```

### Conditional Time-Based Actions

```
You: "If CPU usage stays above 80% for more than 30 minutes during business hours, scale up. After 6 PM, just alert me instead."

Copilot:
1. Sets up time-based conditional rules:
   - Business hours (9 AM - 6 PM): Auto-scale on high CPU
   - After hours (6 PM - 9 AM): Alert only
2. Monitors CPU metrics continuously
3. During business hours:
   - Detects sustained high CPU
   - Automatically scales up
   - Notifies of action taken
4. After hours:
   - Detects sustained high CPU
   - Sends alert without scaling
   - Waits for manual intervention
```

    1. "First, set up the infrastructure..."
    2. "Next, configure the services..."
    3. "Finally, validate everything..."
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Use Checkpoints">

  <Accordion title="Define Success Criteria">

    "Deploy and consider it successful only if error rate stays below 0.1%"
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Plan for Failures">

    "Try to deploy, but if it fails, automatically rollback and notify me"
  </Accordion>

# Qovery CLI
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview

> Install the Qovery CLI, log in, set a default context and run your first commands from the terminal

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Overview

The Qovery CLI (Command Line Interface) enables you to interact with Qovery directly from your terminal. Deploy applications, manage environments, stream logs, and more - all without leaving your command line.

## Installation

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Linux">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="*nix">
        To download and install Qovery CLI on any Linux distribution:

        ```bash
        curl -s https://get.qovery.com | bash
        ```

        <Warning>
        The install script does not verify the binary's integrity. For security-sensitive environments, use the **Manual** tab to download a pinned release and verify its checksum against the official [checksums.txt](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) published with each release.
        </Warning>
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Arch Linux">
        Qovery is part of [AUR](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages) packages, so you can install it with [yay](https://github.com/Jguer/yay):

        ```bash
        yay qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on Linux manually from a [pinned release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) to ensure you control what version is installed.

        Replace `X.Y.Z` with the version you want to install:

        ```bash
        VERSION=1.180.0  # version number without the 'v' prefix
        ARCH=amd64      # use arm64 for ARM64
        ARCHIVE="qovery-cli_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"

        # Download the binary and checksums for your platform
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ARCHIVE}" -o "${ARCHIVE}"
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" -o checksums.txt

        # Verify the checksum of the downloaded file only (fails if tampered)
        grep "${ARCHIVE}" checksums.txt | sha256sum --check

        # Extract and install
        tar -xzf "${ARCHIVE}"
        mv qovery /usr/local/bin/qovery
        chmod +x /usr/local/bin/qovery
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="MacOS">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Homebrew">
        The common solution to install a command line binary on the MacOS is to use [Homebrew](https://brew.sh).

        ```bash
        # Add Qovery brew repository
        brew tap Qovery/qovery-cli

        # Install the CLI
        brew install qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Script">
        To download and install Qovery CLI from the command line:

        ```bash
        curl -s https://get.qovery.com | bash
        ```

        <Warning>
        The install script does not verify the binary's integrity. For security-sensitive environments, use the **Manual** tab to download a pinned release and verify its checksum against the official [checksums.txt](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) published with each release.
        </Warning>
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on macOS manually from a [pinned release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) to ensure you control what version is installed.

        Replace `X.Y.Z` with the version you want to install:

        ```bash
        VERSION=1.180.0  # version number without the 'v' prefix
        ARCH=amd64      # use arm64 for Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)
        ARCHIVE="qovery-cli_${VERSION}_darwin_${ARCH}.tar.gz"

        # Download the binary and checksums for your platform
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ARCHIVE}" -o "${ARCHIVE}"
        curl -sL "https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt" -o checksums.txt

        # Verify the checksum of the downloaded file only (fails if tampered)
        grep "${ARCHIVE}" checksums.txt | shasum -a 256 --check

        # Extract and install
        tar -xzf "${ARCHIVE}"
        mv qovery /usr/local/bin/qovery
        chmod +x /usr/local/bin/qovery
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Windows">
    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="Scoop">
        The classic way to install binaries on Windows is to use [Scoop](https://scoop.sh).

        ```bash
        # Add Qovery bucket
        scoop bucket add qovery https://github.com/Qovery/scoop-qovery-cli

        # Install the CLI
        scoop install qovery-cli
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Manual">
        Install the Qovery CLI on Windows manually by downloading the [latest release](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases), and uncompress its content to `C:\Windows`.
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Docker">
    Install Docker on your local machine and run the following command:

    ```bash
    # Pull and Run the latest Qovery CLI
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:latest help
    ```

    Change `latest` by the version you want to use. For example, to use the version 0.58.4, run:

    ```bash
    docker run ghcr.io/qovery/qovery-cli:0.58.4 help
    ```

    <Info>
    `ghcr.io` is the [GitHub Container Registry](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/pkgs/container/qovery-cli).
    </Info>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Verify Installation

```bash
qovery version
```

## Authentication

Before using the CLI, you need to authenticate:

```bash
qovery auth
```

This will open a browser window for authentication. Once completed, you'll be ready to use the CLI.

### API Token Authentication

You can also authenticate using an API token. Every command then uses the token directly, so you do not need to run `qovery auth`:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-api-token"
qovery auth status
```

Generate an API token from the [Qovery Console](https://console.qovery.com/platform/organization/api-tokens).

## Configuration

The CLI stores configuration in `~/.qovery/context.json`. You can manage multiple contexts for different organizations or clusters.

### Set Default Context

```bash
qovery context set
```

### Show the Current Context

```bash
qovery context
```

## Watching Operations

Most deployment commands accept the `--watch` (`-w`) flag to wait until the targeted services finish and report their final status. The command exits with a non-zero status if a watched service fails, is canceled, ends in an unexpected state, or no longer exists, which is useful in CI/CD pipelines.

By default, a watch stops after **1 hour** and exits with an error if the services have not finished. To wait longer (for example for long builds or Terraform runs), set the `QOVERY_CLI_WATCH_TIMEOUT` environment variable to a [Go duration](https://pkg.go.dev/time#ParseDuration) such as `2h`:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_WATCH_TIMEOUT="2h"
qovery environment deploy --watch
```

## Blueprint Databases

Databases created from a database blueprint are Terraform services, and the CLI supports them like native databases.

### List Blueprint Databases

`qovery database list` lists the blueprint databases of the current environment together with the native databases. Blueprint databases appear with the type `Blueprint database`, and the output shows their status, host, and port:

```bash
qovery database list
```

Add `--show-credentials` to display the login and password, as for native databases. If the credentials are not available (the database is not deployed yet, or you are not allowed to read them), only the host and port are shown.

With `--json`, blueprint databases are included in the output with the same fields as native databases. The `login` and `password` fields are only filled when `--show-credentials` is set.

### Port-Forward to a Blueprint Database

`qovery port-forward` accepts the Console URL of a Terraform service, such as a blueprint database. Pass the URL of the service followed by the ports to forward, in the `local_port:remote_port` format:

```bash
qovery port-forward "$SERVICE_CONSOLE_URL" --port 5432:5432
```

If the service ID in the URL does not exist in the environment, the command fails with a `not found in environment` error.

## Blueprints

### Point a Blueprint at a Newer Major Version

`qovery blueprint upgrade-major` points a blueprint service at the latest tag of a newer major version, for example PostgreSQL 14 to 18. It is built for AWS RDS PostgreSQL databases: Qovery checks the version the database runs and handles the upgrade end to end. Other blueprint services are accepted, but Qovery does not check that their new major can be applied safely, so review that template's upgrade notes first. Run it without `--major` to list the newer majors and what moving to each one would do:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major -n "$SERVICE_NAME"
```

Then pick a major:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major -n "$SERVICE_NAME" --major 18
```

The command shows what will happen and asks for confirmation (`--yes` or `-y` skips it), then updates the blueprint and deploys it. Add `--watch` (`-w`) to follow the deployment.

- **Relabel:** the service already runs that major, for example a database upgraded with an AWS Blue/Green deployment. Only Qovery's records change; the service is not touched. Qovery detects this for AWS RDS databases only.
- **Upgrade:** the service runs an older major.
  - For an AWS RDS PostgreSQL database, the deployment upgrades it in place and takes it offline while AWS upgrades it. Use this for non-production databases.
  - For a production database, upgrade with an [AWS Blue/Green deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/upgrading-rds-instance) first, then run the command: it only relabels the blueprint.
  - Other blueprints always take this path; what happens then depends on their template's own upgrade behavior.
- **Not supported:** the move is refused and the command explains why, for example a lower major than the one running. If the command reports an unknown switch mode, update the Qovery CLI.

See [Moving to a newer major version](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints#moving-to-a-newer-major-version) for details.

## Environment Variables

### Override a Variable That Already Exists at a Higher Scope

The `env create` commands (`application`, `container`, `cronjob`, `environment`, `helm`, `lifecycle`) accept an `--override-if-exists` flag. By default, creating a variable whose key already exists at a higher scope fails with a conflict. With the flag set, Qovery creates an override of that variable at the target scope instead:

```bash
qovery application env create --key DATABASE_URL --value "postgres://..." --override-if-exists
```

# qovery api
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/api

> Call any Qovery API endpoint from the terminal with your CLI login, and print the OpenAPI specification

## Overview

Make authenticated HTTP requests to the Qovery API directly from the CLI. This command acts as a lightweight, `curl`-like client that automatically handles authentication and supports context variable interpolation.

Context variables `{organizationId}`, `{projectId}`, and `{environmentId}` are automatically replaced with values from the current CLI context (set via `qovery context`).

## Usage

```text
qovery api <endpoint> [flags]
```

The `<endpoint>` is the API path relative to the Qovery API base URL (e.g., `organization`, `organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/project`).

## Examples

### List Resources

```bash
# List organizations
qovery api organization

# Get a specific organization
qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID"
```

### Use Context Variables

When you have an active CLI context, placeholder variables are automatically resolved:

```bash
# List projects in current organization
qovery api organization/{organizationId}/project

# List services in current environment
qovery api organization/{organizationId}/project/{projectId}/environment/{environmentId}/service
```

### Create Resources with --field

Build a JSON body from key=value pairs:

```bash
qovery api organization --field name=my-org --field plan=FREE
```

### Send a JSON Body from Stdin

```bash
# Pipe JSON directly
echo '{"name":"my-org","plan":"FREE"}' | qovery api organization --input -

# Send a JSON file as body
qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/project" --input - < body.json
```

### Delete a Resource

```bash
qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID" --method DELETE
```

### Show Response Headers

```bash
qovery api organization --include
```

### Add Custom Headers

```bash
qovery api organization -H "X-Request-Id: abc123"
```

### Use a Custom API URL

```bash
QOVERY_API_URL=https://staging.api.qovery.com qovery api organization
```

{/* BEGIN GENERATED: qovery api --help, CLI v1.180.0 */}
## Command reference

Generated from `qovery api --help` (CLI v1.180.0). Every command also accepts `-h, --help` and the [global flags](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/overview#global-flags).

### `qovery api`

Make an authenticated request to the Qovery API

```text Description from qovery api --help
Make an authenticated HTTP request to the Qovery API.

EXAMPLES

  # List organizations
  $ qovery api organization

  # Get a specific organization
  $ qovery api organization/<id>

  # List projects in current organization (from context)
  $ qovery api organization/{organizationId}/project

  # Get current environment's services (fully from context)
  $ qovery api organization/{organizationId}/project/{projectId}/environment/{environmentId}/service

  # Create an organization using --field
  $ qovery api organization --field name=my-org --field plan=FREE

  # Pipe body from stdin
  $ echo '{"name":"my-org","plan":"FREE"}' | qovery api organization --input -

  # Send a JSON file as body
  $ qovery api organization/<id>/project --input - < body.json

  # Delete a resource
  $ qovery api organization/<id> --method DELETE

  # Show response headers
  $ qovery api organization --include

  # Add a custom header
  $ qovery api organization -H "X-Request-Id: abc123"

  # Use a staging environment
  $ QOVERY_API_URL=https://staging.api.qovery.com qovery api organization
```

```text Usage
qovery api <endpoint> [flags]
qovery api [command]
```

| Subcommand | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| `qovery api spec` | Print the Qovery API's OpenAPI specification |

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--field` | `-f` | stringArray |  |  | Add a key=value pair to the JSON body (repeatable, smart type coercion) |
| `--header` | `-H` | stringArray |  |  | Additional request headers in 'Key: Value' format (repeatable) |
| `--include` | `-i` | bool |  |  | Print HTTP response status and headers before body |
| `--input` |  | string |  |  | Body: '-' for stdin (pipe JSON to command) |
| `--method` | `-X` | string |  |  | HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) |

### `qovery api spec`

Print the Qovery API's OpenAPI specification

```text Description from qovery api spec --help
Fetch and print the Qovery API's OpenAPI specification (YAML), sourced from
https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-openapi-spec.

Use it to discover valid endpoints, methods, and request/response shapes before
calling 'qovery api <endpoint>' — instead of guessing or relying on a copy that
may be out of date. This command does not require authentication.

EXAMPLES

  # Print the spec to stdout
  $ qovery api spec

  # Save it to a file
  $ qovery api spec -o openapi.yaml

  # Look up one path with a YAML query tool
  $ qovery api spec | yq '.paths["/organization"]'
```

```text Usage
qovery api spec [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--output` | `-o` | string |  |  | Write the spec to a file instead of stdout |

# qovery application
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/application

> Deploy, redeploy, restart, stop, clone or delete applications, and manage their domains, variables and secrets

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Overview

Deploy and manage applications within your Qovery environment.

## Commands

### List Applications

List all applications in current environment:

```bash
qovery application list
```

Output as JSON:

```bash
qovery application list --json
```

### Deploy Application

Deploy a specific application:

```bash
qovery application deploy --application "my-api"
```

Deploy with a specific commit:

```bash
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --commit-id "abc123def"
```

Deploy the newest commit of the branch with `latest`. The CLI resolves it to a commit SHA, prints the resolved SHA, and deploys it:

```bash
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --commit-id latest
```

Deploy multiple applications at once:

```bash
qovery application deploy \
  --applications "app1,app2,app3"
```

Watch deployment progress:

```bash
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --watch
```

### Redeploy Application

Redeploy the same version:

```bash
qovery application redeploy --application "my-api"
```

Redeploy a specific commit, or the newest commit of the branch with `latest`. When `--commit-id` is omitted, the currently deployed commit is reused:

```bash
qovery application redeploy --application "my-api" --commit-id "a1b2c3d"
qovery application redeploy --application "my-api" --commit-id latest
```

### Restart Application

Restart a running application without redeploying it:

```bash
qovery application restart --application "my-api"
```

Restart multiple applications and wait until they are restarted:

```bash
qovery application restart \
  --applications "app1,app2" \
  --watch
```

<Note>
With `--watch`, the command follows only the selected applications and exits with code 1 if one of them fails, is canceled, or no longer exists.
</Note>

### Stop Application

Stop a running application:

```bash
qovery application stop --application "my-api"
```

Stop multiple applications:

```bash
qovery application stop --applications "app1,app2"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel an ongoing deployment:

```bash
qovery application cancel --application "my-api"
```

### Delete Application

Delete an application:

```bash
qovery application delete --application "my-api"
```

### Update Application

Update application configuration (branch or auto-deploy setting):

```bash
qovery application update \
  --application "my-api" \
  --branch "main"
```

Enable auto-deploy:

```bash
qovery application update \
  --application "my-api" \
  --auto-deploy
```

## Examples

### Deploy Application

```bash
# Set context first if not already set
qovery context set

# Deploy latest commit
qovery application deploy --application "my-api"

# Deploy with specific commit
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --commit-id "a1b2c3d"

# Watch deployment progress
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --watch
```

### Deploy Multiple Applications

```bash
qovery application deploy \
  --applications "frontend,backend,worker"
```

### Rollback Deployment

```bash
# Deploy a previous commit
qovery application deploy \
  --application "my-api" \
  --commit-id "previous-commit-sha"
```

### Update Branch

```bash
qovery application update \
  --application "my-api" \
  --branch "feature/new-branch"
```

## Additional Subcommand Groups

The `application` command also has the following subcommand groups for more advanced management:

- **`qovery application clone`**: clone an application to another environment
- **`qovery application domain`**: manage custom domains (`list`, `create`, `delete`, `edit`)
- **`qovery application env`**: manage environment variables and secrets (`list`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `alias`, `override`)
- **`qovery application external-secret`**: manage external secrets (`create`, `update`, `delete`)

# qovery audit-log
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/audit-log

> Export your organization's audit logs for a date range to a CSV file

## Overview

Use `qovery audit-log export` to download the audit logs of an organization to a CSV file named `audit_logs_<date>_<time>.csv` in the current directory. The command first prints how many days of history your organization plan keeps.

`--from-date` is required. Dates must use the ISO-8601 format with a `T` between the date and the time, and a time zone, for example `2026-10-01T00:00:00Z` or `2026-10-01T02:00:00+02:00`. Without `--to-date`, the export runs until now.

## Examples

Export from a date until now:

```bash
qovery audit-log export \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --from-date "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z"
```

Export a date range:

```bash
qovery audit-log export \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --from-date "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z" \
  --to-date "2026-10-31T23:59:59Z"
```

```text Description from qovery audit-log export --help
This command provides an easy way to download audit logs.
```

# qovery auth
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/auth

> Log in to Qovery from a browser or a headless session, check your login status and print the access token

## Overview

The `auth` command handles authentication with Qovery. You can authenticate using interactive login or API tokens.

## Commands

### Login

Authenticate with Qovery interactively:

```bash
qovery auth
```

This will open your browser to complete the authentication flow.

### Headless Login

For environments without a browser (CI/CD, servers), use headless mode:

```bash
qovery auth --headless
```

This will provide a URL that you can open manually to complete authentication.

### Login with API Token

Set your API token as an environment variable. Every command then uses the token directly, so you do not need to run `qovery auth`, which always starts the browser or headless login flow:

```bash
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-api-token"
qovery auth status
```

<Info>
You can generate an API token from the Qovery Console under **Settings** → **API Tokens**.
</Info>

### Token

Output the current valid access token (refreshing it if expired). Useful for making direct API calls to the Qovery API.

For security reasons, the token is not printed by default. You must explicitly use `--print` or `--json` to output the token value.

```bash
qovery auth token [flags]
```

**Examples:**
```bash
# Print the raw token value
qovery auth token --print

# Use directly in a curl command
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(qovery auth token --print)" \
  https://api.qovery.com/organization

# Print the full Authorization header value
qovery auth token --print --authorization-header

# Get structured JSON output
qovery auth token --json
```

## Examples

### Interactive Login

```bash
qovery auth
# Opens browser for authentication
# Credentials saved locally
```

### Headless Authentication

```bash
qovery auth --headless
# Displays URL: https://auth.qovery.com/...
# Copy and paste URL in a browser
# Complete authentication manually
```

### CI/CD Authentication

```bash
# In your CI/CD environment
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="${{ secrets.QOVERY_TOKEN }}"
# No `qovery auth` needed: the CLI uses QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN directly
qovery application deploy --application "my-app"
```

### Server/Remote Authentication

```bash
# On a remote server without browser
qovery auth --headless
# Copy the displayed URL
# Open URL on your local machine
# Authentication will be saved on the server
```

### `qovery auth status`

Show authentication status without exposing the access token

```text Description from qovery auth status --help
Show whether the CLI is currently authenticated, as whom, which organization
is selected, and when the session expires.

This command never prints the access token or any other secret value, regardless
of flags. Use it as the safe way to check authentication from scripts, CI, and
automation, instead of parsing the output of 'qovery auth token':

  qovery auth status >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo authenticated || echo "not authenticated"

Unlike most other commands, this always makes a live call to the Qovery API to
confirm the token is currently accepted — a token that is present and well-formed
but has been revoked or expired server-side is reported as not authenticated,
whether it came from a browser login or from QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN / Q_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN.

Exit code is 0 when authenticated, 1 otherwise.
```

```text Usage
qovery auth status [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--json` |  | bool |  |  | JSON output |

### `qovery auth token`

Output the current valid access token

```text Description from qovery auth token --help
Output the current valid access token (refreshing it if expired).

This command provides a valid access token that can be used to make direct API calls 
to the Qovery API. The token is automatically refreshed if it has expired.

For security reasons, the token is not printed by default. You must explicitly
use --print or --json to output the token value.

If you only need to check whether the CLI is authenticated (e.g. from a script
or an automated agent), use 'qovery auth status' instead — it never prints the
token, even with --json.
```

```text Usage
qovery auth token [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--authorization-header` |  | bool |  |  | Output the full Authorization header value (e.g. 'Bearer eyJ...') |
| `--json` |  | bool |  |  | Output as JSON with token, type, expiration, and API URL |
| `--print` |  | bool |  |  | Print the raw access token value to stdout |

Examples printed by `qovery auth token --help`, verbatim.

```text qovery auth token --help
# Print the raw token value
qovery auth token --print

# Use directly in a curl command
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(qovery auth token --print)" https://api.qovery.com/organization

# Print the full Authorization header value
qovery auth token --print --authorization-header

# Get structured JSON output with token, type, expiration, and API URL
qovery auth token --json

# Get JSON with the authorization header pre-formatted
qovery auth token --json --authorization-header
```

# qovery blueprint
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/blueprint

> Move a blueprint service, such as an RDS database, to a newer major version from the terminal

## Overview

Use `qovery blueprint` to move a [blueprint](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/blueprints) service to the latest tag of a newer major version, for example PostgreSQL 14 to 18.

The command is built for AWS RDS PostgreSQL databases. Other blueprint services are accepted, but Qovery does not check that their new major can be applied safely, so review that template's upgrade notes first. See [Point a Blueprint at a Newer Major Version](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview#point-a-blueprint-at-a-newer-major-version) for what each kind of move does.

## Examples

List the newer majors and what moving to each one would do:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major --name "my-postgres"
```

<Warning>
An in-place major upgrade takes the database offline while AWS upgrades it. For a production database, upgrade with an [AWS Blue/Green deployment](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/advanced-tutorials/upgrading-rds-instance) first, then run the command: it only relabels the blueprint.
</Warning>

Move to major 18, skip the confirmation prompt and follow the deployment:

```bash
qovery blueprint upgrade-major \
  --name "my-postgres" \
  --major 18 \
  --yes \
  --watch
```

```text Description from qovery blueprint upgrade-major --help
Point a blueprint service at the latest tag of a newer major version (e.g. PostgreSQL 14 to 18).

Without --major, lists the newer majors and what moving to each one does:
  RELABEL      the service already runs that major (e.g. upgraded on AWS): only Qovery's records change
  UPGRADE      the service runs an older major: the next deploy upgrades it in place (downtime for databases)
  UNSUPPORTED  the move is refused, with the reason
```

```text Usage
qovery blueprint upgrade-major [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--environment` |  | string |  |  | Environment Name |
| `--major` |  | string |  |  | Major version to move to (e.g. 18). Without it, lists the available majors |
| `--name` | `-n` | string |  | Yes | Blueprint service name |
| `--organization` |  | string |  |  | Organization Name |
| `--project` |  | string |  |  | Project Name |
| `--watch` | `-w` | bool |  |  | Watch the service status until it's ready or an error occurs |
| `--yes` | `-y` | bool |  |  | Skip the confirmation prompt |
{/* END GENERATED */}

# qovery cluster
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/cluster

> List, install, deploy, upgrade, stop and lock clusters, download a kubeconfig and open a debug pod

## Overview

View and manage Kubernetes clusters in your Qovery organization.

## Commands

### List Clusters

List all clusters in current organization:

```bash
qovery cluster list
```

### Deploy Cluster

Deploy a cluster:

```bash
qovery cluster deploy --cluster "cluster-name"
```

### Stop Cluster

Stop a cluster:

```bash
qovery cluster stop --cluster "cluster-name"
```

### Install Cluster

Install Qovery on the cluster of your current kubeconfig context. Use it for clusters other than EKS, GKE and Kapsule, which use the Qovery Operator installation instead:

```bash
qovery cluster install
```

Besides the Qovery engine and agents, the generated Helm values install Envoy Gateway with the Gateway API CRDs, cert-manager, ExternalDNS, metrics-server, Loki and Alloy. If the cluster already runs cert-manager, ExternalDNS or Envoy Gateway, turn off the Qovery copy in the values file or remove the existing one. Run `qovery cluster preflight` first to spot these components. See [Installation with the Qovery CLI](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy) and [Supported cluster setups](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups).

### Check a Cluster Before Installing

Check that the cluster of your current kubeconfig context can run Qovery before you install the Qovery Operator. The command only reads from the cluster and needs no Qovery account. It exits with status `1` when a check fails.

```bash
qovery cluster preflight
```

See [Supported cluster setups](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-supported-setups) for the list of checks.

### Upgrade Cluster

Upgrade a cluster to the next Kubernetes version:

```bash
qovery cluster upgrade --cluster "cluster-name"
```

### Download Kubeconfig

Download kubeconfig file for kubectl access:

```bash
qovery cluster kubeconfig --cluster-id "cluster-id"
```

This command writes a `kubeconfig-<cluster-id>.yaml` file in the current directory that allows you to connect to your cluster using kubectl.

For read-only access, add `--read-only`. The file is then named `kubeconfig-readonly-<cluster-id>.yaml` and uses a Kubernetes service account with the `view` ClusterRole:

```bash
qovery cluster kubeconfig --cluster-id "cluster-id" --read-only
```

### Get Cluster Token

Get an auth token for a cluster:

```bash
qovery cluster get-token --cluster-id "cluster-id"
```

### Lock Cluster

Lock a cluster to prevent changes:

```bash
qovery cluster lock \
  --cluster-id "cluster-id" \
  --reason "maintenance"
```

### Unlock Cluster

Unlock a cluster:

```bash
qovery cluster unlock --cluster-id "cluster-id"
```

### List Cluster Nodes

List nodes of a cluster:

```bash
qovery cluster list-nodes --cluster-id "cluster-id"
```

### Open Debug Pod

Launch an interactive debug pod with kubectl pre-configured:

```bash
qovery cluster debug-pod \
  --organization-id "org-id" \
  --cluster-id "cluster-id"
```

This opens a debug shell inside your cluster with kubectl access, perfect for troubleshooting.

## Examples

### List All Clusters

```bash
# List clusters of an organization
qovery cluster list --organization "My Org"

# List clusters with JSON output
qovery cluster list --json
```

### Deploy and Watch Cluster

```bash
qovery cluster deploy \
  --cluster "prod-us-east" \
  --watch
```

### Get kubectl Access

```bash
# Download kubeconfig file
qovery cluster kubeconfig --cluster-id "abc123"

# Set kubectl to use the downloaded config
export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig-abc123.yaml

# Test connection
kubectl get nodes
```

### Open Debug Pod for Troubleshooting

```bash
# Launch debug pod
qovery cluster debug-pod \
  --organization-id "org-abc123" \
  --cluster-id "cluster-abc123"

# Launch privileged debug pod on a specific node
qovery cluster debug-pod \
  --organization-id "org-abc123" \
  --cluster-id "cluster-abc123" \
  --node-selector "kubernetes.io/hostname=my-node" \
  --full-privilege

# Inside the debug pod, you can run kubectl commands:
# kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
# kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace>
# exit
```

### Upgrade Cluster

```bash
# Upgrade with confirmation prompt
qovery cluster upgrade --cluster "prod-us-east"

# Upgrade without confirmation and watch progress
qovery cluster upgrade \
  --cluster "prod-us-east" \
  --skip-confirmation \
  --watch
```

## Tips

<Tip>
Use `qovery cluster deploy --watch` to monitor cluster deployment progress in real time.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Use `qovery cluster kubeconfig` to get full kubectl access to your cluster for advanced operations.
</Tip>

<Tip>
The `debug-pod` command is perfect for quick troubleshooting without needing to configure kubectl locally.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Use `qovery cluster lock` during planned maintenance to prevent accidental changes to your cluster.
</Tip>
