### `qovery cluster preflight`

Check that your Kubernetes cluster is ready before you install Qovery on it

```text Description from qovery cluster preflight --help
Check that your Kubernetes cluster is ready before you install Qovery on it.

Qovery runs on any Kubernetes cluster, with one of two installations:
  - EKS (AWS), GKE (GCP) and Scaleway Kapsule: the Qovery Operator installation, the Helm
    command shown in the Qovery Console.
  - Every other cluster (AKS, k3s, RKE2, OpenShift, on-premise, ...): the installation with
    the Qovery CLI, qovery cluster install.
    https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/kubernetes/byok-legacy

The preflight detects the provider of your nodes, tells you which installation to use and
runs the checks of that installation. Use --install-path to force one. The checks for an
existing cert-manager, ExternalDNS, Envoy Gateway or Gateway API CRDs fail on the Operator
installation, which does not share them. Both installations install these components, so on
the CLI installation they warn: turn off the Qovery copy in the Helm values file that
qovery cluster install generates, or remove the existing one. An existing qovery Helm release
fails only on the Operator installation; on the CLI installation it is Qovery itself.

The preflight runs against the current context of your kubeconfig, or the one given with
--kubeconfig and --context. It only reads from the cluster: it creates, changes or deletes
nothing, and it reads no Secret data. It needs no Qovery account.

It exits with status 1 when at least one check fails. A failed check would make the
installation or the first deployment of the cluster fail; fix it before installing.
Warnings do not block the installation but can break a feature.
```

```text Usage
qovery cluster preflight [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--context` |  | string |  |  | Kubeconfig context to check (default: the current context) |
| `--install-path` |  | string | `"auto"` |  | Installation to check for: operator (EKS, GKE, Scaleway Kapsule), cli (qovery cluster install, any other cluster) or auto (picked from the provider of the nodes) |
| `--json` |  | bool |  |  | JSON output |
| `--kubeconfig` |  | string |  |  | Path to the kubeconfig file (default: $KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config) |
| `--loki-object-storage` |  | bool |  |  | Loki will store logs in object storage (s3, gcs or s3Compatible), so no default StorageClass is needed |

# qovery completion
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/completion

> Turn on tab completion for Qovery CLI commands and flags in bash, zsh, fish or PowerShell

## Overview

Use `qovery completion` to generate the autocompletion script for your shell, so that Tab completes Qovery commands, subcommands and flags. Add `--no-descriptions` to leave the descriptions out of the suggestions.

## Setup

### bash

```bash
# Load completions in current session
source <(qovery completion bash)

# Load completions for every new session
qovery completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/qovery
```

### zsh

```bash
# Load completions in current session
source <(qovery completion zsh)

# Load completions for every new session (Oh-My-Zsh)
qovery completion zsh > ~/.oh-my-zsh/completions/_qovery
```

### fish

```bash
# Load completions in current session
qovery completion fish | source

# Load completions for every new session
qovery completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/qovery.fish
```

### PowerShell

```powershell
# Load completions in current session
qovery completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression

# Add to PowerShell profile for every new session
qovery completion powershell >> $PROFILE
```

### Without descriptions

```bash
qovery completion zsh --no-descriptions > ~/.oh-my-zsh/completions/_qovery
```

# qovery console
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/console

> Open the service selected in your CLI context in the Qovery Console in your browser

## Overview

Use `qovery console` to jump from the terminal to the Qovery Console page of a service. The command opens the service selected in your [context](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/context) in your default browser and prints the URL it opens.

If no organization, project, environment or service is selected yet, the command asks you to pick them first. The command takes no flags and no arguments: to open another service, change the context with `qovery context set`.

## Examples

Open the service in the current context:

```bash
qovery console
```

Open another service:

```bash
qovery context set
qovery console
```

## Tips

<Tip>
Use `qovery console` when you need to perform actions that are easier in the web interface, like viewing metrics or managing complex configurations.
</Tip>

# qovery container
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/container

> Create, deploy, restart, stop or clone container services, and manage their domains, registries, variables and secrets

## Overview

Manage container services within your Qovery environment. Containers allow you to deploy pre-built Docker images.

## Commands

### List Containers

List all containers in current environment:

```bash
qovery container list
```

### Create Container

Create a new container service:

```bash
qovery container create \
  --container "my-container" \
  --registry "$REGISTRY_ID" \
  --image-name "nginx" \
  --tag "latest"
```

### Deploy Container

Deploy a container:

```bash
qovery container deploy --container "my-container"
```

Deploy with specific image tag:

```bash
qovery container deploy \
  --container "my-container" \
  --tag "v1.2.0"
```

Deploy multiple containers at once:

```bash
qovery container deploy \
  --containers "container1,container2"
```

### Redeploy Container

Redeploy with same image:

```bash
qovery container redeploy --container "my-container"
```

### Restart Container

Restart a running container without redeploying it:

```bash
qovery container restart --container "my-container"
```

Restart multiple containers at once:

```bash
qovery container restart --containers "container1,container2"
```

<Note>
With `--watch`, the command follows only the selected containers and exits with code 1 if one of them fails, is canceled, or no longer exists.
</Note>

### Stop Container

Stop a running container:

```bash
qovery container stop --container "my-container"
```

Stop multiple containers at once:

```bash
qovery container stop --containers "container1,container2"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel a container deployment:

```bash
qovery container cancel --container "my-container"
```

### Update Container

Update a container's image name or tag:

```bash
qovery container update \
  --container "my-container" \
  --tag "v2.0.0"
```

### Clone Container

Clone a container to another environment or project:

```bash
qovery container clone --container "my-container"
```

### Delete Container

Delete a container service:

```bash
qovery container delete --container "my-container"
```

Delete multiple containers at once:

```bash
qovery container delete --containers "container1,container2"
```

## Examples

### Deploy Container

```bash
# List containers
qovery container list

# Deploy container
qovery container deploy --container "nginx-proxy"

# Watch deployment status
qovery container deploy --container "nginx-proxy" --watch
```

### Deploy Specific Image Version

```bash
# Deploy with specific tag
qovery container deploy \
  --container "nginx-proxy" \
  --tag "1.21-alpine"
```

### List Containers as JSON

```bash
qovery container list --json
```

# qovery context
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/context

> Show or set the organization, project, environment and service the CLI targets by default

## Overview

Use `qovery context` to see or change the organization, project, environment and service the CLI targets by default, so you do not have to pass them to every command.

## Commands

### Show the current context

```bash
qovery context
```

Prints the organization, project, environment and service the CLI currently targets.

### Set the context

```bash
qovery context set
```

`qovery context set` is an interactive picker: it asks you to select an organization, then a
project, an environment and a service. It takes no flags to select them.

<Note>
**Scripts, CI and AI agents** cannot answer the interactive picker. Skip the context and pass names
explicitly instead: commands accept `--organization`, `--project` and `--environment` (for example
`qovery environment list --organization "Acme Corp" --project "Backend Services"`), and
`qovery api` takes IDs in the path (`qovery api "organization/$ORGANIZATION_ID/project"`).
</Note>

## Examples

### Switch to another organization, project or environment

```bash
qovery context set
# Select organization -> project -> environment -> service
qovery context
# Check what is now selected
```

### Target an organization without changing the context

```bash
qovery project list --organization "Acme Corp"
```

# qovery cronjob
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/cronjob

> Deploy, redeploy, stop, clone or delete cron jobs, and manage their variables and secrets

## Overview

Manage cronjobs within your Qovery environment. Cronjobs run on a scheduled basis (similar to cron in Unix/Linux).

## Commands

### List Cronjobs

List all cronjobs in current environment:

```bash
qovery cronjob list
```

### Deploy Cronjob

Deploy a cronjob:

```bash
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "my-cron"
```

Deploy multiple cronjobs at once:

```bash
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjobs "cron1,cron2"
```

Deploy with a specific commit ID or image tag. For a git-sourced cronjob, `latest` deploys the newest commit of the branch:

```bash
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "my-cron" --commit-id "abc123"
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "my-cron" --commit-id latest
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "my-cron" --tag "v1.2.0"
```

### Redeploy Cronjob

Redeploy an existing cronjob with the same configuration:

```bash
qovery cronjob redeploy --cronjob "my-cron"
```

### Stop Cronjob

Stop a cronjob:

```bash
qovery cronjob stop --cronjob "my-cron"
```

### Delete Cronjob

Delete a cronjob:

```bash
qovery cronjob delete --cronjob "my-cron"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel a cronjob deployment:

```bash
qovery cronjob cancel --cronjob "my-cron"
```

### Update Cronjob

Update cronjob source configuration (branch, tag, or image name):

```bash
# Update git branch (for Dockerfile-based cronjobs)
qovery cronjob update --cronjob "my-cron" --branch "main"

# Update image tag (for image-based cronjobs)
qovery cronjob update --cronjob "my-cron" --tag "v2.0.0"

# Update image name
qovery cronjob update --cronjob "my-cron" --image-name "my-registry/my-image"
```

### Clone Cronjob

Clone a cronjob to another environment or project:

```bash
qovery cronjob clone --cronjob "my-cron"
```

## Examples

### Deploy Cronjob

```bash
# List cronjobs
qovery cronjob list

# Deploy cronjob
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "backup-job"

# Deploy and watch status
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "backup-job" --watch
```

### Update Cronjob and Redeploy

```bash
# Update branch for a git-based cronjob
qovery cronjob update --cronjob "backup-job" --branch "feature/new-schedule"

# Redeploy to apply changes
qovery cronjob redeploy --cronjob "backup-job"
```

### Deploy Cronjob with Specific Tag

```bash
qovery cronjob deploy --cronjob "backup-job" --tag "v2.1.0"
```

```bash
qovery cronjob list --json
```

# qovery database
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/database

> List, deploy, redeploy, restart, stop or delete databases, and show their connection credentials

## Overview

Manage databases within your Qovery environment.

## Commands

### List Databases

List all databases in current environment:

```bash
qovery database list
```

Show credentials in the output:

```bash
qovery database list --show-credentials
```

### Deploy Database

Deploy or start a database:

```bash
qovery database deploy --database "my-db"
```

Deploy multiple databases at once:

```bash
qovery database deploy --databases "db1,db2"
```

### Redeploy Database

Redeploy an existing database:

```bash
qovery database redeploy --database "my-db"
```

### Restart Database

Restart a running database without redeploying it:

```bash
qovery database restart --database "my-db"
```

Restart multiple databases at once:

```bash
qovery database restart --databases "db1,db2"
```

<Note>
With `--watch`, the command follows only the selected databases and exits with code 1 if one of them fails, is canceled, or no longer exists.
</Note>

### Stop Database

Stop a running database:

```bash
qovery database stop --database "my-db"
```

Stop multiple databases at once:

```bash
qovery database stop --databases "db1,db2"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel a database deployment:

```bash
qovery database cancel
```

<Note>
Despite its help text ("Cancel a database deployment"), `qovery database cancel` does not cancel the deployment itself: it only tells you to use [`qovery environment cancel`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/environment), which cancels the deployment of the environment the database belongs to.
</Note>

### Delete Database

Delete a database:

```bash
qovery database delete --database "my-db"
```

Delete multiple databases at once:

```bash
qovery database delete --databases "db1,db2"
```

<Warning>
Deleting a database will permanently delete all data. Make sure you have backups before proceeding.
</Warning>

## Examples

### Deploy Database

```bash
# Set context
qovery context set

# List available databases
qovery database list

# Deploy database
qovery database deploy --database "postgres-main"

# Watch deployment status
qovery database deploy --database "postgres-main" --watch
```

### Stop Database for Maintenance

```bash
# Stop database
qovery database stop --database "postgres-main"

# Perform maintenance...

# Start the database again
qovery database deploy --database "postgres-main"
```

### List Databases with Credentials

```bash
qovery database list --show-credentials
```

### List Databases as JSON

```bash
qovery database list --json
```

# qovery demo
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/demo

> Create a local Kubernetes cluster with Qovery installed to try the platform, then destroy it

## Overview

Try Qovery on your local machine with a demo environment. The `demo` command has two subcommands: `up` to create a local cluster and install Qovery, and `destroy` to tear it all down.

## Commands

### demo up

Set up a local Kubernetes cluster and install Qovery:

```bash
qovery demo up
```

### demo destroy

Destroy the local demo cluster:

```bash
qovery demo destroy
```

## Prerequisites

Before running the demo:

- **Docker**: installed and running
- **k3d**, **helm** and **kubectl**: installed and on your `PATH`
- **A Qovery account**: run `qovery auth` first. The Free plan is enough.
- **macOS or Linux**: on Windows, run the command in WSL

The demo cluster counts as a cluster on your plan. On the Free plan, it uses the one included cluster. Run `qovery demo destroy --delete-qovery-config` to free it.

## Examples

### Start the Demo

```bash
# Start with default cluster name
qovery demo up

# Start with a custom cluster name
qovery demo up --cluster-name "my-demo"

# Start with debug output enabled
qovery demo up --debug
```

### Destroy the Demo

```bash
# Destroy the local cluster
qovery demo destroy

# Destroy the local cluster and remove Qovery-side config
qovery demo destroy --delete-qovery-config

# Destroy a specific named cluster
qovery demo destroy --cluster-name "my-demo"
```

## Tips

<Tip>
The demo runs entirely on your local machine. It's safe to experiment without affecting any cloud resources.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Use the demo to learn Qovery CLI commands before working with production environments.
</Tip>

<Warning>
Give Docker at least 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory.
</Warning>

## Troubleshooting

When `qovery demo up` fails, it prints the step that failed, an error code, a short hint and a diagnostic ID. The debug log is uploaded to Qovery, so the diagnostic ID is enough when you contact support.

| Error code | What to do |
|------------|------------|
| `MISSING_DEPENDENCY` | Install the commands it lists (Docker, `k3d`, `helm`, `kubectl`), then run `qovery demo up` again. |
| `DOCKER_NOT_RUNNING` | Start Docker, then run the command again. |
| `AUTHENTICATION_FAILED` | Run `qovery auth` (or `qovery auth --headless`). |
| `ORGANIZATION_NOT_RESOLVED` | Run `qovery context set` and pick your organization. |
| `DEMO_SUBNET_IN_USE` | Another Docker network uses `172.42.0.0/16`. Run the `docker network rm` or `k3d cluster delete` command from the hint. |
| `LOOPBACK_SETUP_FAILED` | The local address `172.42.0.3` could not be added. On macOS, run `sudo ifconfig lo0 alias 172.42.0.3/32 up` and try again. |
| `UNSUPPORTED_OS` | On Windows, run the command inside WSL. |
| `OPERATOR_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT`, `CLUSTER_DEPLOYMENT_FAILED`, `CLUSTER_DEPLOYMENT_TIMEOUT` | Run `qovery demo up` again. If it fails a second time, contact support with the diagnostic ID. |

Running `qovery demo up` again is safe: it restarts a stopped local cluster instead of creating a new one, and it waits for a cluster deployment already in progress. The cluster is registered in your Qovery organization only after the local setup succeeds.

To pause the cluster without deleting it, use `k3d cluster stop <cluster-name>` and `k3d cluster start <cluster-name>`.

## Next Steps

After trying the demo:

1. [Set up Qovery](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart) on your infrastructure
2. [Deploy your first app](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/getting-started/deploy-your-first-application)
3. Explore [advanced features](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/guides/use-cases/production-environment-management)

# qovery enterprise-connection
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/enterprise-connection

> View and update SSO enterprise connections and map identity provider groups to Qovery roles

## Overview

Use `qovery enterprise-connection` to view and update the [SSO](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/sso) enterprise connection of an organization, and to map identity provider (IdP) groups to Qovery roles.

- `get` and `update` read and change the connection: its default role for new users and whether group synchronization is enforced.
- `group-mappings` lists, adds or changes, and deletes the mappings between IdP groups and Qovery roles.

`--qovery-role` and `--default-role` take the name of a [role](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac), built-in or custom. The name is not case-sensitive.

## Examples

Show an enterprise connection:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection get \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --connection "$CONNECTION_NAME"
```

Set the default role for new users and enforce group synchronization:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection update \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --connection "$CONNECTION_NAME" \
  --default-role "viewer" \
  --enforce-group-sync
```

List the group mappings:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings get \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --connection "$CONNECTION_NAME"
```

Map two IdP groups to a Qovery role:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings add \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --connection "$CONNECTION_NAME" \
  --qovery-role "admin" \
  --idp-group-names "platform-team,sre"
```

Remove the mapping of a role:

```bash
qovery enterprise-connection group-mappings delete \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --connection "$CONNECTION_NAME" \
  --qovery-role "admin"
```

# qovery env
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/env

> Import variables and secrets from a .env file into a service, or turn a Heroku config into a .env file

<Note>
**No configuration file in your repository.** Qovery does not read a `qovery.yml`, `.qovery.yml` or `.qovery.toml`, and there is no `qovery init`. Projects, environments and services are created in the Console, with `qovery api`, or with [Terraform](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview). For the full path from a repository to a running app with commands only, see [Deploy with the CLI and API](https://www.qovery.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/cli-and-api).
</Note>

## Overview

Manage environment variables and secrets for your Qovery services. This command helps you import and parse environment variables.

## Commands

### Import Environment Variables

Import environment variables/secrets for a Qovery service:

```bash
qovery env import
```

Optionally pass a `.env` file path as an argument:

```bash
qovery env import ./my-vars.env
```

This command allows you to bulk import environment variables from a `.env` file into your Qovery application or container. It will interactively prompt you to select which variables to import, whether to import as environment variables or secrets, and whether to overwrite existing values.

### Parse Environment Variables

Parse environment variables and create a `.env` (dot env) file:

```bash
qovery env parse --heroku-json
```

This command parses environment variables from external sources and outputs them in `.env` format. Currently supports parsing Heroku config JSON from stdin.

## Examples

### Import Variables from File

```bash
# Prepare your environment variables in a file
cat > vars.env <<EOF
API_KEY=your-api-key
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb
FEATURE_FLAG=enabled
EOF

# Import to Qovery service (interactive)
qovery env import vars.env
```

### Import Variables Sorted by Key

```bash
qovery env import vars.env --sort
```

### Parse Variables from Heroku

```bash
# Export config from Heroku and pipe to qovery env parse
heroku config -a "$HEROKU_APP_NAME" --json | qovery env parse --heroku-json
```

### Development Workflow

```bash
# 1. Parse environment variables from Heroku and save to .env
heroku config -a my-app --json | qovery env parse --heroku-json > .env

# 2. Use .env file locally
cat .env

# 3. Run your application locally with same variables
npm run dev  # or your local dev command
```

## Managing Service-Specific Variables

For managing environment variables of specific services, use the service-specific commands:

```bash
# Application environment variables
qovery application env list
qovery application env create --key "API_KEY" --value "secret"

# Container environment variables
qovery container env list

# Cronjob environment variables
qovery cronjob env list

# Lifecycle job environment variables
qovery lifecycle env list
```

## Tips

<Tip>
Use `qovery env import` to migrate environment variables from another platform or bulk-update variables for your services.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Use `qovery env parse --heroku-json` to keep your local development environment in sync when migrating from Heroku.
</Tip>

<Warning>
Never commit `.env` files containing secrets to version control. Add `.env` to your `.gitignore` file.
</Warning>

# qovery environment
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/environment

> Deploy, redeploy, stop, cancel, clone or delete environments, print deployment logs, and manage variables, stages and statuses

## Overview

Manage environments and their lifecycle within your Qovery project.

## Commands

### List Environments

List all environments in current project:

```bash
qovery environment list
```

### Deploy Environment

Deploy all services in an environment:

```bash
qovery environment deploy --environment "env-name"
```

Deploy with specific services or versions:

```bash
qovery environment deploy \
  --environment "env-name" \
  --applications "app1:commit_id,app2:commit_id" \
  --watch
```

### Deployment Logs

Print the deployment logs of an environment: the engine output (build, deploy, health checks) shown in the **Deployment logs** tab of the console. These are the logs of the deployment itself, not the runtime output of a running service. For runtime logs, use [`qovery log`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/log).

```bash
qovery environment deployment logs --environment "env-name"
```

Without `--execution-id`, the logs of the latest deployment are printed (the API returns at most the last 1000 lines). To read a past deployment, pass its execution ID as listed by `qovery environment deployment list`:

```bash
qovery environment deployment logs \
  --environment "env-name" \
  --execution-id "$EXECUTION_ID"
```

Scope the output to a single service with `--service` (by name) or `--service-id` (by UUID); the two are mutually exclusive. Environment-level lines are kept for context:

```bash
qovery environment deployment logs --environment "env-name" --service "my-api"
```

<Note>
The console additionally scopes lines to the deployment stage a service belongs to, which the CLI does not resolve, so a few stage-level lines from other stages may appear in a service-scoped view.
</Note>

### Stop Environment

Stop all services in an environment:

```bash
qovery environment stop --environment "env-name"
```

### Cancel Environment Deployment

Cancel an ongoing environment deployment:

```bash
qovery environment cancel --environment "env-name"
```

### Delete Environment

Delete an environment:

```bash
qovery environment delete --environment "env-name"
```

### Update Environment

Update an environment's name or type:

```bash
qovery environment update \
  --environment "env-name" \
  --name "new-name"
```

### Clone Environment

Clone an existing environment:

```bash
qovery environment clone \
  --environment "production" \
  --new-environment-name "staging-clone"
```

## Examples

### Deploy Environment

```bash
# Set context
qovery context set

# Deploy all services and watch
qovery environment deploy \
  --environment "my-env" \
  --watch

# Deploy specific applications with specific commits
qovery environment deploy \
  --environment "my-env" \
  --applications "api:abc1234,frontend:def5678" \
  --watch
```

### Cancel a Deployment

```bash
# Cancel current deployment
qovery environment cancel --environment "my-env"

# Force cancel and watch
qovery environment cancel \
  --environment "my-env" \
  --force \
  --watch
```

### Clone Production to Staging

```bash
# Clone environment
qovery environment clone \
  --environment "production" \
  --new-environment-name "staging-test" \
  --environment-type STAGING

# Clone to a different project and cluster
qovery environment clone \
  --environment "production" \
  --new-environment-name "staging-test" \
  --target-project "other-project" \
  --cluster "staging-cluster"

# Deploy cloned environment
qovery environment deploy --environment "staging-test"
```

### Update Environment

```bash
# Rename an environment
qovery environment update \
  --environment "old-name" \
  --name "new-name"

# Change environment type
qovery environment update \
  --environment "my-env" \
  --type PRODUCTION
```

### `qovery environment deployment logs`

```text Description from qovery environment deployment logs --help
Print the deployment logs of an environment -- the engine output shown in the "Deployment logs" tab of the console.

These are the logs of a deployment itself (build, deploy, health checks), not the runtime output of a
running service: for that, use "qovery log".

Without --execution-id, the logs of the latest deployment are printed. The API returns at most the
last 1000 lines.

--service matches the service name carried by each log line, so it works for every service type
```

| `--json` |  | bool |  |  | Print the logs as JSON |

### `qovery environment env`

# qovery helm
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/helm

> Deploy, redeploy, stop, clone or delete Helm chart services, and manage their domains, variables and secrets

## Overview

Manage Helm charts within your Qovery environment.

## Commands

### List Helm Charts

List all Helm charts in current environment:

```bash
qovery helm list
```

### Deploy Helm Chart

Deploy or update a Helm chart:

```bash
qovery helm deploy --helm "my-helm"
```

Deploy multiple charts at once:

```bash
qovery helm deploy --helms "helm1,helm2"
```

Deploy with a specific chart version:

```bash
qovery helm deploy --helm "my-helm" --chart_version "1.2.3"
```

For a chart sourced from git, deploy the newest commit of the branch with `latest`:

```bash
qovery helm deploy --helm "my-helm" --chart_git_commit_id latest
```

### Redeploy Helm Chart

Redeploy an existing Helm chart with the same configuration:

```bash
qovery helm redeploy --helm "my-helm"
```

### Stop Helm Chart

Stop a Helm chart:

```bash
qovery helm stop --helm "my-helm"
```

Stop multiple charts at once:

```bash
qovery helm stop --helms "helm1,helm2"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel a Helm chart deployment:

```bash
qovery helm cancel --helm "my-helm"
```

### Update Helm Chart

Update a Helm chart's source configuration. In the CLI help of v1.180.0, `--chart_git_commit_branch` and `--values_override_git_commit_branch` are described as "helm chart version": they set the git branch of the chart and of the values override.

```bash
qovery helm update --helm "my-helm" --chart_version "2.0.0"
```

### Clone Helm Chart

Clone a Helm chart to another environment or project:

```bash
qovery helm clone --helm "my-helm"
```

### Delete Helm Chart

Delete a Helm chart:

```bash
qovery helm delete --helm "my-helm"
```

Delete multiple charts at once:

```bash
qovery helm delete --helms "helm1,helm2"
```

## Examples

### Deploy Helm Chart

```bash
# List Helm charts
qovery helm list

# Deploy Helm chart
qovery helm deploy --helm "redis-cluster"

# Deploy with a specific chart version
qovery helm deploy --helm "redis-cluster" --chart_version "17.0.0"

# Watch deployment status
qovery helm deploy --helm "redis-cluster" --watch
```

### List Helm Charts as JSON

```bash
qovery helm list --json
```

# qovery help
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/help

> Show the usage, subcommands and flags of any Qovery CLI command in the terminal

## Overview

Use `qovery help` to print the usage, subcommands and flags of any command. `qovery help <command>` shows the same text as `qovery <command> --help`.

## Examples

Show the list of all commands:

```bash
qovery help
```

Show help for a command:

```bash
qovery help application
```

Show help for a subcommand:

```bash
qovery help application deploy
```

The same, with the `--help` flag:

```bash
qovery application deploy --help
```

# qovery lifecycle
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/lifecycle

> Deploy, redeploy, stop, clone or delete lifecycle jobs, and manage their variables and secrets

## Overview

Manage lifecycle jobs within your Qovery environment. Lifecycle jobs run at specific points in your environment lifecycle (e.g., before/after deployment, on start, on stop, on delete).

## Commands

### List Lifecycle Jobs

List all lifecycle jobs in current environment:

```bash
qovery lifecycle list
```

### Deploy Lifecycle Job

Deploy a lifecycle job:

```bash
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

Deploy multiple lifecycle jobs at once:

```bash
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycles "lifecycle1,lifecycle2"
```

Deploy with a specific commit ID or image tag. For a git-sourced lifecycle job, `latest` deploys the newest commit of the branch:

```bash
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --commit-id "abc123"
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --commit-id latest
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --tag "v1.2.0"
```

### Redeploy Lifecycle Job

Redeploy an existing lifecycle job with the same configuration:

```bash
qovery lifecycle redeploy --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

### Stop Lifecycle Job

Stop a lifecycle job:

```bash
qovery lifecycle stop --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

### Delete Lifecycle Job

Delete a lifecycle job:

```bash
qovery lifecycle delete --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

### Cancel Deployment

Cancel a lifecycle job deployment:

```bash
qovery lifecycle cancel --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

### Update Lifecycle Job

Update lifecycle job source configuration (branch, tag, or image name):

```bash
# Update git branch (for Dockerfile-based lifecycle jobs)
qovery lifecycle update --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --branch "main"

# Update image tag (for image-based lifecycle jobs)
qovery lifecycle update --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --tag "v2.0.0"

# Update image name
qovery lifecycle update --lifecycle "my-lifecycle" --image-name "my-registry/my-image"
```

### Clone Lifecycle Job

Clone a lifecycle job to another environment or project:

```bash
qovery lifecycle clone --lifecycle "my-lifecycle"
```

## Examples

### Deploy Database Migration Job

```bash
# List lifecycle jobs
qovery lifecycle list

# Deploy migration job
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "db-migration"

# Deploy and watch status
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "db-migration" --watch
```

### Update Lifecycle Job and Redeploy

```bash
# Update branch for a git-based lifecycle job
qovery lifecycle update --lifecycle "db-migration" --branch "feature/new-migration"

# Redeploy to apply changes
qovery lifecycle redeploy --lifecycle "db-migration"
```

### Run Post-Deployment Script with Specific Tag

```bash
qovery lifecycle deploy --lifecycle "post-deploy-script" --tag "v1.5.0"
```

## Lifecycle Job Types

| Event | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **START** | Runs when environment starts |
| **STOP** | Runs when environment stops |
| **DELETE** | Runs before environment deletion |
| **DEPLOY** | Runs during deployment |


# qovery log
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/log

> Stream the logs of an application, container, database or job to your terminal

## Overview

View and stream logs from any service running on Qovery: application, container, database or job.

## Commands

### Stream Logs

Stream real-time logs:

```bash
qovery log
```

Stream logs for a specific service (regardless of its type):

```bash
qovery log --service "httpbin"
```

Stream logs for a specific application:

```bash
qovery log --application "my-api"
```

Stream logs in raw JSON format:

```bash
qovery log --service "httpbin" --raw
```

## Examples

### Stream Logs by Service Name

```bash
# Stream logs, works for any service type
qovery log --service "httpbin"

# Stream logs for a specific application
qovery log --application "my-api"

# Stream logs for a specific database
qovery log --database "postgres-main"

# Stream logs for a specific job
qovery log --job "backup-job"
```

### Use Service ID from Console URL

When you have a Qovery console URL, you can use the service ID directly:

```bash
# Extract the ID from a URL like:
# .../service/2c69dfd4-1c5a-44c3-ac65-8c6399cfbf31/service-logs
qovery log --service-id "2c69dfd4-1c5a-44c3-ac65-8c6399cfbf31"
```

### Raw Log Output

```bash
# Display logs as raw JSON
qovery log --service "my-api" --raw
```

### Specify Context Explicitly

```bash
# Provide full context to skip interactive prompts
qovery log \
  --organization "My Org" \
  --project "Backend" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

## Tips

<Tip>
  Use `--service-id` with the UUID from your Qovery console URL to stream logs
  without needing to know the service name. The ID is visible in the URL when
  you navigate to a service in the console.
</Tip>

<Tip>
  Use `--service` when you don't know (or don't want to specify) the type of
  your service. Qovery will try each API (application, container, database, job)
  until it finds a match. Use a specific flag (`--application`, `--database`,
  etc.) if you want to target a precise service type.
</Tip>

<Tip>
  Use `--raw` / `-r` to get logs in JSON format, which is useful for piping
  output to tools like `jq` for further processing.
</Tip>

# qovery port-forward
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/port-forward

> Forward a local port to a service running on Qovery, such as a database or a private API

## Overview

Forward a local port to a service container port. This allows you to access services running in your Qovery environment from your local machine.

Port-forwarding requires the **Port-forward** permission on the service's environment type. See [Shell and Port-forward permissions](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac#shell-and-port-forward-permissions).

## Command

```bash
qovery port-forward
```

The command requires at least one `--port` flag specifying the port mapping in `local_port:remote_port` format. A single number, such as `--port 5432`, uses the same port on both sides.

Without an argument, the command targets the service in your [context](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/context) and asks you to confirm it, or to pick a service. You can also pass the Console URL of the service as the first argument. To find a pod name for `--pod`, run [`qovery list-pods`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/list-pods).

```bash
qovery port-forward "https://console.qovery.com/organization/$ORG_ID/project/$PROJECT_ID/environment/$ENV_ID/application/$APP_ID" --port 8080:80
```

## Usage

```bash
qovery port-forward [flags]
```

## Examples

### Forward a Single Port

```bash
# Forward local port 8080 to remote port 80
qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8080:80
```

### Forward Multiple Ports

```bash
# Forward multiple ports at once
qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8080:80 --port 5432:5432
```

### Access PostgreSQL Database

```bash
# Forward PostgreSQL port
qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 5432:5432

# In another terminal, connect with psql
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U myuser -d mydatabase
```

### Access Application API Locally

```bash
# Forward application port
qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8080:8080

# Access API on http://localhost:8080
curl http://localhost:8080/api/health
```

## Use Cases

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Database Access">
    Forward database ports to run queries, migrations, or admin tools locally without exposing databases publicly.

    ```bash
    # PostgreSQL
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 5432:5432

    # MySQL
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 3306:3306

    # MongoDB
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 27017:27017

    # Redis
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 6379:6379
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Debugging Applications">
    Access application debug ports or admin interfaces that aren't exposed publicly.

    ```bash
    # Access admin panel
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8080:8080

    # Access debug endpoint
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 9090:9090
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Local Development">
    Connect your local development environment to remote services (databases, APIs, microservices).

    ```bash
    # Forward remote database to local app
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-db-5f7c9b4d2-abc34" --port 5432:5432

    # Run local app connecting to remote DB
    DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb npm run dev
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="API Testing">
    Test APIs or services that aren't publicly accessible.

    ```bash
    # Forward internal API
    qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8080:8080

    # Test with curl
    curl http://localhost:8080/api/test
    ```
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Tips

<Tip>
Port forwarding creates a secure tunnel through Kubernetes. The connection is encrypted and authenticated.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Keep the port-forward command running in a terminal window. The tunnel closes when you stop the command (Ctrl+C).
</Tip>

<Warning>
Port forwarding is for development and debugging. For production access, use proper ingress, load balancers, or VPN solutions.
</Warning>

<Warning>
The connection will drop if the pod restarts. You'll need to restart the port-forward command.
</Warning>

## Troubleshooting

### Port Already in Use

If the local port is already in use:

```bash
# Check what's using the port
lsof -i :8080

# Use a different local port
qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-7d8f9c5b6-xyz12" --port 8081:8080
```

### Connection Rejected

If each connection is rejected with `Port-forward connection rejected: check your permissions or run 'qovery auth'`, run `qovery auth` first, as an expired session gives the same error. If the rejection persists, your role does not have the **Port-forward** permission on this environment type. Ask an organization admin to grant it. See [Shell and Port-forward permissions](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac#shell-and-port-forward-permissions).

### Connection Drops

If the connection drops frequently:

```bash
# Use a specific pod instead of letting Kubernetes choose
qovery port-forward --pod "my-app-pod-name" --port 8080:8080
```

# qovery service
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/service

> List all services of an environment, and deploy one or several services by name whatever their type

## Overview

Manage all types of services within your Qovery environment. This is a unified command to list and deploy services across applications, containers, databases, jobs, and Helm charts.

## Commands

### List Services

List all services in current environment:

```bash
qovery service list
```

This displays all services regardless of type (applications, containers, databases, cronjobs, lifecycle jobs, Helm charts).

### Deploy Service

Deploy a service by automatically detecting its type. Works with applications, containers, databases, jobs (cronjobs and lifecycle), and Helm charts.

```bash
qovery service deploy --service "my-app"
```

Deploy multiple services at once:

```bash
qovery service deploy --services "service1,service2,service3"
```

Deploy with a specific version:

```bash
qovery service deploy --service "my-app" --version "abc123"
```

The `--version` parameter accepts:
- Git commit IDs (for applications, git-based jobs, git-based helms)
- Container image tags (for containers, image-based jobs)
- Helm chart versions (for helm repository charts)

## Examples

### List All Services

```bash
# Set context
qovery context set

# List all services in environment
qovery service list

# Example output:
# NAME              TYPE           STATUS
# my-api            Application    Running
# postgres-db       Database       Running
# redis-cache       Container      Running
# backup-job        Cronjob        Running
# db-migration      Lifecycle      Completed
```

### List Services with JSON Output

```bash
qovery service list --json
```

### List Services with Markdown Output

```bash
qovery service list --markdown
```

### Deploy a Service by Name

```bash
# Deploy an application
qovery service deploy --service "my-api"

# Deploy a container with a specific tag
qovery service deploy --service "my-container" --version "v1.2.3"

# Deploy a helm chart with a specific version
qovery service deploy --service "my-helm" --version "1.2.3"

# Deploy multiple services
qovery service deploy --services "frontend,backend,worker"
```

## Service Types

The `service list` command displays all the following service types:

- **Application** - Applications built from Git repositories
- **Container** - Pre-built Docker images
- **Database** - Managed databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, etc.)
- **Cronjob** - Scheduled jobs
- **Lifecycle** - Lifecycle jobs (run on specific events)
- **Helm** - Helm charts

```text Description from qovery service deploy --help
This command works with applications, containers, databases, jobs (cronjobs and lifecycle), and helm charts.

The --version parameter accepts:
  - Git commit IDs (for applications, git-based jobs, git-based helms)
  - Container image tags (for containers, image-based jobs)
  - Helm chart versions (for helm repository charts)

For helm charts, you can also specify:
  - --values-override-version: Git commit ID for helm values override
```

```text Usage
qovery service deploy [flags]
```

| `--values-override-version` |  | string |  |  | Helm values override version (git commit ID) |
| `--version` | `-v` | string |  |  | Version (git commit ID, image tag, or chart version) |
| `--watch` | `-w` | bool |  |  | Watch service status until it's ready or an error occurs |

# qovery shell
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/shell

> Open a shell or run a command in a service container, or in an ephemeral clone pod or debug container

## Overview

Connect to an application container and execute commands in running service instances, or open an interactive shell session. With `--ephemeral`, open the shell in a temporary pod or container instead.

Opening a shell requires the **Shell** permission on the service's environment type. See [Shell and Port-forward permissions](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/members-rbac#shell-and-port-forward-permissions).

## Usage

```text
qovery shell [flags]
qovery shell <qovery_console_service_url>
```

## Commands

### Interactive Shell (interactive mode)

When run without flags, `qovery shell` prompts you to select your organization, project, environment, and service interactively:

```bash
qovery shell
```

### Shell with explicit flags

```bash
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

### Shell into specific pod or container

```bash
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --pod "pod-name" \
  --container "container-name"
```

### Execute Command

Run a specific command instead of opening an interactive shell:

```bash
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --command "ls,-la"
```

The `--command` flag is a comma-separated string slice and can be repeated to pass multiple arguments.

### Shell via Console URL

Pass the Qovery Console URL directly:

```bash
qovery shell "https://console.qovery.com/organization/$ORG_ID/project/$PROJECT_ID/environment/$ENV_ID/application/$APP_ID"
```

### Ephemeral Shell

`--ephemeral` opens the shell in a temporary pod or in a temporary container, instead of the application container. It requires Qovery CLI v1.162.1 or later. Choose where the shell runs with `--mode`:

| Mode | What it does | Use it to |
|------|--------------|-----------|
| `clone` (default) | Creates a separate pod from the service image. It receives no traffic. | Run one-off commands or inspect the service configuration without touching the running pods |
| `debug` | Adds a debug container to a running pod of the service. That pod keeps serving traffic. | Troubleshoot a running pod, for example an image that has no shell or tools |

#### Clone mode

```bash
qovery shell --ephemeral \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

The new pod uses the same image, environment variables, secrets, volumes, service account, security context and node placement as the service. It runs `sleep infinity` instead of the service entrypoint, so your application does not start in it and the pod receives no traffic.

The pod gets the same CPU and memory as the service. Use `--cpu` and `--memory` to give it more, for example for a heavy script or a data migration. Each flag sets both the request and the limit:

```bash
qovery shell --ephemeral --mode clone \
  --memory 2Gi \
  --cpu 1 \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

The pod is deleted when you exit the shell, and after 24 hours at most. The CLI waits up to 5 minutes for it to start.

<Note>
Clone mode works for applications and containers without persistent storage. It fails with `No deployment found for service` on services that use persistent storage.
</Note>

#### Debug mode

```bash
qovery shell --ephemeral --mode debug \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

Qovery adds a `debian:stable-slim` container to the newest running pod of the service. The container shares the process namespace of the application container, so tools like `ps` and `top` show the application processes. The CLI waits up to 2 minutes for the container to start. `--cpu` and `--memory` do not apply in this mode and are ignored.

<Warning>
Kubernetes cannot remove a debug container from a pod. The container stays in the pod until the pod is replaced, for example by the next deployment. If you open another debug shell on the same pod, Qovery reuses the existing container.
</Warning>

#### Permissions

Clone mode requires the same permissions as `qovery shell`. Debug mode requires admin access to the cluster. Both are recorded in the audit logs.

## Examples

### Debug Application

```bash
# Open interactive shell
qovery shell

# With explicit context flags
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api"
```

### Run Database Migrations

```bash
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --command "npm,run,migrate"
```

### Check Application Files

```bash
# List application files
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --command "ls,-lah,/app"
```

### Run a Script Without Touching Production Pods

```bash
qovery shell --ephemeral \
  --memory 4Gi \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --command "python,scripts/backfill.py"
```

### Debug Specific Container

```bash
qovery shell \
  --organization "my-org" \
  --project "my-project" \
  --environment "production" \
  --service "my-api" \
  --pod "my-api-7d4f9c-xvz" \
  --container "nginx-proxy"
```

## Tips

<Tip>
Use interactive shell (run `qovery shell` without flags) for exploratory debugging when you don't know the exact service name.
</Tip>

<Tip>
You can pass the Qovery Console URL as an argument to `qovery shell` to quickly connect to a service.
</Tip>

<Warning>
Be careful when executing commands in production environments. Changes are not persistent across pod restarts.
</Warning>

# qovery status
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/status

> Print the deployment status of the application or container selected in your CLI context

## Overview

Use `qovery status` to check the state of one service: the application or container selected in your [context](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/context). If no service is selected, the command asks you to pick the organization, project, environment and service first.

The command takes no flags. To check another service, change the context with `qovery context set`. For other service types, or to see all services of an environment, use [`qovery service list`](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/service).

## Examples

Check the status of the service in the current context:

```bash
qovery status
```

Output:

```text
Application | Status
my-api      | DEPLOYED
```

Check another service:

```bash
qovery context set
qovery status
```

The status is the service state from the Qovery API, for example `DEPLOYED`, `DEPLOYING`, `BUILDING`, `STOPPED` or `DEPLOYMENT_ERROR`.

# qovery terraform
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/terraform

> List, plan, apply and delete Terraform services, and manage their state and external secrets

## Overview

Use `qovery terraform` to run and manage the Terraform services of an environment from the terminal: list them, run a plan, plan and apply, delete their resources, unlock or migrate their state, and manage their external secrets.

## Examples

List the Terraform services of an environment:

```bash
qovery terraform list \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --project "Backend Services" \
  --environment "production"
```

Run a plan without applying it, and follow it until it finishes:

```bash
qovery terraform plan --terraform "network" --watch
```

Plan and apply the newest commit of the branch:

```bash
qovery terraform plan-and-apply \
  --terraform "network" \
  --commit-id latest \
  --watch
```

Plan and apply several Terraform services at once:

```bash
qovery terraform plan-and-apply --terraforms "network,database"
```

### Access the Terraform state

`setup-backend` generates a `backend.tf` file that points Terraform at the state Qovery stores for a Terraform service. The command asks before it writes the file in the current directory. The state can contain secret values, so keep `backend.tf` and any local copy of the state out of version control.

`--terraform` (`-t`) takes the **ID** (UUID) of the Terraform service, not its name. Without it, the command uses the service in the current [context](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/context).

```bash
qovery terraform setup-backend --terraform "$TERRAFORM_SERVICE_ID"
```

# qovery token

> Generate an API token for CI/CD pipelines, scripts and other non-interactive use of the CLI

## Overview

## Command

```bash
qovery token
```

This command generates a new API token that can be used for authentication instead of interactive login.

## Usage

```bash

```

## Using API Tokens

### In CI/CD Pipelines

```bash
# GitHub Actions
env:
  QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.QOVERY_TOKEN }}

# GitLab CI
variables:
  QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN: $CI_QOVERY_TOKEN

# CircleCI
environment:
  QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${QOVERY_TOKEN}
```

### In Scripts

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Set token as environment variable
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="qov_abc123def456..."

# No `qovery auth` needed: the CLI uses QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN directly

# Run commands
qovery application deploy --application "my-app"
```

### In Local Development

```bash
# Add to your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc)
export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="qov_abc123def456..."

# Or create a .env file
echo "QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN=qov_abc123def456..." > .env
source .env
```

## Security Best Practices

<Warning>
**Never commit API tokens to version control.** Always use secrets management:
- GitHub Actions: Use secrets
- GitLab CI: Use CI/CD variables
- CircleCI: Use environment variables
- Local: Use environment variables or secure vaults
</Warning>

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Token Storage">
    **Do:**
    - Store tokens in CI/CD secret management
    - Use environment variables
    - Use secure vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
    - Rotate tokens regularly

    **Don't:**
    - Commit tokens to Git
    - Share tokens in plain text
    - Use the same token across multiple systems
    - Store tokens in application code
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Token Rotation">
    Regularly rotate API tokens for security:

    ```bash
    # 1. Generate new token (interactive)
    qovery token

    # 2. Update CI/CD secrets with new token

    # 3. Revoke old token in Qovery Console
    ```
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Limited Scope Tokens">
    Generate separate tokens for different purposes by running `qovery token` for each and providing a descriptive name when prompted:

    ```bash
    # For each token, run:
    qovery token
    # Enter a descriptive name at the prompt, e.g.:
    # "Production CI/CD", "Staging CI/CD", "Monitoring Read-Only"
    ```
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Managing Tokens

Tokens can be managed in the Qovery Console:

1. Go to **Settings** → **API Tokens**
2. View all active tokens
3. Revoke tokens that are no longer needed
4. Set expiration dates for tokens

## Token Permissions

API tokens inherit permissions from your user account:

- **Full Access** - Can perform all operations you can perform
- **Scoped to Organization** - Token permissions apply to specific organization
- **Audit Trail** - All token actions are logged

## Examples by Use Case

### CI/CD Deployment

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy to Qovery

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2

      - name: Install Qovery CLI
        run: curl -s https://get.qovery.com | bash

      - name: Deploy Application
        env:
          QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.QOVERY_TOKEN }}
        run: qovery application deploy --application "my-app"
```

### Automated Monitoring Script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# monitor.sh

export QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN="${QOVERY_MONITORING_TOKEN}"

# No `qovery auth` needed: the CLI uses QOVERY_CLI_ACCESS_TOKEN directly

# Get the status of every service in the environment
qovery environment statuses \
  --organization "My Organization" --project "My Project" --environment "production" \
  --json > status.json

# Check for errors
if jq -e '[.applications[]?, .containers[]?, .databases[]?, .jobs[]?, .helms[]?, .terraforms[]?, .agentic_workflows[]?] | map(select(.state | test("ERROR"))) | length > 0' status.json > /dev/null; then
  echo "ERROR: Services with errors detected"
  # Send alert
fi
```

## Tips

<Tip>
Generate separate tokens for different environments (production, staging, development) to limit blast radius if a token is compromised.
</Tip>

<Tip>
Use descriptive names when generating tokens to easily identify their purpose later.
</Tip>

# qovery upgrade
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/upgrade

> Replace the installed Qovery CLI binary with the latest release in one command

## Overview

Use `qovery upgrade` to update the CLI to the latest release. The command checks for a newer version, downloads it from the [Qovery CLI releases](https://github.com/Qovery/qovery-cli/releases) on GitHub and replaces the current binary. If you already run the latest version, it says so and changes nothing.

The command needs write permission on the CLI binary file. If it does not have it, the upgrade is cancelled and the error shows the path of the binary.

<Note>
`qovery upgrade` is not included in the Windows build of the CLI. On Windows, install the new version the same way you installed the CLI.
</Note>

## Example

```bash
qovery upgrade
```

Check the result:

```bash
qovery version
```

# qovery webhook
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/commands/webhook

> List an organization's webhooks and inspect the events each one sent, with response codes

## Overview

Use `qovery webhook` to list the [webhooks](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/integrations/webhooks) of an organization and check the events each webhook sent, with the target URL, response status code and response body.

## Examples

List the webhooks of an organization:

```bash
qovery webhook list --organization "Acme Corp"
```

List the events sent by one webhook. `--webhook-id` is required; take the ID from `qovery webhook list`:

```bash
qovery webhook list-event \
  --organization "Acme Corp" \
  --webhook-id "$WEBHOOK_ID"
```

Get the events as JSON, including the payload sent:

```bash
qovery webhook list-event --organization "Acme Corp" --webhook-id "$WEBHOOK_ID" --json
```

# Troubleshooting
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/troubleshoot/overview

> Fix common Qovery CLI errors, such as a broken authentication context or an outdated CLI version

This troubleshooting guide helps you resolve common issues you may encounter while using Qovery CLI. Use the sections below to find solutions quickly.

---

## CLI Issues

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Error: invalid character '}' after top-level value" icon="circle-xmark">
  **Symptom:** Your CLI command fails with a "Error: invalid character '}' after top-level value" error message.

  **Common Causes:** This message can occur when there is an error in your CLI authentication.

  **Solutions:**
    <Steps>
      <Step title="Remove your current authentication context">
        Delete the file `.qovery/context.json` from your home directory. 
      </Step>

      <Step title="Authenticate again">
        Use the `qovery auth` command to recreate your authentication context.
      </Step>
    </Steps>
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Error: 400 Bad Request JSON parse error: Cannot coerce empty String" icon="gear">
  **Symptom:** Your CLI command fails with a "Error: 400 Bad Request" error message. If ran with the `--verbose` flag, the error message tells you "JSON parse error: Cannot coerce empty String"

  **Common Causes:** This message can occur when your CLI version is not up to date.

  **Solutions:**
    <Steps>
      <Step title="Upgrade Qovery CLI">
        Use the `qovery upgrade` command to perform the upgrade of the CLI. 
      </Step>
    </Steps>
  </Accordion>  
</AccordionGroup>

# Terraform Provider
Source: https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/overview

> Install and authenticate the Qovery Terraform provider, find resource IDs, and deploy environments, services, and variables from Terraform as code.

The Qovery Terraform provider manages Qovery resources from Terraform: organization settings, cloud credentials, clusters, projects, environments, services (applications, containers, jobs, Helm charts, Terraform services and databases) and their variables. You describe the resources in HCL, review the changes with `terraform plan`, and apply them with `terraform apply`.

Starting a new project? [Start a new project with Terraform or OpenTofu](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/from-scratch) goes from an empty cloud account to an app and a database running in staging and production.

This page covers the setup. The reference of every resource and data source is on the [Terraform Registry](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/qovery/qovery/latest/docs).

<Info>
Upgrading from an earlier version? Read the [upgrade guide](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/qovery/qovery/latest/docs/guides/upgrade-to-1.0) before you change the version constraint.
</Info>

<Card title="Practice it in the training console" icon="graduation-cap" href="https://console-training.qovery.com/?track=terraform&utm_source=docs&utm_medium=practice&utm_content=terraform" horizontal>
  Five lessons, from Terraform basics to running the Qovery provider in production. Hands-on lessons in a sandbox: nothing touches a real cluster.
</Card>

## Requirements

- Terraform. The provider is tested against Terraform 1.15. Earlier versions are expected to work but are not tested.
- Or OpenTofu. The provider is also published on the [OpenTofu Registry](https://search.opentofu.org/provider/qovery/qovery/latest) under the same address, `qovery/qovery`: the configuration is the same, run `tofu` instead of `terraform`.
- A Qovery API token.

## Install the provider

Declare the provider and pin its major version, so that a future major release cannot introduce a breaking change without an explicit upgrade:

```hcl main.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    qovery = {
      source  = "qovery/qovery"
      version = "~> 1.0"
    }
  }
}

# Reads the API token from the QOVERY_API_TOKEN environment variable.
provider "qovery" {}
```

Run `terraform init` to download the provider.

## Authentication

The provider authenticates with a Qovery API token. To create one, see [API Token](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/organization/api-token). The token carries a role: give it one that allows the changes your configuration makes.

Pass the token in one of two ways:

- Set the `QOVERY_API_TOKEN` environment variable. The provider reads it when the `token` argument is not set.

  ```bash
  export QOVERY_API_TOKEN="<your-api-token>"
  ```

- Set the `token` argument from a sensitive input variable:

  ```hcl
  variable "qovery_api_token" {
    type      = string
    sensitive = true
  }

  provider "qovery" {
    token = var.qovery_api_token
  }
  ```

<Warning>
Do not write the token in your configuration files or commit it to version control.
</Warning>

## Find resource IDs

Resources reference each other by ID. To use a resource that your configuration does not manage, such as an existing cluster, pass its ID to the configuration, usually as an input variable.

- **Console**: IDs appear in the page URL, for example `https://console.qovery.com/organization/<organization_id>/project/<project_id>/overview`.
- **CLI**: `qovery organization list`, `qovery project list`, `qovery cluster list` and `qovery environment list` print the ID of each resource. Run `qovery context set` first to select the organization and the project. See the [CLI documentation](https://www.qovery.com/docs/cli/overview).

Data sources look up an existing resource by its `id`, not by its name (`qovery_organization_member` uses the member's `email`). Organization-level data sources, such as `qovery_cluster`, also require `organization_id`:

```hcl
variable "organization_id" {
  type = string
}

variable "cluster_id" {
  type = string
}

data "qovery_cluster" "main" {
  id              = var.cluster_id
  organization_id = var.organization_id
}

output "cluster_name" {
  value = data.qovery_cluster.main.name
}
```

To bring a resource created from the Console or the API under Terraform, declare it in the configuration and add an `import` block. The Registry page of each resource gives its import ID. The [Terraform exporter](https://www.qovery.com/docs/terraform-provider/exporter) generates the configuration of a whole environment.

## How the provider tracks changes

The configuration is the source of truth. `terraform plan` refreshes every resource from the Qovery API, so a change made from the Console or the API shows up as a difference, and the next `terraform apply` reverts it to the configured value. The API never returns secrets, such as secret values, passwords and secret keys: Terraform keeps them as configured, so a change made to them outside Terraform does not show up in the plan. Removing an attribute from the configuration plans its default value or its removal.

A few attributes keep their current value when you remove them, because the Qovery API gives Terraform no way to reset them, for example `deployment_stage_id` and `advanced_settings_json`. The [Managing changes guide](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/qovery/qovery/latest/docs/guides/managing-changes) explains the rules and lists these exceptions.

Change the resources that Terraform manages in the configuration, not in the Console.

## Deploy an environment

Creating or changing a service with Terraform updates its configuration in Qovery but does not deploy it. The [`qovery_deployment`](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/qovery/qovery/latest/docs/resources/deployment) resource deploys, stops or restarts an environment on `terraform apply`. You can also deploy from the Console. Qovery stores no deployment object, so a deployment started from the Console does not show up in `terraform plan`.

<Warning>
Destroying a `qovery_deployment`, or removing it from the configuration, deletes its environment and all the services in it. Only declare it for an environment that the same configuration creates or has imported.
</Warning>
